https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A slide presentation delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education on February 6, 2024, introducing Restorative Practices (RP) as a framework for student discipline and school climate. Presenters Casey Conaton, Assistant Principal at Smith Middle School, and Chantelle Yancy, Supervisor of Educational Equity, Inclusion & Community Relations, explain the RP continuum, the Fair Process elements of Engagement, Explanation and Expectation Clarity, and the restorative discipline language already embedded in the TSD Student Code of Conduct. The deck cites Michigan Legislature Section 380.1310c, under which restorative practices "should be the first consideration" for offenses such as interpersonal conflicts, bullying, theft, property damage, class disruption and cyberbullying.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Item**
Restorative Practices Board Overview — a presentation to the Troy School District Board of Education dated February 6, 2024.

**Presenters**

| Presenter | Role | Restorative training cited |
|---|---|---|
| Casey Conaton | Assistant Principal, Smith Middle School | Foundations in Restorative Practice (2012), Macomb County Intermediate School District training from The Resolution Center; Train the Trainor, Restorative Practices (2022), Troy School District training from IIRP Trainer Bill Boyle |
| Chantelle Yancy | Supervisor, Educational Equity, Inclusion & Community Relations | Restorative Justice Training (2010), Marygrove College Social Justice Program; Foundations in Restorative Practices (2023), Rochester Community Schools |

**Learning Intentions and Outcomes**
Stated goals are gaining knowledge of the principles of RP, learning ways to enact RP in the school environment and why, and discovering ways implementation will impact social change. By the end, participants should be able to explain the model for RP, engage in reflective thinking about personal, student, staff and community lived experiences, and apply the principles of RP. A slide titled "7 Factors to Consider" is included.

**Definition**
Restorative practices is described as a field within the social sciences that studies how to strengthen relationships between individuals as well as social connections within communities. It is presented as a continuum of proactive components supporting strong relationships and safe communities where all members feel they belong, with accountability focused on repairing harm and learning from mistakes. The definition is cited to the International Institute for Restorative Practices at https://www.iirp.edu/restorative-practices/explained.

**Framework — Fair Process ("Do with not to")**
- Engagement: engaging with the individual involved; sharing concern, ideas, problem solving, game planning.
- Explanation: explaining the "why we are here" for the individual.
- Expectation Clarity: whatever the outcome may be, the expectation is clear and understood.
A "Restorative Practices Continuum" slide is also included.

**Rationale**
Schools adopt RP as a "comprehensive way to address disparities in exclusionary discipline i.e., suspensions and expulsions." The approach is framed as proactive and preventative, addressing conflict through collectivity so that harm is repaired through community rather than being confined to two individuals. Restorative justice is presented as an alternative process for accountability and taking responsibility for wrongdoing or harmful actions, ensuring victims or those harmed are heard and are active participants.

**Code of Conduct linkage**
The TSD Student Code of Conduct already states that restorative discipline focuses on the harms, needs and causes of student behavior rather than only rule-breaking and punishment. Students who violate the Code may engage in restorative practices as a consequence, facilitated by school officials, provided the student freely admits wrongdoing and expresses contrition to the offended parties. Listed activities include restitution; alternative suspension including In-School Suspension/Detention; written and verbal apology; participation in diversion programs; community service; outreach and awareness activities; a course of study, book study or other applied learning experience; a behavior plan or behavior contract; counseling in and out of school; engagement with agency and community supports; and student-to-student mediation.

**Practice in schools**
Suite360 modules are used for discipline and restorative measures prior to more severe consequences. Peer conflict resolution has been attempted through circle meetings using reflective questioning ("What happened, what were you thinking? What have you thought about since?"), with ADL learning and apology/restoration between victim and offender. Students have re-entry meetings after major discipline, sometimes including other involved students who are willing to participate. Student-teacher conflicts have been addressed through mutually agreed meetings using the restorative questions. Teachers establish community circles in classrooms to connect academically and non-academically.

**Misconceptions addressed**
That RP does not hold students accountable; that teachers should focus only on academics and not SEL needs; that RP is a one-and-done model; that RP replaces or removes other disciplinary measures, especially for extreme behavior; and that belonging is not essential to RP.

**Legal context**
Michigan Legislature Section 380.1310c is quoted, describing victim-initiated victim-offender conferences approved by the victim's parent or legal guardian, or by the victim directly if the victim is at least age 15.

**Resources**
Restorative Practices Explained; "Do restorative practices work?"; Legal Implications - MI; Klevan, S. (2021), Building a positive school climate through restorative practices, Learning Policy Institute, https://doi.org/10.54300/178.861; and an Improving Student Outcomes interactive worksheet. The deck closes with "Where are We Now?" and "Questions?" slides.

Restorative Practices Board Overview is a slide presentation prepared for the Troy School District Board of Education and dated February 6, 2024. It provides an orientation to Restorative Practices (RP) as a discipline and school-climate framework, connects RP to language already present in the TSD Student Code of Conduct, describes how RP is being used in Troy School District buildings, addresses common misconceptions, and cites the governing Michigan statute.

**Learning Intentions and Outcomes.** The opening slide sets three intentions: gaining knowledge on the principles of RP; learning about ways to enact RP in the school environment and why; and discovering ways that implementation will impact social change. Three outcomes are stated for the end of the session: participants will be able to explain the model for RP; engage in reflective thinking drawing on personal experiences and on student, staff and community lived experiences; and apply the principles of RP. A slide headed "7 Factors to Consider" follows.

**Presenters and their credentials.** Two district staff members present. Casey Conaton is Assistant Principal at Smith Middle School. Her cited experience is Foundations in Restorative Practice (2012), a Macomb County Intermediate School District training delivered by The Resolution Center, and Train the Trainor, Restorative Practices (2022), a Troy School District training delivered by IIRP Trainer Bill Boyle. Chantelle Yancy is Supervisor, Educational Equity, Inclusion & Community Relations. Her cited experience is Restorative Justice Training (2010) through the Marygrove College Social Justice Program, and Foundations in Restorative Practices (2023) through Rochester Community Schools.

**What Restorative Practice is.** The definition slides are cited to the International Institute for Restorative Practices at https://www.iirp.edu/restorative-practices/explained. Restorative practices is defined as a field within the social sciences that studies how to strengthen relationships between individuals as well as social connections within communities. It is characterized as a continuum of proactive components that support setting up strong relationships and safe communities where all members feel they belong, with accountability focused on repairing harm and learning from mistakes.

**Framework: Fair Process.** The framework is summarized by the phrase "Do with not to" and three components. Engagement means engaging with the individual involved, sharing concern and ideas, problem solving and game planning. Explanation means explaining the "why we are here" for the individual. Expectation Clarity means that whatever the outcome may be, the expectation is clear and understood. A separate slide presents the Restorative Practices Continuum.

**Why schools adopt RP.** The presentation states that schools adopt RP as a "comprehensive way to address disparities in exclusionary discipline i.e., suspensions and expulsions," emphasizing proactive and preventative approaches. Conflict is addressed through collectivity, so that harm is addressed through community for repair and the process goes beyond "two individuals." Restorative justice is described as providing an alternative process to accountability and to taking responsibility for wrongdoing and harmful actions, while ensuring victims or those harmed are heard and are active participants in the RJ/RP processes.

**Application to student discipline: the TSD Student Code of Conduct.** The deck reproduces the Code of Conduct's restorative discipline section. A major consideration of the Code of Conduct is to identify appropriate disciplinary actions that will bring about positive student behavior. Restorative discipline focuses on the harms, needs and causes of student behavior, not just the breaking of rules and dispensing of punishment; it attempts to provide students an opportunity to be accountable for the harm caused as well as the opportunity to repair the harm. Students are empowered to help resolve conflict and maintain an environment where the work of the school can happen. The stated goal of restorative discipline is to provide students an opportunity to learn to think differently about harm, to deal with conflict in peaceful and creative ways, to address accountability and responsibility, to focus on one another's humanity, and to problem-solve in terms of community and collaboration.

Student violators of the Code of Conduct may have the opportunity to engage in restorative practices as a consequence of their inappropriate behavior, as facilitated by school officials. The Code notes it is important that any student engaging in restorative practices freely admit to any wrongdoing and express contrition for their actions to the offended parties. Restorative practices developed in response to a Code of Conduct violation may include, but are not limited to: restitution; alternative suspension including In-School Suspension/Detention; apology for the offense, both written and verbal; participation in diversion programs; community service activities; outreach and awareness activities; a course of study, book study, or other applied learning experience; a behavior plan or behavior contract; participation in counseling in and out of school; engagement in agency and community supports; and student-to-student mediation.

**What RP looks like in Troy schools.** The presentation lists Suite360 modules used for discipline and restorative practice measures prior to more severe consequences. Peer conflict and resolution work involves resolving issues with teachers and students, with students assisting with discipline through reflections, ADL learning, and apology or restoration between victim and offender. Staff report having tried to resolve peer conflict through circle meetings, with reflective questioning used to help shed light on the why behind incidents — sample questions include "What happened, what were you thinking? What have you thought about since?" Students have re-entry meetings after any major discipline, often with other students involved if those students are willing to participate. In cases of student/teacher conflict, once both parties agree, a meeting is held and the restorative questions are used to help both sides reach a solution and move forward in a positive manner. Teachers also establish community circles in the classroom to connect with students in both academic and nonacademic ways.

**Misconceptions.** Five misconceptions are enumerated: that RP does not hold students or individuals accountable; that teachers should only focus on academics and not social-emotional learning needs; that RP is a one-and-done model or approach; that RP replaces or removes other disciplinary measures, especially with extreme behavior; and that belonging is not essential to RP.

**Example applications.** Two scenarios contrast punitive and restorative handling. Student A was caught vaping in the bathroom: the traditional or punitive response is detention with no reflection, while the restorative response is student learning with an accountable outcome. Students B and C engaged in a fist fight at school: under the traditional or punitive response, students are immediately removed from the school setting and return without an opportunity to repair harm, a re-entry plan, or learning and reflection; under the restorative alternative, the student may be suspended from school with assigned learning about anger, a re-entry meeting, and an opportunity to repair harm to the students or individuals involved.

**Legal implications.** The deck quotes subsection (2) of Michigan Legislature Section 380.1310c. Restorative practices may include victim-offender conferences that are initiated by the victim; that are approved by the victim's parent or legal guardian or, if the victim is at least age 15, by the victim; that are attended voluntarily by the victim, a victim advocate, the offender, members of the school community, and supporters of the victim and the offender; and that provide an opportunity for the offender to accept responsibility for the harm caused to those affected by the misconduct and to participate in setting consequences to repair the harm. The attendees, known as a restorative practices team, may require the pupil to apologize; participate in community service, restoration, or counseling; or pay restitution. The selected consequences are to be incorporated into an agreement that sets time limits for completion and is signed by all participants. The statute provides that restorative practices should be the first consideration to remediate offenses such as interpersonal conflicts, bullying, verbal and physical conflicts, theft, damage to property, class disruption, and harassment and cyberbullying.

**Closing slides and resources.** The presentation includes slides headed "Where are We Now?" and "Questions?" Additional resources listed are Restorative Practices Explained; "Do restorative practices work?"; Legal Implications - MI; Klevan, S. (2021), Building a positive school climate through restorative practices, Learning Policy Institute, https://doi.org/10.54300/178.861; and an Improving Student Outcomes interactive worksheet.

Minutes of the regular meeting of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, held December 12, 2023 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt and Wilson were present; Dr. Philippart was absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Montante, DiPilato, Griffor, Hall, Zawislak and West, with approximately 60 members of the audience. The minutes carry the notation GH/jh and were submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education.

RECOGNITION - TSD MISSION MOMENT: SILVER HORNETS ROBOTICS. The Board recognized the Boulan Park Middle School Robotics Team, the Silver Hornets. The team of eight students built a robot able to perform certain tasks and functions and won awards in the FIRST Tech Challenge Robotics competition in 2022; the team had just been promoted to States in the recent District Championship competition and received the FIRST Inspire Award and the FIRST Alliance Award. Coach Nivedita Maringanti introduced Ananya Siranjeevi, Sree Dhruthi Maringanti, Maanya Gupta, Aarush Arora, Sai Sathvik Reddy Thumma, Diya Siranjeevi, Mihir Kandage and Samarth Yadav, who spoke about their project and demonstrated the robot for the Board and the Troy community.

RECOGNITION - TSD MISSION MOMENT: WEB TEACHER LEADERS. The Board recognized the WEB teacher leaders. WEB, which stands for "Where Everybody Belongs," is a middle school orientation and transition program that welcomes 6th graders through their first year of middle school. Built on the belief that students can help students succeed, it trains 8th grade mentors as WEB Leaders who guide 6th graders in the transition. WEB also functions as an anti-bullying program by providing a cadre of student leaders who look for bullying behavior and help stop it, creating a safer school environment. Philip Lewan, Allyson Pagnani, Emily Stetson, Judy Morgan, Maria Mendola, Jaclynn Parker, Cortney Walls and Raymond Torres were invited to the podium to share remarks.

RECOGNITION - MICHIGAN SCHOOL PUBLIC RELATIONS ASSOCIATION (MSPRA) AWARDS. The Board recognized the Troy School District Communications Department. The Communications team received a 2023 MSPRA Gold Medallion Award for Troy Bond 2022, Preparing for Tomorrow. The team was also recognized by the 2023 MSPRA Excellence Awards program with the following additional awards: Social Media - Excellence; Audio/Podcast - Excellence; Financial Report - Merit; Website/Mobile App - Merit; Video - Merit; Newsletter - Merit; Marketing Materials - Merit. Staff congratulated and presented with an award by Rebecca Fannon, the Membership & Marketing Co-Chair for MSPRA and the Public Relations and Marketing Coordinator for the West Bloomfield School District, were Kerry Birmingham, Melissa Verduyn, Patrice Rowbal, Thomas Butcher, Adam Burns and Linda Alfonso.

STUDENT SPOTLIGHT. The Student Spotlight recognizes the talents and achievements of students in the Creative Guild. The Board recognized Brianna Johnson, a senior at Athens High School; Thomas Butcher, Creative Content Producer from the TSD Creative Guild, described her work.

ADDITIONS & DELETIONS. None.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (AGENDA ITEMS). Ms. Michele Maleszyk, Troy resident and parent in District, addressed the Board about ELA, student achievement data transparency and LTRS training for teachers, and provided packets with student achievement data. Dr. Audra Melton, retired TSD administrator and parent in District, addressed dyslexia, Reading Recovery and District achievement data, and provided the book Language at the Speed of Sight to each board member. Mrs. Stephanie Zendler, former TSD administrator and parent in District, addressed student achievement data, students with disabilities and the achievement gap, and commented that the current ELA program is ineffective. Mrs. Tracy Owens, TSD parent, addressed the District's ELA curriculum and commented that the data provided at the November workshop was combined into a single graph, which is misleading, saying it would be helpful to have the M-Step data broken down. Mr. Suril Patel, a property owner who will move to Troy soon, addressed the lack of data to support what is being taught and shortcomings of Troy with data collection.

GENERAL - CONSENT AGENDA. It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H and I on the consent agenda: Minutes of the October 3, 2023 Board of Education Workshop; Minutes of the October 17, 2023 Board of Education Meeting; Minutes of the November 14, 2023 Special Board of Education Meeting & Closed Session; Minutes of the November 14, 2023 Board of Education Workshop; Second Reading and Adoption - Revised/Recommended Board Policies; Clergy Member for 2023-24 Sex Education Advisory Board; Treasurer's Report - September 2023; Treasurer's Report - October 2023; General Fund Budget Amendment #1. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

PERSONNEL - ADMINISTRATIVE APPOINTMENT, TECHNOLOGY DIRECTOR. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Wilson that the Board of Education issue a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Mr. Troy Wissink, who will begin his duties as Technology Director as of January 1, 2024. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

PERSONNEL - ELEMENTARY AND SECONDARY. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Anne that the Board approve the personnel recommendations as stated: Sana Mirza, Sara Ranucci. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

CURRICULUM - STUDENT ACHIEVEMENT DATA. Assistant Superintendent of Secondary Instruction Christine DiPilato and Assistant Superintendent of Elementary Instruction Kris Griffor gave a PowerPoint presentation on student assessment data, reviewing SAT, PSAT and MSTEP results plus instructional and benchmarking data such as Fountas & Pinnell, Common Lit, NWEA - Math, exit data for advanced placement assessments and graduation rates. They provided comparisons with other districts in Oakland County and the state of Michigan and reviewed reading, writing and math scores. Celebrations shared included the International Baccalaureate Diploma Program, the International Academy East IB diploma acquisition rate, Advanced Placement courses, AP Honor Roll status for Athens and Troy High, and graduation rates for Troy College and Career High School. The Board discussed learning lost during Covid and supports in place for credit recovery.

BUSINESS - iPAD PURCHASE (BOND). It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Alic that the district purchase iPads and cases from Apple Computers in the amount of $699,110.00, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Funds. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

BUSINESS - SMITH ELECTRICAL GEAR PRE-PURCHASE (BOND). It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mr. Hauff that the bid for the pre-purchase of electrical equipment for Smith Middle School be awarded to Great Lakes Power and Lighting in an amount not to exceed $279,900.00, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

BUSINESS - ROOFING PROJECTS (BOND). It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Wilson that the bid for roof replacement be awarded as follows, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund: JD Candler, Services Building, $59,900.00; Royal West Roofing, Bemis and Transportation, $289,000.00; Quality Roofing, Morse and Wattles, $818,420.00; Contingency (5%), $58,366.00; TOTAL $1,225,686.00. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

BUSINESS - PAVEMENT REPLACEMENT PROJECTS. It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Alic that the bid for the Site Work Paving Program be awarded to Nagle Paving Company in the amount of $1,758,370.00, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

BUSINESS - RETENTION POND RENOVATION PROJECT. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt that the bid for sitework projects be awarded to Eagle Excavation in the amount of $381,776.00, approved as an expenditure of the Building Site and Sinking Fund. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

BUSINESS - FOOD SERVICE, BOULAN & LARSON EQUIPMENT REPLACEMENT. It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mr. Hauff that the removal and replacement of the existing walk-in cooler and freezer at both Boulan Park and Larson Middle Schools be awarded to Stafford Smith in the amount of $227,606.32, approved as an expenditure of the Food Service Fund. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (NON-AGENDA ITEMS). Mrs. Sarah Krieger, Troy resident and parent of students in the District, addressed the Board about Mr. Schmidt's presentation in her children's Criminal Law class at Troy High School and about bringing politics into the classroom.

OTHER - REPORTS FROM STUDENT REPRESENTATIVES TO THE BOARD. Teagan Pruitt (Troy College and Career High School), Nurayda Albeez (International Academy-East), Jayla Turner (Troy High School) and Marlien William (Athens High School) each reported on events and activities at their schools.

BOARD MEMBER COMMENTS. Board members wished everyone happy holidays. Mr. Haupt announced that Teacher of the Year nominations are being accepted and encouraged parents to nominate a teacher. Mrs. Anne shared that Ms. Griffor and the ELA team helped her understand how reading and writing are taught and that the district has many tools at its disposal, including phonics and pictures, with teachers teaching to their students' needs. Mr. Hauff attended the Baker Orchestra and Choir Concert and described the fine arts program as thriving. Dr. Wilson thanked Mr. Haupt and Mrs. Alic for completing their first year on the board and mentioned the recent MASB Conference. Dr. Machesky congratulated the fine arts teachers for the numerous holiday concerts, recognized the SSAB Executive Board for planning the District's annual MLK Day event, noted that donations of fleece are desperately needed for that event, and said there would also be a blood drive and other community activities; he also reported that Oakland Schools' STEMI mobile innovation lab was located in the Services Building parking lot, where students can visit for 45-minute sessions. Mr. Schmidt discussed the preservation of Section 1 and the trust fund grant applied for with Oakland County Parks and Six Rivers Conservancy, and announced that the next Board Workshop would be held January 9, 2024 at 6:00 p.m. at the Administration Building and the Organizational and Regular Board Meeting on Tuesday, January 16 at 7:00 p.m. at the Services Building.

ADJOURNMENT. The meeting adjourned at 9:42 p.m.

The minutes call this a remarkable number of semifinalists and a tribute to the staff and parents of the Troy School District, and state that copies of the resolution will be presented to the students at a reception on November 16th.

The resolution, headed 2023 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists, was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Anne. Its clauses recite that the sixty students earned the prestigious honor of being among those selected nationwide as this year's semifinalists; that student achievement is honored through the National Merit Scholarship semifinalist and finalist recognition programs; and that National Merit students reach semifinalist status by scoring in the top one and one-half percent on the National Preliminary Scholastic Aptitude Test (PSAT) and earning comparable scores on the Scholastic Aptitude Test (SAT). The Board adopted the resolution in honor of the students for their selection as 2024 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

LEARNING DISABILITIES AWARENESS MONTH. The minutes record that national associations for a number of different learning differences have each declared October as an awareness month, including associations for Dyslexia, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, and Down Syndrome, and that the U.S. Department of Education has declared October as Learning Disabilities / Dyslexia / Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder / Down Syndrome Awareness Month. In Michigan, Governor Whitmer has provided a more encompassing definition and declared October as Learning Disabilities Month, and the Troy Board of Education joined the governor with its own resolution.

The resolution was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Dr. Wilson. Its clauses state that the term learning disabilities refers to differences in how our brains work, which may affect the acquisition, organization, retention, understanding, or use of verbal or nonverbal information; that learning disabilities range in severity and may impact the acquisition and use of oral language, reading, written language, and mathematics; that 1 in 5 individuals have a learning disability; that learning disabilities may co-exist with other disabilities and conditions and can affect individuals regardless of race, gender, sexual orientation, or other intersecting factors; that disabilities are a natural part of human diversity but individuals with learning disabilities may face discrimination or marginalization; that every person has strengths and learning disabilities should not keep individuals from realizing their full potential; that specialized assessments and interventions involving home, school, community, and workplace settings can significantly enhance quality of life; and that understanding and celebrating the unique abilities of individuals with learning disabilities is essential to an inclusive society embracing the strengths and potential of all Michigan residents. The Board therefore joined Governor Gretchen Whitmer in commemorating October 2023 as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

Category scores were Research 4.83/5.00, Planning 4.67/5.00, Implementation 4.67/5.00, Evaluation 4.50/5.00, and Overall 4.67/5.00, against an MSPRA threshold requiring a weighted average of 4.50/5.00, or 90%, to receive the award. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Award and scoring**
2023 Gold Medallion Awards judge feedback for Troy School District, issued by MSPRA. Each category is scored on a scale of 1.00 to 5.00, and entries must receive a weighted average of 4.50/5.00, or 90%, to receive the award. Judging is done confidentially by an experienced panel of accredited state and national association members and public relations professionals, who provide constructive feedback for all entries.

| Category | Score | Weight |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Research | 4.83/5.00 | 15% of the score |
| Planning | 4.67/5.00 | 45% of the score |
| Implementation | 4.67/5.00 | 25% of the score |
| Evaluation | 4.50/5.00 | 15% of the score |
| Overall | 4.67/5.00 | - |

**Research comments**
Judges called the section very thorough, praised survey feedback on building needs as necessary primary research, and noted objectives were SMART and aligned with research. Suggestions: add charts and graphs from the community survey for visual variety; compare community survey results with community voting demographics; explicitly label the project goal even if identical to the district goal; tighten the third objective, which one judge said should end at motivating families and staff to vote; and identify which items were primary versus secondary and formal versus informal, plus the specific research methodologies used.

**Planning comments**
Judges described a very detailed plan with set roles, objectives, strategies, and tactics, and commended the environmental scan, the identification of target audiences, the inclusion of the budget and team roles and responsibilities, and the tie to the district strategic plan. One judge highlighted the entry's statement that it was crucial to be flexible and able to adapt to changing conditions. Recommendations: attribute some material (political climate, board election campaigns and results, economics) to research; consider whether the Concurrent Campaign section belongs under evaluation; detail each strategy and tactic and tie each to an objective; and outline the five planning elements - goals, public identification, objectives naming the target public for each strategy, SMART objectives, and defined strategies and tactics.

**Implementation comments**
Judges praised key messages drawn from survey research, clear targeting through research-proven outlets, the real estate agent video promoting district value, visually appealing graphics and branding, per-campus adjustments on flyers, newspaper insert and PowerPoint slides, the introductory video, the principal toolkit, the FAQ, and timeline execution. Noted issues: automatic captions on videos should be reviewed and corrected to meet web accessibility standards; one judge could not access the principal toolkit without login information; and details on specific messages and channels against the timeline, budget, and responsible party would strengthen the section.

**Evaluation comments**
Follow-up interviews to determine messaging effectiveness were cited as strong primary research. Judges recommended returning to each element of GOST (Goals, Objectives, Strategies, Tactics) with supporting data for each strategy - newsletter open rates, social media engagement, website views, video watch time - and sharing specifics on the success of individual objectives, including whether objectives were outcome- or output-based and whether awareness, opinions, behavior, or support changed.

**Overall comments and criteria**
Judges liked the entry's focus on the communications campaign rather than the creation of the bond projects, valued the hyperlinks to additional information, and asked for more on how absentee voters were reached. Two judges recommended submitting the campaign for an NSPRA Gold Medallion. Overall criteria: the project is based in strategic communication best practices; the concept is clear and the writing is free of errors; the content is well-organized, visually appealing, and appropriate; the program, school, and/or district brand is portrayed consistently; and the project fulfills the stated objectives and goals.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The 2023 Gold Medallion Awards judge feedback report for Troy School District records category scores and anonymous panel commentary on the district's bond communications campaign entry. Scores were Research 4.83/5.00, Planning 4.67/5.00, Implementation 4.67/5.00, Evaluation 4.50/5.00, and Overall 4.67/5.00.

RESEARCH (4.83/5.00). One judge called the section very thorough, covering a variety of aspects of the program and types of research conducted, and said the survey feedback on building needs provided necessary primary research, that objectives are in line with the research and are SMART, and that the entry touched on how research and evaluation continued to impact planning and implementation throughout the project. That judge recommended, if the campaign is submitted in other award programs, adding charts and graphs from the community survey to provide visual variety and turn numbers into easy-to-read points, and adding something about the voting demographics of the community and whether the community survey results aligned with those numbers. A second judge praised the detailing of research used to inform decision-making, said it helped tell the story and provide the rationale for the project, and called the variety of data used and cited - both primary and secondary - impressive and appreciated; that judge suggested specifically stating and calling out the goal or goals, noting it can be the exact same as the district goal but should also be labeled as the goal for the project or plan, and suggested tightening the third objective, observing that the first and second detail what is being attempted, by how much, and when, while the third is wordier and loses focus, with much of it better placed as a strategy (how the objective will be carried out) or as a tactic (the tools used to execute a strategy). Other comments: fantastic research reaching all stakeholders and outside assessments; great research, but the third objective is too broad and starts to get into strategies and tactics and should end at motivating families and staff to vote; research could be stronger if the entry had included what items were primary and secondary, formal and informal, and the specific research methodologies used; and the entry demonstrates excellent research and outlines goals and objectives that align to research findings.

PLANNING (4.67/5.00). One judge felt some information in the section could also be attributed to research (political climate, board election campaigns and results, economics) and asked whether the Concurrent Campaign section could be considered part of the evaluation, noting that incorporating additional information to explain actions helps show decisions are informed by research. Another judge commended the identification and detailing of target audiences and specifically appreciated the entry's statement that it was crucial to be flexible and be able to adapt to changing conditions as they developed, calling that a hallmark of a public relations professional. That judge also appreciated that the scope of work was considered and categorized in a way target audiences could more easily understand and remember, praised the completion of an environmental scan and its inclusion in the plan and award submission, and again credited masterful use of research and data to inform decision-making. For future submissions the judge encouraged detailing each strategy and tactic, explaining that strategies detail how objectives will be carried out and each strategy needs to be tied to an objective - for example, if an objective is to increase community awareness in low voter turnout areas by a given percentage by a given date, a strategy could be advertising in targeted neighborhoods, with tactics such as yard signs and billboards - and noted that doing so helps assess whether the plan was successfully implemented and whether it had the desired impact. The judge thanked the district for completing and including its budget and team roles and responsibilities. Additional comments: a very detailed plan with set roles, objectives, strategies and tactics; excellent, with a good job tying the campaign into the strategic plan; planning could only be improved by specifically outlining the five planning elements that provide the framework for all communication plans - goals; public identification to establish clearly defined groups; objectives that indicate the target public for each outlined strategy; SMART objectives; and defined strategies (the how) and tactics (the what); and the entry demonstrates a sophisticated and thorough grasp of planning, reflecting a clear understanding of target audiences and communications tactics.

IMPLEMENTATION (4.67/5.00). Judges noted that research from the initial survey feedback and the community survey showed phrases and needs that resonated with stakeholders and were turned into key messages, and that messages were clear and targeted to appropriate audiences through research-proven outlets; one judge singled out the idea of having a real estate agent create a video to promote the value of the district. Another judge called the graphics visually appealing and attention-grabbing with well-done branding, calling out the adjustments made for each campus on the flyers, newspaper insert, and PowerPoint slides, and describing the language as clear, concise, and appropriate and the videos as great, with the introductory video setting a good tone for the campaign ahead. That judge asked that all materials meet web accessibility standards, specifically reviewing and correcting the automatic captions on videos, so materials are readily available to all audiences; called the principal toolkit a wonderful idea while noting the judge could not access it because login information was required; praised the key messages and the willingness to adjust them throughout the campaign; described the FAQ as well-organized and easy to navigate; and commended the timeline execution. Other comments: beautiful campaign; well-designed graphics and consistent use throughout the campaign; implementation could be improved by including details on the specific messages and channels against the timeline, budget, and designated responsible party, which is also the time to monitor results of actions and messages while tracking campaign milestones; and the campaign was successfully implemented, producing materials of a high quality that supported stated goals in accordance with a clear timeline.

EVALUATION (4.50/5.00). Judges called the evaluation thorough and cited follow-up interviews to determine the effectiveness of messaging and how information was shown as a great example of primary research and as information usable for future campaigns. One judge congratulated the district on a successful campaign and on following up with members of target audiences to understand which tactics were most successful, praised the detailing of next steps and called the tactics visually appealing, easy to read, and key to the campaign's success; that judge advised going back to each element of GOST (Goals, Objectives, Strategies, Tactics) to determine whether the district met or exceeded what it set out to do, including data for each strategy such as newsletter analytics (open rate), social media (engagement), website (views), and videos (watch time), and noted that much of that framework already appears in subsequent pages of the award submission. Additional comments: congratulations on the win and great evaluation; love the data points and the detail, with a good job tying evaluation back to goals and objectives; evaluation could only be improved by sharing specifics on the success of individual objectives, asking whether objectives were outcome- or output-based and whether there was a change in awareness, opinions, behavior, or support for the outlined goal, and identifying ways to improve and recommendations for the future; and it seems clear the campaign achieved its objectives, with follow-up interviews bringing specificity and clarity to what might otherwise have been difficult to measure.

OVERALL (4.67/5.00). One judge liked that the entry focused on the communications campaign rather than the creation of the bond projects, called the quality of materials high, suggested adding more about how absentee voters were reached and what messaging they received, and - anticipating an NSPRA Gold Medallion entry - recommended having a few editors review and clean it up. Another thanked the district for including hyperlinks to additional information, said it made for an even more thorough submission, urged that tactics be tied to strategies, objectives, and goals so impact can be directly demonstrated and measured, and called the campaign inspiring. Other overall comments: great job; this is a great campaign, please consider submitting it for an NSPRA Gold Medallion as well; overall this is a strong submission; and excellent work.

RUBRIC. MSPRA uses an experienced panel of accredited state and national association members and public relations professionals to confidentially review and judge entries, and judges provide constructive feedback for all entries. Each category is scored on a scale of 1.00 to 5.00, and entries must receive a weighted average of 4.50/5.00, or 90%, to receive the award. Overall criteria considered when reviewing the entry in its entirety: the project is based in strategic communication best practices; the concept is clear and the writing is free of errors; the content is well-organized, visually appealing, and appropriate; the program, school, and/or district brand is portrayed consistently; and the project fulfills the stated objectives and goals.

Research counts for 15% of the score, and judges ask whether the reason for the project is explained, whether there is evidence of quality and varied methods of research performed, whether findings were used to guide planning, and whether project goals and measurable objectives are stated. Planning counts for 45% of the score, with judges asking whether target audiences were identified, whether strategies were determined for accomplishing objectives, what stakeholders were involved in the planning process, whether a variety of communication tactics were proposed to reach target audiences, what relevant training was provided for key staff, whether a communications budget was developed, and whether team roles and responsibilities were identified. Implementation counts for 25% of the score, with judges asking whether the team created a timeline and met key dates, whether planned strategies and tactics were implemented, what key messages were used to support the goals and objectives, whether audience response was monitored, whether the design of materials was visually appealing, and whether appropriate and clear language was used. Evaluation counts for 15% of the score, with judges asking whether the project was successful based on the goals and objectives, what indicators were used to measure success, whether specific data was collected on the effectiveness of specific strategies and tactics, whether opportunities for improvement were explored for future projects, and what next steps were identified.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Judge feedback from the 2023 Excellence Awards for Troy School District, compiling panel comments on strengths and recommended improvements for entries in seven categories: Audio/Podcast, Financial Report, Marketing Materials, Newsletter, Social Media, Video, and Website/Mobile App. No numeric scores are reported; instead the report pairs narrative praise with specific criticism, most of it recurring around volume of content, accessibility, and readability. The document closes with the judging rubric, listing the elements considered for all categories plus category-specific criteria, including the requirement that Website/Mobile App content and design be accessible for all users under WCAG 2.1 Level AA.

**Report**
2023 Excellence Awards judge feedback for Troy School District. Each category section lists what judges considered the strengths of the entry and what recommendations they had for improving it. No scores are printed.

**Audio/Podcast**
Strengths: tying past and present under the district's overall legacy; strong interviews and editing; innovative and compelling celebration of a district milestone using storytelling as a window to the past; exceptional storytelling and quality audio. Recommendations: add context near the start for listeners less familiar with district history, and open with a brief word from the team explaining the context of the 1989 Athens State Soccer Championship and its relevance today.

**Financial Report**
Strengths: thorough document offering a wealth of information for voters; multiple points of view (students, board president, Realtor); content broken into small, concise chunks; colorful design; comprehensive overview of Troy's bond issue with images of infrastructure clearly in need of repair. Recommendations: shorten the newsletter or add an index or table of contents; use more bullet points; apply more consistent capitalization, type sizes, and typefaces; make the colors for the four areas of the plan consistent throughout, since it was challenging to track improvements by area and grade level or building.

**Marketing Materials**
Strengths: at-a-glance information, visually appealing and unique to each school's colors; consistency across schools with nice infographics; the Hamilton Elementary homepage with a drone video progressing into Hamilton at a glance and the five-star rating from Troy community parents and students. Recommendations: combine the busy school and district mission sections; check ADA accessibility; replace links showing NEW MISSION INFOGRAPHIC COMING SOON with a placeholder graphic; allow more white space.

**Newsletter**
Strengths: consistent message and appearance; front page of each issue clearly identifies the district; contributions from both superintendent and board president; the roundup on the last page; wide variety of topics and programs with numerous pictures and clear branding. Recommendations: balance photos and text; make recurring content consistent between issues (athlete signings differed each issue); reduce excessive graphics; address low-resolution elements; increase font size; add contact information and ways to stay connected.

**Social Media**
Strengths: consistency across campaign-related posts; use of historical video; simple, clear messages; quick facts and footage. Recommendations: better engage the interactive social functions of social media, and include the date of the vote in videos to direct the audience to take action.

**Video**
Strengths: classroom footage; graphics and an attention-getting opening; natural sound; professional footage with excellent b-roll; the sixth grade teacher's segments; an explainer style suited to answering community questions, with easy-to-read flowcharts illustrating math course sequences. Recommendations: shorten the video and reduce educational jargon; interview the math specialist somewhere other than what looked like a living room; avoid closed captioning covering graphics; simplify the student track graphics; add a clear summary structure connecting the changes to student benefit; reconsider the all-caps title cards with tight bounding boxes, including text such as the one at 4:40.

**Website/Mobile App**
Strengths: a collective location for press-related content, including both press releases and a media coverage area; convenient aggregation of news regardless of outlet; a button for visitors to submit news and story ideas; simple, easy navigation and a good mobile version. Recommendations: the press release module is not mobile-friendly; the media coverage page's last column gets cut off even on a full-screen desktop; rework the media logos without the blue boxes and link to their homepages; add a link back to the main Press Room page; note that the media spreadsheet may be hard to keep updated as media links change, and confirm PDF newsletters are ADA-compliant.

**Rubric**
Elements considered for all categories: purpose and target audience well defined or implied; clear, concise, positive writing; text free of grammatical, spelling, and punctuation errors; well-organized, visually appealing, appropriate content; and consistent portrayal of the program, school, and/or district brand. Additional criteria are listed for Annual Report, Audio/Podcast, Diversity Equity and Inclusion, Financial Report, Marketing Materials, Newsletter, Special Purpose, Video, Social Media, and Website/Mobile App, the last requiring accessibility for all users at WCAG 2.1 Level AA.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The 2023 Excellence Awards judge feedback report for Troy School District collects panel comments on the district's entries, organized by category, with each category divided into what judges considered the strengths of the entry and what recommendations they had for improving it. The categories addressed are Audio/Podcast, Financial Report, Marketing Materials, Newsletter, Social Media, Video, and Website/Mobile App. The report contains no numeric scores.

AUDIO/PODCAST. Strengths cited: a really exciting way to tie in the past and the present under the district's overall legacy in this area, with a great job on the interviews and editing; an innovative and compelling way to celebrate a district milestone using storytelling as a window to the past that also connects the community to today; a judge who really enjoyed the submission and called it a great podcast from start to finish; and exceptional storytelling with quality audio. Recommendations: some additional context near the start would help listeners who are not as familiar with the district history, and many listeners might appreciate a brief word from the team introducing the episode so all listeners better understand the context of the 1989 Athens State Soccer Championship and why it is relevant to today.

FINANCIAL REPORT. Strengths cited: the document appears very thorough and offers a wealth of information for voters, includes a variety of points of view (students, board president, Realtor), breaks content into small, concise chunks, and has a colorful, eye-catching design; it is a very comprehensive overview of Troy's bond issue, providing many examples of what could be in Troy's future and including images of infrastructure clearly in need of repair; it is very detailed in explaining every component of the Bond, which is important to some audiences; and it is visually appealing with creative use of information formatting. Recommendations: either making the newsletter shorter with fewer pages or providing an index or table of contents could have improved the entry, because the volume of information presented without a clear road map could be overwhelming, and more consistent use of capitalization, type sizes, and typefaces could have enhanced the professional appearance; there is a lot of text and bullet points would make it more engaging and easier to digest; and the colors for the four areas of the plan were not consistent throughout, with one judge doubting the average person would read so much content and finding it challenging to keep track of all the improvements by area and grade level or building, while recognizing that it was a financial supplement.

MARKETING MATERIALS. Strengths cited: the at-a-glance information, visually appealing and unique to each school's colors; consistency across the various individual schools with nice infographics and great content; the Hamilton Elementary homepage, described as engaging, with the movement of the drone video up top progressing into Hamilton at a glance, showcasing positive aspects and community feedback such as the five-star rating from Troy community parents and students; and materials that are very well organized and consistent across all schools, inviting, easy to read, and colorful. Recommendations: one judge found the first two sections with the school and District's missions busy and would like them combined, since each school's mission should still fit within the District's overall goal, arguing a cleaner, more streamlined design would push people to read the text rather than skim over it; another worried about how accessible (ADA) the materials are on the website; another reported that clicking some submission links produced a page reading NEW MISSION INFOGRAPHIC COMING SOON and found the graphic design a little overwhelming, noting the brain needs white space to process; and a judge recommended a placeholder graphic for the missing Mission Statement graphic that is currently empty.

NEWSLETTER. Strengths cited: consistency with the message and with the appearance; front pages that make clear the publication comes from the district; coverage of many topics with contributions from both the superintendent and the board president and a roundup on the last page; a wide variety of topics and programs that make it a great community resource; and numerous pictures that enhanced the reading experience, with clear and noticeable branding. Recommendations: in some cases additional photos would help tell the story while in others there are too many photos and not enough text; some pages are very busy and difficult to read because the reader does not know where to focus, and more consistency between issues in how the same type of information is shared would help, with the athlete signings standing out as very different in each issue; the amount of content is a little overwhelming and the extra graphics a little excessive; consider a less-is-more approach, since the many visual elements can be a tad distracting and some graphic elements are strained due to lower resolution than their surrounding elements; and to enhance readability consider increasing the font size and adding contact information or promoting ways to stay connected with the district.

SOCIAL MEDIA. Strengths cited: consistency across campaign-related posts and the use of historical video; the use of video to engage and inform the community; simple, clear messages that are easy to consume; and a highly enjoyed submission with quick facts and footage. Recommendations: aside from information distribution, consider how to better engage the social functions and interaction of social media; one judge offered no recommendations, acknowledging how hard a bond campaign is; and the videos did not include the date of the vote, which would have helped direct the audience to take action.

VIDEO. Strengths cited: good shots of kids doing work in the classroom; nice graphics with an opening that immediately caught a judge's attention and good use of natural sound such as a teacher giving instructions; professional-looking footage with excellent b-roll and great messaging; a sixth grade teacher described as awesome who seems to encompass the whole program in her segments, along with video of her interacting with students; and a slightly longer explainer style that fits the purpose of answering community questions, with solid audio and video quality, classroom footage framed well in a variety of angles that keep it from feeling repetitive, easy-to-read flowcharts illustrating the math course sequences, and speakers and footage fitting together into a very cohesive video. Recommendations: the video was really long and contained quite a bit of educational jargon; one judge would have interviewed the math specialist and a few others in a different location because it looked like a living room, found some speakers too rehearsed, and thought the video too long to hold attention; another suggested shortening it, noted graphics can be difficult to read while listening to the narrator, and observed that closed captioning covers graphics; another suggested making more of preparing students for the future, noted the background sign reading show me what you are thinking might have made a nice b-roll piece, and found the graphics showing student track too busy for video; and a final judge said each speaker communicates well and the individual changes and reasoning behind them are mentioned, but would have liked a clear summary or video structure to connect the dots - observing a situation, investigating all parts of the math program, and implementing specific changes with an explanation of how each helps students - adding that the all-caps title cards with tight bounding boxes look phenomenal visually but are uncomfortable to read and that some of their text, such as at 4:40, could be more succinct or punctuated differently.

WEBSITE/MOBILE APP. Strengths cited: a collective location for press-related content is an excellent idea for a school district, with appreciation for both the press release section and the media coverage area; aggregating all news content in one area makes it convenient for users to find what they want regardless of outlet, with a judge speculating that the Media Coverage page populates automatically and calling that super cool, and praising the button for visitors to submit news and story ideas; the simplicity of the page, which is easy to navigate, makes its exact purpose easy to tell, requires no searching or multiple click-throughs, and has a mobile version that looks great; and a page that is easy to view without too much going on. Recommendations: one judge encountered many issues accessing content on a phone, finding that while the page itself was responsive the content was not, requiring side-to-side scrolling inside the page to reach articles and links; another noted the module that displays press releases is not mobile-friendly and that updating it would be a big improvement, suggested changes to the media coverage page because the last column does not quite fit the view and gets cut off even on a full-screen desktop, proposed a different look for the media logos without the blue boxes with links to their homepages from what appear to be buttons at the bottom of the page, and asked for a link back to the main Press Room page from all linked pages; another thought the media spreadsheet will be difficult to keep updated in the long run because links on media sites often change or do not last, found the newsletter a little slow to load and harder to navigate, and questioned whether a PDF format is ADA-compliant and accessible to all audiences; and a final recommendation was to include a document with the audience and purpose behind the page.

RUBRIC. Elements considered by judges for entries in all categories: the purpose and target audience are well defined or implied; the writing is clear, concise, and positive; the text is free of grammatical, spelling, and punctuation errors; the content is well-organized, visually appealing, and appropriate; and the program, school, and/or district brand is portrayed consistently. Additional elements are listed by category. Annual Report, Special Purpose, and Financial Report share the requirements that font and graphic elements be easy to read and enhance the overall design and that there be an effective balance of written and visual information; Annual Report and Special Purpose add that format and length be appropriate for the content and target audiences, while Financial Report adds that complicated topics be made relevant and easy to understand for the target audiences. Audio/Podcast: editing is smooth, organized, and well-paced; topics are engaging, innovative, and relevant; narration, music, and other sounds are of good and consistent quality. Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion: the project is intentionally designed to positively impact, support, or promote DEI efforts; its message and voice are appropriate, approachable, and engaging; and multiple perspectives were considered and consulted. Marketing Materials: the program, school, or district is presented in a creative, persuasive, and positive way; font and graphic elements are easy to read; and there is a compelling call to action. Newsletter: topics are varied and engaging; font and graphic elements are easy to read; and consistency is shown across multiple issues. Video, listed twice in the rubric with identical criteria: editing is smooth, organized, and well-paced; the video includes closed captioning; and video, narration, still photos, music, and graphics are integrated effectively and consistently. Social Media: posts include a high-quality photo, graphic, or video; audience engagement is apparent and encouraged; and posts reflect platform best practices related to accessibility, frequency, style, and voice. Website/Mobile App: user navigation is intuitive and responsive on a mobile device; content appears current and regularly updated; and the content and design are accessible for all users (WCAG 2.1 Level AA).

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: An Association for Middle Level Education (AMLE) article, "Creating a Culture of Connectedness through Middle School Advisory Programs" by Sarah Brody Shulkind and Jack Foote, printed from amle.org on 3/3/23 and included with Troy School District Board of Education materials for the March 7, 2023 meeting. Drawing on questionnaires, advisor interviews, observations, and student focus groups at three diverse middle schools with successful advisory programs, the authors identify seven characteristics of advisors and advisories that foster connectedness. The most striking reported finding is that 98% of focus-group students answered affirmatively when asked whether advisory helps them academically. The piece was previously published in Middle School Journal, September 2009.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Item**
Browser printout of the AMLE (Association for Middle Level Education) web article "Creating a Culture of Connectedness through Middle School Advisory Programs," captured 3/3/23 at 2:24 PM from https://www.amle.org/creating-a-culture-of-connectedness-through-middle-school-advisory-programs/, pages 1/7 through 6/7. Byline: Sarah Brody Shulkind, Jack Foote (Rick Wormeli also appears in the adjacent page furniture). Filed as Troy School District Board of Education material dated March 7, 2023. Closing note: "Previously published in Middle School Journal, September 2009."

**Premise**
Four Los Angeles middle school students answer the question "Does advisory help you feel connected to school?" A seventh grade girl says that without advisory "school would be more distant"; an eighth grade boy describes a bond in which "from 6th sixth grade to 12th grade, everyone shares that connection with one teacher"; a seventh grade boy calls advisory "a place where you can get stuff off your chest."

**Definitions**
Connectedness is defined as a school culture in which students have meaningful relationships with adults in the school, are engaged in the school, and feel a sense of belonging. The authors state it is linked to higher grades, higher test scores, and lower dropout rates regardless of socioeconomic status, citing Blum & Libbey (2004), Jackson & Davis (2000), Klem & Connell (2004), Mac Iver & Epstein (1991), McNeely & Falci (2004), and the National Association of Secondary School Principals (2006). Advisory programs are configurations in which an adult advisor meets regularly during the school day with a group of students for academic and social-emotional mentorship, personalization, and a small peer community of learners.

**Method**
Every advisor and student at three diverse middle schools with successful advisory programs received a questionnaire designed to establish which advisories fostered high levels of connectedness. The three advisories with the highest connectedness at each site were selected; researchers interviewed the advisors, observed the advisories, and ran focus groups with advisees. Seven characteristics emerged at all three sites.

**Figure 1 - Advisor/advisory characteristics that foster connectedness**

| Characteristic |
| --- |
| Strong advisory programs address issues of community. |
| Strong advisories promote open communication. |
| Strong advisors know and care about their advisees. |
| Strong advisors closely supervise their advisees' academic progress. |
| Strong advisors are problem solvers and advice givers. |
| Students and advisors perceive that advisory directly improves academic performance. |
| Students and advisors perceive that advisory functions as a community of learners. |

**Findings**
Community: advisors used family language ("we are a family"); one school used a conversation protocol for positive feedback and behavior issues; another paired seventh graders with eighth grade buddies, called "a pay it forward thing." Observed students were not self-segregated ethnically and refrained from teasing.
Communication: trust walks, team-building games, spotlight activities, a blindfolded obstacle course, and Monday morning circles. In more than half of the advisories observed, students shared emotions publicly.
Academic monitoring: advisors consulted other teachers, used official quarter and semester progress reports, and posted checklists during weekly advisory work time. Asked whether advisors notice struggles, one student said, "Immediately, they are all on it."
Perceived academic effect: 98% of focus-group students said advisory helps them academically. Advisors agreed but split on immediacy - "right away" versus "in the long run."
Community of learners: peer tutoring and study groups formed during guided work time, with one advisor describing a "slip streaming effect." In one observed advisory the advisor asked, "Who can help Damion with this question?" prompting a debate among five students.

**Authors**
Sarah Brody Shulkind, middle school principal, Milken Community High School, Los Angeles, CA (sshulkind@milkenschool.org). Jack Foote, principal, Joseph Le Conte Middle School, Los Angeles, CA (jackfoote@gmail.com).
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Source and provenance**
Filed with Troy School District (Michigan) Board of Education materials dated March 7, 2023, the item is a browser printout of an Association for Middle Level Education (AMLE) article at https://www.amle.org/creating-a-culture-of-connectedness-through-middle-school-advisory-programs/, timestamped 3/3/23, 2:24 PM and paginated 1/7 through 6/7. Title: "Creating a Culture of Connectedness through Middle School Advisory Programs." Byline: "By: Sarah Brody Shulkind, Jack Foote," with the name Rick Wormeli in the adjacent page furniture. Captured site navigation includes Search, Join, Renew, Login; an "Explore These Topics" list (COVID-19, Literacy, Math, Reading, Student Engagement, Teacher Motivation, Writing, Social Emotional Learning, Student Motivation); a "Categories / Select Category" selector; and a "Most Popular" list ("Schools of Distinction," "Kindness is harder than it looks," "AMLE Celebrates Inaugural," "Reimagining School - What should it look like and who is it for?"). A closing line reads "Previously published in Middle School Journal, September 2009."

**Opening student voices**
In "an ordinary Los Angeles school," four middle school students answer "Does advisory help you feel connected to school?" A seventh grade girl: "Without advisory school would be more distant. It would not be as cheerful." An eighth grade boy: "from 6th sixth grade to 12th grade, everyone shares that connection with one teacher... it is a place where teachers really know you and understand you." An eighth grade girl: "at least there is always one so you are not nervous about going to school." A seventh grade boy names sixth grade as when "you have violence problems or drug problems or even academic problems or personal problems," and calls advisory "a place where you can get stuff off your chest."

**Connectedness and supporting literature**
Connectedness is defined as a characteristic of school cultures in which students have meaningful relationships with adults within the school, are engaged in the school, and feel a sense of belonging to the school. The authors assert it is linked to higher grades, higher test scores, and lower dropout rates regardless of students' socioeconomic status, citing Blum & Libbey, 2004; Jackson & Davis, 2000; Klem & Connell, 2004; Mac Iver & Epstein, 1991; McNeely & Falci, 2004; and National Association of Secondary School Principals, 2006. Schools organized to promote personalization and communities of learners better prepare adolescents for later success as adults (Carnegie Council on Adolescent Development, 1989), and improving connectedness is urgent at the middle level "because the roots of alienation take hold during early adolescence."

**Advisory defined; the evidence gap**
Advisory programs are broadly defined as configurations in which an adult advisor meets regularly during the school day with a group of students to provide academic and social-emotional mentorship and support, to create personalization within the school, and to facilitate a small peer community of learners (Cushman, 1990; Galassi et al., 2004; Galassi et al., 1997; Juvonen et al., 2004; National Association of Secondary School Principals, 2006; Stevenson, 1998). Although promoted in the literature and intuitively valued by practitioners, advisory has had limited empirical support and no accepted basis for identifying best practices, leaving schools to rely on intuition and anecdote when building programs and training advisors.

**Methodology**
Every advisor and student at three diverse middle schools with successful advisory programs completed a questionnaire designed to establish which advisories fostered high levels of connectedness, identifying which students felt most connected, which advisories reported high connectedness, and which advisors perceived the same levels as their advisees. The three advisories with the highest connectedness at each site were selected; the researchers interviewed those advisors, observed the advisories, and conducted focus groups with the advisees. Seven salient characteristics emerged at all three sites (Figure 1).

**Figure 1 - Advisor/advisory characteristics that foster connectedness**

| Characteristic |
| --- |
| Strong advisory programs address issues of community. |
| Strong advisories promote open communication. |
| Strong advisors know and care about their advisees. |
| Strong advisors closely supervise their advisees' academic progress. |
| Strong advisors are problem solvers and advice givers. |
| Students and advisors perceive that advisory directly improves academic performance. |
| Students and advisors perceive that advisory functions as a community of learners. |

**Community**
High-connectedness advisories worked on how students related to one another. One advisor: "I like to stress that we are a family. So, we do not laugh at each other and nobody makes comments... I am trying to break them of snickering." Another discussed friendship and ostracism; a third handled conflict by telling students, "This is like our little family away from home." One school used a conversation protocol for positive feedback that asked students to "address issues that are caused by the behavior of someone in advisory." Another advisor asked advisees to be "big brother or sister" to a struggling classmate. Two comments recurred in every focus group: advisory is a family, and advisory helps students bond. During observations students were not self-segregated ethnically and refrained from teasing and put-downs. Cross-grade work included addressing sixth graders' problems with older students at one school and assigning seventh graders an eighth grade buddy at another - "kind of like a pay it forward thing."

**Open communication**
Advisors described spotlight get-to-know-you activities, trust walks, and team-building games; at one school Monday mornings began with a circle where students shared what was on their minds. One advisor set up a blindfolded obstacle course: "The rest of you are going to have to listen and trust the person that is verbalizing to you." Students called the communication "intense" and said "people are really vulnerable, and we all share our feelings." In more than half of the advisories observed, students shared emotions publicly; in one, a conversation about crying followed an advisor sharing his own feelings, and when a student asked "Are you crying?" the advisees looked on without giggling. Students initiated conversations about parents fighting, disagreements with friends, problems with a teacher, and academic difficulties, and cited lunch and after school as "other good times to talk." Layout pull quotes read "Strong advisors give their advisees individualized attention," "Advisory programs foster meaningful peer relationships," and "Advisory programs strengthen connectedness in middle grades schools."

**Academic supervision**
Students said advisors "know everything" about their academic standing - "Even if she does not know right away, she will find out" - and found that helpful. Advisors talked with other teachers both in reaction to poor work and low grades and proactively when they had not heard about an advisee in a while; almost every advisor cited official progress reports at the end of the quarter and semester. One recounted a boy "amazing in one class and failing another": "You get an A in math and science, and you are failing social studies. How is that possible?" - he saved social studies homework and never got to it. Students at all three sites had time to do work during advisory weekly, and many advisors posted a checklist of tasks on the board, some items for the whole group and some for specific students.

**Problem solving**
Students unanimously said they would go to their advisors for advice on bullying, friendship strife, homework dilemmas, and other middle school "drama." Advisors called problem-solving sessions "organic" and "responsive to the needs of my kids," reporting racial tension, weak grades, misunderstandings with teachers, school policy, bullying and exclusion, and stress at home. They emphasized problem solving with students rather than for them, answering "What should I do about...?" with "How would you solve that problem?" and "What do you think are your next steps?"

**Perceived academic impact**
Survey data at all three schools indicated students and advisors perceived that advisory improved academic performance, and students in high-connectedness advisories were more likely than those in lower-connectedness advisories to perceive that link. In the focus groups, 98% of students responded affirmatively to "Do you think advisory helps you academically?" Students cited focus on studies, critical academic support, strategizing about classes and teachers, goal setting, and belonging to a group of peers striving for success. The advisor survey confirmed the qualitative findings; advisors assigned advisory a significant role in academic success but disagreed on immediacy, some saying "right away" and others "in the long run." One advisor: "create a good climate, and you are going to have kids who perform at a good academic level." Another called advisory "an academic support" because "middle school kids [do not] know how to talk with teachers and advocate for themselves."

**Community of learners**
Students described advisees as an academic resource: "there is a lot of unseen potential when you can have students help one another." Advisors used the language of peer tutoring and study groups; one linked it to connectedness: "They pull out homework and help each other... They feel connected to school and connected to their teacher and curriculum." In observations at one school, desks were clustered in groups of four with students quizzing each other, and another group sat on the floor with their advisor reviewing for a test. At another school, when a boy exclaimed "I do not get this!" a girl explained mathematical functions; two students worked a problem at the board; and an advisor turned a question back to the group - "Are negative numbers real numbers? Who can help Damion with this question?" - producing a debate among five students about the nature of numbers. One advisor described a "slip streaming effect" in which "the group seems to be pulling them along."

**Conclusion**
As students approach adulthood schools often become more isolating and impersonal; advisory is presented as "the one place in school where students are intimately known as a 'whole child,'" with the potential to ensure every child has a meaningful relationship with an adult and belongs to a community of peers.

**Authors**
Sarah Brody Shulkind, middle school principal at Milken Community High School, Los Angeles, CA (sshulkind@milkenschool.org). Jack Foote, principal of Joseph Le Conte Middle School, Los Angeles, CA (jackfoote@gmail.com).

**References**
Blum & Libbey (2004), Journal of School Health, 74(7), 231-235; Carnegie Council on Adolescent Development (1989), Turning points, Carnegie Corporation; Cushman (1990), Horace, 7(1), 5-17; Galassi, Gulledge & Cox (2004), Advisory, National Middle School Association; Galassi, Gulledge & Cox (1997), Review of Educational Research, 67(3), 301-338; Jackson & Davis (2000), Turning points 2000, Teachers College Press; Juvonen, Le, Kaganoff, Augustine & Constant (2004), Focus on the wonder years, RAND Corporation; Klem & Connell (2004), Journal of School Health, 74(7), 262-273; Mac Iver & Epstein (1991), American Journal of Education, 99(4), 587-622; McNeely & Falci (2004), Journal of School Health, 74(7), 284-293; National Association of Secondary School Principals (2006), Breaking ranks in the middle, Reston, VA; Stevenson (1998), Teaching ten to fourteen year olds (2nd ed.), Addison Wesley Longman.

| 3B.16 Gymnasium | Interkal Inc. | $155,758 | $155,758 |

| Line | Amount |
|---|---|

**Bid Irregularities**
The low bidders in Structured Cabling and Acoustical Wall Units did not submit a complete bid and are not recommended.
