In the signage category no bidder submitted a complete and/or qualified bid. The fourth low bidder, DMP Signs, submitted a complete bid but with an alternate product to the one specified; that product is being reviewed for equivalence, after which Barton Malow will either recommend award to DMP Signs or rebid the category. Work related to the traffic signal at the Livernois intersection remains in design and will be bid at a later date; the engineer's estimate for that work is included in the projected cost. The project was advertised on the state website for a total of five and a half weeks and drew 38 bids across these categories. Total construction cost including contingency on all previous award recommendations is fifty four million four hundred twenty four thousand nine hundred and sixty one dollars ($54,424,961). Including the estimated work remaining, the projected cost of the building is fifty five and a half million dollars ($55,500,000).

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Board packet material presenting Troy School District's receipt of the Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting from the Association of School Business Officials International (ASBO), together with the underlying correspondence, press release and review-team comments.

CERTIFICATE. The certificate reads that the Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting is presented to Troy School District for its Annual Comprehensive Financial Report for the Fiscal Year Ended June 30, 2024, and that the district report meets the criteria established for ASBO International's Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting. It carries the signatures of Ryan S. Stechschulte, President, and James M. Rowan, CAE, SFO, CEO/Executive Director.

NOTIFICATION LETTER. Dated June 18, 2025, the letter is addressed to Daniel Trudel, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Rd, Troy, Michigan 48098-4777, and opens "Dear Daniel." Writing on behalf of ASBO, James M. Rowan informs the district that Troy School District has received ASBO's Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2024, characterizing the award as a significant achievement that reflects the district's commitment to transparency and high-quality financial reporting. The letter encourages the district to use the COE recipient's logo to share the achievement in emails and marketing materials. It states that the Certificate of Excellence (COE) Review Team has provided comments for the improvement of the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report, that it is important to review the comments and address them before preparing next year's report, and that the district must include a copy of the original comments and the district's written responses to those comments in next year's application packet. A press release for sharing the achievement with the community and the award certificate were attached. The letter closes with congratulations to Trudel and the staff members who worked to earn the COE and an expression of interest in the district's continued participation in the COE program.

PRESS RELEASE. Marked FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE, with contact Allison Barton-Kramer at abarton-kramer@asbointl.org, and datelined Reston, VA - June 18, 2025. Headlined "Troy School District Honored with ASBO International's Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting," the release announces that Troy School District (Michigan) has been awarded the Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting (COE), an honor that recognizes school districts upholding the highest standards of financial reporting and transparency. The district earned the certificate for its Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR) for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2024. Jim Rowan, CAE, SFO, Executive Director of ASBO International, is quoted: "For over half a century, ASBO International's Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting has been the gold standard for promoting and recognizing excellence in financial transparency. Clear and accurate financial reporting is crucial for engaging school communities and building their trust. Districts that earn the COE have demonstrated an extraordinary commitment to these principles." The release explains that participation in the COE program highlights a district's dedication to financial accountability, that submitted ACFRs are rigorously reviewed by a panel of experienced financial professionals who provide constructive feedback to enhance the quality of future reports, and that districts meeting the program's stringent requirements are awarded the Certificate of Excellence - a distinction that also supports bond rating and continuing bond disclosure processes. The program is proudly sponsored by Strategic Partner American Fidelity, and readers are directed to asbointl.org/COE.

ABOUT THE ORGANIZATIONS. The release notes that ASBO International was established in 1910 and is a nonprofit organization that unites, through its members and affiliates, a global network of approximately 30,000 school business professionals, empowering members with programs, resources and connections intended to set the standard for excellence in school business management; more information at asbointl.org. A companion section on American Fidelity describes the company as familiar with the education community, functioning as an extension of a district's HR department, administering the entire benefits program, educating employees through in-person education and customized communications, providing an enrollment platform for benefits enrollment, and helping keep the district and its program compliant.

REVIEW COMMENTS. Dated June 16, 2025, the Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting Review Comments are addressed to Troy School District, Troy, Michigan, for the Fiscal Year Ended June 30, 2024. The document states that it is the consensus of the review team to award the Certificate of Excellence, that the District is to be commended for its efforts, and that the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report is of high quality. Under the FINANCIAL SECTION heading, one comment is listed at reference page 7, item 1: include analysis of significant balances and transactions of the individual major funds (capital projects), with a citation to eGAAFR chapter 31, page 606.

GASB UPDATES. Provided as a courtesy, the review comments list the Governmental Accounting Standards Board statements the district should consider, as applicable, in preparing future Annual Comprehensive Financial Reports. GASB Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences, issued June 2022, updates the recognition and measurement guidance for compensated absences by aligning that guidance under a unified model and amending certain previously required disclosures; its requirements are effective for periods beginning after December 15, 2023. GASB Statement No. 102, Certain Risk Disclosures, issued December 2023, establishes financial reporting requirements for risks related to vulnerabilities due to certain concentrations or constraints; effective for periods beginning after June 15, 2024. GASB Statement No. 103, Financial Reporting Model Improvements, issued April 2024, improves key components of the financial reporting model to enhance its effectiveness in providing information essential for decision-making and assessing a government's accountability, and addresses certain application issues; effective for periods beginning after June 15, 2025. The page invites attendees to journey beyond the horizon at this year's conference in the Traverse City area, describing ALC as a must-attend event for both new and experienced board members, educators and administrators from across Michigan that brings together the brightest minds in education leadership to collectively shape the future of Michigan's schools. Attendees are told they can choose their own adventure through innovative keynotes, interactive sessions, unique networking activities and transformative learning experiences, with conference tracks designed to build lasting connections and offerings for those seeking certification opportunities, governance insights, or innovative approaches to student achievement. Navigation links include REGISTER NOW, VIEW SCHEDULE and REGISTRATION CHECKLIST, plus a CONTACT US prompt and section anchors for General Sessions, Conference Registration Rates, Schedule At-a-Glance, Add-on Registration Options, Resort Accommodations, General Information, Event Policies, Exhibit Show and For Exhibitors.

**Document**
Draft "Pupil Enrollment Projection Study Report 2023-2027" presented to Troy School District by Plante Moran Cresa, LLC, Southfield, Michigan, February 2023; 118 pages, each marked DRAFT. Contact: Paul R. Wills, AIA, LEED AP, Partner, (248) 223-3316, pmcresa.com. Copyright 2023, Plante Moran Cresa, LLC.

**Method**
Standard Cohort Survival Method using grade-to-grade survival ratios (the report's example: 100 first graders followed by 112 second graders is a 112% ratio). Historical FTE comes from Michigan Department of Education Form DS-4061 or district head counts, sourced to the Office of Pupil Accounting; Oakland County live births drive the kindergarten line (K% Birth). Method 1 averages the 6-year survival ratio, Method 2 the most recent 2-year ratio, Method 3 the two combined. District-wide runs use 2022 Fall FTE and 2022 Blended FTE; building runs use the 2022 Fall head count. Self-contained special education, alternative education and part-time pupils are excluded.

**Oakland County comparison.** County population is 1,202,362, 1,253,598 and 1,253,035 (-563); households 483,698, 511,478 and 513,180; median household income $69,166, $92,150 and $99,296. **Live births.** Oakland County resident live births come from the Michigan Resident Birth Files, Division for Vital Records & Health Statistics, Michigan Department of Health & Human Services, charted with a three-period moving average beginning at 17,008; 2022 live births are noted as estimates based on the previous years' trend. The birth row used across the projection worksheets, birth years 2011 through 2022, is 13,346, 13,307, 13,445, 13,454, 13,547, 13,627, 13,184, 13,152, 12,899, 12,298, 12,876 and 12,976. The Fall FTE K% Birth series is 6.55%, 6.46%, 6.23%, 6.13%, 5.32%, 5.20%, 5.95%, 5.90%, 5.82%, 5.75%, 5.70% and 5.79%; the Blended FTE series is 6.52%, 6.49%, 6.25%, 6.14%, 5.39%, 5.21%, 5.89%, 5.92%, 5.83%, 5.76%, 5.72% and 5.80%. The anticipated non-historical factor is 0.0099%, and projected K% Birth is the average of the previous six years excluding minimum and maximum.

**Methodology.** Plante Moran Cresa applies the standard Cohort Survival Method, comparing pupils in a grade last year with the next advanced grade this year; the illustration given is 100 first graders followed by 112 second graders, a 112% survival ratio. Historical enrollment comes from Michigan Department of Education Form DS-4061 for FTE or from district head counts, sourced to the Office of Pupil Accounting, Troy School District. Live births come from the Michigan Department of Public Health's Office of the State Registrar and Center for Health Statistics, with the current year estimated because county compilation is not complete until at least the fourth quarter of the following year. Special education pupils count as general education to the extent of time in general education classrooms. The process is a two-pass sequence: input pupil counts by grade for the past seven years, run a first-pass projection, establish a baseline, compare to trend and adjust, run a second pass incorporating district demographic trend, then review, verify and confirm. Projections do not account for the opening or closing of a private or chartered school, consolidation, annexation or re-zoning. Method 1 averages the 6-year survival ratio, Method 2 the most recent 2-year survival ratio, and Method 3 averages the two.

**Meeting**
Troy Board of Education regular meeting, Tuesday, May 19, 2026, at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. Called to order by President Anne at 7:00 p.m.; adjourned at 8:27 p.m. Filed under the June 16, 2026 packet.

**Attendance**
Board members Anne, Alic, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts and Zendler. Also present: Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Keegan, Cottone, Wallace, Cronin, Griffin, Hall, Montante, Pagel and Trudel, plus approximately 125 members of the audience.

**Recognitions**
- Outstanding Support Person of the Year: Matt Snitgen, a paraprofessional in the MOCI Room at Athens High School, nominated by Rebecca Roy from a field of 25 nominees.
- Legislative Career Accelerator Program: teachers Brynn Lawrence (Troy Center for Transition) and Mark Chrzanowski (International Academy East) introduced Ava Pittman and Nathan Kohnert; participating students were Ayush Jaganath, Aarshia Soni, Harini Shrii Vengata Raghavan (Troy High), Tasnia Jannah, Sulayma Setiaarif (Athens), Amal Surti and Syeda Tarannum (IAE).
- Schools of Character: Hamilton Elementary and Troy Union Elementary named National Schools of Character by Character.org, two of just 72 schools nationwide; Schroeder Elementary, Troy Union and Boulan Park Middle School named State Schools of Character; Wattles and Barnard Elementary received Honorable Mention; Troy Union and Wattles were the only Michigan schools recognized for Promising Practices.
- Volunteers: Athens - Kristin Kennaugh, Heather and Kevin Blum, Samantha Zoll; IAE - Harj Deol, Minal Kulkarni, Surya Saladi; Troy High - Cheri Armstrong, Sherry Gillespie.

**Actions and votes**

| Item | Moved / supported | Vote |
| --- | --- | --- |
| National Teacher Appreciation Week, May 4-8, 2026 | Zendler / Potts | Yes 7, No 0 |
| Mental Health Awareness Month, May 2026 | Potts / Philippart | Yes 7, No 0 |
| Consent agenda items A through L | Haupt / Alic | Yes 7, No 0 |
| Boulan Park renovation bid, $297,803.00 | Philippart / Zendler | Yes 7, No 0 |
| Food Service and Operations vehicles, $205,610.00 | Alic / Haupt | Yes 7, No 0 |
| Oakland Schools biennial election resolution | Philippart / Haupt | Yes 7, No 0 |

The mental health resolution cited Oakland Community Health Network, stated that one in five Americans experience mental health issues, and referenced National Children's Mental Health Awareness Day on May 7, 2026 and Children's Mental Health Acceptance Week, May 3 through May 9, 2026.

**Consent agenda (A through L)**
Minutes of the April 7, 2026 special meeting and workshop, the April 14, 2026 special meeting, the April 21, 2026 regular meeting, and the April 28, 2026 special meeting, closed session and workshop; the Treasurer's Report for March 2026; approval of the Oakland Intermediate School District budget; a resolution to hold a public hearing on the proposed 2026/2027 school year budget; IA budget approval for 2026/2027; and a K-8 literacy pilot purchase. Personnel and Curriculum had no items.

**Business**
The bid for a complete renovation of Boulan Park Middle School covering architectural, mechanical, electrical and structural work (recommendation 3 of 3) was awarded at $297,803.00 as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund. The bid for a Food Services vehicle and an Operations vehicle was awarded to Gorno Ford at $205,610.00, charged to the Food Services Fund and the Maintenance Improvement Fund.

**Oakland Schools biennial election**
Under Mich. Comp. Laws 380.614, the board designated Kendra Montante as its representative, with a member of the district administration team as alternate, to the 2026 electoral body electing the Oakland Schools Intermediate School District Board of Education; supported candidate Gary Hauff for the one position, a six-year term ending June 30, 2032; and directed Montante to vote for Hauff at least on the first ballot at the June 1, 2026 election.

Student representatives Chloe Gentilini (Troy College and Career High School), Ahyoung Song (International Academy-East), Sara Graunstadt (Athens High School) and Bella Doss (Troy High School) reported. **Identification**
Regular meeting minutes of the Troy Board of Education, Tuesday, May 19, 2026, held at the Troy School District Services Building (Service Center), 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The record is filed as M051926BdMtg within the June 16, 2026 board packet. President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. and it was adjourned at 8:27 p.m. Minutes were respectfully submitted by Matt Haupt, Secretary of the Troy Board of Education, with typist initials MH/jh.

**Attendance**
In addition to Mrs. Anne, board members Alic, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts and Zendler were present. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Keegan, Cottone, Wallace, Cronin, Griffin, Hall, Montante, Pagel and Trudel. Approximately 125 members of the audience attended. The meeting opened with the Pledge of Allegiance.

**Recognition: Outstanding Support Staff**
The board presented the Outstanding Support Person of the Year award, a category covering bus drivers, secretaries, paraprofessionals, student support aides, custodial staff, food service, technology, childcare, security and more. There were 25 nominees. The 2026 honoree is Matt Snitgen, a paraprofessional at Athens High School in the MOCI Room, nominated by Rebecca Roy. The nomination praised his unwavering belief in his students, noting that he sees potential where others often see limitations, and cited his positivity, compassion and work ethic. It described how he models and encourages communication in all forms, including body language, gestures, facial expressions and AAC devices, treating every communicative attempt as meaningful. A student was quoted saying, "We have a secret handshake. Mr. S is a great person because he's nice and he makes me feel happy and excited to be at school." Snitgen's name was engraved on the Support Person Plaque, to be displayed at his building for the next year, and a short video of the surprise visit was shown.

**Legislative CAP Students Report**
Students from the Legislative track of the Career Accelerator Program (CAP) reported on their engagement with the school board, the city, and state senators and representatives. Troy Center for Transition teacher Brynn Lawrence and International Academy East teacher Mark Chrzanowski were invited to the podium to introduce their students. Ava Pittman of IA-East and Nathan Kohnert of TCT described their experience and shared a brief video. CAP students who shared their experiences were Ayush Jaganath (Troy High), Tasnia Jannah (Athens), Sulayma Setiaarif (Athens), Aarshia Soni (Troy High), Amal Surti (IAE), Syeda Tarannum (IAE) and Harini Shrii Vengata Raghavan (Troy High).

**Schools of Character Recognition**
Hamilton Elementary School and Troy Union Elementary School were honored as National Schools of Character, two of just 72 schools nationwide to receive the distinction from Character.org. The designation recognizes schools that use character development to positively impact academics, student behavior and school culture. Schroeder Elementary School, Troy Union Elementary School and Boulan Park Middle School were named State Schools of Character, and Wattles Elementary School and Barnard Elementary School received Honorable Mention. Character.org also recognized Troy Union and Wattles as the only schools in Michigan to earn recognition for Promising Practices, highlighting innovative efforts that strengthen school culture, encourage student leadership and service, and promote goodness in action.

**Volunteer Appreciation**
April is Volunteer Appreciation Month, and the board thanked volunteers whose students graduate from TSD this year. Parents recognized and given a token of appreciation were: Athens - Kristin Kennaugh, Heather and Kevin Blum, and Samantha Zoll; IAE - Harj Deol, Minal Kulkarni, and Surya Saladi; Troy High - Cheri Armstrong and Sherry Gillespie.

**National Teacher Appreciation Week resolution**
Teacher Appreciation Week was celebrated Monday, May 4 through Friday, May 8, 2026. Moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Potts, the resolution recited that teachers inspire and open children's minds, promote and strengthen the principles of democratic equality, develop leaders and encourage critical thinking, and that Troy teachers set the bar for excellence. It resolved that the Troy School District supports National Teacher Appreciation Week, May 4-8, 2026. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Mental Health Awareness Month resolution**
Introduced with reference to Oakland Community Health Network and its service provider network and to other school boards across Oakland County. Moved by Mrs. Potts and supported by Dr. Philippart, the resolution recited that one in five of all Americans, including children, experience mental health issues that could lead to school difficulties, physical problems and even suicide; that May 7, 2026 is designated National Children's Mental Health Awareness Day; and that May 3 through May 9, 2026 is designated Children's Mental Health Acceptance Week. It resolved that the Troy Board of Education recognizes May 2026 as Mental Health Awareness Month. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Procedural**
A five-minute recess followed the recognitions. There were no additions or deletions to the agenda and no public communication on agenda items.

**Consent agenda**
Moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Alic, the board approved items A through L: minutes of the April 7, 2026 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the April 7, 2026 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the April 14, 2026 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the April 21, 2026 Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the April 28, 2026 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the April 28, 2026 Closed Session Meeting; minutes of the April 28, 2026 Board of Education Workshop; the Treasurer's Report for March 2026; Approve Oakland Intermediate School District Budget; a Resolution to Hold a Public Hearing on the Proposed 2026/2027 School Year Budget; IA Budget Approval for the 2026/2027 School Year; and the K-8 Literacy Pilot Purchase. Vote: Yes 7, No 0. The Personnel and Curriculum sections contained no items.

**Business: Boulan Park Renovation Project (Recommendation 3 of 3)**
Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Zendler, the board resolved that the bid for a complete renovation of Boulan Park Middle School, including architectural, mechanical, electrical and structural work, be awarded as attached in the amount of $297,803.00, and that the amount be approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Business: Purchase of Replacement Vehicles for Food Service and Operations**
Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt, the board resolved that the bid for a Food Services vehicle and an Operations vehicle be awarded to Gorno Ford in the amount of $205,610.00, approved as an expenditure of the Food Services Fund and the Maintenance Improvement Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Public communication (non-agenda items)**
One community member addressed the board. No action was taken by the board.

**Other: Oakland Schools Biennial Election**
Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mr. Haupt. The resolution recited that Mich. Comp. Laws section 380.614 requires a constituent school board to designate its representative and identify the Intermediate School Board candidate it supports by a resolution adopted not earlier than 21 days prior to the election; that the statute prescribes consideration of the resolution at not less than one public meeting before adoption; and that the board previously considered the resolution at an open meeting conducted under the Open Meetings Act on May 19, 2026. The board designated Kendra Montante as its representative and a member of the Troy School District administration team as its alternate representative to serve on the 2026 electoral body responsible for electing members to the Oakland Schools Intermediate School District Board of Education. The board supported candidate Gary Hauff for the one position on that board for a term of six years ending June 30, 2032, and directed representative Kendra Montante to vote for Gary Hauff at least on the first ballot taken at the June 1, 2026 election. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Reports from high school student representatives**
Chloe Gentilini reported for Troy College and Career High School; Ahyoung Song for International Academy-East; Sara Graunstadt for Athens High School; and Bella Doss for Troy High School, each on events and activities at their schools.

**Board comments**
Topics raised included Troy Youth Assistance Recognition; the Troy Community Coalition Incredible Kid; a Troy Interfaith Group event and a Faith and Community Leaders breakfast; the TFEE Golf Outing on June 9; the Larson Celebration of Learning event; Operation Belonging at Athens; retirees recognition June 1 at Troy High; Teacher Appreciation Week; thanks to volunteers; an Oakland County Government Relations Committee legislative update by Mrs. Alic; the Oakland County Enhancement Millage; budget reductions in connection with a $12 million deficit; a salmon release at Riverbends Park; TSD and Robotics partnering to find a site for teams to work; the SSAB Middle School Leadership Conference; Mental Health Awareness and the Red Pillar; congratulations to graduating senior board representatives; Coffee with the Superintendent and Board on May 21 at 5:00 pm; and congratulations to the 2026 graduates.

**Upcoming meetings and adjournment**
The next board workshop was scheduled for Tuesday, June 1 at Troy High, and the next regular meeting for Tuesday, June 16 at the Services Building. The meeting was adjourned at 8:27 p.m.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: The Troy School District 2024-2025 Course Description Book, revised January 2024 under Superintendent Dr. Richard Machesky, catalogs the courses offered at Athens High School and Troy High School together with graduation requirements, curriculum flexibility options, Oakland Schools Technical Campus programs, and the district anti-discrimination grievance procedure. All students must earn a total of 22.5 credits to be eligible for a Troy High School or Troy Athens diploma, including 4.0 credits of English, 4.0 of mathematics, 3.0 of science, and 3.0 of social studies. Beginning with the class of 2028, a 0.5-credit personal finance requirement is embedded in Economics.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Publication**
2024-2025 Course Descriptions for Athens High School and Troy High School, Troy School District. Dr. Richard Machesky, Superintendent of Schools. Revised January 2024.

**Schools and contacts**
- Athens High School: Mr. Vernon Burden, Principal, 4333 John R. Road, Troy, Michigan 48085. Main Office 248.823.2900, Fax 248.823.2913, Counseling 248.823.2962, Attendance 248.823.2901.
- Troy High School: Mr. Remo Roncone, Principal, 4777 Northfield Parkway, Troy, Michigan 48098. Main Office 248.823.2700, Fax 248.823.2713, Counseling 248.823.2715, Attendance 248.823.2701.
- Department of Teaching & Learning, 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098, 248.823.5221. Central Office Special Education: 248.823.5096.

**Nondiscrimination**
The book opens with the district policy of nondiscrimination citing Title IX of the Educational Amendments of 1972, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, and the Americans with Disabilities Act. Jordan M. Harris, J.D., Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, is appointed Title IX and Section 504/ADA Coordinator for employment and personnel matters; the District Director of Special Education serves as Section 504/ADA Coordinator for handicapped and suspected handicapped students. Questions are directed to John Pagel, Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, MI 48098-4799, (248)823-4000.

**Graduation requirements, Classes of 2025, 2026, 2027, 2028**

| Requirement | Credits |
| --- | --- |
| English | 4.0 |
| Science | 3.0 |
| Mathematics | 4.0 |
| Social Studies | 3.0 |
| Personal Finance | 0.5 |
| Physical Education | 1.0 |
| Health | 0.5 |
| World Language, Fine & Applied Arts, CTE | 3.0 |
| State Assessments | 0.0 |
| Online Learning Experience | 0.0 |
| Total credits needed for graduation | 22.5 |

Science differs by cohort: the classes of 2027 and 2028 take Biology 1.0, Chemistry 0.5 and Physics 0.5, Earth Science 0.5, and a Science Elective 0.5; the classes of 2025 and 2026 take Biology 1.0, Chemistry or Physics 1.0, and a Science Elective 1.0. Mathematics comprises Algebra 1, Geometry, Algebra 2 (or Algebra 2 Part A and Part B, or CTE program completion), and a math elective, with a required math experience in the final year. Social studies comprises World History/Geography 1 and 2, American History/Geography 1 and 2, Economics, and Government and Civics. The World Language / Fine & Applied Arts / CTE block requires 2.0 World Language credits, or 1.0 World Language plus 1.0 CTE or 1.0 VPAA. The online learning requirement is a 20-hour non-credit experience embedded in Troy classes.

**Flexibility options**
Updated 9.2015 under MCL 380.1278a and MCL 380.1278b. Options include the Personal Curriculum, a Physical Education elective waiver for students completing two seasons of district athletics or two seasons of marching band, World Language flexibility for heritage or international proficiency, and CTE program completion credits exchanged on a 1:1 basis for science, world language, or the Algebra 2 requirement.

**Departments covered**
Business, Career Technical Education, Industrial Technical, Life Skills, English, English Language Development, Fine Arts, Health, Mathematics, Media, Physical Education, Science, Social Studies, Special Education, and World Language.

**Oakland Schools Technical Campus**
OSTC-SE at 5055 Delemere Street, north of 14 Mile between Crooks and Coolidge, serves juniors and seniors on a selective basis, generally 1.5 credits per semester. Session 1 AM is course 08101 and Session 2 PM is 08102; morning classes begin 7:50 AM and dismiss 10:20 AM, afternoon classes begin 12:00 PM and dismiss 2:30 PM. Where regular students carry six credits, OSTC students carry three credits at their home high school plus three at OSTC. Applications are made online at www.ostconline.com by the end of February. Credits offered at OSTC are not NCAA approved.

**Grievance procedure**
A three-step formal anti-discrimination grievance procedure is filed with the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, beginning with a written grievance submitted within 10 workdays of the incident and ending with a final and binding written answer from the Superintendent.

The 2024-2025 Course Descriptions book for Athens High School and Troy High School, issued by the Troy School District under Dr. Richard Machesky, Superintendent of Schools, and revised in January 2024, is the district catalog of high school course offerings, graduation requirements, curriculum flexibility provisions, career-technical options, and civil rights procedures.

POLICY OF NONDISCRIMINATION. The opening statement cites Title IX of the Educational Amendments of 1972, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, and the Americans with Disabilities Act, and states the district does not discriminate on the basis of sex or handicap. A grievance procedure is available through any school office, and employees in a bargaining unit may alternatively use the collective bargaining agreement procedure. In accordance with federal regulations, the district has appointed Jordan M. Harris, J.D., Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, as Title IX and Section 504/ADA Coordinator for employment and personnel matters; the District Director of Special Education is the Section 504/ADA Coordinator for handicapped and suspected handicapped students. Questions are directed to John Pagel, Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, Title IX and Section 504/ADA Coordinator, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, MI 48098-4799, (248)823-4000.

SCHOOL DIRECTORY. Athens High School is led by Mr. Vernon Burden, Principal, at 4333 John R. Road, Troy, Michigan 48085, with Main Office 248.823.2900, Fax 248.823.2913, Counseling 248.823.2962, and Attendance 248.823.2901. Troy High School is led by Mr. Remo Roncone, Principal, at 4777 Northfield Parkway, Troy, Michigan 48098, with Main Office 248.823.2700, Fax 248.823.2713, Counseling 248.823.2715, and Attendance 248.823.2701. The Department of Teaching & Learning is at 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098, 248.823.5221. Central Office Special Education can be reached at 248.823.5096.

GRADUATION REQUIREMENTS, CLASSES OF 2025, 2026, 2027, AND 2028. English requires 4.0 credits: English 9 (1.0), English 10 (1.0, class of 2028 and after), English 11 Lit/Comp plus an English elective or 11 English AP 1 and 2 (1.0), and English 12 Lit/Comp 1 and 2 or 12 English AP 1 and 2 (1.0). Science requires 3.0 credits, with different pathways by cohort: for the classes of 2027 and 2028, Biology 1.0 credit, Chemistry 0.5 credit and Physics 0.5 credit, Earth Science 0.5 credit, and a Science Elective 0.5 credit; current requirements for the classes of 2025 and 2026 are Biology 1.0, Chemistry or Physics 1.0, and Science Elective 1.0. Mathematics requires 4.0 credits: Algebra 1 (1.0), Geometry (1.0), Algebra 2 or Algebra 2 Part A and Part B (1.0, or met through CTE program completion such as OSTC), and a Math Elective (1.0); students must have a math experience in their final year of high school. Social Studies requires 3.0 credits: World History/Geography 1 and 2 (1.0), American History/Geography 1 and 2 (1.0), Economics (0.5), and Government and Civics (0.5). Personal Finance is 0.5 credit embedded into Economics and becomes a graduation requirement beginning with the class of 2028, contingent on taking a TSD Economics or AP Economics course. Physical Education requires 1.0 credit: Intro to Physical Activity (0.5) and a P.E. Elective (0.5). Health requires 0.5 credit, and the same block lists 1.0 credit VPAA, which includes Industrial Technology, Business, and Life Skills classes. State Assessments carry 0.0 credit but require completion of Michigan-required assessments administered during high school. The combined World Language, Fine & Applied Arts, and CTE requirement is 3.0 credits, satisfied by 2.0 credits of World Language (non-sequential accepted) or 1.0 credit of World Language plus either 1.0 credit CTE or 1.0 credit VPAA. The Online Learning Experience is 0.0 credit but requires a 20-hour online learning experience embedded across middle and high school. Credit-bearing high school courses taken before high school matriculation appear on the Troy School District high school transcript with grades earned. Total credits needed for graduation are 22.5 for either a Troy High School or Troy Athens diploma. Courses may be retaken prior to or concurrent with the next course in sequence, with the retaken grade replacing the initial grade unless prior administrative approval is granted.

GRADUATION REQUIREMENT FLEXIBILITY OPTIONS, updated 9.2015 and citing MCL 380.1278a and MCL 380.1278b. The Personal Curriculum allows additional credits in some core academic areas in lieu of other requirements when aligned to the student Educational Development Plan (EDP). The Physical Education Elective option excuses students participating in two seasons of Troy School District athletics or two seasons of marching band from the 0.5-credit P.E. elective, tracked automatically with no forms required. The 2.0-credit World Language Requirement has flexibility for non-English heritage language proficiency, international study and residence proficiency, and substitution of CTE or Visual & Performing or Applied Arts credits, documented through a Personal Curriculum. CTE Program Completion permits a 1:1 credit exchange toward science, world language, or the Algebra 2 requirement. A course key explains that descriptions begin with the course number and title, note the school if not offered at both, and give grade levels, length, credit, retake rules, and prerequisites; no course may be retaken for additional credit unless specifically indicated, except Independent Study.

OAKLAND SCHOOLS TECHNICAL CAMPUS. OSTC-SE, an extension of the home high school, is located at 5055 Delemere Street, north of 14 Mile between Crooks and Coolidge, with a Southeast Campus in Royal Oak, MI and a Northeast Campus in Pontiac, MI. Programs are offered to grades 11-12 on a selective basis, with OSTC recommending high school credit based on the local district requirement, generally 1.5 credits per semester. Session codes are 08101 Session 1 AM and 08102 Session 2 PM; morning session classes begin at 7:50 AM and are dismissed at 10:20 AM, and afternoon session classes begin at 12:00 PM and are dismissed at 2:30 PM. Where regular students carry six credits, OSTC students must carry three credits at their home high school in addition to three credits at OSTC. Programs listed include Automotive Technology (must begin in 11th grade), Collision Repair and Refinishing, Computer Programming, Computer Networking, Construction Technology, Culinary Arts/Hospitality, Electrical and Energy Technologies, Entrepreneurship & Advanced Marketing, Health Sciences, Machining, Mechatronics, Visual Imaging Technology, Welding, Homeland Security (Criminal Justice or Cyber Security), and Cosmetology (must begin in 11th grade). Buses transport students to OSTC-SE and back; afternoon-session students must provide their own transportation home. Sophomores and juniors may apply for the following year, with an exploration tour in the fall and online application at www.ostconline.com by the end of February. A note warns athletes that credits offered at OSTC are not NCAA approved.

ANTI-DISCRIMINATION GRIEVANCE PROCEDURE. Any student or employee who believes he or she has been discriminated against, denied a benefit, or excluded from participation on the basis of sex (including sexual harassment), race, color, religion, national origin, age (employees only), height, weight, marital status, or handicap files a written grievance with the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, the designated compliance administrator; forms are available in the Employee Services Department. Step 1: the written grievance form goes to the immediate supervisor or administrator within 10 workdays of the incident; not later than the next workday a copy goes to the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services; within 5 workdays of the filing date the supervisor meets the grievant; within 3 workdays of the meeting a written answer is given. Step 2: appeal within 3 workdays of receipt of the answer to the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, a meeting within 10 workdays of receipt of the appeal, and a written answer within 5 workdays of that meeting. Step 3: appeal within 3 workdays to the Superintendent, a meeting within 10 workdays of receipt of the appeal, and a written answer within 5 workdays of the meeting, final and binding on all parties. A grievance not filed or appealed within the time limits is deemed abandoned; failure to hold a meeting or render a decision allows automatic appeal to the next level; time limits may be extended only by mutual written agreement; records are confidential and none is kept in a staff member personnel file if the final decision is that there was no reasonable basis for the grievance.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A Troy School District administration update to the Board of Education on middle school mathematics, presenting March 2026 survey feedback on the Illustrative Mathematics curriculum and the middle school course progression adopted in May 2023. Survey participation totaled 2,059 students (72 percent of the population), 398 parents and guardians (14 percent), and 21 staff (81 percent). The staff results were markedly critical: 11 of 21 math teachers (52.4 percent) called for revisiting or revising the math progression model, and the most-cited curriculum theme was insufficient materials and practice problems, named by 12 respondents (57.1 percent). Administration said it would bring a recommendation to the Board at the April 28 workshop.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Purpose**
Middle school math update presenting survey feedback gathered in March 2026 on instructional practices in math classrooms, implementation of Illustrative Mathematics (IM), student learning, and middle school course progression. Presented to the Troy Board of Education for the April 7, 2026 meeting.

**Historical context**
The prior curriculum, Big Ideas, was described as outdated and not aligned to the district's vision for math. The Board of Education adopted the new curriculum and new progression in May 2023. Administration committed to annual review of student achievement data (M-STEP/PSAT), annual review of course enrollment data (Honors Algebra 1), annual collection of staff, student and family feedback, implementation of NWEA, ongoing teacher support, and continued building of MTSS structures. Board commitments were to review annual data sets and understand the implementation timeline, described as a 3-5 year implementation, with a note that adoption does not require a 7 year cycle if other concerns arise.

**Achievement data reviewed**
M-STEP results have been reviewed annually for grades 6 and 7: grade 6 in 2024 (first year of implementation data), grade 6 in 2025 (second year), and grade 7 in 2025 (first year). For the 8th grade PSAT in 2026 no achievement data is available yet; that cohort is the first with full implementation of the new program. The n values printed with the achievement charts are (567), (607), (643), (576), (642) and (677).

**Honors enrollment**
Under '8th Grade Enrollment Trends in Honors Math Courses (Algebra 1 and Above)', the presentation states the middle school math sequence change led to an increase in student enrollment in honors and that the district will continue to monitor. Total students shown across the periods charted: (907), (961), (995), (1023).

**Survey participation**

| Survey group | Participation count | Percentage of total population participating |
|---|---|---|
| Student Survey | 2,059 | 72% |
| Parent/Guardian Survey | 398 | 14% |
| Staff Survey | 21 | 81% |

**Staff survey results (n=21)**

| Response | Count | Percent |
|---|---|---|
| Most students understand the goals of the lessons because the work is at the right level | 7 | 33.3% |
| Most students feel lost even after asking questions or reviewing material | 7 | 33.3% |
| Most students are underchallenged and would like more advanced work | 1 | 4.8% |
| Understand goals + underchallenged | 2 | 9.5% |
| Underchallenged + feel lost | 2 | 9.5% |
| All three responses | 2 | 9.5% |

**Themes needing attention**
Within the progression model: too much content in Honors Algebra 1 combined with Math 8 (7, 33.3%); difficulty with differentiation covering pacing, learning gaps and student supports (5, 23.8%); underchallenged students (5, 23.8%); fear of lower outcomes for Algebra 1 students (4, 19.0%). Within the IM curriculum: insufficient materials/practice problems (12, 57.1%); not enough scaffolding or differentiation (8, 38.1%); pacing too fast (7, 33.3%); concerns about Algebra 1 content combined with Math 8 (7, 33.3%); too much focus on story problems (4, 19.0%); negative CoTeach AI experience (4, 19.0%).

**Teacher view of the progression**
Revisit/revise the model 11 (52.4%); no opinion stated 8 (38.1%); favorable view 1 (4.8%); mixed view 1 (4.8%).

**Next steps**
Free response data from parents and students will be coded and analyzed. Administration will prepare a recommendation for the Board at the 4/28 workshop, anticipated to cover supplemental resources, convening a curriculum review team including middle school math teachers, and exploring accelerated pathways, with formal board consideration in winter/spring 2027 for implementation in fall of 2027.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Identification.** 'MS Math Update Survey Feedback March 2026', a Troy School District administration presentation to the Board of Education carried in the April 7, 2026 packet (file titled MS Math Update BOE 4.6.26).

**Historical context.** The presentation opens by noting outdated math materials and that the former curriculum, Big Ideas, did not align to the district's vision for math. The Board of Education adopted the new curriculum and the new progression in May 2023.

**Commitments made at adoption.** TSD Administration committed to: annual review of student achievement data (MSTEP/PSAT); annual review of student course enrollment data (Honors Alg 1); annual collection of feedback from staff, students and families; implementation of NWEA; investment in ongoing teacher support; and continuing to build MTSS structures to support student growth. The TSD Board of Education committed to review annual data sets, to understand the implementation timeline of the new curriculum, described as a 3-5 year implementation timeline, and noted that adoption does not require a 7 year cycle if other concerns arise.

**Curriculum adoption and implementation cycle.** A four-part cycle is depicted: Explore, Research and Vision, Implementation, and Curriculum Review Cycle. Under Research and Vision the district researches best instructional practices, reviews state standards, ensures alignment with the TSD strategic plan, and examines district data trends to identify needs; it compiles and proposes a list of potential resources for early-adopter and pilot teams; assembles a content area curriculum review team of teachers and administrators as suggested by math leadership teams; and creates partnerships with experts, learning organizations and local school districts. Under Explore the district narrows potential resources with curriculum review teams, explores multiple resources with students through a pilot and/or early-adopter experience, gathers qualitative and quantitative student and teacher data on engagement, student performance, joy and usability, and supports pilot and early-adopter classrooms through professional learning, district-wide collaboration, classroom visits, out-of-district site visits, coaching, and learning beyond the school day. Under Implementation the district implements the new curriculum as recommended by the curriculum review and math leadership teams and seeks School Board approval, supports implementation through professional learning, job-embedded coaching, classroom visits and district-wide collaboration, continues professional learning with in-district, local and national partnerships, and reviews qualitative and quantitative data and adjusts.

**Academic achievement data.** The district has annually reviewed M-STEP data for 6th and 7th grade. The data points listed are: MSTEP 6th grade 2024 (first year of implementation data); MSTEP 6th grade 2025 (second year of 6th grade implementation data); MSTEP 7th grade 2025 (first year of implementation data); and PSAT 8th grade 2026, for which no academic achievement data is available yet, that 8th grade being the first cohort to have full implementation of the new program. The n values printed beneath the achievement charts are (567), (607), (643), (576), (642) and (677).

**8th grade honors enrollment.** A section titled '8th Grade Enrollment Trends in Honors Math Courses (Algebra 1 and Above)' summarizes that the middle school math sequence change led to an increase in student enrollment in honors and that the district will continue to monitor middle school honors math enrollments. The total students figures shown across the four charted periods are (907), (961), (995) and (1023).

**Survey purpose and participation.** The district administered a survey to middle school students, parents/guardians, and math teachers to gather feedback on instructional practices within math classrooms, curriculum implementation of Illustrative Mathematics, student learning, and course progression for middle school math. Participation was: Student Survey 2,059 participants, 72 percent of the total population; Parent/Guardian Survey 398 participants, 14 percent; Staff Survey 21 participants, 81 percent.

**Student and parent response options.** The full text of the survey response choices reported for the student math experience question were: 'I usually understand the goals of the lesson because the work is at the right level for me'; 'I feel underchallenged by lessons and I would like more opportunities for advanced work'; and 'I feel lost even after asking questions or reviewing material'.

**Staff survey responses (n=21).** Seven respondents (33.3 percent) said most students understand the goals of the lessons because the work is at the right level for them. Seven respondents (33.3 percent) said most students feel lost even after asking questions or reviewing material. One respondent (4.8 percent) said most students are underchallenged by lessons and would like more opportunities for advanced work. Two respondents (9.5 percent) selected both the 'understand the goals' and 'underchallenged' statements. Two respondents (9.5 percent) selected both 'underchallenged' and 'feel lost'. Two respondents (9.5 percent) selected all three statements.

**Identified areas of improvement, math progression model.** Main themes needing to be addressed within the current math progression model: too much content in Honors Algebra 1 combined with Math 8, 7 responses, 33.3 percent; difficulty with differentiation covering pacing, learning gaps and student supports, 5 responses, 23.8 percent; underchallenged students, 5 responses, 23.8 percent; fear of lower outcomes for Algebra 1 students, 4 responses, 19.0 percent.

**Identified areas of improvement, IM curriculum.** Main themes needing to be addressed within the current IM curriculum: insufficient materials, specifically practice problems, 12 responses, 57.1 percent; not enough scaffolding/differentiation within the curriculum, 8 responses, 38.1 percent; curriculum pacing too fast, 7 responses, 33.3 percent; concerns about Algebra 1 content combined with Math 8, described as lower rigor and too much content, 7 responses, 33.3 percent; too much focus on story problems, 4 responses, 19.0 percent; negative CoTeach AI experience, 4 responses, 19.0 percent.

**Math teacher perspective on the current math progression.** Revisit/revise the math progression model, 11 responses, 52.4 percent; no opinion stated, 8 responses, 38.1 percent; favorable view of the math progression model, 1 response, 4.8 percent; mixed view of the math progression model, 1 response, 4.8 percent.

**Pending analysis.** The presentation states that in the coming weeks free response survey data from both parents and students will be coded and analyzed to inform next step decision making.

**AI summary.** A slide labeled 'AI Summary (CoPilot)' reproduces the prompt used: attached are survey results from math teachers on current math curriculum and math course progression, provide a summary of the survey responses. The executive summary produced states that the survey reveals significant concerns among math teachers about both the IM curriculum and the current course progression model, particularly around pacing, differentiation, foundational skill gaps, and Algebra 1 in 8th grade; that while some teachers value the instructional philosophy and student discourse supported by IM, the prevailing tone is negative to mixed, with widespread calls for more balance, clearer pathways, and stronger supports. Overall takeaways listed: IM philosophy has merit but materials are insufficient on their own; foundational skills and fluency require far more emphasis; differentiation is difficult without structural changes to courses or curriculum; Algebra 1 in 8th grade is a critical pain point affecting students, teachers, and outcomes; and teachers want clear learning targets, flexible pacing, and defined pathways rather than scripted constraints.

**Next steps.** Administration asked for additional time to review feedback, collaborate with the team, and prepare a recommendation to the Board at the 4/28 workshop. Anticipated topics in the recommendation, based on teacher survey feedback, are: adoption of supplemental resources to support student learning in response to staff, student, and family feedback; convening a curriculum review team inclusive of middle school math teachers; and exploring accelerated pathways for middle school students and accompanying curriculum. The process would include board consideration and adoption of a formal recommendation in winter/spring 2027 for implementation in fall of 2027.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A 21-slide Troy School District secondary mathematics presentation on the Geometry and Honors Geometry program review and curricular adoption, brought to the Board of Education as item 3D. It reports on two years of piloting, in which OpenUp Mathematics was piloted for Quarter 1 of 2024-25 and discontinued on teacher feedback while Illustrative Mathematics was piloted for Quarters 2, 3 and 4 and then across all of 2025-26, with 100 percent of Geometry teachers and 88 percent of Honors Geometry teachers participating. The recommendation is adoption of Illustrative Math Geometry with additional fluency practice through DeltaMath and printed student workbooks.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Item and scope**
Secondary Math, Geometry and Honors Geometry: Program Review and Curricular Adoption, a PowerPoint presented to the Troy Board of Education for April 7, 2026 as item 3D.

**Framing**
The deck reviews the eight Standards for Mathematical Practice (make sense of problems and persevere; reason abstractly and quantitatively; construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; model with mathematics; use appropriate tools strategically; attend to precision; look for and make use of structure; look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning) and the 8 Effective Math Teaching Practices, citing NCTM (2014), Principals to Actions: Ensuring mathematical success for all. The district vision, citing NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics, holds that all students are doers of mathematics and that the program should cultivate positive mathematical identities so students develop deep mathematical understandings, understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience the wonder, joy, and beauty of mathematics.

**Current status**
The current resource has been in use for over 15 years, creating alignment challenges between teachers and across buildings. Current resources present topics taught in sequence rather than a storyline that builds conceptual understanding over time, and do not explicitly provide tools or strategies to make learning accessible for all students. High school math curriculum options are described as more limited, with everything requiring adjustment and supplementation.

**Pilot process**

| Year | Materials piloted | Teacher participation | Structure |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2024-25 | OpenUp Mathematics and Illustrative Math | 70% of Geometry teachers | OpenUp in Quarter 1, discontinued on teacher feedback about time constraints, lack of teacher guidance and explicit practice; IM in Quarters 2, 3 and 4 |
| 2025-26 | Illustrative Math | 88% of Honors Geometry teachers; 100% of Geometry teachers | IM piloted for the school year |

Both years included monthly cohort meetings with job-embedded professional learning. The Geometry cohort partnered with the Michigan Math and Science Leaders Network (MMSLN), which provided professional learning on teaching IM, supported prioritizing Geometry standards to open room for curriculum aligned to postsecondary pathways in Statistics, Quantitative Reasoning or Data Science and the TSD portrait of a learner, is developing a Data Science module based on Troy teachers' input, and facilitated the monthly cohort meetings.

**Course distinction**
Geometry covers conceptual understanding of proof and conceptual understanding and application of geometry. Honors Geometry adds conceptual understanding and application of proof, algebraic application of geometry, additional and more advanced trigonometry concepts, extensions through projects and additional algebra work, and a faster pace.

**Teacher perception data (15 of 16 geometry teachers)**
Celebrations: 10 out of 15 feel confident using IM and 3 out of 15 somewhat confident; 13 out of 15 feel confident navigating IM resources; 13 out of 15 feel IM moves the district toward a problem-based, student-centered curriculum. Challenges: 13 out of 15 feel they lack adequate sample communications and tools for parents; 12 out of 15 feel tools for struggling learners are insufficient; 10 out of 15 feel extension tools are insufficient.

**Recommendation and supports**
Adopt Illustrative Math Geometry with additional fluency practice and printed student workbooks. Supports include the 2026 Math Summer Institute (3 days prior to back-to-school professional learning), back-to-school PL days, a full day of district professional learning, Math Specialist coaching and intervention, quarterly collaboration meetings for Geometry and monthly for Honors Geometry, DeltaMath subscriptions, and IM Family Support Materials and lesson summaries posted on Schoology.

**Monitoring**
Goals are growth in the number of students scoring advanced or proficient on PSAT and SAT exams and improvement in achievement, problem solving and communication of mathematical thinking measured by internal common assessments; measures reported annually include PSAT/SAT with cohort data and NWEA, with unit and common assessments and student grades in higher levels of mathematics studied with staff.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Identification.** '3D 2026 Geometry BOE Presentation', a 21-slide PowerPoint titled Secondary Math, Geometry and Honors Geometry: Program Review and Curricular Adoption, presented to the Troy School District Board of Education for the April 7, 2026 meeting.

**Guiding learning and standards.** The deck states the district has engaged in extensive learning as it continues its secondary math review and adoption process. It lists the Standards for Mathematical Practice: make sense of problems and persevere in solving them; reason abstractly and quantitatively; construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; model with mathematics; use appropriate tools strategically; attend to precision; look for and make use of structure; and look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning. It then presents the 8 Effective Math Teaching Practices, stating that to ensure mathematical success for all students mathematics education will involve these practices and that they allow teachers to implement the Michigan K-12 Math Standards, citing NCTM (2014), Principals to Actions: Ensuring mathematical success for all.

**Vision.** The Troy School District Mathematics Department believes all students are doers of mathematics and that the purpose of the mathematics program is to cultivate students' positive mathematical identities so that all students develop deep mathematical understandings, understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience the wonder, joy, and beauty of mathematics. The citation given is NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics.

**Current status.** The district has used its current resource for over 15 years and has made the curriculum its own, which presents challenges such as alignment between teachers and across buildings. Current resources are topics taught in sequence rather than a storyline that intentionally builds conceptual understanding over time, and do not explicitly provide tools or strategies to support teachers in making learning accessible for all students. The district has collaborated with districts across the county and with national experts, and reports that options for high school math curricula are more limited and that everything requires some adjustments and supplementation.

**Pilot process, 2024-25.** Based on the team's review matrix, the team piloted OpenUp Mathematics and Illustrative Math. Seventy percent of Geometry teachers participated in the pilot. OpenUp was piloted for Quarter 1 and discontinued due to teacher feedback regarding time constraints, lack of teacher guidance, and explicit practice. Illustrative Math was piloted for Quarters 2, 3 and 4 because the team wanted to see the entire story of the year unfold. Professional learning and support consisted of monthly cohort meetings with job-embedded professional learning.

**Pilot process, 2025-26.** The team piloted Illustrative Math. Eighty-eight percent of Honors Geometry teachers participated in the IM pilot and 100 percent of Geometry teachers participated. IM was piloted for the school year. Support again consisted of monthly cohort meetings with job-embedded professional learning, and the Geometry cohort partnered with the Michigan Math and Science Leaders Network.

**MMSLN partnership.** The Michigan Math and Science Leadership Network provided professional learning around teaching the Illustrative Math curriculum; supported the team in prioritizing Geometry standards to create the opportunity for additional curriculum aligned to postsecondary pathways of Statistics, Quantitative Reasoning, or Data Science and to the TSD portrait of a learner; is developing a Data Science module based on Troy teachers' input and direction; and supported facilitation of the monthly meetings with the Geometry cohort.

**IM philosophy and sample items.** Slides assert that IM aligns with the district vision and describe the IM philosophy as problem-based, student-centered teaching and learning. Separate slides display a sample SAT problem and a sample AP exam question.

**Geometry versus Honors Geometry.** Geometry is characterized by conceptual understanding of proof and conceptual understanding and application of geometry. Honors Geometry is characterized by conceptual understanding and application of proof, conceptual understanding and algebraic application of geometry, additional and more advanced trigonometry concepts, extensions in the form of projects and additional work with algebra, and a faster pace.

**Teacher perception data, celebrations (15 of 16 geometry teachers responding).** Ten out of 15 feel confident using IM and 3 out of 15 feel somewhat confident. Thirteen out of 15 feel confident navigating the IM resources. Thirteen out of 15 feel IM moves the district toward its goal of implementing a problem-based, student-centered math curriculum. Two teacher quotations are included: one stating that what the teacher enjoys about the current curriculum is that it encourages students to think about the 'why' behind the math instead of just memorizing steps, with appreciation for the focus on student discussion and multiple ways of approaching problems; and one stating enjoyment that there is a storyline, that students build on previous ideas and use that knowledge to problem solve, and that the curriculum teaches through applications with students often asked to explain their thinking rather than just get to an answer.

**Teacher perception data, challenges.** Thirteen out of 15 feel they do not have adequate sample communications or tools to provide parents with resources for at-home support; the plan is a printed workbook, extra practice with DeltaMath, and IM Lesson Summaries and Family Resources posted on Schoology. Twelve out of 15 feel the tools provided to support struggling learners are not sufficient; the plan is extra practice with DeltaMath, professional learning on Tier 2, UDL, IM routines and formative assessment, and collaboration time. Ten out of 15 feel the tools provided for extension are not sufficient; the plan is extension problems with DeltaMath and collaboration time to develop extension activities.

**Adaptations based on challenges.** A quoted teacher describes being challenged by the lack of resources that come with the curriculum, wanting projects or challenge problems with each section or unit rather than relying on the 'are you ready for more' feature; the plan is regular collaboration time during the school day to create additional resources. A second quoted teacher describes challenges with the accessibility of some lessons, noting that while the curriculum emphasizes conceptual understanding many students still need more structure, clearer examples and more guided practice; the plan is professional learning on the direct instruction moments embedded within IM, plus DeltaMath and CoTeach AI to create more guided and independent practice. The deck states these plans were developed collaboratively with teachers.

**Recommendation.** Illustrative Math Geometry with Additional Fluency Practice and Printed Student Workbooks. The stated rationale: a problem-based curriculum built on a Universal Design for Learning framework; embedded supports for students with disabilities and English Learners; extensions for students who are ready for more; built-in instructional routines that support teachers and students; predictable and purposeful activity and lesson structure; practice problem sets with built-in cumulative review; additional fluency practice using DeltaMath; and printed student workbooks.

**Continued support of implementation.** The 2026 Math Summer Institute consisting of 3 days of learning prior to back-to-school professional learning; back-to-school professional learning days; a full day of learning during district professional learning; Math Specialist support to unpack units, co-plan, co-teach, coach teachers, and do intervention with struggling students; quarterly collaboration meetings including job-embedded learning for Geometry; and monthly collaboration meetings including job-embedded learning for Honors Geometry.

**Support for families.** Every IM unit includes a Family Support Materials section describing in plain language the big ideas students will encounter, providing an overview of the mathematics, details about what to expect as learning deepens, and questions that promote conversation about the mathematics. Every IM lesson includes a lesson summary written to summarize the main mathematical points and any new vocabulary in student-friendly language, intended for students to read on their own time or to catch up after an absence, and useful for families.

**Course materials.** All course resources will be accessed through the IM platform, with additional resources housed in Schoology. Student workbooks will be provided to all students, and student workbooks and family resources will be posted on Schoology. As requested by teachers, DeltaMath subscriptions will be purchased to support additional practice and fluency for classroom use and for work sent home.

**Monitoring success.** Goals are to see growth in the number of students who score advanced or proficient on PSAT and SAT exams, and improvement in student achievement, problem solving skills, and communication of mathematical thinking as monitored through internal common assessment. Measurement may include, reported annually, PSAT/SAT including cohort data and NWEA; and studied with staff, unit assessments and common assessments and student success (grades) in higher levels of mathematics.
