https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Identification**
Draft 2025-26 Troy School District Student Code of Conduct, 16 pages, prepared through Miller Johnson School Policy Services and copyrighted to Miller Johnson for the sole and exclusive use of Miller Johnson and the Troy School District. Presented as item 3C for the April 7, 2026 Board of Education meeting.

**Acknowledgements, athletics, transportation, searches**
Students and parents sign the Acknowledgement of Receipt annually at registration through PowerSchool Forms; a footnote defines 'parents' to include legal guardians. Athletics participation is a privilege, not a right, governed additionally by the TSD Athletic Handbook, acknowledged in Final Forms. Student drivers must be licensed, permitted, registered and parked in designated areas, conditioned on advance consent to vehicle search at any time for any reason. Bus misconduct costing transportation privileges includes insubordination, smoking/vaping, fighting, profane or foul language, and destruction of property. Students have no reasonable expectation of privacy in lockers, desks or assigned technology devices.

**Dress and appearance**
Required: a shirt of opaque fabric with some form of shoulder strap, opaque bottoms, and shoes. Prohibited: violent language or images; drug, alcohol or vaping imagery; body armor or tactical gear; hate speech, profanity, pornography; visible undergarments; swimsuits outside class or practice; dangerous accessories such as handcuffs; and anything obscuring the face except religious observance or PPE. Hats and hooded sweatshirts are allowed if the face stays visible.

**Bullying and cyberbullying**
Each building Principal is primarily responsible for implementing administrative regulation 2006AR and its corresponding policy. The Superintendent reports all verified incidents and consequences to the Board annually. Retaliation is a serious violation of Board Policy 2000.06 independent of substantiation, as are intentionally false reports. Where bullying is alleged to be based on race, color, sex, national origin or disability, the principal notifies the district Compliance Officer or Coordinator under Board Policy 8000.07 and Administrative Regulations 8007AR and 8007.1AR.

**Discipline thresholds**

| Term | Definition in the Code |
|---|---|
| Short-term suspension | 10 school days or fewer |
| Long-term suspension | More than 10 school days; procedurally, 11 school days or more |
| Suspension (definition) | Exclusion for fewer than 60 school days, or until conditions are met |
| Expulsion | Exclusion for 60 school days or more, or permanent exclusion |

Seven factors must be considered and documented before long-term suspension or expulsion: the student's age; disciplinary history; whether the student is disabled within the meaning of IDEA or ADA/Section 504; seriousness of the misconduct; whether it threatened the safety of any pupil or staff member; whether restorative practices will be used; and whether less severe discipline would suffice. The presumption does not apply to short-term suspensions or to a student possessing a firearm in a weapons free school zone. Restorative practices teams may be constituted under Section 1310c(2) of the Revised School Code.

**Attendance**
The Code quotes Revised School Code 380.1561 requiring attendance from age six to the child's eighteenth birthday. Students get one day per excused day to make up work, up to 10 days. Secondary students arriving within five minutes of the start of class are marked tardy and later arrivals get an unexcused tardy, with 3 tardies per class per marking period allowed before detention. A parent must call within 24 hours for an absence to be excused. Long-term absences in excess of 5 days and not to exceed 10 days must be prearranged one week in advance on an Extended Absence form. Email notices go out at the 5, 7 and 9 absence point in any semester; chronic absenteeism brings a staff meeting and referral to the Oakland County Truancy Officer.

**Prohibited acts**
Thirty-six numbered offenses, among them alcohol and marijuana, arson (MCL 750.71 through MCL 750.80), bullying and hazing, criminal sexual conduct (MCL 750.520b-e and g), dangerous weapons including a knife with a blade over 3 inches, drugs, electronic devices and laser pointers, gang insignia, look-a-like weapons, recording without consent, scholastic dishonesty, vaping, acceptable use violations expressly covering artificial intelligence and large language models, and weapons including a knife with a blade length of three inches or less.

**Due process**
A building administrator's suspension of up to ten school days is final and not subject to review or appeal. Suspensions of 11 to 59 days may be appealed in writing to the building principal and Assistant Superintendent within five days. Recommended expulsions require a hearing with the Assistant Superintendent, commencing within ten school days if the student is suspended pending the hearing or scheduled within fifteen school days if not. The decision is given orally within five school days of the close of the hearing with a written decision mailed at the same time; permanent expulsion may be appealed to the Superintendent within five school days, and the Superintendent renders a written decision within fifteen school days.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Identification and copyright.** TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT STUDENT CODE OF CONDUCT, a draft for 2025-26 presented as agenda item 3C in the April 7, 2026 Board of Education packet. The document runs 16 pages and carries a Miller Johnson School Policy Services notice stating it is copyrighted to Miller Johnson, intended for the sole and exclusive use of Miller Johnson and the Troy School District, and that no portion may be reproduced, copied, distributed, or sold without prior written permission.

**Introduction.** The School District must balance the interests of students and the community in a safe and conducive educational environment with its duty to provide educational services to students who engage in misconduct. Board of Education policies and the Code are intended to strike that balance but do not limit the district's lawful authority. All students and parents must sign the Acknowledgement of Receipt of the Student Code of Conduct annually when students are registered for the school year, completed through PowerSchool Forms. A footnote states that 'parents' includes legal guardians and, where required by law, those acting in the place of parents.

**Athletics and transportation.** Participation in interscholastic or extracurricular athletics is a privilege, not a right; student athletes are subject to the Code at all times plus the TSD Athletic Handbook, acknowledged annually by parents and athletes through Final Forms and posted on the TSD Athletics webpage. Student drivers must be licensed and receive district permission to park on district property or use a vehicle during the school day, must register with their school and park only in designated areas, conditioned on advance consent to search of their vehicles at any time, for any reason, with or without notice. Bus riders must obey the driver's direction; misconduct examples that may suspend transportation privileges include insubordination, smoking/vaping, fighting, profane or foul language, and destruction of property.

**Dress and appearance.** Students must wear a shirt with opaque fabric in front, back, and on the sides under the arms plus some form of shoulder strap; bottoms of opaque material including pants/jeans or the equivalent such as skirt, sweatpants, leggings, dress, or shorts; and shoes. Courses that include attire as part of the curriculum, such as professionalism, public speaking, and job readiness, may include assignment-specific dress, and activity- or course-specific shoe requirements are permitted such as athletic shoes for physical education or recess and closed toe shoes for science labs and industrial arts. Prohibited are violent language or images; images or language depicting or suggesting drugs, alcohol, vaping or paraphernalia or any illegal item or activity; body armor, tactical gear, or facsimile; hate speech, profanity, pornography; clothing revealing visible undergarments, though visible waistbands and straps are allowed; swimsuits except as required in class or athletic practice; accessories that could be considered dangerous or used as a weapon such as handcuffs or other metal accessories; and any item that obscures the face except as a religious observance or as personal protective equipment such as medical face masks. Hats, hooded sweatshirts and other head coverings are permitted but must leave the face visible to staff and not interfere with anyone's line of sight.

**Police, search and seizure.** The district cooperates with local police; parents will be notified if police arrest or wish to question their student in school, with timing depending on circumstances, and except as required by law the district retains discretion to report crimes. Students have no reasonable expectation of privacy in school property assigned to them such as lockers, desks and technology devices, and the district reserves the unrestricted right to search and seize such property at any time, for any reason, with or without notice. Illegal or inappropriate items may be confiscated and delivered to police or parents.

**Bullying and cyberbullying.** The Principal of each building is primarily responsible for implementing administrative regulation 2006AR and its corresponding policy. The Superintendent shall report to the Board of Education annually all verified incidents of bullying and the resulting consequences. 'Bullying' means any written, verbal, or physical act, or any electronic communication including cyberbullying, intended or reasonably known to be likely to harm one or more students by substantially interfering with educational opportunities, benefits, or programs; adversely affecting a student's ability to participate in or benefit from educational programs by placing the student in reasonable fear of physical harm or causing substantial emotional distress; having an actual and substantial detrimental effect on physical or mental health; or causing substantial disruption in the orderly operation of the school. 'At school' means in a classroom, anywhere else on school premises, on a school bus or other school-related vehicle, and at a school-sponsored activity or event whether or not on school premises, and includes off-premises use of a telecommunications access device or service provider owned by or under the control of the district. Retaliation against a target, witness, reporter or participant in an investigation is prohibited and is a serious violation of Board Policy 2000.06 independent of whether a complaint is substantiated; intentionally false reports are likewise prohibited. Victims must immediately report to the building principal, assistant principal, or counselor, and the parent must also report; the principal or designee conducts a prompt investigation and may first attempt informal resolution such as restorative practices, with the complainant free to request a formal investigation at any time. Where bullying is alleged to be based in whole or in part on race, color, sex, national origin, or disability, the principal notifies the district's designated Compliance Officer or Coordinator pursuant to Board of Education Policy 8000.07 and Administrative Regulations 8007AR and 8007.1AR.

**Rebuttable presumption and the seven factors.** Consistent with Michigan law the district adopts a rebuttable presumption that students should not be disciplined by long-term suspension, meaning more than 10 school days, or expelled, meaning 60 or more school days, unless the district determines in its sole discretion that the presumption has been rebutted after considering each of seven factors: the student's age; the student's disciplinary history; whether the student is disabled within the meaning of IDEA or ADA/Section 504; the seriousness of the misconduct; whether the misconduct threatened the safety of any pupil or staff member; whether restorative practices will be used; and whether less severe discipline would properly address the misconduct. The presumption does not apply to short-term suspensions of 10 school days or fewer or to a student who possesses a firearm in a weapons free school zone, but the administrator must consider and document the seven factors for all long-term suspensions and expulsions. Restorative practices must be considered in every case as an addition or alternative to suspension or expulsion; a restorative practices team may be constituted and act in the manner described in Section 1310c(2) of the Revised School Code, and restorative practices should be the first consideration for interpersonal conflicts, bullying, verbal and physical conflicts, theft, damage to property, class disruption, and harassment.

**Definitions of discipline.** Administrative intervention is disciplinary action not resulting in suspension and may include removal from a class period, in-school suspension, reprimand, restitution, detention and/or work assignment before or after school, additional classroom assignments, and revocation of the privilege of attending after school functions. Suspension is exclusion from school for fewer than 60 school days or exclusion terminating upon fulfillment of specific conditions. Expulsion is exclusion from the district for 60 school days or more or permanent exclusion.

**Attendance.** The Code quotes the Revised School Code (380.1561) requiring every parent, guardian or other person having control of a child from the age of six to the child's eighteenth birthday to send that child to the public schools during the entire school year. Excused reasons include chronic or serious illness, religious observances, family bereavement, mandatory court appearance, college visits, or other reasons approved by a building administrator. Students receive one day for each day excused absent to make up work, up to 10 days, including tests and quizzes; work assigned before an absence is due on return. School-sponsored activities such as field trips, athletic contests, counselor appointments, student club obligations and school business are exempted absences. Students must sign in or sign out in the designated office when entering or leaving at other times. Elementary schools develop their own truancy procedures, communicated at the beginning of each year. At middle and high school, students arriving within five minutes after the start of class are marked tardy and later arrivals receive an unexcused tardy; students are afforded 3 tardies per class per secondary marking period without penalty, after which detention is assigned. A parent must call the attendance office within 24 hours for an absence to be excused; any absence not excused within 24 hours remains unexcused, and unexcused absences may bar makeup of missed assessments, labs or presentations. Long-term absences in excess of 5 days and not to exceed 10 days must be prearranged and approved one week in advance through an Extended Absence form available in each school's main office. Families receive email communication including class attendance status at the 5, 7 and 9 absence point in any semester, listing the course name, total number of absences, and whether excused or unexcused. Chronic absenteeism results in a meeting with school staff and referral to the Oakland County Truancy Officer and other county resources.

**Range of discipline and jurisdiction.** Penalties range from administrative intervention to expulsion, from suspension to expulsion, or expulsion alone, with the actual penalty depending on the nature and severity of the offense, the facts, the student's age, prior behavioral record, chronic nature of the misconduct, staff recommendation and other relevant circumstances. The Code applies to prohibited acts on school property; in a motor vehicle including one used for a school-related purpose; at a school-related activity, function or event; en route to or from school; involving another student en route to or from school; off school premises where the act is prohibited by law or is serious enough in the building administrator's judgment that continued attendance would endanger health and safety or substantially interfere with the educational process; and acts committed before enrollment in Troy School District or while enrolled elsewhere.

**The 36 prohibited acts.** 1 Alcohol, Marijuana, and Chemical Substances. 2 Arson. 3 Arson Prohibited by Law, citing MCL 750.71 through MCL 750.80 and supplemental to paragraphs 2, 12, 22 and 36. 4 Bullying and Hazing, referencing Board Policy 2000.06 and AR 2006. 5 Coercion, Extortion, and Blackmail. 6 Copyrighted Material. 7 Criminal Acts. 8 Criminal Sexual Conduct as defined by MCL 750.520b-e and g, supplemental to paragraphs 9, 10, 14, 24, 25 and 35. 9 Discriminatory Harassment covering race, color, national origin, religion, sex including sexual orientation and gender identity/expression, marital status, pregnancy status, genetic information, disability or age. 10 Disruption of School. 11 Damage of Property or Theft/Possession. 12 Dangerous Weapons, listing brass knuckles, dagger, dirk, firearm, iron bar, knife with a blade over 3 inches in length, pocket knife opened by a mechanical device, or stiletto. 13 Dress. 14 Drugs, Narcotic Drugs, and Counterfeit Substances. 15 Electronic Communication Devices and Laser Pointers. 16 Failure to Comply with Directions of School Personnel. 17 Failure to Cooperate. 18 False Alarms. 19 False Allegations. 20 Falsification of Records. 21 Fighting, Assault, and Battery on Another Person. 22 Fireworks, Explosives, and Chemical Substances. 23 Gang Insignia/Activity, defining 'gang' as a group of two or more persons whose purpose or activities include illegal acts or Code violations. 24 Improper Communications. 25 Indecency. 26 Look-A-Like Weapons such as a starter pistol, rubber knife or toy gun. 27 Misconduct Prior to Enrollment. 28 Personal Protection Devices such as pepper gas, mace, stun gun or electric shock device. 29 Recording, barring capture or transmission of audio or images of any person at school or school-related events without express consent. 30 Trespassing, Loitering. 31 Scholastic Dishonesty including plagiarism. 32 Smoking/Tobacco/Vaping, including electronic cigarettes and vaporizers. 33 Suspended Student on School Property or Attending School Activities. 34 Violation of Acceptable Use Policy, stating that uses of artificial intelligence, large language models, or similar technology are subject to the Acceptable Use policy and the Code. 35 Violations of Building's Rules and Regulations. 36 Weapons and Dangerous Instruments, covering a knife with a blade length of three (3) inches or less, air soft gun, blackjack, baton, martial arts device, paint ball or splat gun.

**Personal technology guidelines.** Districtwide, students may not use or possess active electronic communication devices in restrooms, locker rooms, offices and other locations with a reasonable expectation of privacy, and laser pointers are barred without express administrative permission. Elementary: phones and personal devices must remain on silent with notifications disabled and stored in backpacks or lockers during school hours, with no one-way or two-way communication during the school day unless approved by a TSD staff member; wearable technology such as Apple Watches and Fitbits is allowed with notifications off and communication features disabled; earbuds or headphones require staff permission. Middle school: personal technology may not be used during the school day and must remain out of sight until the end of the day including passing time and lunch, stored in lockers, though personal cell phones may be used in the main office. High school: phones and personal technology must be stored in a locker or backpack during class time. The district is not responsible for lost, stolen or damaged personal technology; students use district-provided iPads during instruction.

**Due process, short-term suspension.** Before any out-of-school suspension the building administrator will inform the student of the misconduct and, if denied, explain the evidence; allow the student to explain their version of the facts; and consider each of the seven individual factors, including restorative practices. If the student's presence poses an immediate danger or ongoing threat of disruption the administrator may suspend immediately and provide due process as soon thereafter as reasonable. The administrator may impose a suspension not to exceed ten school days, must inform the parent in person or by phone and then in writing, and that decision is final and not subject to further review or appeal.

**Due process, long-term suspension and expulsion.** Step 1: for a suspension of eleven or more school days or expulsion, the student and parent are notified in writing of the charges, the potential range of disciplinary action, the fact that a hearing will be held with the building administrator, and the time, place, location and procedures; that hearing will take place within five days of the disciplinary event to the extent practicable, and the notice documents consideration of the seven factors and of restorative practices. A recommended suspension of 11 to 59 days may be appealed in writing to the building principal and Assistant Superintendent within five days. All recommended expulsions of 60 school days or more, and permanent expulsions, require a hearing with the Assistant Superintendent. If the student is suspended pending the decision the hearing commences within ten school days following the initial suspension after the principal's investigation is complete; if not suspended, it is scheduled within fifteen school days following completion of the investigation, with timelines subject to enlargement on request. Step 2: the Assistant Superintendent hearing determines the truth or falsity of the charges and, if found true, considers the seven factors, restorative practices and appropriate discipline; the student or parent may waive the hearing, in which case the principal's recommended penalty is ordinarily imposed except that expulsion or permanent expulsion remains the Assistant Superintendent's decision; charges may be amended and a greater or lesser penalty imposed. Step 3: the decision is given orally not later than five school days after the close of the hearing, with a written decision mailed at the same time, subject to enlargement for extenuating circumstances. Step 4: a decision to permanently expel may be appealed to the Superintendent by written notice filed with the Assistant Superintendent and Superintendent within five school days; the appeal involves no further testimony or new evidence, the Assistant Superintendent shares the hearing results and a recommendation, the student, parent or legal representative may address the Superintendent, and the Superintendent renders a written decision within fifteen school days. During suspension, expulsion or permanent expulsion a student may not participate in or attend school-sponsored activities on or off campus, nor be on district property.

**Inconsistency clause.** The Code is intended to be consistent with Michigan law, Board of Education policies, and Administrative Regulations promulgated by the Superintendent; inconsistencies are resolved with Michigan law superseding both Board policies and Administrative Regulations, and Board Policy superseding Administrative Regulations.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: The Troy School District's 2025-2026 Course Descriptions booklet catalogs the courses offered at Athens High School and Troy High School, issued under Dr. Richard Machesky, Superintendent of Schools, and marked "Revised, February, 2025." It opens with the district's Title IX and Section 504/ADA nondiscrimination policy, sets out graduation requirements and flexibility options, describes courses department by department with course numbers, grade levels, credits and prerequisites, and closes with Oakland Schools Technical Campus information and the anti-discrimination grievance procedure. The governing requirement stated throughout is that all students must earn 22.5 total credits to be eligible for a Troy High School or Troy Athens diploma.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Publication**
2025-2026 Course Descriptions for Athens High School and Troy High School, Troy School District. Dr. Richard Machesky, Superintendent of Schools. Revised, February, 2025.

**Schools and contacts**
- Athens High School: Mr. Vernon Burden, Principal, 4333 John R. Road, Troy, Michigan 48085
- Troy High School: Mr. Remo Roncone, Principal, 4777 Northfield Parkway, Troy, Michigan 48098
- Department of Teaching & Learning, 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098, 248.823.5221
- Title IX / Section 504 / ADA: John Pagel, Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, MI 48098-4799, (248)823-4000
- Central Office Special Education: 248.823.5096

**Nondiscrimination**
The policy cites Title IX of the Educational Amendments of 1972, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, and the Americans with Disabilities Act. Jordan M. Harris, J.D., Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, is the Title IX and Section 504/ADA Coordinator for employment and personnel matters; the Director of Special Education is the Section 504/ADA Coordinator for students.

**Graduation requirements (Class of 2025 and beyond)**

| Area | Required credits |
| --- | --- |
| English | 4.0 |
| Science | 3.0 |
| Mathematics | 4.0 |
| Social Studies | 3.0 |
| Personal Finance | 0.5 |
| Physical Education | 1.0 |
| Health | 0.5 |
| World Language, Fine & Applied Arts, CTE | 3.0 |
| Online Learning Experience | 0.0 |
| State Assessments | 0.0 |
| Total | 22.5 |

Personal Finance is embedded in Economics and becomes a requirement with the class of 2028. The online learning experience is a non-credit 20-hour requirement. Science differs by cohort: the classes of '27, '28 and '29 take Biology (1.0), Chemistry 1 (0.5) and Physics 1 (0.5), Environmental Science: Human Impact (0.5) and a science elective (0.5); the class of '26 takes Biology (1.0), Chemistry or Physics (1.0) and a science elective (1.0).

**Flexibility options** (updated 9.2015, MCL 380.1278a & MCL 380.1278b)
A Personal Curriculum aligned to the Educational Development Plan; waiver of the 0.5-credit Physical Education elective for two seasons of district athletics or marching band; World Language flexibility for heritage-language proficiency, international study, or substitution of CTE or Applied Arts credits; and CTE completion exchanged 1:1 for science, world language or Algebra 2 credit.

**Career and Technical Education**
Twelve programs: Architecture and Design; Automotive Technology; Business Administration, Management and Operations; Computer Programming; Computer Information Systems and Security; Culinary Arts; Education; Finance; Marketing and Sales; Mechanical Drafting (Woodworking); Mechatronics; and Radio and Broadcasting Technology. Completers take courses in sequential order; a C or better makes a student eligible for credentials including Certiport, Microsoft Office Specialist, ServSafe, ProStart and the Child Development Associate (CDA).

**Oakland Schools Technical Campus**
OSTC-SE, 5055 Delemere Street, Royal Oak, MI, serves grades 11-12 half-days. Morning classes begin 7:50 AM and dismiss 10:20 AM; the afternoon session runs 12:00 PM to 2:30 PM (08101 Session 1 AM, 08102 Session 2 PM). Credit is generally 1.5 credits per semester; if regular students carry six credits, OSTC students carry three at their home school plus three at OSTC. Applications close at the end of February, and OSTC credits are not NCAA approved.

**Grievance procedure**
A written grievance alleging discrimination on the basis of sex, race, color, religion, national origin, age (employees only), height, weight, marital status or handicap is filed with the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services. Step 1 requires filing within 10 workdays, a meeting within 5 workdays and a written answer within 3 workdays; Steps 2 and 3 each allow 3 workdays to appeal, 10 workdays to meet and 5 workdays to answer, with the Superintendent's decision final and binding.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Publication and contacts.** The 2025-2026 Course Descriptions booklet covers Athens High School and Troy High School in the Troy School District, is issued under Dr. Richard Machesky, Superintendent of Schools, and is marked "Revised, February, 2025." Athens High School is listed with Principal Mr. Vernon Burden at 4333 John R. Road, Troy, Michigan 48085; Troy High School with Principal Mr. Remo Roncone at 4777 Northfield Parkway, Troy, Michigan 48098. Back matter lists the Department of Teaching & Learning at 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098, 248.823.5221, main offices 248.823.2900 and 248.823.2700, counseling 248.823.2962 and 248.823.2715, attendance 248.823.2901 and 248.823.2701, and Special Education at 248.823.5096.

**Nondiscrimination policy.** The opening policy cites Title IX of the Educational Amendments of 1972, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and the Americans with Disabilities Act. Jordan M. Harris, J.D., Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, is named Title IX and Section 504/ADA Coordinator for employment and personnel matters; the Director of Special Education is Section 504/ADA Coordinator for handicapped and suspected handicapped students. Questions go to John Pagel, Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, MI 48098-4799, (248)823-4000.

**Graduation requirements.** Requirements are stated for the classes of 2025, 2026, 2027 and 2028, with total credits needed for graduation of 22.5 for a Troy High School or Troy Athens diploma. English requires 4.0 credits: English 9 1.0, English 10 1.0, English 11 Lit/Comp plus an elective or 11 English AP 1 & 2 1.0, and English 12 Lit/Comp or 12 English AP 1 & 2 1.0. Science requires 3.0 credits: the classes of ’27, ’28 and ’29 take Biology 1.0, Chemistry 1 0.5 and Physics 1 0.5, Environmental Science: Human Impact 0.5 and a science elective 0.5, while the class of ’26 takes Biology 1.0, Chemistry or Physics 1.0 and a science elective 1.0; AP Environmental Science (1.0) can replace Environmental Science: Human Impact (0.5). Mathematics requires 4.0 credits: Algebra 1 1.0, Geometry 1.0, Algebra 2 or Algebra 2 Part A and Part B 1.0 (also meetable through CTE program completion such as OSTC), and a math elective 1.0, with a math experience required in the final year. Social Studies requires 3.0 credits: World History/Geography 1 & 2 1.0, with AP Human Geography fulfilling World 1; American History/Geography 1 & 2 1.0; Economics 0.5; Government and Civics 0.5. Personal Finance is 0.5 credit embedded into Economics, required beginning with the class of 2028 and obtainable only through a TSD Economics or AP Economics course. Physical Education requires 1.0 credit and Health 0.5. World Language, Fine & Applied Arts and CTE requires 3.0 credits: 2.0 World Language credits, non-sequential accepted, or 1.0 World Language plus 1.0 CTE or VPAA, in addition to 1.0 VPAA. A 20-hour online learning experience and state assessments are non-credit requirements.

**Flexibility options.** Updated 9.2015 under MCL 380.1278a and MCL 380.1278b: a Personal Curriculum aligned to a student’s Educational Development Plan; excusal from the 0.5-credit Physical Education elective for two seasons of Troy School District athletics or marching band, tracked automatically with no forms required; World Language flexibility for heritage language proficiency, international study and residence, or substitution of CTE or Applied Arts credits; and CTE program completion exchanged 1:1 for science or world language credit or to satisfy Algebra 2.

**Career and Technical Education.** Twelve programs are listed: Architecture and Design; Automotive Technology; Business Administration, Management and Operations (BAMO); Computer Programming; Computer Information Systems and Security; Culinary Arts; Education; Finance; Marketing and Sales; Mechanical Drafting (Woodworking); Mechatronics; and Radio and Broadcasting Technology. Completers take required courses in sequential order, and a C or better in each course confers eligibility for an industry-certified credential.

**Business, marketing and work-based learning.** BAMO comprises 005231 Business Entrepreneurship, 005404 Digital Business and 005415 Business Law & Management, with Certiport Entrepreneurship and Small Business certification worth two ACE credits and a Communication Career Skills Artificial Intelligence certification worth one ACE credit. Finance and Accounting comprises 005011 Financial Accounting 1, 005012 Financial Accounting 2 and 005124 Building Wealth & Investments, each satisfying a half credit of the math-related graduation requirement in 12th grade. Marketing and Sales includes Marketing 1, Advanced Marketing, Sports and Entertainment Marketing, Marketing Research Capstone and School Based Enterprise, with DECA and the Troy Athens Fantasy League. Work-Based Learning students may earn up to 2.0 credits for work of at least 10 hours per week and 200 hours per semester; unpaid students must not exceed 45 hours per training experience.

**Technical and applied programs.** Information Technology covers Computer Programming, Cybersecurity and Digital/Multimedia, with AP Computer Science A, Computer Science Principles AP, Cybersecurity (003172 at Troy High, 103172/203172 at Athens), Web Creation and Game Design. Careers in Education 1 and 2, held at Athens using the Troy Athens Preschool, offer advanced placement credit at Central University, Western Michigan University, Oakland University, Macomb Community College and Davenport University plus a Child Development Associate (CDA) credential. Drafting and mechatronics offerings are Architectural Drawing 1 and 2, Woodworking Design & Fabrication 1 and 2, Engineering & Advanced Manufacturing and Engineering & Digital Manufacturing Systems. Automotive Technology at Troy High runs Auto Tech 1 through 4, with Auto Tech 2 a 2-hour block worth 1 credit per semester with 2 retakes, meeting NATEF Automotive Maintenance and Light Repair standards. Culinary Arts at Athens offers Restaurant Operations / Terrace Cafe (2 hours, 2 credits), Commercial Baking and Commercial Foods on the ProStart curriculum.

**English, ELD and Fine Arts.** English sequences are English 9, English 10, 11 English Literature/Composition or 11 English AP, and 12 English Lit/Comp or 12 English AP, with electives such as Creative Writing, Classical Mythology and Drama, Graphic Novels, Science Fiction, Speech, Debate and Writing for Publication. AP Seminar and AP Research culminate in a paper of approximately 4000-5000 words. ELD placement follows the State of Michigan Entrance Protocol with annual WIDA ACCESS testing, offering Beginner, Intermediate and Advanced ELD, Bridges to Lit/Comp for ELs and EL Tutorial, graded pass/fail. Fine Arts spans Drawing 1 through Advanced Art AP, Campus Band and Freshman Orchestra through Symphony Orchestra, Concert Choir and Madrigal Singers, Music Theory, which counts as a math elective credit for juniors and seniors who have completed all other required math credits, Intro to Music Technology and Recording using ProTools, and Theatre I through III.

**Mathematics, Health and Physical Education.** Mathematics runs from Algebra 1 and Intensified Algebra 1, a double-blocked 2-hour course worth 1 credit per semester, through Geometry, Algebra 2 with Part A and Part B variants, Precalculus, College Algebra, Calculus AB AP, Calculus BC AP, Statistics AP, Calculus 3 and Linear Algebra (dual enrollment with Lawrence Tech), Introduction to Data Science and Data Structures and Algorithms. Health offers 008852 Health, stated as required for graduation, and Peer Mediation; Multi-Departmental offers Innovation Learning and Innovation Lab, influenced by the "D school" at Stanford University, plus LEAP: Linking Education and People. Physical Education requires Intro to Physical Activity Level 1 (007952) or Level 2 (007962), including CPR training, fitness, swimming testing and team sports; Lifeguarding requires students to be 15 years old and costs $40 for Red Cross certification.

**Science, Social Studies, Special Education and World Language.** Science includes Biology, Anatomy and Physiology, Genetics/Bacteriology/Biotechnology/Embryology, Biology AP, Chemistry 1 and 2, AP Chemistry, Organic Chemistry, Physics 1 and 2, Engineering Physics, AP Physics 2 and C, Environmental Science: Human Impact, Astronomy, Forensic Science and Environmental Science AP. Social Studies includes World History/Geography 1 and 2, Human Geography AP, American History/Geography, Economics, Government and Civics, Psychology, Sociology, Mental Health, Philosophy, Comparative Government and Politics AP built around China, Great Britain, Iran, Mexico, Nigeria and Russia, History through Film, Conflicts of the 20th & 21st Centuries, LINK, AP Art History covering 250 works of art, and Stories of Yourself & Others, carrying a half ELA credit and a half History credit. Special Education offers Integrated Studies, Linguistics and Composition, Reading Strategies, Integrated Math, English Language Arts, Math Skills A/B, Life Skills Math and LS sections of core subjects. World Language, keyed to the ACTFL Proficiency Guidelines, runs through level 4 in French, Spanish, Japanese, Chinese and German with AP courses in the first four; Japanese 2 students read and write 120 basic Kanji, Japanese 3 adds another 170+ and Japanese 4 another 180+.

**Oakland Schools Technical Campus.** OSTC-SE, the Southeast Campus at 5055 Delemere Street, Royal Oak, MI, north of 14 Mile between Crooks and Coolidge, serves grades 11-12 through half-day clusters staffed by instructors holding a Michigan Teaching Certificate and Vocational Authorization. Course numbers 08101 (Session 1 AM) and 08102 (Session 2 PM) correspond to a morning session beginning at 7:50 AM and dismissing at 10:20 AM and an afternoon session beginning at 12:00 PM and dismissing at 2:30 PM. Credit is generally 1.5 credits per semester; if regular students carry six (6) credits, OSTC students must carry three (3) credits at their home high school in addition to three (3) credits at OSTC. Offerings include Automotive Technology and, at the Pontiac Northeast Campus, Cosmetology, both of which must begin in 11th grade, plus Collision Repair, Computer Networking, Construction Technology, Culinary Arts/Hospitality, Health Sciences, Machining, Mechatronics, Visual Imaging Technology, Welding and Homeland Security. Students apply at www.ostconline.com by the end of February, and OSTC credits are not NCAA approved.

**Anti-discrimination grievance procedure.** Students or employees alleging discrimination on the basis of sex (including sexual harassment), race, color, religion, national origin, age (employees only), height, weight, marital status or handicap file a written grievance with the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, the designated compliance administrator. Step 1 requires filing with the immediate supervisor within 10 workdays of the incident, a meeting within 5 workdays of filing and a written answer within 3 workdays. Step 2 allows appeal within 3 workdays, a meeting with the Assistant Superintendent or Deputy Superintendent within 10 workdays and an answer within 5 workdays; Step 3 follows the same intervals with the Superintendent, whose decision is final and binding. A grievance not filed or appealed within the time limits is deemed abandoned.

**Submission**
Elementary Mathematics Materials Adoption, March 2023, submitted by Natalie Haezebrouck and Julia Alder.

**Rationale**
Troy School District reviews curricular materials every nine years. The last curricular adoption was Middle and High-School Health in 2020; the last elementary math adoption was in 2010. The philosophy of review has since broadened from seeking new materials to examining instructional practices, intervention, assessment and current data so that curricular, structural and staffing needs align. Teachers have been supplementing the current resource with three act tasks, number sense routines and additional materials; a resource addressing deep conceptual learning, number sense and mathematical fluency is sought. Reference points are the Michigan Math State Standards and the National Council of Teachers of Mathematics (NCTM).

**Process**
The Math Leadership Team (MLT) was assembled in September 2019 with representation from all grade levels and roles. MLT reviewed student performance data, surveyed all elementary teachers, and studied NCTM's Principles to Action, concluding that both a math specialist role and new curricular materials were needed. MLT members and colleagues from the Oakland County Math Leadership Team identified candidate publishers and materials, evaluated against the Standards for Mathematical Practice and NCTM's 8 Effective Math Teaching Practices. Early Adopter teachers spent over a year evaluating materials. In January 2021 the list was narrowed and select publishers were invited to Troy to demonstrate online features; materials were piloted in January and February. Ninety-five early adopter teachers volunteered to implement Bridges in Mathematics and Number Corner during 2022-23.

Elementary Mathematics Materials Adoption report, March 2023, submitted by Natalie Haezebrouck and Julia Alder to the Troy School District Board of Education.

RATIONALE. The district reviews its curricular materials every nine years. Since the last curricular adoption, Middle and High-School Health in 2020, the district has updated its philosophy of curricular review: rather than simply seeking new materials, it takes stock of programming as a whole, including instructional practices, intervention, assessment and current data, so that curricular, structural and staffing needs can be aligned. The last elementary math adoption was conducted in 2010. Since then the district reports better understanding of the Michigan Math State Standards, better aligned elementary math resources, and continued guidance from the National Council of Teachers of Mathematics (NCTM) on best practice. Teachers have been supplementing the current resource with three act tasks, number sense routines and additional materials to address missed opportunities, and a resource that fully addresses deep conceptual learning, number sense and mathematical fluency is desired.

PROGRAM REVIEW TIMELINE (Image 1). The timeline traces comprehensive math program development and the development of MTSS: learning and implementing Math Recovery and Tier 1 research in research classrooms; 2019 Bridges early adopters with Tier 1 focus on conceptual understanding and modeling; '20 COVID, extension of ME and math specialists, support for intensive intervention in math and research of resources for Tier 1; '21 review of TSD data and focus on math mindset, noting a trend of fewer students proficient in math over time; and 22-23.

PROCESS AND SELECTION. The review began in September 2019 with the assembly of the Math Leadership Team (MLT), an interdepartmental team with representation from all grade levels and roles across the system that meets several times per year to plan and monitor progress toward the district vision. MLT reviewed student performance data and administered a survey to all elementary teachers about their own and their students' experience with mathematics, and studied the NCTM publication Principles to Action. Through that work the team identified a need for the role of math specialist as well as a need for new curricular materials. Members of MLT and colleagues from the Oakland County Math Leadership Team identified potential publishers, materials and resources, using the standards of math practice (Table 2) and the NCTM Effective Math Teaching Practices to focus the evaluation, with the Michigan Standards for Mathematics as the foundation. Image 2 presents the 8 Effective Math Teaching Practices, cited to NCTM (2014), Principals to Actions: Ensuring mathematical success for all. Once selections were narrowed, the Early Adopter Team vetted the resources and began using lessons in classrooms; all early adopter teachers spent over a year evaluating materials. In January 2021 the resource list was narrowed and select publishers were invited to Troy to demonstrate online features accompanying the text resources; materials were piloted in January and February. Ninety-five early adopter teachers volunteered to implement the recommended curriculum, Bridges in Mathematics and Number Corner, during the 2022-23 school year.

EARLY ADOPTER TEAM AND MATH SPECIALISTS (Table 1). Building totals: Barnard 6, Bemis 6, Costello 9, Hamilton 18, Hill 6, Leonard 17, Martell 12, Morse 6, Troy Union 9, Wass 4, Wattles 2, for a total of 95. Grade-level column totals are 13 for kindergarten, 22 for grade 1, 13 for grade 2, 15 for grade 3, 16 for grade 4 and 16 for grade 5.

MATERIALS REVIEWED (Table 3). Illustrative Mathematics develops conceptual understanding with tasks that call for hands-on learning, but was not fully available during the 2021-2022 pilot and review timeline; its format was in Google Drive, publishers are not developing more supports for elementary level IM, hands-on materials and mathematical modeling tools are not integrated within the resource, and online Google Drive modules for teachers require multiple downloads and integration to Schoology. It is now more available from Kendall Hunt and through online modules, and is quoted as rigorous, problem-based, fully aligned to the standards, available in print and digital, and highly rated by EdReports across all three review gateways. Math Expressions 2013 Edition is the current resource; its approach to mathematical fluency was limited and only partially addressed number sense, it aligned with grade-level content but did not adequately address differentiation, ELD and students with special needs, its online personal math trainer provided extra practice, hands-on materials and modeling tools are not integrated, and online teacher resources are available but difficult to utilize. Bridges Mathematics including Number Corner offers a fluency approach embedded in Number Corner with monthly opportunities for students to share, model and develop numeracy; it aligns with grade-level content and integrates research and models supporting Math Recovery learning progressions; tasks build in varying levels of sophistication; modeling tools provide access for differentiation including ELD, students with special needs, and students with high sophistication in math; teacher website and materials are available in PDF; online apps and family supports come through the Math Learning Center website; an active online support blog draws on a national network of educators; and a Fluency Pathway sits in Number Corner. Number Corner is described as a skill-building program revolving around the classroom calendar that provides daily practice and continual encounters with broader mathematical concepts in 15-20 minutes of additional engaging daily instruction.

FEATURES OF RECOMMENDED MATERIALS (Table 4). Features include a number sense focus through Number Corner; grade-level alignment through Bridges units addressing the Michigan State Standards; teacher implementation supports through the Math Learning Center Educator Website, which requires an educator login and which math specialists use to find recommendations and resources for early adopter classroom teachers; parent communication through Math At Home and Home Learning Resources; digital features through Math Learning Center iPad apps and Work Place games with sharable QR codes; fluency and practice through Home Connections and student workbooks, with the district holding an option to print or purchase workbooks; an assessment system with pre-assessments, check points, post-assessments, checklists, and both interview-based and written forms; support for high aptitude, ELD, special needs and DEI through low-floor high-ceiling task design with built-in mathematical tools and models; and implementation support including multiple professional learning sessions included in the purchase, partnership with a local facilitator for job-embedded learning, and the Bridges educator blog. The recommendation is that Bridges Math and Number Corner 3rd edition move forward.

IMPLEMENTATION PLAN. All resources will be available for instruction on the first day of school for the 2023-24 academic year. Teachers will have the option of training on Number Corner and Bridges Unit 1 in June, and all teachers will participate in a kick-off during back-to-school professional development in August 2023 in collaboration with math specialists and the Bridges team during the OneTroy kick-off. Teachers will participate in job-embedded PD, math specialists will support each building throughout the year, and the district will work with principals to create master schedules incorporating 75-90 minutes of instructional time per day.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of April 18, 2023, held at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, called to order by President Schmidt at 7:00 p.m. with all seven members present and approximately 150 people in the audience. The Board approved four two-year probationary administrative contracts, awarded a gym floor renovation bid of $63,930.00 to Floor Care Concepts and an elementary audio upgrade bid of $498,676.00 to TelSystems, and authorized Superintendent Dr. Richard Machesky to negotiate a lease with the Troy Racquet Club for a tennis facility on the Troy High School site. That resolution carried 6 to 1, with Mrs. Alic dissenting.

**Meeting and Attendance**
Regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education, April 18, 2023, Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Present with Mr. Schmidt were Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart, and Wilson. Superintendent Machesky attended along with administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Detmer, Duda, Roncone, Jansen, Canfield, Griffin, Naus, Cottone, Young, Henry, Barsh, Keen, Recker, DiPonio, Keyser, Conaton, Harris, and West. Approximately 150 members of the audience were present. The meeting adjourned at 9:20 p.m.

**Recognitions**
President Schmidt changed the order of the Recognition items. The Mission Moment honored Leonard Elementary ASD teacher Megan Murray and Literacy Specialist Nancy Haboush for an adapted version of LLI intervention; Dr. Erin Detmer and Sarah Young introduced them. The Student Spotlight featured Grace Cafagna, a senior at Athens High School in the TSD Creative Guild, introduced by Thomas Butcher. Stefanie Gervais was named 2023 Outstanding Support Staff Employee of the Year from 25 nominees, with a reception set for May 11th. The Outstanding Teacher of the Year program drew 62 nominations; a reception for all nominees was set for April 25th.

| Outstanding Teacher 2023 | Position |
|---|---|
| Erich Beregszaszy | Science Teacher, Athens High School |
| Shannon Dziwanowski | Science Teacher, Larson Middle School |
| Patricia Grandy | Teacher, Troy Preschool |
| Karen Rosewarne | 5th Grade Teacher, Leonard Elementary School |

Mrs. Rosewarne was also selected Overall TSD Teacher of the Year for 2023. Winners were sent to Oakland Schools for the Countywide Outstanding Teacher Award program.

**Consent Agenda (23-024)**
Moved by Mr. Hauff, supported by Mr. Haupt; items A through F approved 7 yes, 0 no: minutes of the March 7, 2023 Workshop; minutes of the March 11, 2023 Retreat; minutes of the March 21, 2023 Board Meeting; Treasurer's Report for February 2023; Ancillary Fund(s) Budget Amendment; and rescheduling the June 20 Board meeting to June 13 at 7:30 pm at Troy High School.

**Personnel Actions (all effective July 1, 2023; all 7-0)**

| Res. | Appointee | Position | Mover / Support |
|---|---|---|---|
| 23-025 | Mr. Patrick Griffin | Principal, International Academy East | Wilson / Hauff |
| 23-026 | Ms. Gabrielle Naus | Assistant Principal, International Academy East | Anne / Philippart |
| 23-027 | Mr. John Pagel | Assistant Superintendent, Employee Services | Haupt / Alic |
| 23-028 | Mr. Brian Canfield | Director, Employee Services | Alic / Anne |

Each received a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure. Resolution 23-029 (Philippart / Wilson) approved elementary and secondary personnel recommendations including new hire Szczepanski, 7-0. Curriculum items: none.

**Business**
Resolution 23-030 (Alic / Hauff) awarded the THS gym floor renovation bid to Floor Care Concepts for $63,930.00, payable from the Building Site & Sinking Fund and/or the 2023 Bond Fund; 7-0. Resolution 23-031 (Hauff / Haupt) awarded Elementary Audio Upgrades to TelSystems for $498,676.00 from the 2023 Bond Fund; 7-0.

**Troy Racquet Club Partnership (23-032)**
Moved by Mrs. Anne, supported by Dr. Philippart. The resolution contemplates a tennis facility on the Troy High School site with 12-15 courts, up from the 8 that currently exist, domed approximately October through April, with outdoor lighting for later summer play. Play would be membership-based for community members and for students outside the school day; Troy High students and staff get free exclusive access during tennis sections of the Physical Education curriculum, district tennis programs get free in-season access, and TRC would provide free membership to students showing proof of economically disadvantaged status. Dr. Richard Machesky or his designee was authorized to negotiate and execute a lease subject to legal counsel review. Mrs. Alic said the project would likely serve mostly private use. Yes: 6 (Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson). No: 1 (Alic).

**Public Comment and Board Comments**
Fifteen speakers addressed the Board under non-agenda public communication, limited to one minute each to allow a full hour; all but one spoke against removal of the honors program. Board members reported on the TSD Business Education Roundtable, the NSBA Conference, and the district art show. The next workshop was announced for Tuesday, May 2nd at the Administration Building and the next regular meeting for Tuesday, May 16th at 7:00 pm at the Services Building.

Minutes of a regular meeting of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, held April 18, 2023 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present were Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart, and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Detmer, Duda, Roncone, Jansen, Canfield, Griffin, Naus, Cottone, Young, Henry, Barsh, Keen, Recker, DiPonio, Keyser, Conaton, Harris, and West. There were approximately 150 members of the audience. The minutes are signed by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, and bear the notation GH/jh.

RECOGNITION. President Schmidt changed the order of the Recognition items on the agenda. The first item was the Mission Moment, recognizing the work of two teachers at Leonard Elementary School: ASD teacher Megan Murray and Literacy Specialist Nancy Haboush, who worked together to create an adapted version of LLI intervention, with the minutes describing its impact on students in the ASD room as nothing short of amazing. Dr. Erin Detmer and Sarah Young were invited up to introduce the teachers and share more about their work. The next item was the Student Spotlight, in which the Board recognizes the creative achievements of students in the TSD Creative Guild; Thomas Butcher was invited up to introduce Grace Cafagna, a senior at Athens High School, and share more about her special work.

Outstanding Support Staff. The Board recognized its Outstanding Support Staff employee of the year, a category that includes bus drivers, secretaries, paraprofessionals, student support aides, custodial staff, food service, technology, childcare, security and more. The district received 25 nominees for Outstanding Support Staff Employee of the Year. Stefanie Gervais was honored as the 2023 Outstanding Support Staff employee of the year. A short video clip was shared of the district's visit to surprise Stefanie, along with words from those who nominated her. She and the rest of the nominees were to be recognized at a reception on May 11th. Stefanie was invited up to say a few words to the Board and receive congratulations.

Outstanding Teachers. The Outstanding Teacher of the Year program received 62 nominations, with educators from every building nominated by families, students and colleagues at the preschool, elementary, middle, and high school levels. Four teachers were selected. A short video was shared of the district's administrative team surprising the winners in their classrooms. All nominees were to be recognized at a reception on April 25th, where they would receive their nomination packets, a small token of appreciation, and the chance to visit with those who nominated them. The four Outstanding Teachers for 2023 are: High School, Erich Beregszaszy, Science Teacher, Athens High School; Middle School, Shannon Dziwanowski, Science Teacher, Larson Middle School; Preschool, Patricia Grandy, Teacher, Troy Preschool; and Elementary, Karen Rosewarne, 5th Grade Teacher, Leonard Elementary School. Mrs. Rosewarne was also selected as the Overall TSD Teacher of the Year for 2023. The winners were sent to Oakland Schools to represent Troy in the Countywide Outstanding Teacher Award program.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS: None. PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (AGENDA ITEMS): None.

Resolution 23-028, moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Anne: a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure to Mr. Brian Canfield, who will begin his duties as Director, Employee Services effective July 1, 2023. Yes: 7. No: 0. Resolution 23-029, under the heading Elementary and Secondary, moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Dr. Wilson: the Board approves the personnel recommendations as stated, listing New Hire: Szczepanski. Yes: 7. No: 0.

CURRICULUM: None.

BUSINESS. Resolution 23-030, THS Gym Floor Renovation, moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Hauff: the bid for gym floor renovation work be awarded to Floor Care Concepts in the amount of $63,930.00, with that amount approved as an expenditure of the Building Site & Sinking Fund and/or the 2023 Bond Fund. Yes: 7. No: 0. Resolution 23-031, Elementary Audio Upgrades, moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Haupt: the bid for Elementary Audio Upgrades be awarded to TelSystems in the amount of $498,676.00, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Bond Fund. Yes: 7. No: 0.

Resolution 23-032, Public-Private Partnership (Troy Racquet Club), moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Philippart. The whereas clauses state that the School District and TRC desire to enter a Public-Private Partnership that positively impacts the students of Troy; that both desire to expand tennis and pickleball offerings to students of Troy School District and the community of Troy through development of a tennis facility on the Troy High School site; that the design of the facility and site will seek to minimize additional concrete and traffic flow issues; that the design will seek to minimize adverse environmental impact through retention of current trees or planting of new trees; that, subject to design and construction approval, the facility would include 12-15 tennis courts, an expansion of the 8 courts that currently exist; that, subject to design and construction approval, the facility would be domed approximately October through April to allow winter play and include outdoor lighting to allow later evening play in the summer; that the facility would be membership-based pay to play for community members and likewise for students outside of the school day; that Troy High School students and staff will have free exclusive access during tennis sections of the Physical Education curriculum; that Troy School District Tennis Programs will have free access during their season; that TRC will provide free membership and access to the club for Troy students who show proof of economically disadvantaged status; that the Board will explore additional sites and opportunities to provide free access to tennis for students and community through development of new tennis courts; and that the District desires to authorize the Superintendent, Dr. Richard Machesky, or his designee, to negotiate and execute a lease agreement with TRC consistent with the resolution, subject to review and approval by the School District's legal counsel. The resolved clause authorizes Dr. Machesky or his designee accordingly. Mrs. Alic explained why she would vote no, stating that while the project would provide some benefit to students it would likely serve mostly private use, and adding that although she was voting no she would support the Board's overall decision in moving forward on the partnership. Yes: 6 (Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson). No: 1 (Alic).

REPORTS FROM STUDENT REPRESENTATIVES. Sara Ali, student representative for Athens High School, reported on events and activities at Athens. Nish Palepu, student representative for Troy High School, was absent. Alexi Papadelis, student representative for Troy College and Career High School, reported on events at her school and announced Arts Beats & Treats on May 12th from 2:30 to 5:00 pm. Yara Mashal, student representative for International Academy-East, reported on events at her school and invited everyone to the Senior Art Show and Empty Bowls Dinner on April 25th.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (NON-AGENDA ITEMS). Mr. Schmidt explained the guidelines for public comment and informed the audience that due to the number of requests submitted, each person would have only one minute to speak, allowing a full hour of public comment. Mr. Joseph Olivier, TSD parent, addressed the Board regarding the Exchange Student Enrollment policy at Troy High and Athens. The following speakers addressed the Board regarding removal of the honors program and supported keeping that as an option for students: Mr. Toby Tang, TSD parent; Mr. Victor Li, 6th grade student at Boulan Park Middle School; Jing Dai, TSD parent; Hengguang Li, TSD parent; Krish Mathrani, junior at IA-East; Mr. Carol Toppi, TSD parent; Mr. Andrew Sosnoski, TSD parent; Ms. Yue (Luna) Xuan, TSD parent; Mr. Steven Sheng, TSD parent; Amy Luo, TSD parent; Le Xia, TSD parent; Mark Gunn, Troy community member who ran for state representative in the 2022 elections; Yan Liang, TSD parent; and Mr. Shan Jiang, TSD parent.

OTHER: None.

BOARD MEMBER COMMENTS. Dr. Philippart described attending the TSD Business Education Roundtable meeting that week and thanked the TSD administration, Doug Tietz, Corewell Health, Magna, and AT&T for participating, speaking about public/private partnerships and project-based learning as an opportunity for students to experience the world of work. Mrs. Anne said she attended the NSBA Conference, where she learned about student voice and the possibility of students having outside mentors. Mrs. Alic noted that Ramadan was coming to a close and wished everyone a belated Happy Passover. Mr. Hauff spoke about the importance of celebrating fine arts and said he visited the Art Show at the Troy Community Center. Dr. Wilson discussed events being showcased around the District and said the Art Show would be open until May 3rd; she thanked the community for voicing concerns and opinions and invited them to watch the District's YouTube channel for recorded Community Conversations about upcoming curriculum changes. Mr. Schmidt announced the next Board Workshop for Tuesday, May 2nd at the Administration Building and the next regular meeting for Tuesday, May 16th at 7:00 pm at the Services Building.

ADJOURNMENT. The meeting adjourned at 9:20 p.m.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education regular meeting held October 15, 2024 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, called to order by President Schmidt at 7:00 p.m. with seven Board members present and roughly 25 people in the audience. Recognitions dominated the evening: resolutions for Learning Disabilities Month and Principal Appreciation Month, 11 national NSPRA awards for the Communications Department, and a resolution honoring sixty-nine 2025 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists. The most consequential action was the award of the new Smith Middle School construction bid in the amount of $8,915,483.00, charged to the Capital Projects Fund, Sinking Fund, and Food Services Fund.

**Meeting and Attendance**
Troy Board of Education regular meeting, October 15, 2024, Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m.; it adjourned at 8:11 p.m. Minutes submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary. Present besides Mr. Schmidt: Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart, and Wilson; Superintendent Machesky; administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Foren, and Trudel. Approximately 25 members of the audience attended.

**Recognition and Mission Moment**
Student Spotlight recognized creative achievement in the TSD Creative Guild; Thomas Butcher introduced Athens senior Maisie Justes and described her journey as a filmmaker. The U.S. Department of Education designates October as Learning Disabilities / Dyslexia / ADHD / Down Syndrome Awareness Month; Governor Whitmer declared October Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan.

**Resolutions adopted**

| Resolution | Moved by | Supported by | Vote |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Learning Disabilities Awareness Month, October 2024 | Dr. Wilson | Dr. Philippart | Yes 7 / No 0 |
| Principal Appreciation Month | Mrs. Alic | Mr. Haupt | Yes 7 / No 0 |
| 2025 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists | Dr. Philippart | Mrs. Alic | Yes 7 / No 0 |

**Meeting identification.** Minutes of a Board Meeting of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, held October 15, 2024 at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois. The meeting of the Troy Board of Education was held at the Troy School District Services Building located at 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present were Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart, and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Foren, and Trudel. There were approximately 25 members of the audience. The meeting adjourned at 8:11 p.m. The minutes are respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the typist notation GH/jh.

**Recognition - Student Spotlight.** The Board introduced the evening's Student Spotlight, the segment in which students are recognized for creative achievements they accomplish in the TSD Creative Guild. The Board invited Thomas Butcher to the podium to introduce Athens senior Maisie Justes and to share about her success in her journey as a filmmaker.

**Mission Moment - Learning Disabilities Awareness Month.** National associations for a number of different learning differences have each declared October as an awareness month, including associations for Dyslexia, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, and Down Syndrome. To honor and magnify those efforts, the U.S. Department of Education has declared October as Learning Disabilities / Dyslexia / Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder / Down Syndrome Awareness Month. In Michigan, Governor Whitmer provided a more encompassing definition and declared October as Learning Disabilities Month, and the Troy Board of Education adopted its own resolution in response.

The resolution, titled Learning Disabilities Awareness Month, October 2024, was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Dr. Philippart. Its recitals state that the term learning disabilities refers to differences in how our brains work, which may affect the acquisition, organization, retention, understanding, or use of verbal or nonverbal information; that learning disabilities range in severity and may impact the acquisition and use of oral language, reading, written language, and mathematics; that 1 in 5 individuals have a learning disability; that learning disabilities may co-exist with other disabilities and conditions and can affect individuals regardless of race, gender, sexual orientation, or other intersecting factors; that disabilities are a natural part of human diversity but individuals with learning disabilities may face discrimination or marginalization; that every person has strengths and learning disabilities should not keep individuals from realizing their full potential; that specialized assessments and interventions involving home, school, community, and workplace settings can significantly enhance quality of life; that appropriate supports and services allow individuals with learning disabilities to achieve their goals and participate fully in society; and that celebrating unique abilities is essential to an inclusive society embracing the potential of all Michigan residents. The resolving clause has the Troy School District Board of Education join Governor Gretchen Whitmer in commemorating October 2024 as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan. Vote: Yes 7, No 0. Resolution adopted.

**Principal Appreciation Month.** Throughout the State of Michigan, October has traditionally been celebrated as Principal Appreciation Month in recognition of the work of building-level educational leaders. The resolution commending elementary and secondary principals was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt. Its recitals state that energetic and inspiring school leadership is essential if teachers, schools, and districts are to ensure that all Troy students are college and career ready; that K-12 school principals play a vital role in student success and act as liaison between the school and the community it serves, ensuring parents and the community are aware of student and school achievements; that Troy School District principals are dedicated, quality educational professionals committed to providing sound leadership and guidance to their staff and students; and that during this month the district joins educators, parents, and students throughout Michigan to raise awareness of the importance of educational leadership and to thank all principals working in Troy. The resolving clause officially recognizes October as Principal Appreciation Month in Troy. Vote: Yes 7, No 0. Resolution adopted.

**2024 National School Public Relations Association (NSPRA) Awards.** The Board recognized the Troy School District Communications Department and invited them forward. The Communications team received 11 national awards this year through the National School Public Relations Association National School Communication Awards: 6 Awards of Excellence, 4 Awards of Merit, and 1 Honorable Mention. The Board expressed pride in the department's creative talent and its work strengthening the bond between the schools and the community.
