https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: The Troy School District Middle School Curriculum Guide for 2024-2025 describes the philosophy, goals, outcomes, and full course catalog for grades 6 through 8 across the district's middle schools. It lays out a three-year scheduling framework in which sixth graders take five academic classes plus every-other-day physical education and an optional every-other-day music or art elective, while seventh and eighth graders take four academic classes plus required Health/Physical Education and Digital Applications 1.0, a full-year music option, and a growing elective load. The most consequential structural feature is that eighth-grade Algebra 1 Honors, Geometry Honors, and World Language I carry high school credit and are figured into the student's high school GPA.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
Overview
The Troy School District Middle School Curriculum Guide for 2024-2025 is an 18-page catalog covering middle school philosophy, goals, student outcomes, a three-year scheduling overview, and course descriptions for grades 6, 7, and 8.

Philosophy, Goals, and Outcomes
Troy middle schools state a commitment to academic excellence and to being developmentally responsive to adolescents' innate curiosity, desire to expand their environment, and need for recognition and personal achievement. The program is characterized by a research-based curriculum with effective assessment and evaluation; a shared vision fostering respect for learning, diversity, and responsible behavior; and a cooperative partnership with parents and community. Goals 1 through 9 cover developmental appropriateness, a diverse student population, core-subject skills, discovery of special interests and aptitudes, diversified cultural/social/civic/vocational/recreational experiences, guidance services promoting self-esteem and independence, community partnerships, transition from elementary to high school, and modeling healthy lifestyles. The stated outcomes are a self-directed learner, a quality worker, a positive communicator, a collaborative and cooperative contributor, and an involved and visionary citizen.

Three-Year Scheduling Overview

| Grade | Academic load | Additional requirements | Elective allowance |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | Five academic classes | Physical Education (EOD, required) | Orchestra, Choir, Band, or Art, all EOD |
| 7 | Four academic classes | Health/Physical Education (1/2 year), Digital Applications 1.0 (1/2 year); music students take Concert Band, Chamber Orchestra, or Choir full year | One full year total (two 1/2-year electives or one full-year elective) |
| 8 | Four academic classes | Music students take Symphonic Band, Advanced Orchestra, or Choir full year | Non-music students: two full years total (four 1/2-year classes, two 1/2-year plus one full-year, or two full-year classes) |

EOD denotes Every Other Day.

Grade 6 Courses
Required full-year courses are ELA 6, Language Arts 6, Mathematics 6 (or another math class), Science 6, Social Studies 6, and Physical Education 6 (full year EOD). Mathematics 6 is organized in ten units: Area and Surface Area; Introducing Ratios; Linear Relationships; Unit Rates and Percentages; Dividing Fractions; Arithmetic in Base Ten; Expressions and Equations; Rational Numbers; Data Sets and Distributions; and Putting it all Together. Grade 6 electives, which meet every other day alternating with PE, are Art 6, Band 6 or Orchestra 6, and 6th Grade Choir.

Grade 7 Courses
Required courses are Digital Applications 1.0 (half year), English 7, Health and Physical Education 7 (half year), Mathematics 7 or another math class, Science 7, and Social Studies 7. Health topics include nutrition, recognizing influences, human sexuality, and choosing healthy behaviors, with information on AIDS and sexually transmitted diseases; parents may excuse their child from human sexuality and AIDS sessions. Social Studies 7 covers ancient world history and geography from the beginning of human history until around 1500.

Grade 8 Courses
Required courses are English 8, Science 8, United States History 8 (Native Americans to 1877), and a math class: Mathematics 8, Algebra 1 Honors, or Geometry Honors. Algebra 1 Honors covers five critical areas and Geometry Honors covers six; both count toward high school credit and are figured into the high school GPA.

Electives
Half-year electives for grades 7 and 8 include 2D Visual Art, 3D Visual Art, Applied Engineering, Art Expressions, Ceramics, Communication Arts, Computer Programming, Computer Science Discoveries, Creation Lab, Digital Applications 2.0, Innovation Incubator, Life Skills, LINKS (teacher recommendation only), Money Matters, Science and Engineering Explorations, Theatre Arts, Video Technology, and Video Technology 2. Full-year offerings include Chamber Orchestra, Choir 7, 7th/8th Choir, Concert Band, Graphic Design/Yearbook, Advanced Orchestra, Choir 8, Fundamentals of Fitness, Jazz Band, Physical Education (Grade 8), Symphonic Band, WEB Leadership, and World Language I in Chinese, French, German, Japanese, or Spanish.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Troy School District Middle School Curriculum Guide for 2024-2025 is an 18-page document setting out the district's middle school philosophy, goals, student outcomes, three-year scheduling structure, and complete course descriptions for grades 6, 7, and 8. Each page carries the running footer "TSD Middle School Curriculum Guide" with the page number and "2024-2025."

Middle School Philosophy. Troy middle schools provide a program that creates an environment recognizing, accepting, respecting, and meeting the diverse needs and characteristics of young adolescent students, with a commitment to academic excellence and to being developmentally responsive to adolescents' natural characteristics: an innate curiosity, a desire to expand their environment, and the need for recognition and personal achievement. The program is characterized by a research-based curriculum with effective assessment and evaluation that is challenging, integrative, and exploratory; sharing a vision with all members of the educational community to foster respect for learning, diversity, and responsible behavior; and a cooperative partnership with parents and members of the community.

Middle School Goals. Goal 1: all programs will be developmentally appropriate. Goal 2: ensure all programs meet the needs of a diverse student population. Goal 3: ensure all students develop skills and knowledge in the core subject areas. Goal 4: provide students the opportunity to discover their special interests, attitudes, aptitudes, and abilities as the basis for determining future actions. Goal 5: provide students with diversified experiences in cultural, social, civic, vocational, and recreational programs. Goal 6: provide guidance services and programs to promote self-esteem, independence, and responsible behavior. Goal 7: provide the opportunity for students to establish partnerships with the community. Goal 8: provide a transition from elementary to high school. Goal 9: provide a model for healthy lifestyles for students.

Middle School Outcomes. In cooperative partnership with home and community, the district commits to preparing each student to become a self-directed learner who is responsible, enthusiastic, and intellectually curious; a quality worker who designs a plan, applies the best possible resources, technologies, and organizational strategies, creates products and performances, monitors development, maintains high standards, and assesses results; a positive communicator; a collaborative and cooperative contributor who creates and sustains productive group relationships; and an involved and visionary citizen who develops an awareness of global issues, contributes positively to local and world communities, advocates for the environment, and prepares to meet future challenges.

Three-Year Middle School Overview. In sixth grade all students are required to take five academic classes plus Physical Education on an every-other-day (EOD) basis; music students may add Orchestra EOD, Choir EOD, or Band EOD, and non-music students may take Art EOD. In seventh grade all students take four academic classes plus required Health/Physical Education for a half year and Digital Applications 1.0 for a half year. Seventh-grade music students take one of Concert Band (full year), Chamber Orchestra (full year), or Choir (full year), with an elective allowance totaling one full year (two half-year classes or one full-year class); non-music seventh graders take elective courses totaling one full year (two half-year electives or one full-year elective). In eighth grade all students take four academic classes; music students take one of Symphonic Band (full year), Advanced Orchestra (full year), or Choir (full year) plus an elective totaling one full year, while non-music eighth graders take a total of two full years of electives, structured as four half-year classes, two half-year classes and one full-year class, or two full-year classes.

Grade 6 required courses. ELA 6 (full year) has students study literature of various genres and informational text including literary nonfiction, with a standards-based focus on comprehension of complex texts, inferences based on textual evidence, thematic and character development, claims and evidence, academic vocabulary, and independent choice reading. Language Arts 6 (full year) covers narrative, informational, and argumentative writing using mentor texts, the writing process, conventions, short and sustained research through inquiry, and digital media presentation. Mathematics 6 (full year, required or another math class) covers ratio and rate, dividing fractions by fractions, negative numbers, and variables, organized into ten units: Unit 1 Area and Surface Area; Unit 2 Introducing Ratios; Unit 3 Linear Relationships; Unit 4 Unit Rates and Percentages; Unit 5 Dividing Fractions; Unit 6 Arithmetic in Base Ten; Unit 7 Expressions and Equations; Unit 8 Rational Numbers; Unit 9 Data Sets and Distributions; Unit 10 Putting it all Together. Physical Education 6 (full year EOD) runs either as a yearlong every-other-day program or an everyday semester class, combining cardio-respiratory fitness with games, skills development, and recreational activities. Science 6 (full year) covers life and earth science with units on cells and heredity, ecology, Earth's changing surface, and species adaptation and survival. Social Studies 6 (full year) is a geography-based course covering physical and human geography, migration and settlement, culture and cultural diffusion, population and demographic changes, resource use, trade and economic interdependence, and the responses of local, national, and international governmental and non-governmental organizations.

Grade 6 electives, which meet every other day alternating with PE, are Art 6 (elements and principles of art, comparing artwork across time and culture), Band 6 or Orchestra 6 (reinforcing fifth-grade skills; students should have taken band or orchestra in fifth grade or had formal instruction), and 6th Grade Choir (organized within the National Core Arts Standards around Perform, Create, Respond, and Connect, with day and evening performances in the schools and community).

Grade 7 courses. Digital Applications 1.0 (half year, required) explores 21st Century or Web 2.0 online tools for interactive information sharing. English 7 (full year) deepens reading comprehension, application, literary response, analysis, and vocabulary development. Health and Physical Education 7 (half year, required) is a combined ten-week course continuing the sixth-grade skill areas; health topics include nutrition, recognizing influences, human sexuality, and choosing healthy behaviors, along with countering messages encouraging tobacco, alcohol, and other drug usage and information on the spread of AIDS and sexually transmitted diseases; parents may excuse their child from class sessions covering human sexuality and AIDS. Mathematics 7 (full year, required or another math class) extends rates and ratios to equivalent ratios and proportional relationships and expands fractions to all rational numbers. Science 7 (full year) covers earth science, physics, and chemistry, including Earth's waters, weather and climate, astronomy, waves, energy, physical and chemical changes, and chemical properties. Social Studies 7 (full year) covers ancient world history and geography with a deliberate focus on content literacy, investigating human history from the beginning until around 1500, early migration and settlement patterns, and pastoral and agrarian societies leading to empires, trade networks, and diffusion of people, resources, and ideas.

Grade 8 courses. Algebra 1 Honors (full year, required or another math class) is a first-year high school algebra course for advanced students with five critical areas: linear equations and inequalities; functions including sequences interpreted graphically, numerically, symbolically, and verbally; regression techniques for approximately linear relationships; equations, inequalities, and systems involving exponential, quadratic, and rational expressions; and specialized functions including absolute value, step, and piecewise-defined functions. The course counts toward a high school credit and is figured into the high school GPA. English 8 (full year) continues study of literature of various genres and informational text. Geometry Honors (full year) is for advanced students who have completed Algebra 1 Honors and covers six critical areas: congruence in terms of rigid motions, geometric constructions, and theorems; similarity transformations and right triangle trigonometry; geometric relationships in the coordinate plane; theorems about circles; geometric measurement for two- and three-dimensional objects; and geometric concepts in modeling situations. It also counts toward a high school credit and is figured into the high school GPA. Mathematics 8 (full year) extends proportional relationships to linear relationships, linear equations in one and two variables, functions, and irrational numbers. Science 8 (full year) covers advanced earth science topics including energy, biogeochemical cycles, resources and human impacts on Earth systems, advanced rock cycle, interior of Earth, plate tectonics theory, earthquakes, volcanoes, hydrogeology, severe weather, Earth in space, the sun, Earth history and geologic time, and climate change, with cooperative lab work and an online Moodle project. United States History 8 (full year) surveys U.S. history from the time of the Native Americans to 1877, treating the American Revolution, formation of the national government, westward movement, and the Civil War and Reconstruction in detail, with periodic study of Michigan history and U.S. foreign affairs.

Grades 7 and 8 half-year electives. 2D Visual Art (painting, collage, drawing, printmaking); 3D Visual Art (papier-mache, clay, batik, mixed media); Applied Engineering (design, computer modeling, advanced manufacturing and construction, stress analysis, mechanical engineering, renewable energy systems, aerodynamics, space and rocketry); Art Expressions (ceramics, drawing, painting, sculpture, printmaking); Ceramics (pinch, coil, and slab construction, plus paper, wire, plaster, wood, and found objects); Communication Arts (public speaking, pantomime, role playing, interviews, listening skills, improvisation); Computer Programming (Introduction to JavaScript: Drawing and Animation; JavaScript: Games and Visualizations; HTML/CSS: Making Webpages; HTML/JS: Making Webpages Interactive; plus building and programming a robot); Computer Science Discoveries (problem solving, programming, physical computing, user-centered design, and data); Creation Lab (S.T.E.A.M. projects including bridge building, soldering, coding, game creation, projectiles); Digital Applications 2.0 (Adobe Creative Suite, video production, animation, digital imaging, Dreamweaver; prerequisite is successful completion of Digital Applications 1.0); Innovation Incubator (design thinking and entrepreneurship, with the cornerstone Larson Innovation Shark Tank project pitched to Metro Detroit business community members including market researchers, patent attorneys, and engineers, plus coding and 3-D printer skills); Life Skills (foods preparation and hand and machine sewing); LINKS, a peer-to-peer support program pairing general education students with students with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and other special needs, available by teacher recommendation only; Money Matters (Michigan Career Pathways, budgets, bank accounts, credit, interest, investing, responsible spending); Science and Engineering Explorations (Science and Engineering Practices, research and experimentation methodologies, the engineering and design cycle, entering work into competitions such as the Science and Engineering Fair of Metro Detroit, or SEFMD); Theatre Arts (acting, improvisation, scene study, with a public performance); Video Technology (digital video cameras, Windows Movie Maker and Apple iMovie editing, PSAs, commercials, music videos, television studio positions, daily live morning news broadcasts, media literacy and copyright ethics); and Video Technology 2, an extension of Video Technology 1.

Full-year electives. Grade 7 offerings include Chamber Orchestra (for students who successfully participated in Orchestra as a sixth grader; many evening performances required), Choir 7, 7th/8th Choir, Concert Band (continuation of sixth-grade band, placement by student proficiency, meeting daily), and Graphic Design/Yearbook, which connects students with the Boulan Park School Community and is open to seventh and eighth graders. Grade 8 offerings include 7th/8th Choir, Advanced Orchestra (for students who successfully participated in Orchestra as a seventh grader; includes a Saturday performance at the MSBOA Orchestra Festival), Choir 8, Fundamentals of Fitness, Graphic Design/Yearbook, Jazz Band (open by audition or teacher approval, previous band experience required, members also participate in a concert band ensemble), Physical Education (Grade 8), Symphonic Band (placement by proficiency, meets daily, two Saturday performances including MSBOA Band Festival), and WEB Leadership, where WEB stands for "Where Everyone Belongs" and student leaders organize school-wide initiatives such as sixth-grade orientation, character and culture programs, charity opportunities, and student mentoring. World Language I (Grade 8) is a full-year, every-day course that counts toward high school credit and is figured into the GPA; the guide notes the class may only be offered at the high school during first hour, requiring parents to provide transportation to the high school with a shuttle returning students to the middle school. The World Language I offerings are Chinese I, French I, German I, Japanese I, and Spanish I, each a full-year elective.

Meeting Details
Board of Education, Troy, Michigan. Board meeting minutes for January 21, 2025, held at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. Vice President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Present in addition to Mrs. Anne were Board members Alic, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts, and Zendler, along with Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Montante, Trudel, and Henry. The four high school student representatives were absent because schools were closed that day due to extreme cold temperatures. Approximately 25 members of the audience attended. The meeting was adjourned at 8:57 p.m.

Organizational Actions
Dr. Philippart was elected acting chairperson (7-0, moved by Mrs. Alic, supported by Mr. Haupt) and appointed Judy Holmes temporary secretary. Officer elections followed by roll call, all unanimous among the seven members:

| Office | Elected | Nominated by | Term |
|---|---|---|---|
| President | Dr. Philippart | Mrs. Alic | until December 31, 2025 |
| Vice President | Mrs. Anne | Mrs. Alic | until December 31, 2025 |
| Secretary | Mrs. Alic | Mr. Haupt | until December 31, 2025 |

The Board adopted the resolution on Fund Depositories and Investments for January through December 2025, designating Bank of America, Citizens Bank, JP Morgan Chase Bank, Comerica Bank, Huntington Bank, Fifth Third Bank, Flagstar Bancorp, MILAF (Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Plus, managed by PFM Asset Management, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank), and PNC Bank. Funds may be invested according to Board Policy 5000.06, and the Treasurer may combine money from more than one fund under subsection (1)(h) of Section 380.1223 of the Revised School Code. Clark Hill, PLC, Collins & Blaha, P.C., Miller Johnson, Thrun Law Firm, P.C., and Miller Canfield were continued as legal counsel for calendar year 2025. The Superintendent was continued as Deputy Secretary, and Judy Holmes, Secretary to the Superintendent of Schools, was designated to post meeting notices. The 2025 meeting schedule and Board Committee Memberships were adopted, each 7-0.

Recognition and Reports
The TSD Mission Moment on the IA-East Capstone Experience / IB Middle Years Programme was moved to the February 25, 2025 meeting due to the school cancellation. Dr. Machesky read a statement for School Board Appreciation Month and presented gifts of appreciation. Melissa Prowse, Manager of Planning and Development for Oakland County Parks, introduced Brian Marzolf, Land Protection Manager of Six Rivers Land Conservancy, standing in for executive director Chris Bunch, who reported on Turtle Woods Nature Preserve: after an unfunded 2023 Trust Fund application, a 2024 application with increased match was awarded $2,175,000 in December, with construction projected to begin 2026-2027 for a parking lot, restrooms, trails, and boardwalks.

Business Actions

| Project | Total | Fund |

Minutes of the Troy Board of Education meeting of January 21, 2025, held at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan. Vice President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mrs. Anne, present were Board members Alic, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts, and Zendler. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Montante, Trudel, and Henry. The four high school student representatives were not in attendance because schools were closed that day due to extreme cold temperatures. Approximately 25 members of the audience were in attendance. Mrs. Anne explained that the evening's meeting is where the Board selects officers, appoints committee members for the upcoming year, and approves or authorizes items that must be considered on an annual basis, with the regular Board meeting following the organizational portion.

Election of Acting Chairperson. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt that Dr. Philippart serve as acting chairperson to officiate the meeting until the election of a president was completed. The vote was Yes: 7, No: 0.

Appointment of Temporary Secretary. Dr. Philippart appointed Judy Holmes to act as temporary secretary until the secretary of the Troy Board of Education had been elected.

Nomination and Election of President. Acting Chairperson Philippart declared nominations in order for the office of Board president. Mrs. Alic nominated Dr. Philippart. It was moved by Mrs. Potts and supported by Mrs. Anne that nominations be closed; Yes: 7, No: 0. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt that Dr. Philippart serve as president of the Troy Board of Education until December 31, 2025. On the roll call vote, Alic, Anne, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts, and Zendler all voted Yes.

Nomination and Election of Vice President. President Philippart declared nominations in order for vice president. Mrs. Alic nominated Mrs. Anne. It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Anne that nominations be closed; Yes: 7, No: 0. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Anne that Mrs. Anne serve as vice president until December 31, 2025. On the roll call vote, Anne, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts, Zendler, and Alic all voted Yes.

Nomination and Election of Secretary. President Philippart declared nominations in order for secretary. Mr. Haupt nominated Mrs. Alic. It was moved by Dr. Melton and supported by Mr. Haupt that nominations be closed; Yes: 7, No: 0. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Haupt that Mrs. Alic serve as secretary until December 31, 2025. On the roll call vote, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts, Zendler, Alic, and Anne all voted Yes.

Appointment of School Board Treasurer. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Haupt that Dan Trudel, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, be appointed as Treasurer of the Troy Board of Education for the period January through December 2025. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Establish Fund Depositories and Investments. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Anne that the Board adopt the resolution on Fund Depositories and Investments for the period January through December 2025, with a copy of the attached resolution incorporated in its entirety as part of the official minutes. The resolution recites that public monies belonging to or held for the State, County, or other political units of the State may come into the hands of Daniel Trudel, Treasurer of Troy School District, and that under the laws of Michigan the Board is required to provide by Resolution for the deposit of all public monies, including tax monies. The Treasurer is directed to deposit and/or invest all public monies in his name as Treasurer into the following depository institutions: Bank of America; Citizens Bank; JP Morgan Chase Bank; Comerica Bank; Huntington Bank; Fifth Third Bank; Flagstar Bancorp; MILAF (Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Plus, managed by PFM Asset Management, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank); and PNC Bank. Monies may be withdrawn by checks signed with a facsimile signature of Treasurer Daniel Trudel, and in emergencies the handwritten signature of Daniel Trudel or Superintendent Richard M. Machesky, who may sign on the General Fund account and the Payroll account at Bank of America. Monies in the accounts established at PNC Bank for paying Troy Career Center expenses may be withdrawn by checks with the handwritten signature of the Troy Career Center Manager, Assistant Manager, or Program Coordinators. The Treasurer may open or close accounts with the listed institutions provided it is in the interest of the District. District funds may be invested according to Board Policy 5000.06, and the Treasurer is authorized to combine money from more than one fund for the purpose of making an investment authorized by subsection (1)(h) of Section 380.1223 of the Revised School Code. The maximum amount to be invested with the above institutions is regulated by the school code. The certification reads: "I, Emina Alic, Secretary of Troy School District, Oakland County, Michigan, certify that the Resolution was adopted by said Board at a meeting thereof held on the date specified above," given under hand and seal of the Troy School District in the County of Oakland in the State of Michigan this 21st day of January 2025. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Designation of Board and District Legal Counsel. It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Anne to continue the designation of Clark Hill, PLC; Collins & Blaha, P.C.; Miller Johnson; Thrun Law Firm, P.C.; and Miller Canfield as legal counsel to advise and/or represent the Troy School District and Board of Education as necessary for the 2025 calendar year, with the superintendent authorized to consult additional counsel as needed with prior notification to the board. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Designation of Superintendent to be Deputy Secretary. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Dr. Melton to continue the designation of the Superintendent of Schools as Deputy Secretary of the Board with authority to act for the secretary for the 2025 calendar year. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Designation of Person for Posting Notices of Meetings. It was moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Anne that the person designated for posting notices of meetings for the 2025 calendar year shall be Judy Holmes, Secretary to the Superintendent of Schools. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Meeting Schedule and Committee Assignments. It was moved by Mrs. Potts and supported by Mrs. Alic that the Board adopt the schedule of meetings for the 2025 calendar year as indicated on the attached calendar; Yes: 7, No: 0. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Board adopt the Board Committee Memberships for the 2025 school year as attached; Yes: 7, No: 0.

Recognition. Dr. Machesky announced that the TSD Mission Moment on the IA-East Capstone Experience / IB Middle Years Programme had been moved to the February 25, 2025, Board of Education Meeting due to the cancellation of school that day. For Board Recognition Month, Dr. Machesky read a statement noting that each January the Troy School District honors and celebrates the trustees of its Board of Education, that School Board Appreciation Month recognizes the critical role board members play in reinforcing the district mission of ensuring learning for all, and thanking members for shaping policies, fiscal stewardship, and support of world-class teaching and learning. He then presented the members with a gift of appreciation.

Turtle Woods Update. Melissa Prowse, Manager of Planning and Development for Oakland County Parks, shared that Chris Bunch, Executive Director of Six Rivers Land Conservancy, was ill and unable to attend. She introduced Brian Marzolf, Land Protection Manager of Six Rivers Land Conservancy, who provided a report updating the community on the progress of the Turtle Woods Nature Preserve. Partners in the initiative with Oakland County Parks have been Six Rivers Land Conservancy, Troy School District, City of Troy, and Stage Nature Center. They applied to the Trust Fund in 2023 and were not funded; they applied in 2024 with increased match and were awarded $2,175,000 in December. Construction is projected to begin 2026-2027 and will include a parking lot, restrooms, trails, and boardwalks. Turtle Woods Nature Preserve will become a public park as soon as the project is complete. Dr. Machesky recognized Ida Edmunds, a Troy School District Board Member for over 30 years and a proponent of preserving the property who helped initiate the project, and also recognized former Troy School Board President Karl Schmidt, who helped push the project over the finish line.

Additions and Deletions: none. Public Communication (non-agenda items): Dr. Philippart provided the opportunity for community members to address the Board for both agenda and non-agenda items; seven community members addressed the Board during public communication and no action was taken by the Board.

Consent Agenda. It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Alic that the Board approve items A, B, and C on the consent agenda: minutes of the December 3, 2024, Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the December 17, 2024, Board of Education Meeting; and the Treasurer's Report for November 2024. Yes: 7, No: 0. Personnel: none. Curriculum: none.

Business: THS Kitchen Server Project. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mrs. Alic that the bid for remodeling the kitchen serving area at Troy High be awarded as follows and that the amount be approved as an expenditure of the Food Services Fund: Selective Demolition, Graham Construction, $48,700.00; General Trades, Graham Construction, $219,335.00; Hard Tile, Omega Floors, $51,500.00; Food Service Equipment, Great Lakes Hotel Supply, $675,491.00; Mechanical, Quality Air Systems, $148,800.00; Electrical, Innovative Energy Controls, $206,815.00; TOTAL $1,350,641.00. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Business: 2025 Paving Replacement Project. It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Anne that the bid for Site Work Paving Projects be awarded as follows and that the amount be approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund: Paving, T&M Asphalt Paving Replacement/Resurfacing, $2,193,770.00; 6% Contingency, $131,626.00; Great Lakes Landscape Design, Barnard Drainage System & Installation, $112,537.00; TOTAL $2,437,933.00. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Business: 2025 Flooring Replacement Project. It was moved by Dr. Melton and supported by Mr. Haupt that the bid for flooring replacement work be awarded as follows and that the amount be approved as an expenditure of the Building Site & Sinking Fund: Conventional Carpet, Flooring Demo/Replacement, $744,015.21; Diamond Shine Polishing, Floor Polishing, $85,450.00; Additional/Emergency Flooring, $50,000.00; TOTAL $879,465.21. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Public Communication (non-agenda items), second call: Dr. Philippart noted that he had provided an opportunity for all community members who wished to speak during the evening's meeting to address the board at the beginning of the meeting under agenda items.

Other: Attendance Area Review Update Report. Dr. Machesky introduced Paul Wills, partner at Plante Moran Realpoint, who shared a PowerPoint presentation with the Board and community providing an update on the Attendance Area Review process. He shared the background for why the process was started and the work of the group to date, discussed each phase of the process, and indicated that the district will seek community feedback in Phase 3 between February and April. TSD will hold four listening sessions for families, one at each middle school, and will send out a community survey for additional feedback. He reviewed enrollment history and projected enrollment and discussed elementary schools that are split to different middle schools, and shared Option C in more detail. Board members discussed the process and raised questions about transportation for siblings who are grandfathered in and about building utilization and current use of buildings.

Board Comments: Board members offered sentiments and comments before the close of the meeting.

Adjournment. Dr. Philippart announced that the next Board Workshop will be held on Tuesday, February 11th at 6:00 pm in the Administration Building and the next Board Meeting will be held on Tuesday, February 25th at 7:00 pm in the Services Building. The meeting was adjourned at 8:57 p.m. Respectfully submitted, Emina Alic, Secretary, Troy Board of Education. Reference notation: EA/jh.

Overview
TMP Architecture, Inc. of Bloomfield Hills submitted a furnishing recommendation dated August 31, 2023 to Ms. Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Education, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, MI 48098. The package covers the Troy Central Office Board Room (TMP Project No. 22106A, 4400 Livernois Road) and the Troy Services Building Board Room (TMP Project No. 22107A, 4420 Livernois Road). Quotes were obtained based on pre-existing bid contracts (consortiums). The letter is signed by Keri Seeney, NCIDQ, Associate | Interior Designer, with a copy to Laura Casai of TMP Architecture.

Recommended Awards

| Category | Manufacturer | Dealer | Quote Amount |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | KI | Interior Office Source | $74,738.10 |
| B | VS America | Great Lakes Furniture Supply | $3,162.60 |
| C | Media Technologies | Dew-El | $2,651.69 |
| D | Steelcase | NBS | $886.18 |
| E | SurfaceWorks | NBS | $3,067.38 |
| | | TOTAL AMOUNT | $84,505.95 |

Specified Furniture
Category A (KI) covers item A1, 18 PINR2460T Pirouette nesting training tables, 29 inches high, 24 x 60 inches, for the Central Office Board Room; item A2, 18 PINR3060T Pirouette tables, 30 x 60 inches, for the Services Building Board Room; item A3, 36 LLA200 LimeLite four-leg nesting armless chairs, seat height 18-1/4 inches, Central Office; item A4, 72 LL2200 LimeLite four-leg stacking chairs with casters, Services Building; and item A5, 8 LL6200 LimeLite height-adjustable task stools, seat height 22-3/4 to 32-3/4 inches, Services Building. Category B is item B1, VS America model 01471 Team Table, 65 x 44-7/8 inches, 40 inches high, anthracite finishes, Services Building Board Room. Category C is item C1, a Media Technologies CS7236-24 Rubix mobile storage unit, 72 inches wide by 24 inches deep by 36 inches high, Central Office Board Room. Category D is item D1, two Steelcase PFLHUB Thread power hubs at 37-1/8 inch desk height in Merle (7360) finish. Category E is item E1, a SurfaceWorks RLNLECT2730SL Dewey Collection lectern with technology storage, pneumatic height adjustment, overall height 37 to 44 inches.

Contract Terms
The Owner may hold quotes ninety days. Each quote must carry a notarized familial relationship disclosure under Public Act 232 of 2004, a Non-Collusion Affidavit, and a Certification of Compliance with the Iran Economic Sanctions Act (Michigan Public Act No. 517 of 2012, with a civil penalty of not more than $250,000.00 or two times the contract amount, whichever is greater, and three-year bid ineligibility for a false certification). Dealers must carry Comprehensive General Liability and Automobile Liability insurance of $1,000,000 per person and $1,000,000 per occurrence, and $1,000,000 property damage per occurrence, with thirty days written notice of cancellation and Troy School District named as insured. Delivery is between 8:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. in Fall 2023, with installation complete by Fall 2023 and a pre-installation notice issued three to four weeks ahead. Payment reaches 80 percent of the bid category after installation and the Architect's initial punch list, with the balance on final approval; invoices go to Mr. Rick West, Assistant Superintendent for Business Services. The project is not subject to prevailing wage rate requirements for Oakland County, and warranties run one year from project completion and Owner acceptance. Submittal review allows 15 working days for an initial review and 15 working days for a resubmittal.

Recommendation Letter
TMP Architecture, Inc., 1191 West Square Lake Road, Bloomfield Hills, Michigan 48302-0374 (PH 248.338.4561, FX 248.338.0223), wrote to Ms. Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Education, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, MI 48098, on August 31, 2023, transmitting a furnishing recommendation for the Central Office Board Room and Services Board Room under TMP Project No. 22106A / 22107A. Quotes were obtained based on pre-existing bid contracts (consortiums). TMP recommended awards as follows: Category A, KI product through dealer Interior Office Source, $74,738.10; Category B, VS America through Great Lakes Furniture Supply, $3,162.60; Category C, Media Technologies through Dew-El, $2,651.69; Category D, Steelcase through NBS, $886.18; Category E, SurfaceWorks through NBS, $3,067.38; TOTAL AMOUNT $84,505.95. Enclosures comprised dealer assurances, specifications, pricing quotes and drawings. The letter was signed by Keri Seeney, NCIDQ, Associate | Interior Designer, copied to Laura Casai (TMP Architecture).

Package Structure
The furnishings package, dated 08/31/2023 and marked ISSUED FOR BOARD APPROVAL, lists the Owner as Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Road, and the Architect as TMP Architecture, Inc. (info@tmp-architecture.com). Its table of contents covers proposal requirements sections 007000-F General Conditions, 008050-F Contractor Code of Conduct, and 013300-F Submittal Procedures; furnishing specifications for Categories A through E; and drawings A12.1A Furniture Plan for the Central Offices Board Room and A12.1A Furniture Plan for the Services Building Board Room. Project locations are the Troy Central Office Board Room Furnishings at 4400 Livernois Road and the Troy Services Building Board Room Furnishings at 4420 Livernois Road.

General Conditions
The Owner and Architect may stop work to ensure proper interpretation; the Owner's representative accepts deliveries and reports missing or damaged items through the Architect; a final inspection is conducted jointly. The Architect interprets all work, visits periodically, prepares a punch list, and approves materials, fabrics, finishes, colors and details. The Owner reserves the right to hold quotes ninety (90) days. Each quote must be accompanied by a sworn, notarized familial relationship statement, a Non-Collusion Affidavit, and a signed Certification of Compliance with the Iran Economic Sanctions Act; consortium or cooperative pricing must reference the specific contract. Contract award occurs on issuance of a Purchase Order, perfected on delivery of a Certificate of Insurance. The Owner is not subject to Michigan State or Federal excise taxes. Required insurance is Comprehensive General Liability and Automobile Liability covering personal injury or death at $1,000,000 per person and $1,000,000 per occurrence and property damage of $1,000,000 per occurrence, plus Workmen's Compensation and Employer's Liability, with thirty (30) days written notice of cancellation and Troy School District specifically named. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A Board presentation summarizing the data-gathering phase of the Troy School District Portrait of a Graduate exercise, drawing on parent surveys, a K-12 principals discussion, and classroom conversations with students. The research produced twelve traits expected of a Troy graduate, ranging from Visionary and Connected to Organized and Confident Communicator, and reported near-perfect overlap in the priorities named by students, parents and principals. Parent input alone comprised 308 completed surveys generating more than 24,000 words of transcript, of which 94 percent of remarks were positive and constructive.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
Purpose
The exercise was launched because outside experts such as Tony Wagner emphasize seeking input from the stakeholders most influenced by district policy, because the strategic plan refresh surfaced a call for stronger student voice, and because the Board had asked for a clearer measure of success from a student perspective. The stated goal was to identify what traits should be visible in students if the District is delivering on its promise of a world class education.

Sample

| Group | Method | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| Parents | 3-question open-ended survey | 308 completed surveys; 60+ pages of transcripts; 24,000+ words; 94% positive and constructive remarks |
| Principals | 45-minute discussion | All-principals K-12 meeting |
| Students | 30-minute discussions | 4 high schools, 3 middle schools, 4 elementary, 1 preschool; 16 total classrooms; 320+ students |

Core Question Progression
Participants were asked what the best of what the District is doing to date is; what the most critical hard and soft skills are that should be fostered before students leave; and what the secret sauce is that should mark a Troy graduate as an adult.

Findings
Students, parents and principals showed an almost perfect overlap in stated priorities, and those priorities aligned tightly with the District Strategic Plan. The presentation frames the net conclusion as either District strategy matching parent and student ideals, effective communication of the Pillars to key stakeholders, or both. A Leonard second grader supplied the framing quote: a portrait is two things, a picture of you and the best parts of you.

Twelve Traits of a TSD Graduate
Visionary; Connected; Kind, compassionate, and inclusive; Joyous about discovery; Eager for challenge; Tenacious; Intellectual crackerjack; Adaptable; Self-starter; Good team player; Organized; Confident communicator. Each trait carries a definition plus supporting observations. Recurring student themes include a felt disconnect between classroom content and future degree programs or careers, the primacy of teacher relationships, a preference for project-based exploration over what high schoolers described as informational cramming, and the value of trial-and-error work. Students at the two larger high schools felt caring teachers were more the exception than the rule, while students at TCCHS and IAE identified adult engagement and emotional investment as a primary reason for their success. Parent themes include interpersonal connection, grit, source discernment, intellectual flexibility, organization and time management, and communication across changing media.

Mapping and Takeaways
The twelve traits were mapped to the strategic plan areas of EC to Career, Equity and Well-Being, Deep Learning, and Building Capacity. Six broad takeaways were reported: parents hold clear expectations beyond academic success; students know and appreciate deep learning when they experience it; students recognize the need for broader skill sets; everyone grasps the importance of student-adult connections; the more advanced the grade, the less ideal the educational and skill set delivery; and outstanding adults modeling the strategic ideals exist at every level, making the central challenge expanding those examples until they become the norm.

Next Steps
The Board of Education led the research, analysis and creation of the initial construct. Central Administration is now tasked with integrating the findings into professional development across the organization, which will shift the original structure. The presentation suggests sharing the results in their original form with parents and parent groups, and using the traits as a common Board framework for assessing the impact of new pedagogies and the depth of student work across grade levels and subject areas.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Rationale
The Portrait of a Graduate Data Gathering Summary opens by citing outside experts like Tony Wagner, who continue to emphasize the importance of and value in seeking the input of stakeholders most influenced by district policies and focus, namely students. When feedback was gathered for the strategic plan refresh, the organization said loudly and clearly that stronger student voice was needed as part of building a world class experience for Troy students. The Board had also consistently asked for a clearer measure of success from a student perspective as the central tenets of the strategic plan are executed. The District pursued a Portrait of a Troy Graduate exercise as a way to better identify what student traits should be visible if the District is successfully delivering on its promise of a world class education.

Sample and Method
Parents completed a 3-question open-ended survey: 308 completed surveys, more than 60 pages of transcripts, more than 24,000 words, with 94% positive and constructive remarks. Principals participated in a 45-minute discussion at an all-principals K-12 meeting. Students took part in 30-minute discussions across 4 high schools, 3 middle schools, 4 elementary schools and 1 preschool, comprising 16 total classrooms and more than 320 students. The core question progression asked what the best of what the District is doing to date is; what the most critical hard and soft skills are that should be fostered and developed in students before they leave; and, as an adult, what the secret sauce is that should mark a Troy graduate.

Consensus
The presentation reports a near perfect consensus among students, parents and principals, describing an almost perfect overlap in stated priorities that were in tight alignment with the District Strategic Plan. The stated net conclusion is that either District strategy is in line with parent and student ideals, the District has effectively communicated the value of the Pillars to key stakeholder groups, or both. Framing the concept, Karl asked how a portrait differs from a regular picture of someone, and a Leonard second grader answered that a portrait is two things, a picture of you and the best parts of you.

The Twelve Traits
Visionary: can confidently connect formal education and student experiences to the real world and to immediate and long-term futures. Highlight educational experiences almost always made strong connections between subject material and reality, and students described aha moments when those connections were made. Students, particularly high schoolers, often described a disconnect between classroom work and how learning applies to a specific degree program or career, and complained that career planning was disconnected from academics.
Connected: a person who has built meaningful relationships with peers and adults and understands the deep value in those connections. In a world recently marked by isolation and a generation trapped in social media, parents were emphatic about a school experience that builds strong interpersonal relationships for social and emotional stability as well as career advancement. Students at all grade levels also spoke about feeling connected to peers and teachers. High schoolers held teacher relationships up as one of the most important elements of academic and social success, tied to whether they were confident their teachers cared about them as people. In the two larger high schools, students felt caring teachers were more the exception than the rule, while at TCCHS and IAE students identified adult engagement, including emotional investment, as a primary reason for their success.
Kind, compassionate, and inclusive: intrinsically treats others with kindness, respect and fairness. These themes were prominent in parent responses, which tied them to interpersonal skills and broader productive citizenship. Asked what a satisfied employer might see in someone that would suggest a Troy origin, students said they want to be recognized as people who care about and take care of those around them. Both groups stressed recognizing and valuing differences in an increasingly multicultural world.
Joyous about discovery: an enthusiastic lifelong learner, curious about the world and eager to explore new topics and ventures, often just for fun. Parents want children who continue to grow intellectually because they value learning for its own sake. Students did not name this as a desired future differentiator but demonstrated joy, curiosity and excitement about past opportunities to explore on their own terms, experiment and learn by trial and error. The summary paraphrases a common student sentiment: graduates should want to learn something because it fascinates them, not because it is going to be on the test.
Eager for challenge: excited to tackle any challenge and unafraid of Big Hairy Audacious Goals. The trait describes someone bold and confident whom people ask to lead a difficult situation. For parents this linked tightly to tenacity and grit; for students it was more about who they want to be and how they want to be viewed. Ambitious student projects outside core academics, such as Charity Week, are highly valued because they let students tackle a BHAG and see results greater than they thought themselves capable of, breeding confidence for future ones.
Tenacious: marked by grit, a determination to work through challenges and persevere to resolution, and adept in situations requiring productive struggle. Parents worry about educational environments or teaching styles that spoon feed information or provide easy assistance. For students at every grade level tenacity is highly valued, and one of the most commonly desired employer-identified traits was confidence that a Troy graduate given a task will figure out how to make it happen and will not stop pressing until the goal is reached.
Intellectual crackerjack: proficient at drawing meaningful conclusions and developing implications from informational sources, data, research and people, an adept synthesizer of input. One parent described wanting their child to have the intellectual skills to understand reality, while most described recognizing the validity of information sources, drawing conclusions from trustworthy pieces, and adjusting them as new valid information appears. Rather than learning about things, these parents want students taught how to explore, discern and develop their own informed perspectives. Students describe wanting to be seen as smart because they know how to gather good data and figure things out, one reason large, in-depth, longer-deadline projects were a perennial favorite way of learning.
Adaptable: possesses the flexibility to incorporate new information and the willingness to pivot when necessary or beneficial. Many parents railed against intellectual rigidity. Students did not name this as a desired trait but repeatedly held up assignments requiring trial and error or a pivot as situations where their learning went into hyperdrive, saying the process of figuring it out and adjusting from initial errors shifted learning from short-term cramming to long-term, deeper understanding.
Self-starter: confident and willing to tackle deep, complex projects with little assistance. Parents framed this as the ability to take on individual projects and manage them effectively. Students value collaborative work but also want regular opportunities to execute multi-week, multi-layered projects on their own, both for higher education and work and for the control over what they research or create. High schoolers in particular described most current classwork as informational cramming aimed at retention testing rather than applied mastery, and turned repeatedly to project-based exploration as their preferred approach.
Good team player: can lead or contribute as a group member with ease, understanding interpersonal dynamics, allocation of responsibilities, intellectual humility when others have higher expertise, and how to move a group forward productively and positively. Parents and students at all grade levels recognized the need to master group work. All stakeholder groups noted the binary temptation to see a student as either driving a group project or leeching off it, and observed that meaningful contribution means continuous curiosity so that students who did not start as the expert can become one. Students consistently asked for a mix of team and individual work.
Organized: possesses top-notch organization, time management and project management skills. Parents begged the District for help in this area to emphasize how important the skill is. Students were less likely to list it as a desired trait, though some at every level wanted to hone organizational skills before graduating, and noted that complex, longer-term projects require mapping out the entire process and completing steps in a timely manner.
Confident communicator: able to easily convey ideas, information and their own perspective through one-on-one conversation, writing and a variety of interactive media. Described as universally valued, with both parents and students wanting communications practice incorporated across every aspect of a student's academic career, and parents attentive to the constantly changing and fractured communications landscape.

Mapping to the Strategic Plan
The twelve traits were mapped against the strategic plan areas listed as EC to Career, Equity and Well-Being, Deep Learning, and Building Capacity.

Six Broad Takeaways
Parents have clear, powerful expectations of the District that go well beyond academic success. Students know and appreciate deep learning when they experience it. Students recognize the need to develop broader skill sets for later success. Everyone grasps the extreme importance of strong connections between students and District adults. Currently, the more advanced the grade, the less ideal the educational and skill set delivery. At every grade level there are outstanding adults modeling the strategic ideals, making the biggest challenge expanding those examples until they become the norm.

So Now What
As requested, the Board of Education was given the opportunity to lead the research, analysis and creation of the initial Portrait of a Graduate construct. Central Administration is now tasked with integrating the findings into professional development across the organization in a way staff can digest and that becomes part of the life blood of the District, so the original structure will shift. The presentation notes possible value in sharing the results in their original form with parents and parent groups so they understand the broader educational and personal goals for all students, and suggests the Board could use the traits as a common framework for assessing the impact of new pedagogies and the depth of student work across grade levels and subject areas.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education meeting held July 18, 2023 at the Administration Building, 4400 Livernois, called to order by President Schmidt at 9:30 a.m. and adjourned at 9:58 a.m. The Board adopted a seven-item consent agenda and approved five personnel resolutions, including two-year probationary administrative contracts for Larson Middle School Principal Brian Zawislak and Communications Director Kendra Montante, contract extensions through June 30, 2025 for building administrators and the three assistant superintendents, and an extension of the Superintendent's contract running July 1, 2023 through June 30, 2028. Every recorded vote was 6 yes, 0 no, with Mrs. Alic absent.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
Attendance
The meeting was held at the Troy School District Administration Building, 4400 Livernois. President Schmidt called it to order at 9:30 a.m. Present with Mr. Schmidt were Board members Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart and Wilson; Mrs. Alic was absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky; administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Fulcher, Keyser and West; and approximately 4 other members of the audience. There were no recognitions and no additions or deletions.

Public Communication
Mr. Schmidt adjusted the agenda to move public comment for non-agenda items up and invited two audience members who had submitted forms. Mr. Jeff Schaeper, a Troy resident, addressed de-tracking students in ELA and de-tracking in the middle school math honors program, saying the Board will bear responsibility for the outcome of the change in teaching and curriculum. Ms. Kristin Pingree, a TSD parent, addressed math curricula in Washington and Texas, said increased communication is important, and asked the District to put forth more of an outreach effort.

Consent Agenda (Resolution 23-050)
Moved by Mr. Hauff, supported by Mr. Haupt, approving items A through G: minutes of the June 6, 2023 Special Board of Education meeting; the June 6, 2023 Closed Session; the June 6, 2023 Board Workshop; the June 13, 2023 Board of Education Meeting; the June 28, 2023 Special Board of Education Meeting; the Treasurer's Report for May 2023; and the Michigan High School Athletic Association (MHSAA) Membership Resolution 2023/2024. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Alic.

Personnel Actions

| Resolution | Action | Mover / Support | Vote |
|---|---|---|---|
| 23-051 | Two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure to Mr. Brian Zawislak, Principal, Larson Middle School, effective July 19, 2023 | Anne / Philippart | 6-0, Alic absent |
| 23-052 | Two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure to Ms. Kendra Montante, Director of Communications and Strategic Initiatives, effective August 1, 2023 | Wilson / Hauff | 6-0, Alic absent |

| 23-054 | Extension of contracts for Rick West, Kris Griffor and Christine DiPilato through June 30, 2025 | Philippart / Anne | 6-0, Alic absent |
| 23-055 | Extension of the Superintendent contract, July 1, 2023 through June 30, 2028 | Philippart / Hauff | 6-0, Alic absent |

Discussion
Dr. Wilson asked why the TCCHS principal was not included with the administrative contracts presented. Dr. Machesky said the TCCHS principal position has never been part of the Administrative Handbook and that the Board could discuss adding the position at the September or October workshop to bring it more in line with the others.

Other Business
Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Haupt, the Board approved the Sex Education Advisory Board membership for the Troy School District for the 2023/2024 school year as shown on the attached list. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Alic. Mrs. Anne asked whether all schools have someone representing them in the SEAB membership; Ms. DiPilato said they do not.

Adjournment
Mr. Schmidt announced the next Board of Education meeting for August 16th at 6:00 p.m. in the Administration Building. The meeting adjourned at 9:58 a.m. Minutes submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: An administrative report to the Troy School District Board of Education, dated February 7, 2023, summarizing the annual revisions to the High-School Course Description Book (CDB) for the 2023/2024 school year. The CDB is described as a OneTroy document developed collaboratively by administrators and department heads from both high schools together with the teaching and learning team, and it is updated each year as part of the district's curriculum review process. The most consequential change is a restructured science and English pathway: newly developed Chemistry 1 and 9 English courses become required for all students beginning with the class of 2027, while Active Chemistry/Earth Science and the two existing English 9 courses are removed.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
Purpose
The High-School Course Description Book (CDB) sets out course requirements and opportunities for Troy School District high school students. It is organized by department so that students and families understand the offerings. It is identified as a OneTroy document developed collaboratively by administrators and department heads from both high schools and the teaching and learning team. The CDB is updated annually as part of the curriculum review process, with department teams determining where course descriptions should be updated to reflect new curriculum and instruction, and where courses should be added or deleted. The report lists the changes made for the 2023/2024 school year.

Courses Added

| Course | Grades | Length / Credit | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Chemistry 1 | 9-12 | 1 semester, ½ credit, No Retake | Newly developed revision of the previously taught full year Chemistry class; required for all students beginning with the class of 2027; satisfies ½ credit of the math related graduation requirement during the 12th grade year |
| Chemistry 2 | 9-12 | 1 semesters, ½ credit, No Retake | Pre-requisite: Chemistry 1; in development, to begin running in the second semester of the 23/23 school year; satisfies 1/2 credit of the math related graduation requirement during the 12th grade year; pre-requisite for Advanced Placement Chemistry |
| 9 English | 9th grade | 2 semesters, 1 credit, ½ credit per semester | Newly developed revision of previously taught 9th grade English courses; required for all students beginning with the class of 2027 |
| Intensified Algebra 1 | Grades 9 | 2 semesters, 1 credit per semester, No retake | Prerequisite: None; currently being piloted at THS and AHS; scheduled in collaboration with the math specialist |
| Mindful Art | — | 1 semester, ½ credit per semester, Retakes: 1 | New course designed in collaboration with the counseling and art departments |

Course Content Highlights
Chemistry 1 covers energy, atomic structure, bonding, chemical reactions, solution, and combustion, with analytical problem solving of real-life phenomena and laboratory techniques. Chemistry 2 extends this to atomic structure, bonding, chemical reactions, solutions, acid-base chemistry, thermodynamics, equilibrium, and gas laws, noting that a strong foundation in algebra is important and that students interested in any STEM related field are encouraged to take it. 9 English is a foundational course emphasizing in-depth study of multiple genres of reading and modes of writing and speaking, with novels, short stories, poetry, nonfiction texts, mentor texts, and book clubs, and essays including literary analysis, informational, argumentative, and narrative. Intensified Algebra 1 targets conceptual understanding, mathematical skills, and problem-solving and reasoning, including metacognition and multiple representations of linear, absolute value, quadratic, rational, polynomial, power, and exponential functions; successful completers will be prepared for Geometry. Mindful Art combines mindfulness concepts with art activities addressing personal identity, stress reduction and coping skills, relationship skills through collaboration and community work, and gratitude.

Courses Removed
Advanced Swimming and Lifetime Sports & Fitness (to be combined with lifeguarding as Lifeguarding, Advanced Swimming and Lifetime Sports & Fitness); Active Chemistry/Earth Science (both removed due to the newly restructured science course pathway); Beginning & Intermediate Swimming and Lifetime Sports & Fitness (combined with Learning to Swim as Learning to Swim: Beginning & Intermediate Swimming and Lifetime Sports & Fitness); Emerging Engineering (re-titled Mechatronics); English 9 Literature and Compositions and English 9 Literature and Composition Honors (removed in favor of the newly designed required English course beginning with the class of 2027); Intermediate Tumbling and Gymnastics (combined with Beginner Tumbling and Gymnastics); Metals 1 and Advanced Metals (removed due to lack of student interest over the past several years, rising material costs, and safety concerns).

Course Descriptions Updated
Advanced Placement Biology: description updated and GBBE removed as a pre-requisite. Algebra 2 Honors, Geometry Honors, and Precalculus Honors: prerequisites updated to show ability to move tracks. Team Sports courses will no longer have gender attached.

Presented to the Troy School District Board of Education for the February 7, 2023 meeting, this administrative report describes updates to the High-School Course Description Book (CDB) for the 2023/2024 school year.

Background and process
The High-School Course Description Book shows the course requirements and opportunities for students and is organized by department so that students and families have an understanding of the offerings. It is characterized as a OneTroy document developed collaboratively by administrators and department heads from both high schools together with the teaching and learning team. The CDB is updated annually as part of the district's curriculum review process; each year department teams work to determine where course descriptions should be updated to reflect new curriculum and instruction, or where courses should be added or deleted.

COURSES ADDED

Chemistry 1. Described as the newly developed course, a revision of the previously taught full year Chemistry class, required for all students beginning with the class of 2027. Catalog line: Grades 9-12. 1 semester. ½ credit. No Retake. The course satisfies ½ credit of the math related graduation requirement during the 12th grade year. Students will study theories and concepts in chemistry related to energy, atomic structure, bonding, chemical reactions, solution, and combustion. Many topics are developed through analytical problem solving of real-life phenomena. Experiments will be performed which will drive the learning of concepts, and students will execute a variety of laboratory techniques throughout the semester. Students are expected to work with a group, follow procedures, ask questions, organize data, make observations, develop models, and apply concepts learned to real-life.

Chemistry 2. The report states the course is in development and will begin running in the second semester of the 23/23 school year. Students interested in taking a full year of chemistry in order to access AP Chemistry will enroll in both Chemistry 1 and Chemistry 2. Catalog line: Grades 9-12. 1 semesters. ½ credit. No Retake. Pre-Requisite: Chemistry 1. The course satisfies 1/2 credit of the math related graduation requirement during the 12th grade year. Students will extend their learning of theories and concepts of chemistry related to atomic structure, bonding, chemical reactions, solutions, acid-base chemistry, thermodynamics, equilibrium, and gas laws. Many topics are developed through analytical problem solving of real-life phenomena, and experiments will be performed in a collaborative setting which will drive the learning of concepts. A strong foundation in algebra will be important in understanding class concepts. Students interested in any STEM related field are encouraged to take the course, and the course is a pre-requisite for taking Advanced Placement Chemistry.

9 English. Identified as the newly developed 9th grade English course, a revision of previously taught 9th grade English courses, required for all students beginning with the class of 2027. Catalog line: 2 semesters. 1 credit. ½ credit per semester. This foundational English course is required for all 9th grade students. Completion of both 9th and 10th grade English courses will prepare students to engage with future English courses including Advanced Placement should they elect to do so. The course offers a rigorous curriculum and includes in-depth study and analysis of multiple genres of reading and a variety of modes of writing and speaking in a class structure that allows students the opportunity to practice skills and strategies daily. This repertoire of skills and strategies enables students to approach reading, writing, and speaking experiences with confidence and proficiency. Students hone their reading skills through frequent and increased engagement with novels, short stories, poetry, nonfiction texts, mentor texts, and book clubs. Daily writing in the forms of drafts and revisions based on teacher modeling and timely feedback will lead to skilled final essays which include literary analysis, informational, argumentative, and narrative. Class structure, including dedicated in-class time for reading, writing, and speaking, choice, and frequent timely feedback, will foster growth in students' reading, writing, and speaking skills.

Intensified Algebra 1. The report states the course is currently being piloted at THS and AHS. It covers all content of Algebra I as well as additional enrichment skills to build background knowledge quickly to ensure success in future high school math courses. Catalog line: Grades 9. 2 semesters. 1 credit per semester. No retake. Prerequisite: None. The course is scheduled in collaboration with the math specialist. It targets conceptual understanding, mathematical skills, and problem-solving and reasoning. Students are re-engaged in the curriculum through visualizations and multiple representations of mathematical ideas. Students also study metacognition to motivate and build students' positive beliefs about their academic abilities. Content includes multiple representations of linear, absolute value, quadratic, rational, polynomial, power, and exponential functions. The course builds foundational math skills used throughout high school, and students who successfully complete it will be prepared for Geometry.

Mindful Art. A new course designed in collaboration with the district's counseling and art departments. Catalog line: 1 semester. ½ credit per semester. Retakes: 1. Mindful Art combines mindfulness concepts with engaging art activities to encourage expression, self-awareness, and stress reduction. The class will focus on exploring personal identity, learning about and practicing stress reduction and coping skills, developing relationship skills through collaboration and community work, and fostering gratitude.

COURSES REMOVED

Advanced Swimming and Lifetime Sports & Fitness is to be combined with lifeguarding; the new course name will be Lifeguarding, Advanced Swimming and Lifetime Sports & Fitness.

Active Chemistry and Earth Science: both courses are being removed due to the newly restructured course pathway for science.

Beginning & Intermediate Swimming and Lifetime Sports & Fitness will be combined with Learning to Swim; the new course name will be Learning to Swim: Beginning & Intermediate Swimming and Lifetime Sports & Fitness.

Emerging Engineering is re-titled Mechatronics.

English 9 Literature and Compositions and English 9 Literature and Composition Honors: both courses are being removed to show the newly designed required English course beginning with the class of 2027.

Intermediate Tumbling and Gymnastics will be combined with Beginner Tumbling and Gymnastics.

Metals 1 and Advanced Metals are being removed due to lack of interest by students over the past several years. The report adds that the course was becoming costly due to rising prices of materials, and that safety was also a concern in the course.

COURSE DESCRIPTIONS UPDATED

Advanced Placement Biology: course description updated and GBBE removed as a pre-requisite.

Algebra 2 Honors, Geometry Honors, and Precalculus Honors: prerequisites updated to show ability to move tracks.

Team Sports courses will no longer have gender attached.

Significance
The additions and removals together restructure two required freshman pathways. In science, the full-year Chemistry class is replaced by a semester-length Chemistry 1 required of the class of 2027 onward, with an optional companion Chemistry 2 leading to Advanced Placement Chemistry, while Active Chemistry and Earth Science exit the catalog. In English, the two former ninth-grade offerings, English 9 Literature and Compositions and English 9 Literature and Composition Honors, are replaced by a single required 9 English course, also beginning with the class of 2027. Remaining changes consolidate overlapping physical education and swimming offerings, retire the metals program on cost, interest, and safety grounds, retitle Emerging Engineering as Mechatronics, and remove gender designations from Team Sports courses.
