https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Carried on the Troy School District Board of Education agenda for the meeting of April 1, 2025, this PDF is titled "TSD PEPS Report - March 2025" and is the district's PEPS (Pupil Enrollment Projection Study) report. The most consequential fact about the copy supplied for summarization is that its text layer did not extract as text: every page came through as raw font glyph-index codes - slash-delimited integer sequences - rather than characters, so no narrative sentence, table value, projection, or enrollment figure is recoverable from the source provided.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Identification**
- Title: TSD PEPS Report - March 2025
- Board meeting date: April 1, 2025
- Format: PDF
- Subject: the district's PEPS report, i.e. its pupil enrollment projection study

**Extraction status**
The PDF's embedded fonts are subset fonts with no usable character mapping, so the text extraction produced glyph indices instead of letters and digits. Each line of the supplied source appears as a run of slash-delimited numbers with a repeating token standing in for the space character. The numbering restarts and is reassigned from one embedded font to the next, so the same index refers to different characters on different pages.

**What can be stated**
The file is long and page-structured, with a running header repeated at the top of many pages and with the bulk of the body consisting of dense tabular material - long rows of uniform-width numeric tokens, consistent with enrollment counts, grade-level breakdowns, and multi-year projection grids - interspersed with shorter caption and section-label lines and with graphic-heavy pages carrying little text. Section-heading structure and district map or figure pages are discernible from the layout alone.

**Caveat**
No figure from this report is reproduced here. Any enrollment count, birth count, projection year, grade cohort, building name, or percentage that a reader might expect from a pupil enrollment projection study is present in the original PDF but absent from the extracted text, and none has been inferred or supplied from other sources. A summary with substantive content will require re-extracting this PDF with optical character recognition or with a glyph-mapping decoder rather than the standard text layer.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Agenda item for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of April 1, 2025, filed under the title "TSD PEPS Report - March 2025" and attached as a PDF. PEPS is the district's pupil enrollment projection study, the periodic demographic and enrollment forecast used to inform capacity, staffing, boundary, and facilities planning.

The controlling fact for this summary is a technical one. The PDF supplied for re-summarization does not carry a readable text layer. Its embedded fonts are subsetted without a ToUnicode mapping, and the extraction step therefore emitted raw glyph indices rather than characters. Every content line in the source arrives as a run of slash-delimited integers, with a single repeated token occupying the position of each space. The index-to-character assignment is local to each embedded font subset and is reassigned as new fonts are introduced, so the mapping changes from page to page and even between typefaces on the same page. Nothing in the extracted stream is legible as English text or as Arabic numerals.

Consequently no substantive content of the report is transcribed here. That includes, and is not limited to: total district enrollment, enrollment by building, enrollment by grade, kindergarten entry counts, resident live-birth counts, cohort-survival ratios, housing or development counts, Schools of Choice or non-resident counts, capacity or utilization figures, and every projected year in the forecast horizon. None of these were legible, none have been carried over from any other Troy School District document, and none have been reconstructed by inference. Writing any such figure would be fabrication rather than summarization, which is precisely the failure mode this re-summarization effort exists to eliminate.

What the source does permit is a description of the document's physical shape. It is a multi-page, page-formatted report. A short running header line repeats at the top of the majority of pages, and a second, shorter line beneath it varies from page to page in the manner of a section or figure label. The body is dominated by tabular material: long lines composed of many uniform-length numeric tokens arranged in regular columns, with left-hand label tokens of consistent length, which is the signature of grade-by-year or building-by-year projection grids. Several pages consist of only a handful of short lines, consistent with map, chart, or full-page graphic content whose labels sit outside the text layer. Other pages carry short stacked single-token lines of the sort used for chart axis tick labels and legends. Toward the end of the file the density of numeric tokens falls and short label-style lines predominate, consistent with summary or methodology pages.

For downstream use, this item should be treated as an unindexed attachment. Full-text search against it will return nothing, and the tiered summaries stored for it should not be relied on for any enrollment number. Recovering the content requires re-processing the original PDF - either by rendering the pages and running optical character recognition, or by reconstructing the per-font glyph-index tables and decoding the existing stream. Until one of those is done, the record for this document is limited to its title, its format, its identification as the district's pupil enrollment projection study report for March 2025, and its placement on the April 1, 2025 Board of Education agenda.

Minutes of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, for the Board Meeting of February 25, 2025, held at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Philippart called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Dr. Philippart, present were Board members Alic, Anne, Haupt, Melton, Potts, and Zendler. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Montante, Griffor, Griffin, Jansen, and Trudel. There were approximately 75 members of the audience. The minutes close "Respectfully submitted, Emina Alic, Secretary, Troy Board of Education," with the notation EA/jh.

RECOGNITION - ALL-STATE ATHLETES FALL 2024. Mr. Matt Jansen, Director of Athletics, recognized students named All-State Athletes in their respective sports: Graham Bauman (Boys' Soccer, 2nd Team), Marc Delikat (Boys' Soccer, 3rd Team), Dhruv Gupta (Boys' Tennis, 1st Team), Audrey Hamilton (Girls' Cross Country), Jesse Hao (Boys' Tennis, 1st Team), Prabath Inturi (Boys' Tennis, 1st Team), Daniel Kadiu (Boys' Soccer, 1st Team), Nick Kamugunga (Boys' Soccer, 3rd Team), Derrick Kim (Boys' Tennis, 1st Team), Nahuel Larroquette (Boys' Soccer, 2nd Team), Madie Miller (Girls' Cross Country), Neel Nagappala (Boys' Tennis, 1st Team), Ishan Patel (Boys' Tennis, 1st Team), Kian Schneeweis (Boys' Cross Country), Varun Shetty (Boys' Tennis, 1st Team), and Anthony Wu (Boys' Tennis, 1st Team). Coaches Adam Spinks, Kevin McConnell, Mike Messina, Andrew Shipp, and Brian Miska were also recognized. The students came up to receive a certificate and congratulations from the Board.

TSD MISSION MOMENT - IA-EAST CAPSTONE EXPERIENCE, IB MIDDLE YEARS PROGRAMME. The Board recognized Thyra Foronda, a sophomore at the International Academy East, for excellence in her MYP Personal Project, the capstone experience of the IB Middle Years Programme, in which all sophomores spend a semester investigating a topic of their choice. Foronda is the founder of YPLA (Youth Peace & Language Association), a nonprofit focused on English language learning for people in the Middle East, with multiple departments offering internships and volunteer opportunities. Her passion for languages, particularly Arabic, inspired the initiative, which also explores the impact of globalization and combines language learning with cultural understanding and leadership development.

TSD MISSION MOMENT - SSAB EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE MLK DAY OF SERVICE. The Board recognized the Superintendent Student Advisory Board Executive Committee, which leads the 56-member SSAB meetings by planning, setting agendas, running meetings, and orchestrating activities and events. The minutes note this is the second year the group has had an executive board, refer to "these eight students" and later to "these six individuals," and record that the committee organized and executed the MLK Citywide Celebration and Day of Service, which hundreds of families attended; photos were shared on the district Facebook page and were to appear in the Friday newsletter. The executive board members called forward for recognition and a token of appreciation were Nurayda Albeez, Elyse Lazrado, Maaz Ali, Vihaan Gehlaut, Angelina Matti, and Reah Pawar.

STUDENT SPOTLIGHT. The Board recognized creative achievement in the TSD Creative Guild, welcoming Student Board Representative from IA-East Nurayda Albeez; Mr. Thomas Butcher, Creative Guild advisor, was invited up to speak about her accomplishments.

PERSONNEL: None. CURRICULUM: None.

Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

BUSINESS - NETWORK AND WIRELESS PROJECT. It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Anne that the purchase and implementation of a network and wireless solution from Cisco Networks be awarded to People Driven Technology in the amount of $2,154,355.01 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Board members inquired about E-rate funding; Mr. Trudel said the district would be eligible for E-rate funding after April 1st. The minutes as extracted do not print a vote tally for this item.

BUSINESS - EPIC PA, BELL, AND SECURITY SYSTEM. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt that the purchase of the EPIC System be awarded to VSC, Inc. in the amount of $1,826,553.30 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

BUSINESS - MARTELL CAFETERIA TABLES. It was moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Anne that the purchase of cafeteria tables be awarded to School Specialty in the amount of $39,786.15 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (NON-AGENDA ITEMS). Dr. Philippart provided the opportunity for community members to address the Board on non-agenda items. Four community members addressed the Board during public communication. No action was taken by the Board.

OTHER - IDEA FULL FUNDING ACT RESOLUTION. Background recorded in the minutes: the K-12 Alliance of Michigan held a press conference to launch efforts both to celebrate the success of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) on the 50th anniversary of its passage and to press the federal government to fund it adequately; Congress has never funded the program higher than 18%, and this year funding has dropped all the way back to 10.3%, costing Michigan roughly $650 million this year alone. School boards in Michigan were asked to pass a resolution in support of the IDEA Full Funding Act, with signed resolutions to be shared with members of Congress at the K-12 Alliance symposium in April. It was moved by Dr. Melton and supported by Mrs. Alic. The whereas clauses state that public education is the cornerstone of democracy; that in the decade following the Great Recession students across the U.S. lost nearly $600 billion from the states' disinvestment in their public schools; that prior to the COVID-19 pandemic both state and federal funding for public schools was already failing to meet critical student needs; that since the pandemic students have needed additional academic, social, emotional, and mental health supports through targeted programming, additional personnel, enhanced professional development, new technology, and critical facility updates; that research consistently shows increased education funding positively affects academic performance, increases graduation rates, and future earnings; that when IDEA was passed in 1975 the federal government committed to pay 40 percent of the average per pupil expenditure for special education; that the financial pledge has never been met and is currently funded at approximately 10.7 percent, leaving a gap of billions of dollars; that Troy School District serves a student population that includes 10.69 percent of students with disabilities; that unfunded IDEA costs require the district to reallocate money from other programs; and that federal underfunding has negatively impacted the academic opportunities of all students for generations. The resolution calls on Congress to immediately pass the IDEA Full Funding Act (S.2217/H.R. 4519), which would create a 10-year mandatory path to fully fund IDEA, and calls on the state legislature to provide adequate, equitable, and sustainable funding increases to districts. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

OTHER - MASB BOARD OF DIRECTORS' ELECTION, REGION 8. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Troy Board of Education cast its ballot for the following candidate to serve on the 2025 Michigan Association of School Boards' Board of Directors: Randel Meisner, Region 8, three-year term. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

Bids were opened December 15, 2022 across four trade categories, drawing twelve bids in all. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Item and source**
Board agenda item 11.A., meeting of January 17, 2023: "RFP 9951TSD 2023 Athletics Letter of Rec 230105." The packet contains a letter dated January 5, 2023 from Foresite Design (3269 Coolidge Highway, Berkley, Michigan 48072; phone 248-547-7757; www.foresitedesign.com), signed by Michael Sims, addressed to Rob Carson, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, MI 48098. Subject: Troy High School & Boulan Park Middle School, 2023 Synthetic Turf and Track Renovations, Letter of Recommendation. Copies to Larry Franckowiak of Troy School District; Michelle Kerns/Mark Paulus of Lecole Planners; and the FDI file. One enclosure — the bid tabulation.

**Bidding process**
Bids were submitted December 15, 2022 (bids due 12/15/22 at 11:00 A.M.). The project was separated into four trade categories, and a total of twelve bids were received. Post-bid interviews with the apparent low bidders were conducted on December 16, 2022 and January 3, 2023. Tabulation sheets are dated 12/16/2022 and track bid security, Iran sanction disclosure, familial disclosure, Addendum #1 acknowledgment, base bid, and remarks.

**Recommended awards**

| Proposal | Recommended contractor | Location | Contract sum |
|---|---|---|---|
| A — Site Work | S&H Trucking and Excavating | Fort Gratiot, Michigan | $483,000.00 |
| B — Synthetic Turf | Shaw Integrated and Turf Solutions, Inc. | Dalton, Georgia | $580,458.00 |
| C — Track Surface | Goddard Coatings Company | Pontiac, Michigan | $144,105.00 |
| D — Site Work Track | Nagle Paving Company | Novi, Michigan | $534,790.00 |
| | | **Total** | **$1,742,353.00** |

**Breakdowns and alternates**
Proposal A: base bid $343,000.00 plus Voluntary Alternate No. 1 at $140,000.00, total $483,000.00. The alternate covers complete removal of the existing E-layer and its replacement with a pre-manufactured performance pad carrying a 24-year warranty, described as adding benefits for safety, athlete performance, and maintenance.
Proposal B: base bid $515,905.00 plus Voluntary Alternate No. 1 at $64,553.00, total $580,458.00. The alternate substitutes the proprietary "GameOn" turf system for the base bid; over 90% of the inlays are fully tufted, yielding a more consistent playing surface and reduced maintenance.
Proposal C: the letter cites a contract sum of $194,105.00 and shows base bid $194,105.00 with Voluntary Alternate No. 1 at $-50,000.00 for a total of $144,105.00. Accepting S&H's Voluntary Alternate #1 reduces Goddard's scope by eliminating the new E-layer work; Goddard offered a $50,000.00 credit, which Foresite deems fair value.
Proposal D: base bid $534,790.00, total $534,790.00.

**Bid tabulation (base bids)**
Proposal A — Site Work Turf: S&H Trucking & Excavating $343,000.00 (Vol Alt 1); Gibraltar Construction Company $487,400.00; Eagle Excavation Incorporated $770,000.00.
Proposal B — Synthetic Turf: Sprinturf $460,440.00 (Vol Alt 1); Astroturf Great Lakes $462,365.00 (Vol Alt 2); A-Turf, Inc. $477,500.00 (Vol Alt 1); Shaw Integrated Turf Solutions $515,905.00 (Vol Alt 1); Act Global Americas, Inc. $529,927.00.
Proposal C — Track Surface: Goddard Coatings Company $194,105.00; Star Trac Enterprise, LLC $282,000.00.
Proposal D — Site Work Track: Nagle Paving Company $534,790.00; Asphalt Specialists, LLC $750,000.00.

Foresite asks the district to advise what additional information may be required from the recommended contractors so it can be secured for presentation at the next Board of Education meeting.

**Identification**
This packet is Board of Education agenda item 11.A. for the Troy School District meeting of January 17, 2023, titled "RFP 9951TSD 2023 Athletics Letter of Rec 230105." It comprises a two-page letter of recommendation dated January 5, 2023 and its single enclosure, a four-page bid tabulation. The letter is on the letterhead of Foresite Design, 3269 Coolidge Highway, Berkley, Michigan 48072, phone 248-547-7757, website www.foresitedesign.com, with the practice areas footer "Athletic Facility Planning – Site Planning – Consulting – Landscape Architecture." It is addressed to Rob Carson, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, MI 48098, and signed by Michael Sims (initials MDS). The subject line reads: "Troy School District – Troy High School & Boulan Park Middle School – 2023 Synthetic Turf and Track Renovations – Letter of Recommendation." One enclosure is noted. Copies were sent to Larry Franckowiak of Troy School District; Michelle Kerns and Mark Paulus of Lecole Planners; and the FDI file.

**Procurement history**
Bids for the Troy School District 2023 Synthetic Turf and Track Renovations project were submitted on December 15, 2022; the tabulation sheets record the bid deadline as 12/15/22 at 11:00 A.M. The project was separated into four trade categories — Proposal A Site Work (Site Work Turf), Proposal B Synthetic Turf, Proposal C Track Surface, and Proposal D Site Work Track — and a total of twelve bids were received across them. Post-bid interviews were conducted with the apparent low bidders on December 16, 2022 and again on January 3, 2023. The enclosed tabulation sheets are each dated 12/16/2022 and are headed "Troy School District 2023 / Troy High School Turf Track / Boulan Park MS Track." Each sheet carries columns for bid security, Iran sanction disclosure, familial disclosure, Addendum #1 acknowledgment, base bid, and remarks, with the note "**Bold Indicates Apparent Low Bidder."

**Proposal A – Site Work**
Foresite recommends S&H Trucking and Excavating of Fort Gratiot, Michigan to complete the work identified in Proposal A Site Work for a contract sum of $483,000.00. The breakdown is: Proposal A Base Bid $343,000.00; Voluntary Alternate No. 1 $140,000.00; Total $483,000.00. The recommended sum is based on acceptance of one voluntary alternate, which includes the complete removal of the existing E-layer and its replacement with a pre-manufactured performance pad. The new performance pad carries a 24-year warranty and, per the letter, would provide added benefits toward safety, athlete performance, and maintenance.

**Proposal B – Synthetic Turf**
Foresite recommends Shaw Integrated and Turf Solutions, Inc. of Dalton, Georgia to complete the work identified in Proposal B Synthetic Turf for a contract sum of $580,458.00. The breakdown is: Proposal B Base Bid $515,905.00; Voluntary Alternate No. 1 $64,553.00; Total $580,458.00. The recommended sum is based on acceptance of one voluntary alternate implementing the proprietary "GameOn" turf system in lieu of the base bid. The letter states the technology of this turf system allows for over 90% of the inlays to be fully tufted, providing a consistent playing surface as well as reduced maintenance efforts and expenses. Shaw's base bid was not the lowest of the five base bids listed on the Proposal B tabulation.

**Proposal C – Track Surface**
Foresite recommends Goddard Coatings Company of Pontiac, Michigan to complete the work identified in Proposal C Track Surface, citing a contract sum of $194,105.00 in the narrative. The breakdown shown is: Proposal C Base Bid $194,105.00; Voluntary Alternate No. 1 $-50,000.00; Total $144,105.00. The letter explains that by recommending acceptance of Voluntary Alternate #1 from S&H Trucking & Excavating, Goddard Coatings Company's scope of work will be reduced to eliminate the new E-layer work. During post-bid evaluations Goddard Coatings Company offered a credit of $50,000.00 for the reduced scope, which Foresite's office deems to be of fair value.

**Proposal D – Site Work Track**
Foresite recommends Nagle Paving Company of Novi, Michigan to complete the work identified in Proposal D Site Work Track for a contract sum of $534,790.00. The breakdown is: Proposal D Base Bid $534,790.00; Total $534,790.00. No alternates are applied to this proposal.

**Total recommended award**
The letter summarizes the total amount recommended for award as: S&H Trucking and Excavating $483,000.00; Shaw Integrated and Turf Solutions, Inc. $580,458.00; Goddard Coatings Company $144,105.00; Nagle Paving Company $534,790.00; Total $1,742,353.00.

**Bid tabulation – Proposal A, Site Work Turf**
Three base bids are recorded: S&H Trucking & Excavating $343,000.00, with the remark "Vol Alt (1)"; Gibraltar Construction Company $487,400.00; and Eagle Excavation Incorporated $770,000.00. Four additional bidder rows are blank.

**Bid tabulation – Proposal B, Synthetic Turf**
Five base bids are recorded: Sprinturf $460,440.00, remark "Vol Alt (1)"; Astroturf Great Lakes $462,365.00, remark "Vol Alt (2)"; A-Turf, Inc. $477,500.00, remark "Vol Alt (1)"; Shaw Integrated Turf Solutions $515,905.00, remark "Vol Alt (1)"; and Act Global Americas, Inc. $529,927.00. Three additional bidder rows are blank.

**Bid tabulation – Proposal C, Track Surface**
Two base bids are recorded: Goddard Coatings Company $194,105.00 and Star Trac Enterprise, LLC $282,000.00. Five additional bidder rows are blank.

**Bid tabulation – Proposal D, Site Work Track**
Two base bids are recorded: Nagle Paving Company $534,790.00 and Asphalt Specialists, LLC $750,000.00. Five additional bidder rows are blank.

**Closing**
Foresite Design asks the district to advise its office of additional information that may be required from the recommended contractors so that it may be secured on the district's behalf for presentation at the next Board of Education meeting, and invites questions or concerns. The letter functions as the professional recommendation supporting the Board's award of the turf and track renovation contracts for Troy High School and Boulan Park Middle School under RFP 9951TSD.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Character | Student-Friendly Deep Learning Progression is a two-page rubric written in first-person student language, describing growth in the Character competency across four dimensions and five levels of evidence. The stated aim is learning to deep learn, to keep trying, to have integrity, empathy, and compassion, and to always be a learner. The material is credited to Copyright 2019 by Education in Motion (New Pedagogies for Deep Learning), with reproduction authorized for educational use by educators, local school sites, and noncommercial or nonprofit entities that have purchased the book.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What It Is
A student-facing learning progression for the Character competency, part of a Learning Progressions series. The header describes Character as learning to deep learn, to keep trying, to have integrity, empathy, and compassion, and to always be a learner. It runs across two pages, the second labeled Character (Cont'd).

Structure
Four dimensions are each described at five levels: Limited Evidence, Emerging, Developing, Accelerating, and Proficient. Every descriptor is written as an I statement for student self-assessment.

| Dimension | Page |
|---|---|
| Proactive stance toward life and learning to deep learn | 1 |
| Grit, tenacity, perseverance, and resilience | 1 |
| Empathy, compassion, and integrity | 2 |
| Using technology for learning (leveraging digital) | 2 |

Proactive Stance Toward Life and Learning to Deep Learn
At Limited Evidence the student is not clear about what needs to be learned or why, can complete teacher-prepared tasks but needs help reflecting, and does not yet find learning a positive experience. Emerging adds identifying with help what is known and needed, choosing a topic and finding information with help, beginning to see peer and teacher feedback as opportunities, and believing learning and achievement are possible. Developing describes interests, knowledge, and learning needs, creating or designing a project, using feedback to improve, and experiencing learning as positive and leading to accomplishment. Accelerating adds skill at working out how to learn, reflecting on progress, seeking feedback, applying learning to current and future projects, and balancing work with play. Proficient describes finding and creating one's own learning opportunities, continually building knowledge and skills for success in life, creating meaningful solutions that impact life and the world, and actively seeking feedback even when challenging.

Grit, Tenacity, Perseverance, and Resilience
Limited Evidence describes usually giving up when facing unexpected challenges or negative feedback and being unable to work through hard tasks. Emerging describes needing a lot of support with setbacks and beginning to work through challenges with encouragement. Developing describes learning to persevere, being thrown off track by major setbacks sometimes but handling small or medium challenges by pausing, reflecting, adapting, and finding new solutions. Accelerating describes persevering and never giving up on the most challenging tasks, and working through major setbacks or negative feedback. Proficient describes grit, tenacity, perseverance, adaptability, and resilience that allow the student to work through any challenge and help others do the same, and understanding character qualities as essential to creating meaningful change.

Empathy, Compassion, and Integrity
Progresses from being unsure what others feel, to beginning to put oneself in others' shoes, to imagining how others experience the world and wanting to be courageous about doing the right thing, to regularly reflecting on feeling more empathy and showing more compassion as an authentic goal, to regularly modeling compassion, empathy, and integrity even when unnoticed or inconvenient, with sincerity, fairness, trustworthiness, and bravery as valued virtues.

Using Technology for Learning (Leveraging Digital)
Progresses from using some digital without seeing how it supports learning, to occasional use and beginning to use digital to develop empathy, compassion, and grit, to regular use with understanding of how digital deepens those traits, to explaining how digital helps learning and reflection, to effortless use throughout the learning experience and using digital to support others by encouraging them and providing feedback.

Attribution
Source line on both pages: Copyright 2019 by Education in Motion (New Pedagogies for Deep Learning). All rights reserved. Reproduction authorized for educational use by educators, local school sites, and noncommercial or nonprofit entities that have purchased the book.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Character | Student-Friendly Deep Learning Progression, a two-page rubric distributed with the Troy School District Board of Education materials for the meeting of October 3, 2023, under the file name student-friendly-Character. It belongs to a series headed Learning Progressions and is written entirely in first-person student voice so that students can locate their own practice on the scale.

Framing statement. The subtitle on both pages reads: Learning to deep learn, to keep trying, to have integrity, empathy, and compassion, and to always be a learner.

Architecture. The rubric is a matrix. Rows are dimensions of the Character competency; columns are five levels of evidence, labeled Limited Evidence, Emerging, Developing, Accelerating, and Proficient. Page one covers two dimensions, Proactive stance toward life and learning to deep learn, and Grit, tenacity, perseverance, and resilience. Page two, headed Character (Cont'd) | Student-Friendly Deep Learning Progression, repeats the dimension and level headers and covers Empathy, compassion, and integrity, and Using technology for learning (leveraging digital).

Dimension 1: Proactive stance toward life and learning to deep learn. Limited Evidence: the student is not clear about what needs to be learned and why; can complete tasks the teacher prepares but needs help to reflect on and understand how a task is going; learning is not yet a positive experience. Emerging: with help, the student can identify what is known, what needs to be learned, and why; with help, can choose a topic and find needed information; is learning to see peer and teacher feedback as opportunities to learn and improve; believes learning and achievement are possible. Developing: the student can describe interests, existing knowledge, learning needs, and reasons for learning; can choose a topic and create or design a project to support learning; listens to peer and teacher feedback and uses it to improve how learning happens; experiences learning as positive, leading to a feeling of accomplishment and achievement. Accelerating: the student understands what needs to be learned and is skilled at working out how to learn it; reflects on progress and seeks feedback while learning; uses what is learned to improve current and future projects; enjoys learning as a way to improve life; tries to balance work with play. Proficient: the student has the skills to find and create personal learning opportunities; is continually building knowledge and skills for success in life; creates meaningful solutions that impact both personal life and the world; actively seeks out feedback and uses it to better understand how learning happens and what supports growth; looks for any opportunity to learn something new even when it is challenging; balances work with play.

Dimension 2: Grit, tenacity, perseverance, and resilience. Limited Evidence: the student usually gives up when facing an unexpected challenge or receiving negative feedback, and when a task or experience is too hard is unable to work through the challenge to find a solution. Emerging: the student needs a lot of support to deal with setbacks, negative feedback, and difficult challenges, and is starting to work through challenges but still needs support and encouragement not to give up. Developing: the student is learning to persevere and not give up even when tasks are challenging; major setbacks or difficulties may throw the student off track sometimes, but small or medium challenges can be handled by pausing, reflecting, adapting, and finding new solutions. Accelerating: the student perseveres and never gives up, even on the most challenging tasks; when faced with major setbacks or negative feedback, pauses, reflects, adapts, and works through the challenge to find a solution; understands and can talk about why the character qualities matter for life. Proficient: grit, tenacity, perseverance, adaptability, and resilience allow the student to work through any challenge or setback and to help others do the same; the student seeks out feedback and uses it to help learning; and understands that the character qualities are essential for creating meaningful change in personal life and in the world.

Dimension 3: Empathy, compassion, and integrity. Limited Evidence: the student is not sure what other people might feel when interacting with them or when hearing about issues happening in the world. Emerging: the student is beginning to put himself or herself in others' shoes and can sometimes see what their experiences must be like. Developing: more and more, the student can imagine how others experience the world even without having experienced those things personally; would like to be courageous about doing the right thing in class and beyond it; wants to develop empathy, compassion, and integrity in order to be a better person. Accelerating: the student regularly reflects on how to feel more empathy and show more compassion for others, describing this as an authentic personal goal, and strives to be courageous within the class and beyond it. Proficient: the student regularly shows and models compassion, empathy, and integrity even when no one notices or when it is inconvenient; virtues such as sincerity, fairness, trustworthiness, and bravery matter and are how the student wishes others to describe both the person and the work produced.

Dimension 4: Using technology for learning (leveraging digital). Limited Evidence: the student uses some digital during the learning process but does not see how it supports learning. Emerging: the student uses digital to assist with learning occasionally and is beginning to use digital to develop empathy, compassion, and grit. Developing: the student regularly uses digital to support learning and understands how digital can deepen traits like empathy, compassion, and grit. Accelerating: the student knows and can explain how digital helps with learning, reflection, and developing traits like empathy, compassion, and grit. Proficient: the student effortlessly uses technology throughout the learning experience and uses digital to support others with their learning by encouraging them and providing feedback.

Attribution and permissions. Both pages carry the identical source line: Copyright 2019 by Education in Motion (New Pedagogies for Deep Learning). All rights reserved. Reproduction authorized for educational use by educators, local school sites, and/or noncommercial or nonprofit entities that have purchased the book. No Troy School District author, department, or presenter is named in the document itself, and it contains no figures, dollar amounts, dates other than the copyright year, or board action language.

**Meeting**
Troy Board of Education regular meeting, December 16, 2025, held at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Philippart called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. and it adjourned at 7:50 p.m. Minutes submitted by Emina Alic, Secretary (EA/jh).

**Attendance**
Present in addition to Dr. Philippart: Board members Alic, Anne, Haupt, Melton, Potts, and Zendler. Also present: Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Recker, Jansen, and Trudel. Approximately 50 members of the audience attended.

**Recognition**
The Troy High Boys' Tennis Team was honored. Following runner-up finishes in each of the past two seasons and returning 11 of 12 starters from the 2024 season, the team won a State Championship. Recognized: Sourish Daruri, Quentin Gatto, Krish Gupta, Jesse Hao, Jonathan Jung, Raghav Karur, Vyom Kashi, Jyotiraditya Kashyap, Derrick Kyung Chan Kim, Solmin Kim, Jackson Kraus, Neel Nagappala, Nikhil Nair, Varun Shetty, Zain Taqi, Nathan Wanstreet, Anthony Wu, and Dheeraj Yelleti.

**Consent Agenda**
Moved by Mr. Haupt, supported by Mrs. Alic, to approve items A, B, C, and D. Items listed: Minutes of the November 11, 2025 Workshop; Minutes of the November 18, 2025 Board Meeting; Treasurer's Report - October 2025; AP French & Spanish Resources; Schools of Choice 105 & 105C. Yes: 7, No: 0.

**Personnel**
Moved by Mrs. Anne, supported by Mr. Haupt, that the Board issue a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure to Dr. Jordan Dennis, who begins duties as Supervisor, Data and Research effective January 5, 2026. Yes: 7, No: 0. Nothing was presented under Curriculum.

**Business Actions**

| Item | Vendor | Amount | Fund | Vote |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Food Service equipment - slatwall enclosure | Stafford Smith | $37,455.00 | Food Service Fund | 7-0 |
| Electrical & utility gear pre-purchase | O'Donnell Electric | $587,874.00 | Capital Projects Fund | 7-0 |
| 2026 Roof Replacement Project | award schedule not reproduced in the text | not stated | Capital Projects Fund and Building Site and Sinking Funds | 7-0 |
| Site Work - Paving Projects | Nagle Paving | $3,367,085.00 | Capital Projects Fund and Building Site & Sinking Funds | 7-0 |

Motions came from Mrs. Potts (support Mrs. Anne) for food service, Mrs. Zendler (support Mr. Haupt) for the electrical pre-purchase, Dr. Melton (support Mrs. Alic) for roofing, and Mrs. Anne (support Mrs. Alic) for paving.

**Public Communication**
None on agenda items. During non-agenda public communication, one community member addressed the Board; no action was taken.

**Other Business**
Moved by Dr. Philippart, supported by Mrs. Zendler, to approve a proposed new OCSBA resolution supporting non-partisan school board elections. Yes: 7, No: 0. Moved by Mrs. Anne, supported by Mr. Haupt, to approve a proposed new OCSBA resolution supporting full funding of Early On Michigan, an early intervention program for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with disabilities, developmental delays, or at risk for delays. Yes: 7, No: 0.

**Student Representatives**
Sara Graunstadt (Athens High School), Bella Doss (Troy High School), and Chloe Gentilini (Troy College and Career High School) reported on school events. Ahyoung Song (International Academy-East) was absent.

**Board Comments and Announcements**
Topics included the Reading Literacy Summit on the Science of Reading and Reading Intervention, a Girl Botz Newsletter 1st Place Award, a visit to Bemis 1st and 3rd grade classrooms, the January 19th MLK Day of Service, and certification training completed by three new Board members. Dr. Philippart announced the next Board Workshop for January 13th at 6:00 p.m. and the next regular and organizational meeting for January 20th at 7:00 p.m., both in the Services Building.

Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Recker, Jansen, and Trudel. There were approximately 50 members of the audience.

**Recognition - Troy High Boys' Tennis Team**
The Board recognized the Troy High Boys' Tennis Team. The narrative notes the team was motivated by runner-up finishes in each of the past two seasons and entered the year determined to represent their city with pride. Returning 11 of 12 starters from the 2024 season, the group consistently demonstrated maturity, discipline, and experience throughout the year. The defining lesson of the season was that yesterday's setbacks can become today's success, a mindset the players embraced from the first day forward, and their commitment was ultimately rewarded with a State Championship. The players recognized and celebrated were Sourish Daruri, Quentin Gatto, Krish Gupta, Jesse Hao, Jonathan Jung, Raghav Karur, Vyom Kashi, Jyotiraditya Kashyap, Derrick Kyung Chan Kim, Solmin Kim, Jackson Kraus, Neel Nagappala, Nikhil Nair, Varun Shetty, Zain Taqi, Nathan Wanstreet, Anthony Wu, and Dheeraj Yelleti.

**Other - OCSBA Resolution on Full Funding of Early On Michigan**
It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Board of Education approves the proposed new resolution as presented: OCSBA supports full funding of Early On Michigan, an early intervention program for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with disabilities, developmental delays or who are at risk for delays due to certain health conditions. The vote was Yes: 7, No: 0.

**Reports from High School Student Representatives**
Sara Graunstadt, student representative for Athens High School, shared a report on the events and activities happening in her school. Bella Doss, student representative for Troy High School, shared a report on the events and activities happening in her school. Chloe Gentilini, student representative for Troy College and Career High School, shared a report on the events and activities happening in her school. Ahyoung Song, student representative for International Academy-East, was absent.

**Board Comments**
Board members wished everyone a Merry Christmas and Happy Holidays. Comment topics listed in the minutes were: the Reading Literacy Summit on the Science of Reading and Reading Intervention; the Girl Botz Newsletter and a shout out for a 1st Place Award; thanks to the Bemis principal and staff for hosting Board members' visit to 1st and 3rd grade classrooms to see the updated curriculum in action; the January 19th MLK Day of Service, to which the community is invited; and thanks to the three new Board members for completing all training courses in a short period of time to maintain full Board certification.

**Announcements and Adjournment**
Dr. Philippart announced that the next Board Workshop will be held in the Services Building on January 13th at 6:00 p.m., and that the next regular and organizational meeting will be held on January 20th at 7:00 p.m. in the Services Building. The meeting adjourned at 7:50 p.m.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Presentation Identification**
Middle School Math Update: Board Workshop - January 2026, prepared for the Troy School District Board of Education. The deck reviews the district's middle school mathematics program change, the evidence behind it, perception data collected in May 2025, and current honors enrollment trends.

**TSD Vision for Mathematics**
All students are doers of mathematics. The stated purpose of the mathematics program is to cultivate students' positive mathematical identities so that all students develop deep mathematical understandings, understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience the wonder, joy, and beauty of mathematics. The vision is attributed to NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics.

**Findings (May 2023)**
Finding 1, explore curricular changes: program data from the last 5 years preceding COVID revealed that student performance was slightly decreasing or stagnant, and that cohort data showed a decrease in the number of students who achieved at advanced and proficient along with an increase in students who were not proficient. Finding 2, explore course sequencing: students are not able to, or do not, fluidly move between tracks in middle school. Finding 3, explore classroom pedagogy: explore task-based, inquiry-based instruction that builds procedural fluency through conceptual understanding.

**Recommendation: Illustrative Math (May 2023)**
The recommended resource was Illustrative Math, characterized as problem-based; grounded in Universal Design for Learning; with embedded supports for students with disabilities and English learners; extensions for students who are ready for more; built-in instructional routines that support teachers and students; activity and lesson structure that is predictable and purposeful; and practice problem sets with built-in cumulative review.

**Choosing Math 8 or Honors Algebra 1 (May 2023)**
Math 8 is described as a natural transition from a Math 7 experience, in which students explore ideas of linearity, functions, and geometry and establish a solid foundation for future work in Algebra 1 and Geometry. Honors Algebra 1 embeds Math 8 standards into Algebra 1, with students moving to formalizing and generalizing their understandings with a focus on efficiency and mastery. In the spring of 7th grade, buildings host information nights to discuss and illustrate the differences between Math 8 and Honors Algebra 1 so families can make informed decisions, and families engage with math teachers to discuss individual student needs. Student performance in problem solving skills, communication of mathematical thinking and ideas, math assessment feedback, and standardized test scores should be considered.

**Supporting All Students (May 2023)**
Supports listed include deep levels of learning; investing in staff through professional learning; enrichment materials embedded within Illustrative Math under the Are You Ready For More? feature; enrichment and enhancement opportunities such as Math Club and Robotics; and traditional test-out opportunities to move more quickly through grade levels.

**Monitoring Our Success (May 2023)**
Goal 1: see growth in the number of students who score advanced or proficient on the MSTEP math assessment, PSAT and SAT exams. Goal 2: increase enrollment in and successful completion of Honors Algebra 1 in 8th grade as measured through enrollment data and end of course summative exams. Goal 3: build student problem solving skills and communication of mathematical thinking as monitored through internal common assessment. Measurement of student achievement may include, reported annually, MSTEP/PSAT/SAT including cohort data and math benchmark assessments; and, studied with staff, unit assessments and common assessments, student enrollment in Algebra 1, and student success (grades) in higher levels of mathematics.

**2023 Reflections on Program Change**
The reflections state the intent to align course work with the district vision of deep learning for all students, noting the then-current system does not lend itself to that goal; that the district learned from the field that emphasis should be on depth and fluency, not speed; that the new curriculum provides additional instruction in number sense and procedural fluency and additional access to rich tasks that elicit meaningful discourse and deep understandings; that the new curriculum is designed to offer multiple entry points allowing true differentiation in the general education setting; and that students who desire to accelerate will have the opportunity to reach Algebra 1 by Grade 8 or before, with test-out continuing every spring.

**Student Perception Data (May 2025), n = 1,932**
Celebrations: 93% of students said their math class is a welcoming place for everyone; 87% said they had lots of opportunities to interact with each other; 88% agreed that in math class it is important to try rather than to get things right the first time; 90% agreed with the statement I know I can be good at math; 79% feel prepared for the next level of math; and 59% said the lessons are just right for them. Challenges: 34% of students would like to receive more specific feedback on how to improve their work; 45% of students do not enjoy learning math; 24% said the lessons are too easy; and 17% said the lessons are too hard.

**Student Voice (May 2025)**
Positive comments quoted include enjoyment of interactions with peers and being at a level where the math is not too easy or too hard; appreciation for a teacher who explains math equations with real life examples; appreciation that there are different ways to learn math; and a student who feels confident enough to raise a hand without being judged and enjoys working with friends, bouncing ideas off them or helping them. Suggestions quoted include adding a difficulty level to assignments to show improvement; more interactive projects or activities so class does not get too boring; a pre-test so the teacher can understand what students know; more repetitive practice per activity to aid retention before tests; and learning more things students will use in real life.

**Teacher Perception Data (May 2025), n = 19**
Celebrations: 95% of teachers say they are comfortable navigating the resource, and 79% say they have the tools they need to accurately measure student progress. Quoted teacher comments praise that there is not just one way to learn or know most of the content, material, skills or strategy and that the curriculum figures out the why; the conceptual content and the different ways of doing math, the Are You Ready For More feature, tasks that are good for students to work together on, and the effort put into getting students to talk and write math; and how the curriculum connects math to real-life situations along with a low floor approach that is inviting for students who may be struggling. Challenges: 37% of teachers need more resources for families and 42% of teachers are using the IM instructional routines that support student access. Quoted concerns include the need for more support for ELD students and students with low reading and comprehension skills, noting that reading a problem three times is not always doable and frequently does not help; requests for more supplemental practice, assessments that match the learning activities, and guidance on what can be combined or eliminated from lessons or units; and a wish for more at-home resources with more written-out examples beyond the online workbook and videos.

**Professional Learning for Middle School Teachers**
2024/25: monthly meetings with Honors Algebra 1, district release professional learning days covering PLCs, UDL, and NWEA learning, building-level PLCs, and support from Math Specialists. 2025/26: district release professional learning days covering PLCs, UDL, and NWEA learning, building-level PLCs, and support from Math Specialists.

**Honors Enrollment Goal and Data**
Under the goal to increase enrollment in and successful completion of Honors Algebra 1 in 8th grade as measured through enrollment data and end of course summative exams, the deck presents 8th Grade Enrollment Trends in Honors Math Courses (Algebra 1 and Above). The chart labels total students as 907, 961, 995, and 1023 across the periods shown. The summary states that the middle school math sequence change led to an increase in student enrollment in honors, and that the district will continue to monitor middle school honors math enrollments. A second chart, Representation of Federal Demographic Categories in Honors Math, carries the values 159, 451, 486, and 348, with population labels n = 1023 and n = 529; the extracted text does not preserve the category labels attached to those values.

**Data To Come**
Future reporting is to include successful completion of Honors Algebra I in 8th grade, measured by course enrollment fall/spring and course enrollment the following year as sequential data; achievement and growth data referencing the November 2025 Board presentation; MSTEP; and NWEA.

**Document type and parties**
Report to the Board of Education from Plante & Moran, PLLC, signed by Chris Geck, CPA, covering the audit of Troy School District's basic financial statements as of and for the year ended June 30, 2025. The report is organized as Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), and Informational Items (pages 7-19). **Results of the audit**
For the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2024 the District adopted GASB Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences; the opinion is not modified with respect to the new policy. **MPSERS plan status**

**Fund balance and other district-specific items**

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Plante & Moran, PLLC issued this Report to the Board of Education of Troy School District in connection with the audit of the School District's basic financial statements as of and for the year ended June 30, 2025. The transmittal letter is dated October 13, 2025 and thanks Mr. Dan Trudel, Mr. Aurel Malutan, and the entire business office for their assistance and preparedness. The report is divided into Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), and Informational Items (pages 7-19). The Results of the Audit letter is signed by Plante & Moran, PLLC and Chris Geck, CPA.

RESPONSIBILITIES AND SCOPE. The engagement letter is dated June 3, 2025. The auditors' responsibility is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements prepared by management are fairly presented in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles, obtaining reasonable but not absolute assurance that the statements are free of material misstatement. Internal control was considered solely to determine audit procedures, not to provide assurance on internal control. The audit was also conducted in accordance with Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, and a separate letter dated October 13, 2025 addresses internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance with laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements. The audit followed the scope and timing communicated at the planning meeting of June 18, 2025.

SIGNIFICANT AUDIT FINDINGS. For the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2024, the School District adopted the provisions of Governmental Accounting Standards Board Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences; the opinion is not modified with respect to this new accounting policy. Significant accounting policies are described in Note 2. No significant transactions were recognized in a different period than when they occurred. The most sensitive estimates were the District's share of the MPSERS net liability for pension and net asset for other postemployment benefits recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75; the District's estimates as of June 30, 2025 were $211.6 million for pension and $36.6 million for OPEB, based on data received from the Office of Retirement Services. Disclosures were described as neutral, consistent, and clear. No significant difficulties were encountered, no disagreements with management arose, and no misstatements were detected as a result of audit procedures. A management representation letter is dated October 13, 2025. There were no consultations with other independent accountants. The auditors read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and nothing came to their attention suggesting material misstatement or inconsistency.

OTHER RECOMMENDATIONS AND OBSERVATIONS. The Food Service Fund's fund balance continues to exceed the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures. The School District should continue to monitor its spenddown plan, entered into with the Michigan Department of Education, for reducing the balance to an acceptable level.

MANAGING THE CHANGING LANDSCAPE. The State did not meet its self-imposed July 1 deadline to complete the school aid budget for fiscal year 2025/2026. The May 2025 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference produced upward revisions to short- and long-term revenue growth projections for the General Fund and School Aid Fund, with cautionary notes about macroeconomic events including evolving federal trade policies. The federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act was signed on July 4, 2025 and is estimated to significantly reduce State revenue and to make Medicaid changes affecting the State budget. The U.S. Department of Education is undergoing major changes in 2025 following an executive order to dismantle it; billions of dollars in education funding were initially frozen, primarily related to Title I, and the president's budget proposal eliminates funding for Title 1-C, Title III, Title II, and Title IV-A.

2024/2025 SCHOOL FUNDING. The target foundation allowance stayed at $9,608 per pupil for public schools, while public school academies received a 3.9 percent increase estimated at $9,983. The blended pupil count used 90 percent weighting for the October 2024 count and 10 percent for the February 2024 count, with a two-year blended count available under Section 29 for districts whose 2024 final membership was lower than 2023. Under Section 147a(4), state funding historically covering the OPEB UAAL was about $669 million statewide; the 2024/2025 School Aid Bill redirected about $598 million of savings back to districts through the 147a(4) categorical, representing approximately 5.75 percent of the District's 2024 MPSERS-related payroll. For fiscal year 2024/2025 the School District received $5,055,278 under 147a(4), approximately $411 on a per pupil basis. Section 147c(2) appropriated $250 million in additional one-time payments to the retirement system, with no fund balance impact because the District was invoiced for the same amount it received. Section 147g was new in 2024/2025 and reimbursed employees for their 3 percent employer contribution to the OPEB plan, providing no additional general operating resources. GSRP funding increased, with families below four times the federal poverty level eligible for free preschool. At-risk funding is now over $1 billion. Transportation, Future Educator Fellowship, Student Teacher Stipend, and ISD Operations support continued without substantive change. The most significant reduction was mental health and school safety under Section 31aa, cut from $328 million to initially only $26.5 million on an opt-in basis, later increased by a $125 million supplemental.

2025/2026 SCHOOL FUNDING. Michigan's Legislature, split between a Republican-led House and a Democratic-led Senate, missed the July 1 statutory deadline; negotiations continued past the July 1, 2025 start of the school fiscal year and past the State's October 1, 2025 fiscal year start, forcing an emergency one-week stopgap. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act was expected to shrink Michigan's 2026 revenue by roughly $677 million if the State adopted the federal tax rule changes. The school aid budget is $21.3 billion, about $0.5 billion higher than last year, while continuing to shift approximately $1.3 billion in 2026 from the School Aid Fund to colleges and universities. Key provisions: the per pupil foundation allowance rises to $10,050 from $9,608, approximately a 4.6 percent increase; the 147a(1) MPSERS cost offset of $100 million, roughly $75 per student statewide, was eliminated; 147a(4) was completely removed compared with the 2025 budget, equating to $598 million or approximately $400 per student, reflecting the statutory reduction in the MPSERS UAAL required contribution from 20.96 percent to 15.21 percent of covered payroll; Section 30d universal free school meals continues with about $200 million; Section 31a at-risk funding increased 25 percent, adding roughly $258 million, with a new parent reporting and feedback requirement; Section 41 English Language Learner grants received a 25 percent boost to approximately $62.7 million; Section 51e foundational special education grants grew about 4 percent, roughly $25 million statewide; $65 million in one-time funds was set aside for K-3 class size reduction; Section 31aa provides over $169 million, an increase from roughly $151.5 million allocated last year including supplemental funds; and $100 million in one-time infrastructure grant funding was allocated.

LOOKING FORWARD. The State's 2026 budget is approximately $81 billion, boosting road and bridge funding by approximately $1.1 billion per year through a new 24 percent wholesale tax on marijuana producing $420 million and by replacing the 6 percent sales tax on gasoline with a 20 cents per gallon fuel tax increase, aligning with Governor Gretchen Whitmer's "fix the roads" promise; the new tax measures are expected to generate over $1.5 billion per year once fully implemented. Statewide enrollment has historically been slightly under 1.5 million students, was declining by about 10,000 students per year before the pandemic, and decreased in excess of 50,000 students during the pandemic. On average it takes about 10 students to fully fund a teacher position. The next Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference occurs in January 2026. The federal government missed its October 1 deadline and is in a shutdown.

MICHIGAN SCHOOL MEALS. The state-funded free breakfast and lunch initiative launched in the 2023/2024 school year under State Aid Act amendments, with Section 30d funds allocated to the Food Service Fund. For 2024/2025 the School District received $3,719,300 in Section 30d state funding. Districts apply through the Coordinated Application in the State's NexSys system and must participate in the National School Lunch Program, serve breakfast and lunch at no cost to pre-K through 12th grade students, adopt the Community Eligibility Provision, collect family income information, and write off outstanding negative student balances using resources outside the Food Service Fund. Funding continued in the 2026 state budget with a new provision allowing MDE to withhold 5 percent of state aid payments for non-adherence to federal school meal rules or failure to require completion of the federal free and reduced-price meal application.

OTHER INFORMATIONAL ITEMS. Davis Bacon prevailing wage requirements apply when federal funding is used for remodeling, renovation, repair, or construction contracts over $2,000. MPSERS, which has a September 30 year end, had a net pension liability of approximately $24.5 billion at September 30, 2024, a decrease of approximately 24 percent from $32.4 billion at September 30, 2023, and a net OPEB asset of approximately $4.3 billion compared with $566 million at September 30, 2023, an increase of approximately 660 percent; the plan's annual investment rate of return was 15.5 percent for the year ended September 30, 2024 versus 8.3 percent for the prior year. During 2024/2025 the School District's General Fund expenditures exceeded revenue by approximately $3.1 million, reducing General Fund fund balance to approximately $33.7 million at June 30, 2025; the statewide average at June 30, 2024 was approximately 24.7 percent of operating expenditures excluding transfers, equal to about a 13-week period, while the School District's fund balance percentage is 17.4 percent, equal to approximately 9 weeks of operation. GASB Statement No. 103, Financial Reporting Model Improvements, and GASB Statement No. 104, Disclosure of Certain Capital Assets, are both effective for the District's June 30, 2026 year end. Sinking fund legislation effective August 6, 2023 allows sinking fund millages approved by voters after May 7, 2023 to be used for student transportation vehicles and related parts, supplies, and equipment, and for trucks and vans registered under the Michigan vehicle code, 1949 PA 300, MCL 257.1 to 257.923; sinking funds authorized prior to March 29, 2017, between March 29, 2017 and May 7, 2023, and after May 7, 2023 must be accounted for separately with annual independent audit. RESPONSIBILITIES AND SCOPE. The engagement letter is dated June 3, 2025. The auditors' responsibility is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements prepared by management are fairly presented in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles, obtaining reasonable but not absolute assurance that the statements are free of material misstatement. Internal control was considered solely to determine audit procedures, not to provide assurance on internal control. The audit was also conducted in accordance with Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, and a separate letter dated October 13, 2025 addresses internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance with laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements. The audit followed the scope and timing communicated at the planning meeting of June 18, 2025.

SIGNIFICANT AUDIT FINDINGS. For the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2024, the School District adopted the provisions of Governmental Accounting Standards Board Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences; the opinion is not modified with respect to this new accounting policy. Significant accounting policies are described in Note 2. No significant transactions were recognized in a different period than when they occurred. The most sensitive estimates were the District's share of the MPSERS net liability for pension and net asset for other postemployment benefits recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75; the District's estimates as of June 30, 2025 were $211.6 million for pension and $36.6 million for OPEB, based on data received from the Office of Retirement Services. Disclosures were described as neutral, consistent, and clear. No significant difficulties were encountered, no disagreements with management arose, and no misstatements were detected as a result of audit procedures. A management representation letter is dated October 13, 2025. There were no consultations with other independent accountants. The auditors read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and nothing came to their attention suggesting material misstatement or inconsistency.

OTHER RECOMMENDATIONS AND OBSERVATIONS. The Food Service Fund's fund balance continues to exceed the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures. The School District should continue to monitor its spenddown plan, entered into with the Michigan Department of Education, for reducing the balance to an acceptable level.

MANAGING THE CHANGING LANDSCAPE. The State did not meet its self-imposed July 1 deadline to complete the school aid budget for fiscal year 2025/2026. The May 2025 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference produced upward revisions to short- and long-term revenue growth projections for the General Fund and School Aid Fund, with cautionary notes about macroeconomic events including evolving federal trade policies. The federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act was signed on July 4, 2025 and is estimated to significantly reduce State revenue and to make Medicaid changes affecting the State budget. The U.S. Department of Education is undergoing major changes in 2025 following an executive order to dismantle it; billions of dollars in education funding were initially frozen, primarily related to Title I, and the president's budget proposal eliminates funding for Title 1-C, Title III, Title II, and Title IV-A.

2024/2025 SCHOOL FUNDING. The target foundation allowance stayed at $9,608 per pupil for public schools, while public school academies received a 3.9 percent increase estimated at $9,983. The blended pupil count used 90 percent weighting for the October 2024 count and 10 percent for the February 2024 count, with a two-year blended count available under Section 29 for districts whose 2024 final membership was lower than 2023. Under Section 147a(4), state funding historically covering the OPEB UAAL was about $669 million statewide; the 2024/2025 School Aid Bill redirected about $598 million of savings back to districts through the 147a(4) categorical, representing approximately 5.75 percent of the District's 2024 MPSERS-related payroll. For fiscal year 2024/2025 the School District received $5,055,278 under 147a(4), approximately $411 on a per pupil basis. Section 147c(2) appropriated $250 million in additional one-time payments to the retirement system, with no fund balance impact because the District was invoiced for the same amount it received. Section 147g was new in 2024/2025 and reimbursed employees for their 3 percent employer contribution to the OPEB plan, providing no additional general operating resources. GSRP funding increased, with families below four times the federal poverty level eligible for free preschool. At-risk funding is now over $1 billion. Transportation, Future Educator Fellowship, Student Teacher Stipend, and ISD Operations support continued without substantive change. The most significant reduction was mental health and school safety under Section 31aa, cut from $328 million to initially only $26.5 million on an opt-in basis, later increased by a $125 million supplemental.

2025/2026 SCHOOL FUNDING. Michigan's Legislature, split between a Republican-led House and a Democratic-led Senate, missed the July 1 statutory deadline; negotiations continued past the July 1, 2025 start of the school fiscal year and past the State's October 1, 2025 fiscal year start, forcing an emergency one-week stopgap. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act was expected to shrink Michigan's 2026 revenue by roughly $677 million if the State adopted the federal tax rule changes. The school aid budget is $21.3 billion, about $0.5 billion higher than last year, while continuing to shift approximately $1.3 billion in 2026 from the School Aid Fund to colleges and universities. Key provisions: the per pupil foundation allowance rises to $10,050 from $9,608, approximately a 4.6 percent increase; the 147a(1) MPSERS cost offset of $100 million, roughly $75 per student statewide, was eliminated; 147a(4) was completely removed compared with the 2025 budget, equating to $598 million or approximately $400 per student, reflecting the statutory reduction in the MPSERS UAAL required contribution from 20.96 percent to 15.21 percent of covered payroll; Section 30d universal free school meals continues with about $200 million; Section 31a at-risk funding increased 25 percent, adding roughly $258 million, with a new parent reporting and feedback requirement; Section 41 English Language Learner grants received a 25 percent boost to approximately $62.7 million; Section 51e foundational special education grants grew about 4 percent, roughly $25 million statewide; $65 million in one-time funds was set aside for K-3 class size reduction; Section 31aa provides over $169 million, an increase from roughly $151.5 million allocated last year including supplemental funds; and $100 million in one-time infrastructure grant funding was allocated.

LOOKING FORWARD. The State's 2026 budget is approximately $81 billion, boosting road and bridge funding by approximately $1.1 billion per year through a new 24 percent wholesale tax on marijuana producing $420 million and by replacing the 6 percent sales tax on gasoline with a 20 cents per gallon fuel tax increase, aligning with Governor Gretchen Whitmer's "fix the roads" promise; the new tax measures are expected to generate over $1.5 billion per year once fully implemented. Statewide enrollment has historically been slightly under 1.5 million students, was declining by about 10,000 students per year before the pandemic, and decreased in excess of 50,000 students during the pandemic. On average it takes about 10 students to fully fund a teacher position. The next Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference occurs in January 2026. The federal government missed its October 1 deadline and is in a shutdown.

MICHIGAN SCHOOL MEALS. The state-funded free breakfast and lunch initiative launched in the 2023/2024 school year under State Aid Act amendments, with Section 30d funds allocated to the Food Service Fund. For 2024/2025 the School District received $3,719,300 in Section 30d state funding. Districts apply through the Coordinated Application in the State's NexSys system and must participate in the National School Lunch Program, serve breakfast and lunch at no cost to pre-K through 12th grade students, adopt the Community Eligibility Provision, collect family income information, and write off outstanding negative student balances using resources outside the Food Service Fund. Funding continued in the 2026 state budget with a new provision allowing MDE to withhold 5 percent of state aid payments for non-adherence to federal school meal rules or failure to require completion of the federal free and reduced-price meal application.

OTHER INFORMATIONAL ITEMS. Davis Bacon prevailing wage requirements apply when federal funding is used for remodeling, renovation, repair, or construction contracts over $2,000. Sinking fund legislation effective August 6, 2023 allows sinking fund millages approved by voters after May 7, 2023 to be used for student transportation vehicles and related parts, supplies, and equipment, and for trucks and vans registered under the Michigan vehicle code, 1949 PA 300, MCL 257.1 to 257.923; sinking funds authorized prior to March 29, 2017, between March 29, 2017 and May 7, 2023, and after May 7, 2023 must be accounted for separately with annual independent audit. TITLE AND PURPOSE. "Pieces of One Troy: Building Belonging Through Data and Action" was presented to the Troy School District Board of Education in November 2025. The stated purposes were to review student performance on state assessments and how performance has changed over time, district-by-district performance, performance gaps between student groups, and areas of focus and celebrations. The deck cautions that state assessments are summative assessments designed to be a snapshot in time, are one part of a balanced assessment system, help policy makers and decision makers understand overall levels of achievement and identify schools, groups, and students for support, and are not designed to be diagnostic or to drive day-to-day teaching and learning.

M-STEP GRADES 3-7 BY GRADE. GAP ANALYSIS. The implications slide states that districts have historically struggled to raise the performance of students with disabilities, economically disadvantaged students, and English learners on par with countywide and statewide rates, a phenomenon commonly known as the Performance Gap and also referred to as an Opportunity Gap. The Multi-Tiered System of Support slide lists district commitment to building coherence in process, focus on systems that support all students, commitment to Professional Learning Communities in process at all schools, universal supports, review of progress monitoring of any student on a plan, development of a district handbook, interventions taught by content strong teachers, and focus on Tier 1 instruction. ANALYSIS. Strengths listed: TSD consistently outperforms county and state averages, demonstrating strong and effective instructional practices; all subgroups (economically disadvantaged, special education, English learners) are performing above their statewide peers, indicating effective support systems; performance stability over three years underscores resilience and sustainability of current practices; and third grade is first in the county in ELA and math. Focus areas for continuous improvement: special education, described as the largest and most persistent achievement gap, addressed through inclusive practices with a focus on Tier 1 instruction and targeted interventions provided by content strong teachers; economically disadvantaged students, who outperform state and county peers but of whom fewer than half meet proficiency; and English learners, who perform strongly compared with county and state peers but for whom a performance gap remains and ongoing language acquisition and academic language development support is essential.

MIDDLE SCHOOL MATH. Cohort performance slides cover the current 9th grade Class of 2029, described as the last split cohort with the 6/7 and 7/8 track and IM 6/7 and the first cohort with a choice after 7th grade of Honors Algebra 1, and the current 8th grade Class of 2030, described as IM 6th/IM 7th.
