https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Presentation.** 6-8 Math Curriculum Adoption, May 2023, delivered at the Troy School District Board workshop on May 2, 2023, documenting the 6-8 curriculum review process for 2019-2023 across three phases: Phase 1 Research and Vision, Phase 2 Explore, and Phase 3 Implementation.

**Phase 1: Research and Vision.** The district notes it has used its current resources, Math Expressions and Big Ideas Math, for almost 10 years, and that a great deal of learning has occurred in the last 10 years. Learning partnerships are listed as Michael D. Steele, PhD, University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee professor and National Science Foundation Program Officer; Ted Coe, PhD, VP, Academic Advocacy - Mathematics at NWEA and, from 2014-2020, Director of Mathematics at ACHIEVE, INC.; and Jonathan Bostic, PhD, Bowling Green State University professor of mathematics education. Data slides present 6th grade M-STEP data over time, 7th grade M-STEP data over time, and 8th grade M-STEP data over time, with a note that in the 2018/19 school year students took the PSAT 8. A math cohort chart for grades 3-7 tracks student performance on Math M-STEP for the same cohort of students from grade 3 in 2015 through grade 7 in 2019. A further slide addresses students' opportunities for choice.

**Standards and pedagogy reflection.** The deck lists the eight Standards for Mathematical Practice: make sense of problems and persevere; reason abstractly and quantitatively; construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; model with mathematics; use appropriate tools strategically; attend to precision; look for and make use of structure; and look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning. It presents the 8 Effective Math Teaching Practices as the means to implement the Michigan K-12 Math Standards, citing NCTM (2014), Principles to Actions: Ensuring mathematical success for all.

**Vision and findings.** The vision, citing NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics, states that all students are doers of mathematics and that the program's purpose is to cultivate students' positive mathematical identities so all students develop deep mathematical understandings, understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience the wonder, joy and beauty of mathematics. Finding 1, explore curricular changes: program data from the last 5 years preceding COVID showed student performance slightly decreasing or stagnant, with cohort data showing a decrease in students achieving advanced and proficient and an increase in students not proficient. Finding 2, explore course sequencing: students are not able to fluidly move between tracks in middle school. Finding 3, explore classroom pedagogy: explore task-based, inquiry-based instruction that builds procedural fluency through conceptual understanding.

**Phase 2: Explore.** Questions framed for the curricular pilot asked how TSD would align middle school math programming with its vision and beliefs; what world-class middle school mathematics programming looks like; how conceptual understanding is built and what learning trajectory students experience; what opportunities students experience in a task-based, inquiry-based classroom; and how a teacher can meet the needs of all learners in a collaborative, student-centered environment.

**Review matrix.** The Middle School Math Curriculum Review Matrix is organized into Blue, Red, Gold and Green sections, each with Evidence and Overall rating/impression fields. Blue covers Deep Learning opportunities, student discussion and talk, inquiry and/or task basis, cohesive topic sequencing in an engaging storyline or learning arc, and support for the standards for mathematical practice. Red covers valuing students' mathematical ideas, inviting all students in, choice and voice, eliciting joy, and differentiation opportunities. Gold covers support for teachers in using the 8 effective math practices, what professional learning is offered and how it is structured and who runs it, ongoing teacher support, support for differentiation, and connection to a research base or learning organization such as a university. Green covers support for students in future pathways and relevance to students' lives and college and career interests.

**Pilot process.** The team investigated 8 different curricula and narrowed to two using the review matrix. 50% of middle school math teachers participated, with representation from each course - Math 6, Math 6/7 Honors, Math 7, Math 7/8 Honors and Math 8 - and all four middle schools participating. Semester 1 piloted Connected Mathematics Project (CMP) and Semester 2 piloted Illustrative Mathematics (IM), with two or more units of each curriculum taught by all pilot teachers. Both curricula were described as task-based, inquiry instruction with enhanced opportunities to access the Math Practice Standards, specifically making sense of problems and persevering, constructing viable arguments and critiquing the reasoning of others, and modeling with mathematics.

**Professional learning during the pilot.** 1.5 day of professional learning was provided during the school day to all piloting teachers prior to the start of each pilot, and 4 job-embedded professional learning opportunities were offered to every pilot teacher during the piloting experience. All middle school math teachers engaged in job-embedded professional learning around technology and the pilot curriculum, and during district PD all teachers engaged in 2 days of learning on best practice and pedagogy with Dr. Bostic and MSU facilitators. Pilot teachers met as PLCs supported with building subs, Math Specialists co-planned, co-taught and coached throughout the pilot, and pilot teachers were paid to work after hours. Data collected included student and teacher surveys, work samples, videos and assessments.

**Pilot teacher input.** For CMP, celebrations were that the curriculum provides multiple ways for students to solve problems, allows students to deepen learning through talk and collaboration, and that some teachers believed the support provided was sufficient to implement with fidelity. Areas of need included some concerns about the curriculum being invitational and relevant to students, many concerns about providing enough guidance because materials were not manageable to use, and some concerns about supporting the needs of all learners. For Illustrative Math, celebrations were that the curriculum invites all students into the mathematics, provides multiple ways to solve problems, allows students to deepen learning through talk and collaboration, that teacher materials provide enough guidance and are manageable to use, that teacher support was sufficient to implement with fidelity, and that teachers felt confident to implement. Areas of need were more guidance about fostering an engaging learning environment and more professional learning on supporting the needs of all learners. The team then revisited the review matrix.

**Recommendation: Illustrative Mathematics (IM).** IM curriculum is authored and maintained exclusively by Illustrative Mathematics, a non-profit organization led by noted mathematician and standards author Dr. Bill McCallum. IM began at the University of Arizona, where Dr. McCallum served as a professor, and has been developed into a complete K-12 curriculum through grants from the National Science Foundation, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, the Carnegie Corporation of New York and others. IM is described as a research organization that consistently monitors implementation and impact, with a link to illustrativemathematics.org/impact/. IM is characterized as problem-based, built on universal design for learning, with embedded supports for students with disabilities and English learners, extensions for students ready for more, built-in instructional routines, predictable and purposeful activity and lesson structure, and practice problem sets with built-in cumulative review. Slides cover preparing for problem-based teaching and learning, the problem-based lesson structure, a sample SAT problem, a sample AP exam question, and school districts in Michigan utilizing or exploring IM.

**Course sequencing and choice (Finding 2).** District data showed students tend to stay in the track they are placed in throughout middle school, and it is difficult, even for students doing well in math, to move to the Honors track; the current structure requires families to purchase summer learning opportunities in order for students to move between tracks. IM is presented as enabling deep levels of engagement and differentiation for all math learners.

**Research base.** A timely research summary quotes The Effect of School Tracking on Student Achievement and Inequality: A Meta-Analysis by Eder Terrin and Moris Triventi of the University of Trento, reporting that applying meta-analytical techniques to studies from the last two decades yields a mean effect size of tracking on efficiency that is null while positive for inequality, providing no support for an equality-efficiency trade-off (quoting Skopek et al., 2019, p. 224), and concluding that de-tracking reforms which postpone tracking, reduce the number of tracks, or smooth out distinctions across tracks have potential to reduce inequality of educational opportunity based on social background without harming overall student achievement. Research from ACT notes that high school teachers often prioritize covering a broad range of advanced topics while college-level teachers think high school students should receive in-depth coverage of foundational topics like number sense and basic algebra (Chait & Venezia, 2009), and that students with a solid understanding of middle school mathematics are better prepared for advanced high school courses, improving success rates in college-level courses (ACT 2009, 2012). Two Other Resources slides list references including Boaler (2000), Bressoud (2017), Clotfelter, Ladd and Vigdor (2012) of Duke University, the Common Core State Standards Initiative (2010), Daro and Asturias (2019), Gamoran and Hannigan (2000), the Kansas State Department of Education White Paper (2015), Loveless (2016), Ma and Wilkins (2007), Morton and Riegle-Crumb (2019), NCEE (2013), Patall, Cooper and Robinson (2008), Rosenstein (2014) of Rutgers, and US Department of Education reports from 2012 and 2018.

**Middle school pathways and FAQ.** Pathway slides reference Grade 8, Grade 9 and Grade 10 sequences. The FAQ asks whether Math 8 content is being skipped, answering that Math 8 content will be intentionally and thoughtfully embedded into the middle school Algebra 1 course, work to be completed in partnership with the Michigan Math and Science Leadership Network (MMSLN) and IM. It also asks what information families might use to choose Math 8 versus Algebra 1, answering that buildings will host family information nights to discuss and illustrate the differences.

**Supporting all students.** Advancement and acceleration measures include deep levels of learning, investing in staff through professional learning, enrichment materials embedded within Illustrative Math under "Are You Ready for More?", enrichment and enhancement opportunities such as math club and robotics, and traditional test-out opportunities to move more quickly through grade levels.

**Phase 3: Implementation.** Implementation principles are that teachers practice IM's problem-based instructional model with integrity and believe all students are capable of learning grade-level mathematics; that teachers engage in IM Professional Learning with implementation support through IM coaching, university partners and a Math Specialist at each building; that school leaders and administrators understand and support the systemic changes necessary to change teachers' practice; and that families and communities engage with and support their students' learning. The 2022/23 middle school math implementation PD days are full day meetings with 8 subs each day, scheduled May 30 for Math 6, May 31 for Math 7, June 1 for Math 8, June 5 for Math 6, June 7 for Math 7 and June 12 for Math 8, with a Summer Institute tentatively August 8-11. For 2023/24, back-to-school professional learning will focus on using the new resources, with job-embedded professional learning with IM coaches throughout the school year, a full time Math Specialist in each building to unpack units, co-plan, co-teach, coach teachers and provide intervention with struggling students, and monthly afterschool PLC meetings with after school pay.

**Support for families.** For 2022/23 to date, middle school parent nights were held at Baker on April 18, Boulan on April 19, Larson on April 20 and April 24, and Smith on April 17, with a Community Round Table to answer family questions on April 13, plus a video explaining the review process, curriculum changes and a classroom sneak peek, an Academics website, and ongoing one-on-one conversations with families. For 2023/24, the district plans parent learning sessions at buildings with math teachers, math specialists and CIS, parent learning sessions from experts in the field, and classroom video examples on the website. Every IM unit includes Family Support Materials describing the big ideas in plain language, and every IM lesson includes a lesson summary in student-friendly language covering the main mathematical points and new vocabulary.

**Monitoring success.** The district will continuously gather teacher feedback about supports, next learning and the implementation process, and measure student achievement regularly - reported annually via M-STEP, PSAT and SAT including cohort data, plus benchmarks, and studied with staff via unit assessments, student enrollment in Algebra 1, and student success as measured by grades in higher levels of mathematics.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Presented to the Troy School District Board of Education on December 3, 2024, the Accountability Plan slide deck reports progress against the four "World Class for All" pillars: Green (Early Childhood to Career), Red (Equity and Well-Being), Blue (Deep Learning), and Gold (Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families). Each pillar is laid out as objectives, December 2024 celebrations and key results, and challenges and recommendations. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Format and purpose**
PowerPoint presentation delivered at the December 3, 2024 Troy School District Board of Education meeting. The framing slide states that the "World Class for All" pillars hold the team accountable to Objectives and Key Results. Each of the four color-coded pillars is presented in the same sequence: objectives, December 2024 celebrations and key results, and challenges and recommendations.

**Green Pillar - Early Childhood to Career**
Objectives: invest in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for universal preschool for all three- and four-year-olds; expand college and career pathways through high-quality CTE that connects underrepresented students to in-demand careers; and build a consistent K-12 career readiness plan.
Key results: GSRP slots increase from 98 to 160; Portrait of A Learner; K-8 career readiness engagement with Media Specialists and Maker Space; the 99b Computer Science / Computational Thinking Grant; K-12 CS alignment with Oakland Schools and MDE; Early Middle College with LTU; a Business Round Table; Career Accelerator Program increase to 60 students; 8th grade interviews and portfolio integrated with middle school Celebrations of Learning; and Athens named one of two schools in the state to pilot the Ignite Program (Mechatronics). More than 290 students from the class of 2024 earned CTE completer status across eleven listed fields including Mechatronics, Automotive Technician, Computer Programming, Finance, and Woodworking.
Challenges: transition to a 5 Day Model; preparation for universal preschool; the stigma of career readiness; embedding career readiness through building leaders; digital citizenship K-12; growing computer science; and shifting from electives to CTE programs.

**Red Pillar - Equity and Well-Being**
Objectives center on equity and well-being, funding investments for the whole child, an elevated district-wide focus on Alignment, Access, and Agency, and assessing needs for a world class learning environment. Key results: an SEL curriculum pilot and SEL-focused programming K-12; Behavioral Threat Assessment and Suicide Risk Assessment committee work; Belonging Focus Group Sessions and Student Equity Council expansion; the Community Book Read; and all building teams trained in restorative culture as of November 2024. Challenges note over 1600 SEL lessons in Everyday Speech utilized September through November, partnership with Margaret Coggins and the BTA Team, NTAC adoption, and suicide awareness professional learning in Winter 2024.

**Blue Pillar - Deep Learning**
Objectives: MTSS systems of support that empower student voice, improved technology access and training, global best practices (NPDL, The 6 C's, learning partnerships), and upgraded facilities. Slides cover furniture, playgrounds, and student designs and input, noting 36 teachers piloting furniture K-12 alongside student quotations. Curriculum and pedagogy items include full days of professional learning on October 31st and November 1st, implementation of NWEA and Common Lit standardized assessments, pilot work in Geometry, review in Spanish and French, an elementary ELD Newcomer curriculum pilot, and a Grades 11/12 ELA Course Study Team. MTSS work includes partnership with New Solutions K-12 and Solution Tree, a teacher consultant model for Special Education, and an artificial intelligence leadership committee. Challenges: coordinating MTSS across teams, substitute teacher coverage, and systemness.

**Gold Pillar - Building Capacity**
Objectives address educator preparation, pipelines for underrepresented educators, job-embedded professional learning, and co-designed experiences for the OneTroy community. Key results list the Fielding International Partnership, NSK12, Solution Tree, Community Book Read, Learning Nights at all schools, counseling systemness 6-12, website launch feedback sessions, and WEB, LEAP, and the Student Leadership Conference. Challenges include partnership with Celebrate Hope, attracting experienced staff from outside the district, retention strategies, leadership cohorts, and a new teacher learning series.

**Closing**
A "What's Next?" slide quotes that the world's best school systems ensure all stakeholders understand the purpose, priorities, and goals of the system, with leaders clarifying a few very specific non-negotiables while encouraging autonomy and creativity at all levels.

Troy School District Accountability Plan presentation delivered to the Board of Education on December 3, 2024, in PowerPoint form. The opening slides identify the district and school (Troy) and establish the framework: the "World Class for All" Pillars hold the team accountable to Objectives and Key Results. The body of the deck walks through four color-coded pillars in turn, each with an objectives slide, a December 2024 celebrations and key results slide, and a challenges and recommendations slide.

GREEN PILLAR - EARLY CHILDHOOD TO CAREER
Objectives: continue to invest in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for access to universal preschool for all three- and four-year-olds; expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students by offering high-quality career and technical education, with the plan connecting underrepresented students to in-demand careers in high-growth industries through partnerships with colleges, employers, and stakeholders, enabling work-based learning, credential earning, and college credit opportunities; and build a consistent career readiness plan for students K-12.
December 2024 celebrations and key results: an increase in GSRP slots from 98 to 160; consistent priority on percent Preschool Experience Data; Portrait of A Learner; career readiness engagement opportunities K-8 partnered with Media Specialists and Maker Space; the 99b Computer Science / Computational Thinking Grant; K-12 computer science alignment with Oakland Schools and the Michigan Department of Education; expanded maker-centered learning spaces to the high school; continued prioritization of post-secondary learning partnerships throughout K-12; Early Middle College with LTU; a Business Round Table; a Career Accelerator Program increase to 60 students; 8th grade interviews and portfolio integrated with middle school Celebrations of Learning; Athens named as one of two schools in the state to pilot the Ignite Program (Mechatronics); and a process of reviewing and updating CTE programs to make improvements, build stronger connections with business and industry, and provide students the opportunity to earn credentials.
A dedicated slide records that more than 290 students from the class of 2024 earned completer status in one of the district's CTE courses, listing Education, Radio & Television Broadcasting, Marketing, Finance, Drafting & Design Technology, Cooking and Culinary Arts, Automotive Technician, Computer Programming, Mechatronics, Business, and Woodworking.
December 2024 challenges and recommendations: transition to a 5 Day Model; preparation for universal preschool (expanding access); mindshifting the stigma of career readiness to prioritize relevance to learning in classrooms; supporting all building leaders to embed career readiness initiatives in classrooms and beyond; Portrait of a Learner, leveraging and embracing its connection to the current strategic plan; prioritizing digital citizenship for K-12; growing and developing computer science in the K-12 curriculum; and shifting from electives to CTE programs.

RED PILLAR - EQUITY AND WELL-BEING
Objectives: ensuring a focus on equity and well-being; funding additional investments to support the needs of the whole child; an elevated district-wide focus on Alignment, Access, and Agency; and assessing needs and taking action to meet the demands of a world class learning environment in all school communities.
December 2024 celebrations and key results: an SEL curriculum pilot and SEL-focused programming K-12; Behavioral Threat Assessment (BTA) and Suicide Risk Assessment committee work; elevating student experience through Belonging Focus Group Sessions and Student Equity Council expansion; family and community engagement via the Community Book Read and the Continuing the Conversation Series; and restorative culture and community, with all building teams trained as of November 2024.
Challenges and recommendations: community engagement and partnerships with continued intentional collaboration and connection; encouraging and implementing aligned structures; equity teamwork across buildings; SEL curriculum and SEL support/instruction K-12, noting that over 1600 SEL lessons in Everyday Speech were utilized September through November; continued partnership with Margaret Coggins and the BTA Team, including behavioral threat assessment consistency through NTAC adoption, suicide awareness professional learning in Winter 2024, and consistent expectations across all levels and teams; restorative practices including counseling, team, and department fundamentals training, train-the-trainer work to build capacity, and community involvement and awareness; and Belonging as a North Star, continued through an Inclusive Newsletter, professional learning, and student support.

BLUE PILLAR - DEEP LEARNING
Objectives: create and sustain systems of support at all levels that deepen learning and empower student voice (MTSS), with access to deep learning described as imperative for all children; improve technology access for students and families while providing quality training to leverage technology to deepen learning; continue to pursue the global best practices of all content areas (NPDL, The 6 C's, learning partnerships); and assess the need and take action for upgraded facilities to meet the demands of a world-class learning environment in all school communities.
Separate slides are devoted to Furniture, Playgrounds, and Student Designs and Input for Playgrounds and Furniture. The student input slide records 36 teachers piloting furniture K-12 and quotes students: "We need places to climb and play sports to get our energy out!"; "I like rockers because I can rock on them and sit on the carpet to read. It's easy to concentrate and it's comfy."; "My favorite stuff is something I can move with."; and "We want shade and nice places to relax with our friends in nature."
Curriculum and pedagogy: focused attention on Professional Learning Communities at the secondary level; targeted learning on Universal Design and MTSS at the secondary level; continued learning around learning environments in coordination with bond initiatives; development of an Artificial Intelligence leadership committee; development of a Computer Science leadership team; and continuing to grow digital portfolios for students to document learning over time. A second curriculum slide lists October 31st and November 1st as full days of professional learning - elementary on classroom environments and MTSS in mathematics, secondary on universal design, plus choice sessions - along with implementation of NWEA and Common Lit standardized assessments and ongoing development of the MTSS process, and continued curricular work comprising pilot work in Geometry, a review process in Spanish and French, a pilot of the elementary ELD Newcomer curriculum, and a Grades 11/12 ELA Course Study Team.
Multi-Tiered Systems of Support: partnership with New Solutions K-12 and a plan for implementation of its recommendations. Elementary MTSS work continues to monitor benchmark data, develop capacity in math, and solidify tier-one instruction in all classrooms. Secondary MTSS teams meet regularly to support student needs, consider system data to be utilized, build a continuum of services to include a teacher consultant model for Special Education, and partner with Solution Tree to build instructional leadership capacity.
Challenges and recommendations: coordinating MTSS implementation across teams (principals, teachers, content areas, support staff); continuously supporting all content areas; substitute teacher coverage; systemness and building capacity of all staff; and helping staff see connections across content area and level.

GOLD PILLAR - BUILDING CAPACITY OF STUDENTS, STAFF, AND FAMILIES
Objectives: improving educator preparation, strengthening pipelines for underrepresented educators, and supporting current educators; continuing to provide job-embedded professional learning experiences for all staff; and providing professional learning opportunities for staff, community, and students with the goal of co-designing impactful experiences to better the OneTroy community.
Key results: job-embedded learning for staff through the Fielding International Partnership, NSK12, Solution Tree, the Community Book Read, and Learning Nights at all schools; use of early release days to prioritize conversations with collaborative teacher teams around student learning and emerging professional learning communities; building systemness with counseling 6-12 around program opportunities; engaging stakeholders in feedback sessions on the website launch; and building student capacity through WEB, LEAP, and the Student Leadership Conference.
Challenges and recommendations: continued partnership with Celebrate Hope; continued investigation into attracting experienced staff from outside of the district; retention strategies; building community partnerships; continued collaboration among departments within Sub Cabinet; leadership cohorts; and a new teacher learning series.

CLOSING
The final content slide is titled "What's Next?" and carries the quotation: "The world's best school systems ensure that all stakeholders understand the purpose, priorities, and goals of the system. Leaders clarify a few very specific non-negotiables that must be honored throughout the system and at the same time they encourage autonomy and creativity at all levels to foster ownership and innovation."

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
"Exploring Our Data Story" was presented to the Troy School District Board of Education at its meeting of November 19, 2024. The stated objectives were to review district goals, provide context to enhance understanding of data, and share how data is utilized to drive district systems and processes.

ASSESSMENT FRAMEWORK
A slide titled "Beyond the Cover: Understanding Summative & Formative Assessment" organizes the district's measures: building a strong foundation and early childhood enrollment; district-level summative assessments consisting of M-STEP (Gr 3-7), PSAT 8 / SAT 11, and College Board Advanced Placement; classroom-level formative assessments consisting of Fountas & Pinnell (K-5), Bridges Math (K-5), Common Lit (ELA 6-12), and NWEA - Math (6-Alg 1); and exit data, specifically the TCCHS graduation rate.
Under "Snapshots of Progress," the presentation recognizes the limitations of summative M-STEP and PSAT/SAT data: cohort tracking allows monitoring of student cohort performance over time; comparative insights allow assessment against other districts; and granularity issues mean summative data lacks detailed analysis for specific performance insights.

M-STEP
Chart slides are presented for ELA M-STEP Grades 3-7 with county comparison and FRL rate, for M-STEP Math Grades 3-7 with county comparison and FRL rate, and for Middle School M-STEP Grades 6 and 7 covering English Language Arts and Mathematics. The underlying values for these graphics are not carried in the document text.

PSAT 8 RESULTS
The PSAT 8 Evidence-Based Reading & Writing (EBRW) chart plots Troy School District (TSD), Oakland Schools, and the State across 2018-19, 2021-22, 2022-23, and 2023-24. TSD: 87.1, 81, 85.6, 84.2. Oakland Schools: 70.3, 67, 68.4, 71.4. State: 61.9, 59.7, 59.7, 64.5.
The PSAT 8 Math chart, over the same four periods, shows TSD at 75.1, 67.5, 69, and 64.3; Oakland Schools at 52.5, 44.6, 45.5, and 42.3; and the State at 41.4, 36.2, 36.2, and 32.6. A further slide is labeled "2023-24 PSAT 8" and compares the OS LEA Average with TSD.

SAT 11TH GRADE RESULTS
SAT 11th grade Evidence Based Reading & Writing (EBRW) over 2018-19, 2021-22, 2022-23, and 2023-24: TSD 82.9, 75.3, 76.9, 77.3; Oakland Schools 62.9, 59, 59.3, 59.6; State 55.3, 51.6, 52.2, 51.3.
SAT 11th grade Math over the same periods: TSD 73.6, 61.6, 61.3, 59.5; Oakland Schools 46.7, 39.3, 38.9, 35.7; State 36.3, 30, 29.9, 26.3.
SAT Overall Performance, defined as the percent of 11th grade students who meet or exceed expectations in both Math and EBRW, is charted on an axis spanning 2018-19, 2019-20, 2020-21, 2021-22, 2022-23, and 2023-24 with a 0 to 80 scale. Plotted values are 69.8, 58.8, 59.7, and 57 for TSD; 44.5, 37.3, 37.1, and 34.4 for Oakland Schools; and 33.9, 28.1, 28.2, and 25.1 for the State. TSD exceeds both Oakland Schools and the State on every summative measure shown.

REFLECTIONS AND USES OF SUMMATIVE DATA
Summative data informs the MTSS process, collaboration, and ongoing adjustments, along with a partnership with NSK12 to evaluate supports and structure for students with services in ELD, Special Education, and other areas. Areas of focus are access to Tier 1 core instruction for all; access to content-strong staff, framed as who is teaching the content and intervention; additional time for learning, framed as more time with content-strong staff; and ongoing professional learning, with the October 31 and November 1 Trailguide given as an example.

USING DATA TO INFORM INSTRUCTION
Under MTSS Decision Making, "MTSS Time" covers building data and trends; the principle that MTSS is for all children; bringing students with IEPs into scheduling discussions; reviewing progress monitoring of any student on a plan; working on team dynamics; starting with celebrations; and reviewing all data points. Chart slides display the Fountas & Pinnell Benchmark by grade level and a Math Benchmark by grade.
For NWEA mathematics, the district has established a universal screener for middle school mathematics; middle school math specialists use it to identify which students need further, more diagnostic assessment within the MTSS process; and it allows the district to participate in a third-party study with Illustrative Mathematics. A slide addresses NWEA informing classroom-level decisions.
The Common Lit assessment is described in five functions: assessment as a baseline, establishing a starting point for student performance; identifying needs, recognizing students who require immediate support; data-driven instruction, using results to inform whole-class lessons and small group activities; monitoring growth, measuring student progress over time; and goal setting, engaging students in setting personal learning objectives based on assessment results. A sample classroom report from Common Lit is shown.

NEXT STEPS
"Reading Between the Lines" lists district improvement needs: examples such as screening and diagnostic tools to improve the MTSS process; formation of work groups to build capacity and continued partnership; and shared ownership of the MTSS process.

CELEBRATIONS
Investment in Early Childhood is listed first among celebrations.
International Academy East IB Diploma acquisition is reported by graduation year: 82% in 2019, 90% in 2020, 87% in 2021, 88% in 2022, 72% in 2023, and 81% in 2024.
AP Honor Roll results are given for Troy High School and Athens High School across 2023-24 and 2022-23:
| AP School Metric | Troy HS 2023-24 | Troy HS 2022-23 | Athens HS 2023-24 | Athens HS 2022-23 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| School Overall | Gold | Gold | Gold | Silver |
| College Culture | 75% (381/510) | 69% (364/527) | 70% (253/362) | 61% (232/378) |
| College Credit | 67% (341/510) | 65% (341/527) | 58% (209/362) | 50% (189/378) |
| College Optimization | 30% (153/510) | 30% (158/527) | 23% (83/362) | 27% (102/378) |
Definitions given: College Culture is the percent of students in the graduating class who took an AP exam at any point in high school regardless of score; College Credit is the percent of the graduating class who score 3 or higher on an AP exam in high school; College Optimization is the percent of the graduating class who took 5 or more AP exams in high school, where at least 1 exam was taken in 9th or 10th grade. The document notes that research finds 6 or more APs do not improve college graduation rates beyond the optimal total of 5 such courses in high school, and that the Honor Roll also recognizes schools that encourage students earlier on their AP journey so as not to overload them with AP courses in their junior or senior years. Award thresholds are listed as Platinum, Gold, Silver, and Bronze: College Culture 80%, 65%, 50%, 40%; College Credit 50%, 35%, 30%, 25%; College Optimization 15%, 10%, 5%, 2%.
Enrollment in AP 11 ELA by school year, showing percent of 11th graders enrolled, total 11th graders, and 11 English AP enrollment:

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2020 | 38% | 935 | 357 |
| 2021 | 34% | 905 | 307 |
| 2022 | 39% | 924 | 356 |
| 2023 | 34% | 932 | 315 |
| 2024 | 42% | 948 | 402 |
A College Board quotation states that AP courses help students tackle college-level work, develop critical and useful skills for future AP courses, college, and career, and stand out to scholarship organizations and in the college application process.
Seal of Biliteracy recipients by year of graduation: 9 in 2019, 3 in 2021, 3 in 2022, 5 in 2023, 15 in 2024, and 18 marked with an asterisk for 2025.
The TCCHS 4-year graduation rate, expressed as the percent of students who graduated in four years, is charted for 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024 at 32, 48, 47, 64, 77, and 83.
Career and Technical Education completer status: more than 290 students from the Class of 2024 earned completer status in one of the district's CTE courses, spanning Mechatronics, Computer Science, Automotive Technician, Cooking & Related Culinary Arts, Drafting & Design Technology, Finance & Financial Management Services, Education, Television & Radio Broadcasting, Woodworking, Merchandizing, Sales & Marketing Operations, and others.

CLOSING
The presentation ends with "Sharing Troy's Success Stories" and a thank you.

**Procurement notes**

**Item.** Attendance Area Review Committee (AARC) proposal presentation to the Troy School District Board of Education, January 21, 2025. It revises the January 14 deck by replacing Options A through E with Option C and three Option C variants developed after the 1/14/25 Board workshop.

**Background.** Prior AARC groups convened in 2015 and 2018, and a 62-member Facilities Review Committee ran a 6-month process in 2021/22 producing recommendations for the 2022 bond proposal. Middle school enrollment ranges from 590 to 870 per building. Plante Moran was hired as demographers. The 2024 AARC had 25 members (15 administrators, 10 community members) and met October 14, October 28, November 11, November 25 and December 9; cabinet discussions have been weekly since August 2024.

**Optimal size model.** Learning Community size of 125 students; average class size 25; full-time teachers teach 5 sections (5x25 = 125); two learning communities per grade level (250 in grade 6); grades 6-8 totaling 750 students, flexing up to 900. The new Smith Middle School was built for an optimal enrollment of 750, and all four middle schools rank in Metro Parent's Top 6 in Michigan.

**Goals.** Goal 1 - right-size middle schools with equal student ratios. Goal 2 - resolve double splits. Goal 3 - no impact on high schools.

**Baseline enrollment.**

| Middle school | Existing boundary (Dec 2024) | Maintain existing boundary (2027) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Baker (Blue) | 631 | 556 |
| Boulan (Orange) | 847 | 721 |
| Larson (Green) | 863 | 713 |
| Smith (Yellow) | 599 | 536 |

Four middle schools total 2,940 pupils (2024) and a projected 2,526 pupils (2027).

**Options presented.**

| Option | Baker | Boulan Park | Larson | Smith | Schools affected | Students moved | Goals met |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Option C | 616 | 603 | 625 | 682 | 5 | ~630 | 3 |
| Option C - ONLY TU | 517 | 793 | 625 | 591 | 3 | ~250 | 2 |
| Option C - ONLY SA | 616 | 603 | 750 | 557 | 3 | ~380 | 2 |
| Option C - TU to Larson | 616 | 603 | 830 | 477 | 6 | ~380 | 2 |
| No Change | 517 | 793 | 750 | 466 | 0 | n/a | 1 |

**Driver populations.** Troy Union Elementary is projected at 205 students for Fall 2027: 100 assigned to Smith, 105 assigned to Larson, with 20 open-enrolled from Smith to Larson, yielding actual counts of 80 to Smith and 125 to Larson. Somerset Apartments is projected at 319 elementary students for Fall 2027, all of whom attend Boulan Park Middle School under current policy.

**Impacts.** Each option notes potential special education staffing effects, continued building-by-building staffing for special education and English learners, and transportation in which routes and bus numbers may shift while keeping driver numbers consistent and the longest route at 30 minutes or less.

**Timeline and next steps.** 2025/2026 prepare for adjustments; 2026/2027 changes implemented. Students in grades 5-8 (classes of 2032, 2031, 2030, 2029) are not impacted and may continue in their Fall 2025 building; current 5th and 6th graders slotted for a new school may move in 2025/2026. Community meetings at the four middle schools in February/March, a community survey in March/April, and Board consideration and decision in April/May.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Document and setting.** Attendance Area Review Committee (AARC) Proposal presentation, Troy School District, delivered to the Board of Education on January 21, 2025. It is a revision of the AARC deck given at the January 14, 2025 Board workshop: the earlier Options A through E are removed and replaced with Option C plus three Option C variants built in response to Board and committee questions.

**Why the review.** Historic district practice is to review enrollment patterns and challenges every 5-10 years. Previous AARC groups convened in 2015 and 2018, and a 62-member Facilities Review Committee ran a 6-month process in 2021/22 to create recommendations for the 2022 bond proposal with staff, student, cabinet and Board of Education feedback. Challenges include enrollment 'splits' as students transition from elementary to middle school or middle to high school, a double split at Troy Union, single splits at Smith, Baker, Wattles and Hamilton, and current ratios at each middle school, where enrollment ranges from 590 to 870 per building. Additional factors listed are enrollment projections, birth rate and schools of choice, the new Smith Middle School built for an optimal enrollment of 750, and Metro Parent rankings placing all four middle schools in the Top 6 in Michigan.

**Optimal middle school size.** Ideal parameters are a Learning Community size of 125 students, an average class size of 25 students, full-time teachers teaching 5 sections (5 x 25 = 125), two Learning Communities per grade level (250 in grade 6), and grades 6-8 totaling 750 students. Learning Communities can flex up to 900 students as class size increases above an average of 25, and to fewer than 750 students as class size dips below 25, which increases costs. Cited benefits include more full-time elective staff and 3 lunch periods aligned with grade levels.

A smaller school risks more partial staff, impact on school culture, limited course availability (example: only 2 sections of art offered), increased costs from lower class sizes, staff split across two content areas, and too few students for extracurriculars such as jazz band, theatre and yearbook. A larger school may require staffing 'overages' (example: more than a 1.0 orchestra teacher), teachers giving up prep periods, congestion in classrooms, hallways and cafeteria, saturated club and athletic opportunities, and limited ability to support new or move-in families.

**Process to date.** The district hired Plante Moran as demographers for yearly and future enrollment projections. The AARC group was formed in 2024 with 25 members representing each elementary and middle school - 15 administrators and 10 community members - drawn from applications requested in September. The 3-month process met on October 14, October 28, November 11, November 25 and December 9, and cabinet discussions have occurred weekly since August 2024. Criteria and data used included enrollment, grade cohorts and boundaries, birth rates, resident/non-resident/employee feeder paths, current maps, demographic data (ethnicity, English learners, students with disabilities, economics, content area performance), transportation implications, historical cohort data, and previous AARC information. Historical enrollment data slides are labeled January 2024. TSD directed the committee to focus on a four middle school future; committee feedback gave the district pause regarding community priorities and values such as programmatic experience, location and community schools, enrollment size, and duration of bus ride.

**Surrounding districts.** Rochester Community School District, Utica Community Schools, Walled Lake Consolidated Schools, Huron Valley Schools, West Bloomfield School District and Chippewa Valley Schools are described as considering or moving through the same process.

**Goals.** Goal 1: right-size middle schools, equal student ratios. Goal 2: resolve double splits. Goal 3: no impact on high schools.

**Current pathways.** Troy Union to Smith/Larson to Athens/Troy; Wass, Hill and Costello to Larson to Athens; Barnard to Baker to Athens; Morse and Wattles to Baker to Athens/Troy; Martell and Leonard to Smith to Troy; Hamilton to Smith/Boulan to Troy; Schroeder and Bemis to Boulan to Troy. The double split is Troy Union Elementary students splitting between Smith and Larson middle schools, with Smith students splitting again between Athens and Troy High. The elementary single split is Wattles and Morse students attending Baker MS splitting between Troy HS and Athens HS. The middle school single split is Hamilton students splitting between Smith and Boulan Park MS, with both feeding Troy HS.

**Current and future student counts.** All prior options presented assumed Somerset Apartment students would follow the feeder pattern. Four middle schools hold 2,940 pupils (2024) and a projected 2,526 pupils (2027). Existing Boundary (December 2024): Baker (Blue) 631 students, Boulan (Orange) 847 students, Larson (Green) 863 students, Smith (Yellow) 599 students. Maintain Existing Boundary (2027): Baker (Blue) 556, Boulan (Orange) 721, Larson (Green) 713, Smith (Yellow) 536.

**Fall 2027 projected middle school feeder enrollment (2,526 students).** Hamilton 226, Schroeder 216, Bemis 237, Martell 189, Leonard 212, Wattles 205, Morse 204, Troy Union 205, Costello 219, Wass 219, Hill 187, Barnard 207. All options are based on the Fall 2027 projected enrollment.

**Troy Union Elementary detail.** Fall 2027 projection of 205 students. Middle school students from Troy Union: 205. Troy Union assigned to Smith: 100. Troy Union assigned to Larson: 105. Troy Union open enrolled from Smith to Larson: 20. Actual students Troy Union to Smith: 80. Actual students Troy Union to Larson: 125.

**Somerset Apartments detail.** Fall 2027 elementary projection of 319 students, distributed as Hamilton 0, Schroeder 60, Bemis 69, Martell 39, Leonard 52, Wattles 52, Morse 47, Troy Union 0, Costello 0, Wass 0, Hill 0, Barnard 0. All Somerset Apartments students go to Boulan Park Middle School.

**Option C.** Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 625, Smith 682. Updated after the AARC concluded, based on questions asked by the group. All Troy Union students go to Smith. All students living in community housing follow their currently assigned elementary school to that elementary school's assigned middle school. Somerset Apartments' 319 students go to Boulan Park from 6 elementary schools. Number of schools affected: 5. Approximate students moved: 630. Number of goals met: 3. Pros: right sizes middle schools, resolves double splits, meets all three goals, keeps cohorts of students together. Cons: unresolved single splits, Hamilton splits from elementary to middle school, and Wattles, Smith and Baker have a split from middle to high school. Special education impact notes potential staffing increases at Smith, an opportunity for students with IEPs receiving services only or a resource room program to remain in a cohort with peers, potential for students placed in categorical programs to be displaced from peers if the placement is not at Smith, and continued staffing based on building need. English learner staffing continues based on need. Transportation routes and bus numbers may shift, with a goal of consistent routes and driver numbers and a longest route of 30 minutes or less.

**Option C - ONLY TU.** Baker 517, Boulan Park 793, Larson 625, Smith 591. Updated after the BOE Workshop on 1/14/25. All Troy Union students go to Smith; all students living in community housing go to Boulan Park Middle School (current policy); Somerset Apartments' 319 students go to Boulan Park from 6 elementary schools. Schools affected: 3. Approximate students moved: 250. Goals met: 2. Pro: resolves double splits. Cons: unresolved single splits, Hamilton splits from elementary to middle school, and Wattles, Smith and Baker have a middle-to-high school split. Special education and English learner staffing continue based on building need; transportation goals match Option C, with a longest route of 30 minutes or less.

**Option C - ONLY SA.** Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 750, Smith 557. Updated after the BOE Workshop on 1/14/25. Troy Union has no changes; all students living in community housing follow their currently assigned elementary school to that school's assigned middle school; Somerset Apartments' 319 students currently go to Boulan Park from 6 elementary schools. Schools affected: 3. Approximate students moved: 380. Goals met: 2. Pro: keeps cohorts of students together. Cons: does not resolve the Troy Union double split, unresolved single splits, Hamilton splits from elementary to middle school, and Wattles, Smith and Baker have a middle-to-high school split.

**Option C - TU to Larson.** Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 830, Smith 477. Updated after the BOE Workshop on 1/14/25. Troy Union all to Larson; all students living in community housing follow their currently assigned elementary school to that school's assigned middle school; Somerset Apartments' 319 students go to Boulan Park from 6 elementary schools. Schools affected: 6. Approximate students moved: 380. Goals met: 2. Pros: resolves double splits, keeps cohorts of students together. Cons: unresolved single splits, Hamilton splits from elementary to middle school, and Wattles, Smith and Baker have a middle-to-high school split.

**No Change.** All Somerset Apartment students go to Boulan Park. Four middle schools with 2,940 pupils (December 2024) and 2,526 pupils (2027). Existing Boundary (2024): Baker (Blue) 631, Boulan (Orange) 847, Larson (Green) 863, Smith (Yellow) 599. Maintain Existing Boundary/Policy (2027): Baker (Blue) 517, Boulan (Orange) 793, Larson (Green) 750, Smith (Yellow) 466. Schools affected: 0. Goals met: 1. Pros: no students affected, community support. Cons: does not right size middle schools, continues the disparity, maintains the double splits.

**Timeline and assumptions.** 2025/2026 - prepare for adjustments; 2026/2027 - changes implemented. Students will continue to have access to advanced programming. TSD will ensure families with multiple middle school students enrolled at the same time have the option to keep siblings at the same middle school. Middle school legacy: students currently enrolled in 5th, 6th, 7th or 8th grade (classes of 2032, 2031, 2030 and 2029) will not be impacted and may continue in the building they are in the Fall of 2025. Option to move: a current 5th or 6th grader slotted to attend a new school may do so in the 2025/2026 school year, ahead of the proposed changes. Curriculum is consistent across all four middle schools and athletics are uniform.

**Phases and next steps.** Phase 1 Discovery - committee formed, research and planning, potential recommendations developed. Phase 2 Recommendation (January) - the committee provides the Board with options and the Board determines whether to move forward. Phase 3 Feedback (February - April) - four listening sessions, one at each middle school, plus a community survey. Phase 4 Determination (April/May) - TSD provides the Board a summary of feedback and the Board determines any future changes. Next steps: February/March community meetings at the 4 middle schools; March/April community survey; April/May Board of Education consideration and decision.

Pros: right sizes middle schools, resolves a double split at Troy Union, middle school boundaries are geographically close to their middle school location, resolves all elementary-to-middle school splits, meets all three goals. Cons: Morse and Wattles maintain a middle-to-high school split, it affects the highest number of schools and students, it has two middle-to-high school splits at Baker and Boulan Park, and it impacts 4 elementary schools.

**Option B.** Baker 563, Boulan Park 739, Larson 611, Smith 613. Hamilton split, current, total 226: 150 to Boulan Park (2/3) and 76 to Smith (1/3). Morse split, new, total 204: 136 to Boulan Park (2/3) and 68 to Baker (1/3). Wattles split, current, total 205: 136 to Smith (2/3) and 69 to Baker (1/3). All of Costello goes to Baker, all of Troy Union goes to Larson, and all of Wattles goes to Smith. Number of schools affected: 8. Number of goals met: 2. Pros: partially right sizes middle schools, resolves a double split at Troy Union, resolves all middle-to-high school splits, meets most of the goals, and creates two distinct feeders to Athens and Troy High with the split happening after elementary. Cons: Morse, Wattles and Hamilton have an elementary-to-middle school split, several schools and students are affected, and a lot of disruption at the elementary level.

**Option C.** Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 625, Smith 682. Updated after the AARC concluded, based on questions asked by the group. Hamilton split, total 226, current practice: 150 to Boulan Park (2/3) and 76 to Smith (1/3). All Troy Union students go to Smith. All students living in community housing follow their currently assigned elementary school to that elementary school's assigned middle school. Number of schools affected: 5. Number of goals met: 3. Pros: right sizes middle schools, resolves double splits, meets all three goals, keeps cohorts of students together. Cons: unresolved single splits, Hamilton splits from elementary to middle school, and Wattles, Smith and Baker have a middle-to-high school split.

**Option D.** Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 611, Smith 696. Hamilton split, current, total 226: 150 to Boulan Park (2/3) and 76 to Smith (1/3). All of Troy Union goes to Larson and all of Costello goes to Smith. Number of schools affected: 4. Number of goals met: 3. Pros: right sizes middle schools, resolves a double split at Troy Union, impacts fewer schools. Cons: Hamilton splits from elementary to middle school; Costello, Wattles and Morse split from middle to high school.

**Option E.** Baker 563, Boulan Park 589, Larson 611, Smith 763. Wattles split, current, total 205: 136 to Smith (2/3) and 69 to Baker (1/3). Morse split, total 204: 136 to Boulan Park (2/3) and 68 to Baker (1/3). All of Troy Union goes to Larson and all of Costello goes to Baker. Number of schools affected: 9. Number of goals met: 3. Pros: partially right sizes middle schools, resolves a double split at Troy Union, resolves all middle-to-high school splits, meets all three goals, and creates two distinct feeder patterns to Athens and Troy High with the split happening after elementary. Cons: Morse and Wattles have an elementary-to-middle school split, several schools and students are affected, and it impacts 9 buildings.

**No Change.** Current middle school boundary with four middle schools, 2,940 pupils (December 2024) and 2,526 pupils (2027). Existing Boundary (2024): Baker (Blue) 631, Boulan (Orange) 847, Larson (Green) 863, Smith (Yellow) 599. Maintain Existing Boundary (2027): Baker (Blue) 556, Boulan (Orange) 721, Larson (Green) 713, Smith (Yellow) 536. Number of schools affected: 0. Number of goals met: 1. Pros: no students affected, community support. Cons: does not right size middle schools, continues the disparity, maintains the double splits.

**Timeline and assumptions.** 2025/2026 - prepare for adjustments; 2026/2027 - changes implemented. Advanced programming: students will continue to have access. Siblings: TSD will ensure families with multiple middle school students enrolled at the same time have the option to keep siblings at the same middle school. Middle school legacy: students currently enrolled in 5th, 6th, 7th or 8th grade (classes of 2032, 2031, 2030 and 2029) will not be impacted and will have the option to continue in the building they are in the Fall of 2025. Option to move: a current 5th or 6th grader slotted to attend a new school may do so in the 2025/2026 school year, ahead of the proposed changes. Curriculum: the curriculum offered at all four middle schools is consistent across the district, and athletics are uniform.

**Phases and next steps.** Phase 1 Discovery - the committee was formed and developed potential recommendations. Phase 2 Recommendation (January) - the committee provides the Board of Education with options and the Board determines whether to move forward. Phase 3 Feedback (February - April) - four listening sessions, one at each middle school, plus a community survey. Phase 4 Determination (April/May) - TSD provides the Board a summary of feedback and the Board determines any future changes. Next steps: February/March community meetings at the 4 middle schools; March/April community survey; April/May Board of Education consideration and decision.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Presentation slides titled "School Start Time," prepared for a Troy Board of Education Workshop dated March 2, 2021 and carried in the April 4, 2023 board packet, reporting the results of a district-wide survey on moving high school start times later. Troy has operated a 5-tier bus schedule with a 7:20am high school start since 2011, a shift that reduced the bus fleet by 14 busses and cut transportation costs by about $800,000 per year. Survey responses came from 3,297 parents, 2,208 students and 878 staff. The deck's stated key finding is that between two-thirds and three-fourths of stakeholders say the District should follow the research and change the high school start time to later in the morning.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**What this is**
Slide deck presented at a Troy Board of Education Workshop dated March 2, 2021 and included in the April 4, 2023 board packet as "Start Times Survey Report 3-2." Stated key takeaways (Slide 2): review of survey data, next steps, and timeline.

**Background (Slide 3)**
The Board had been studying high school start times for four years. When state funding was cut to its lowest point in 2011, the District moved from a 3-tier schedule (one start time each for elementary, middle and high schools) to a 5-tier bussing schedule. The change produced staggered start times for different elementary and middle school buildings, reduced the bus fleet by 14 busses, and reduced transportation costs by about $800,000 per year. To keep the latest-starting elementary buildings from releasing close to 5pm, high school start times were shifted earlier to 7:20am. The deck notes this burdened teens with early "get-ups" and made after-school teacher professional development and collaboration difficult because teachers of similar grades end their teaching day at different times. The District has operated on this schedule since 2011 to be as cost-efficient as possible.

**Research cited**
National studies show high schoolers' melatonin levels do not permit a healthy night's sleep when schools start before 8:00am, with 8:30am cited as closer to optimal. Associated outcomes listed: higher rates of tardiness, absenteeism and truancy; lower academic achievement across the entire school day, not only first hour; double-digit increases in teen driving accidents throughout the day and evening; higher rates of juvenile delinquency and arrest; and higher rates of teen depression and stress-related health disorders. Studies also show students in high schools that shift later do get more sleep. Both the Center for Disease Control and Prevention and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommend high schools start at least at 8:00am and ideally 8:30am or later.

**Arguments for keeping early starts (Slide 4)**
Cheaper bus routing; earlier high school starts let elementary and middle schools start later; earlier dismissal lets after-school activities start earlier (though Oakland County game times typically start after 4pm, so a later Troy end time would not affect them); students leave before parents depart for work and can be home to care for younger siblings.

**Survey samples**
| Group | Respondents |
|---|---|
| Parents | 3,297 |
| Students | 2,208 |
| Staff | 878 |

High-school-only cross-tabs used parent and student subgroups of 1,670 and 1,360 plus 321 staff. Parents-only breakouts: elementary 1,679, middle school 1,282, high school 1,670. Students-only: 5th graders 420, middle school 428, high school 1,360. Staff-only: elementary 390, middle school 217, high school 321.

**Reported results**
On the importance question, the three response options ("not a significant problem," "good to correct but can wait until school funding is better," and "a critical problem that needs to be corrected as soon as possible") drew 50%/45%/38%, 34%/35%/41% and 16%/20%/21% from parents, students and staff. The high-school-only version drew 51%/46%/36%, 30%/28%/31% and 18%/26%/32%. On the action question — keep the current 5-tier schedule with high schools at 7:20am, or increase the school budget assigned to bus service to move high school start times later — the split was 73%/66%/62% against 27%/34%/38%; the high-school-only version showed 62%/69%/54% against 38%/31%/46%.

**Key findings (Slide 14) and next steps (Slide 15)**
Between two-thirds and three-fourths of stakeholders say follow the research and change the high school start time to later in the morning; about 30% of each respondent group are willing to provide some leeway as to when the change is adopted; the traditional cadence (HS, MS, EL) is preferred. Next steps: Board questions, budget prioritization, and a decision point in early April.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Slide deck titled "School Start Time," prepared for a Troy Board of Education Workshop dated March 2, 2021 and carried in the April 4, 2023 board packet under the title "Start Times Survey Report 3-2." Slide 2 lists the key takeaways as review of survey data, next steps, and timeline.

**History of the 5-tier schedule (Slide 3).** The deck states the Board of Education had been studying the topic for the past four years. When state funding was cut to its lowest point in 2011, the District made the decision to shift from a 3-tier schedule — one start time for elementary, one for middle schools, and one for high schools — to a 5-tier bussing schedule. That produced staggered start times for different elementary and middle school buildings but allowed the District to use busses more efficiently: the bus fleet was reduced by 14 busses and transportation costs fell by about $800,000 per year. The change was not without problems. To make sure the latest-starting elementary buildings did not end so late that children were arriving home close to 5pm, the District shifted high school start times earlier, to 7:20am. That put an added burden on teens in terms of early "get-ups" and made after-school teacher professional development and collaboration very difficult, because teachers of similar grades now end their teaching day at different times. The District has operated on this schedule since 2011, recognizing those negative impacts, in order to be as cost-efficient as possible.

**Research basis.** In the past five years a growing body of evidence suggests the decision to push high school start times to 7:20am may not be optimal for the social/emotional health or the academic achievement of Troy's high school students. Recent national studies show high schoolers' melatonin levels do not allow them to fall asleep early enough to capture a healthy night's sleep when schools start before 8:00am, and that high schools should ideally start closer to 8:30am for optimal sleep. National research associates consistent lack of sleep in early-start high schools with higher rates of tardiness, absenteeism and truancy; lower academic achievement, not only in first hour but across the entire school day; double-digit increases in teen driving accidents throughout the day and evening; higher rates of juvenile delinquency and arrest; and higher rates of teen depression and stress-related health disorders. Studies have also shown that students in high schools that shift to later start times do in fact get more sleep, countering a common argument that students will just stay up later. In light of those findings, both the Center for Disease Control and Prevention and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommend that high schools shift start times to at least 8:00am, and ideally to 8:30am or later. That recommendation prompted the Board of Education to begin studying a possible return to a 3-tier bus schedule so the District could shift high school start times to 8:00am or later.

**Why early high school start times persist (Slide 4).** Reasons listed: more efficient bus routing, timing and sharing that lowers district transportation costs; an earlier high school start time allows elementary and middle schools to start later; an earlier high school end time allows extracurricular and after-school activities to start earlier — although because high school game times across Oakland County typically start after 4pm, a later end time in Troy would not impact high school game times for Troy students; early-start high school students are more likely to leave for school in the morning before their parents leave for work; and early-start high school students can be home in time to receive younger siblings and provide after-school care for them.

**Survey participation.** The survey drew 3,297 parents, 2,208 students and 878 staff. On the question of which grades respondents have students enrolled in, are enrolled in, or teach — offering preschool, elementary, middle school, high school and post-secondary, with multiple responses allowed so totals add to more than 100% — the printed chart values are 4%, 62%, 19%, 44%, 39%, 19%, 25%, 51%, 62%, 37% and 3%. A footnote indicates the student sample at the elementary level consists of 5th graders only.

**Importance of moving high school start times later.** Respondents chose among "To me, this isn't a significant problem and probably doesn't need addressing," "This is something that would be good to correct, but we can wait to fix it until school funding is better at some point," and "This is a critical problem that needs to be corrected on as soon as possible." Across all parents (n=3,297), students (n=2,208) and staff (n=878), the printed shares are 50%, 45% and 38%; 34%, 35% and 41%; and 16%, 20% and 21%. A high-school-only version of the same question, with respondent counts of 1,360, 1,670 and 321, shows 51%, 46% and 36%; 30%, 28% and 31%; and 18%, 26% and 32%.

**Action preference.** Asked to weigh the research on teen sleep patterns and the negative impact of early high school start times against the additional bus service costs of a later high school start, respondents chose between keeping the current 5-tier bus schedule with staggered start times for different elementary and middle school buildings (high schools continuing to start at 7:20am) and increasing the amount of money in the school budget assigned to bus service so high school start times could move later in the morning. Across all parents, students and staff the printed shares are 73%, 66% and 62% against 27%, 34% and 38%. The high-school-only version shows 62%, 69% and 54% against 38%, 31% and 46%.

**3-tier schedule options.** If the District moved to a 3-tier bus schedule, six approximate start/end combinations were offered: Elementaries 8:00am to 2:58pm / Middle schools 8:30am to 3:14pm / High schools 9:00am to 3:50pm; Elementaries 8:00am to 2:58pm / High schools 8:30am to 3:20pm / Middle schools 9:00am to 3:44pm; Middle schools 8:00am to 2:44pm / Elementaries 8:30am to 3:28pm / High schools 9:00am to 3:50pm; Middle schools 8:00am to 2:44pm / High schools 8:30am to 3:20pm / Elementaries 9:00am to 3:58pm; High Schools 8:00am to 2:50pm / Elementaries 8:30am to 3:28pm / Middle schools 9:00am to 3:44pm; and High Schools 8:00am to 2:50pm / Middle schools 8:30am to 3:14pm / Elementaries 9:00am to 3:58pm. On the combined chart (parents n=3,297, students n=2,208, staff n=878) the printed option shares range from 7% to 44%. A parents-only chart, asking which set would be most ideal for the household over the rest of their children's time in Troy Schools, breaks parents out by elementary (n=1,679), middle school (n=1,282) and high school (n=1,670) children, with printed shares ranging from 3% to 48%. A students-only chart, asking which set would be best for everyone in the District, breaks out 5th graders (n=420), middle school (n=428) and high school (n=1,360) students, with printed shares ranging from 4% to 52%. A staff-only chart, asking which set would be best for the District as a whole, breaks out elementary (n=390), middle school (n=217) and high school (n=321) staff, with printed shares ranging from 2% to 56%.

**Key findings (Slide 14).** Between two-thirds and three-fourths of stakeholders say follow the research and change high school start time until later in the morning. About 30% of each respondent group are willing to provide some leeway as to when that change is adopted. The traditional cadence (HS, MS, EL) is preferred.

**Next steps and timeline (Slide 15).** Board questions; budget prioritization; decision point in early April.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Board of Education presentation titled "Project 2026 Blueprint," delivered to the Troy School District board on June 6, 2024, reporting the district Accountability Plan against the four "World Class for All" pillars. Each pillar objective is reported in a uniform format of Objectives, Key Results, and Challenges and Recommendations, covering Deep Learning (Blue Pillar), Building Capacity (Gold Pillar), Equity and Well-Being (Red Pillar), and Early Childhood to Career (Green Pillar). The most concrete outcome reported is the personalized transition of 326 students into Troy School District kindergarten, alongside an increase in GSRP slots for 2024-25.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**What this is**
Slide deck presented to the Troy School District Board of Education on June 6, 2024, branded "Project 2026 Blueprint" and "Troy School District." It presents the district ACCOUNTABILITY PLAN, stating that the "World Class for All" Pillars hold the team accountable to Objectives, Key Results, and Challenges and Recommendations.

**Pillar framework**

| Pillar | Color | Objectives reported |
|---|---|---|
| Deep Learning | Blue | 4 |
| Building Capacity | Gold | 3 |
| Equity and Well-Being | Red | 2 |
| Early Childhood to Career | Green | 2 |

**Deep Learning (Blue Pillar)**
Objective 1 is to create and sustain systems of support at all levels that deepen learning and empower student voice (MTSS), asserting that access to deep learning is imperative for all children. Key results cite partnership and learning with New Solutions K-12 (student supports K-12), Solution Tree (PLC model 6-12), and Oakland Schools (MTSS). Challenges for elementary and secondary MTSS are to continue monitoring benchmark data, continue developing capacity in math, and solidify tier-one instruction in all classrooms. Objective 2 addresses improving technology access for students and families with quality training; items listed include development of an Artificial Intelligence leadership committee, development of a computer science leadership team, continuing to grow digital portfolios for students to document learning over time, and building understanding of meaningful use of AI in the classroom. Objective 3 is to continue pursuing global best practices in all content areas (NPDL, The 6 C's, learning partnerships), with key results of Solution Tree Professional Learning Communities K-12, NSK12 Supporting All Students, hosting the Midwest Literacy Institute, and Math Recovery K-12. Objective 4 is to take action for upgraded facilities, referencing Fielding International comprehensive guiding principles for MS and HS Redesign, involvement of all stakeholders in the design process, ongoing staff learning tied to curriculum, ongoing bond project work, and supporting vision and implementation efforts.

**Building Capacity (Gold Pillar)**
Objective 1 covers improving educator preparation, strengthening pipelines for underrepresented educators, and supporting current educators: attending university job fairs, "Grow Your Own" programs, hosting job fairs for educators, employee support groups, a leadership cohort, and a New Teacher Learning Series. Challenges named are teacher shortage and limited university education enrollment. Objective 2 covers job-embedded professional learning for all staff, use of release days to prioritize conversations with collaborative teacher teams, emerging professional learning communities, and building systemness with counseling 6-12 around program opportunities. Objective 3 covers professional learning for staff, community, and students to co-design impactful experiences for the OneTroy community, citing continued partnership with Celebrate Hope, community engagement (Community Book Read and Experience Panel), building student capacity through WEB, LEAP and a Student Leadership Conference, and Learning Nights at all schools for parents and community.

**Equity and Well-Being (Red Pillar)**
Objective 1 is to fund additional investments supporting the needs of the whole child, listing SEL curriculum and programming, a Behavioral Threat Assessment (BTA) committee, community engagement, SEL curriculum and program implementation, PLC collaborative work, and district training on a new BTA tool.
