**Meeting identification.** Minutes of a regular meeting of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, held June 17, 2025 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. President Philippart called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m. In addition to Dr. Philippart, Board members Alic, Anne, Haupt, Melton, Potts, and Zendler were present. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Montante, DiPilato, Pagel, Griffor, Haezebrouck, Recker, Detmer, Singh, Cross, and Trudel. Approximately 150 members of the audience attended. The meeting adjourned at 8:58 p.m. The minutes are submitted by Emina Alic, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, and carry the typist notation EA/jh.

**Public hearing on the 2025/2026 proposed budget.** The business portion opened with a public hearing on the proposed 2025/2026 budget. Mr. Trudel presented the details of the proposed budget to the Board and community and shared a PowerPoint presentation. He noted the proposed budget had been reviewed in great detail with the Board at the June workshop. His presentation addressed tax values, homestead and non-homestead millage, general fund adjustments and assumptions, ancillary funds, the sinking fund, and the capital projects fund. He also reviewed student enrollment, the District's foundation allowance history, and revenues and expenditures. The Board indicated it had reviewed the proposed budget in its entirety at the June 3rd Workshop. President Philippart invited questions from the audience related to the proposed budget; one question was asked by a community member to clarify what the sinking funds are and how they are used.

**Recognition: Ava Bunao.** The Board recognized recent graduate Ava Bunao, named a runner up for the 2025 Gold Award Girl Scout Young Women of Distinction for her project "On the Spot Community First Aid Awareness for Outdoor Recreation." The project focused on providing access to first aid resources in local outdoor recreation areas and on teaching community members how to use them. It also earned the GSUSA Gold Award Scholarship, which is awarded to one Gold Award Girl Scout per council. Ava graduated from Athens High School with high honors and numerous scholarships and will begin college at Michigan State University as a biochemistry major and a student in the Osteopathic Medical Scholars Program on a pre-medicine track. She was invited to the podium to describe her Gold Award project.

**Recognition: Bemis Math Pentathlon team.** A second Mission Moment honored the Bemis Math Pentathlon team for earning the 2025 National Math Pentathlon First Place Gold Trophy. Mrs. Harleen Singh, Principal of Bemis, came to the podium to describe the achievement and introduce the champion team. The following students received a certificate of achievement and congratulations from Board members: Aashvi Vatsa, Aiden Rajbhandari, Anika Gollamudi, Aryian Majjhoo, Elias Roumayah, Ishan Vankadara, Shardul Joshi, Vihaan Palepu, Atharv Salimath, Ayona Chauhan, Bhashith Thulugu, Mannat Thakur, Navneeth Sheshathri, Ryka Kashi, Sanvika GopalaKrishnan, Sarah Farah, Vihaa Chethan, Alexander Majjhoo, Aniket Pagi, Ayla Majjhoo, Cali Hoskins, Charles Carlisle, Dhruhi Bhatt, Eleanor Roumayah, Feruz Mamarasulov, Gourika Kurkimatt, Grace Thomas, Irene Thommana, Naaga Nainika Dhavala, Nainika Chowdhury, Nate Zhang, Prarthana Gowda, Srihith Gattupalli, Varun Prasanth Kumar, Anushka Sonar, Asha Thabolingam, Bruno Redondo, Fatima Bilal, Hari Kern, Kaira Singh, Ritwika Thanigaivel, Saisha Fegade, Tiyasa Giri, Adam Majjhoo, Anirudh Ganesh, Isaac Thommana, Padmesh Lekkala Haribabu, Pugal Suresh Babu, Rayan Pedaballe, Shrivatsav Santapuri, Dheeya Gopalakrishnan, Satyapavana Gattupalli, Shilpa Manni, and Varnika Prasanth Kumar.

**Student Spotlight.** The Student Spotlight recognized creative achievement in the TSD Creative Guild, described at this meeting as more accurately an Alumni Spotlight. Recent graduates Akshaya Rachamadugu (2025 Troy High graduate) and Anoush Rophael (2025 Athens graduate) were recognized for dedication to Creative Guild throughout their high school careers. Mr. Thomas Butcher was invited up to share the achievement.

**Resolution in Support of Gun Safety and Safe Gun Storage.** Moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Anne. The whereas clauses state that the safety and well-being of students, teachers, and staff is a top priority in the Troy School District; that firearm-related deaths are the leading cause of death among children and adolescents; that rates of death from firearms among ages 14 to 17 are now 22.5% higher than motor vehicle-related death rates, and that in the U.S. middle and high school age children are now more likely to die as the result of a firearm injury than from any other single cause of death; that according to a report from the US Secret Service, in incidents of gun violence on school grounds 76% of attackers acquired a firearm from the home of a parent or another close relative; that every year roughly 350 children under the age of 18 unintentionally shoot themselves or someone else; that nearly 22,000 Americans die by firearm suicide every year, including over 950 children and teens; that research indicates 47% of firearm owners who have children living in their homes do not safely store at least one of their weapons; that evidence strongly suggests secure firearm storage is an essential component of any effective community safety strategy; that keeping students, teachers and staff safe from the threat of gun violence should be the responsibility of all adult stakeholders in the district; and that preventative measures require action now.

The resolving clauses direct the Superintendent to periodically communicate the importance of safe firearm storage and other firearm safety and violence prevention measures during gun violence awareness month, and to disseminate material on an annual basis stressing the importance of secure storage of firearms by including it in the District's annual notification materials. A further clause commits the Board and Superintendent to continue working with local law enforcement agencies, medical and mental health agencies, and non-profit organizations to increase efforts to inform District parents of their obligations regarding secure storage of firearms in their homes and other gun violence prevention safety measures. A final clause provides that the resolution shall not be construed to conflict with any existing Michigan or federal law. The vote was Yes 7, No 0, and the resolution was declared adopted. Emina Alic, Secretary, Board of Education, certified the resolution as a true and complete copy duly adopted at a regular meeting held on the 17th day of June, 2025, with notice given in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976. Citations appended to the resolution reference news.umich.edu, labblog.uofmhealth.org, the US Secret Service publication Protecting America's Schools, Everytown Research's "Not an Accident" map and its report on the rise of firearm suicide among young Americans, a Pew Research Center guns report, and David C. Grossman et al., "Gun Storage Practices and Risk of Youth Suicide and Unintentional Firearm Injuries," JAMA 293, no. 6 (2005): 707-14.

**Additions and deletions; agenda-item public communication.** None recorded for either.

**Consent agenda.** Moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Alic that the Troy Board of Education approve items A through K on the consent agenda: minutes of the May 6, 2025 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the May 20, 2025 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report for April 2025; Food Service Contract Renewal; Michigan High School Athletic Association (MHSAA) Membership Resolution 2025/2026; 2024/2025 Budget Amendment; 2025/2026 Budget Appropriations Resolution; District Pavement Crackfill & Striping; Troy Preschool Playground Pavillion Purchase/Installation; Schools of Choice 2025-26; and First Student Contract Renewal. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Personnel.** Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Board issue a two-year administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Ms. Ebert, who will begin her duties as Assistant Principal, Baker Middle School commencing with the 2025-26 school year. Vote: Yes 7, No 0. Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mrs. Potts that the Board issue a two-year administrative contract without tenure to Dr. David Recker, who will begin his duties as Director, Teaching & Learning commencing with the 2025-26 school year. Vote: Yes 7, No 0. Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Anne that the Board issue a two-year administrative contract without tenure to Ms. Reba McNally, who will begin her duties as Principal, Hamilton Elementary School commencing with the 2025-26 school year. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Curriculum: Elementary Writing Units of Study.** The Director of Teaching and Learning, with members of the Teaching & Learning team, provided information to Board members on recommended materials for grades K-5 for the upcoming school year; Board members had reviewed the plan and asked questions following the Board Workshop. Moved by Mrs. Potts and supported by Mrs. Alic that the recommended materials for grades K-5 be approved starting in the 2025-2026 school year. Mrs. Zendler shared a statement informing the community and fellow board members that she would be voting no on the proposed writing curriculum. Dr. Melton shared that upon further research and investigation she would not support the adoption. Mrs. Anne shared sentiments about the proposed writing curriculum but indicated she would support its adoption. Vote: Yes 5 (Alic, Anne, Haupt, Philippart, Potts), No 2 (Melton, Zendler).

**Business: Smith Middle School EPIC system.** Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Anne that the purchase of an EPIC system for Smith Middle School be approved through VSC Inc. in the amount of $173,978.00, and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Public communication (non-agenda) and other.** Ten community members addressed the Board during public communication; no action was taken by the Board. Under Other, no items were recorded, but Dr. Philippart shared a statement indicating that the Board recently completed Superintendent Dr. Richard Machesky's performance evaluation and shared a brief assessment with the community: Dr. Machesky is once again a highly effective leader and the Board will be extending his contract for another three years. Board members shared sentiments about the end of the school year, congratulated graduates and retirees, wished the community a safe summer, and congratulated and welcomed the new administrators. An update on pending legislation and budgets from the recent OCSBA meeting was shared. Dr. Philippart announced the next regular Board meeting for July 15th at 9:30 a.m. at the Administration Building and the August 19th Board meeting also at the Administration Building at 6:00 p.m.

**Meeting identification.** Minutes of a regular meeting of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, held May 20, 2025 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. **Legislative CAP students report.** The Board welcomed students from the Legislative track of the District's Career Accelerator Program (CAP), who have been engaged in learning about levels of government from the school board and the city to state senators and representatives. Two students shared experiences, insights, and how CAP affected their educational journey. The students named were Aarav Akolkar (THS), Tanmayee Choudary Gudi (IAE), Jackson Kanczuzewski (AHS), Amarachi Obiakor (IAE), Melita Pereira (IAE), Naina Rodrigues (THS), Jyostsna Shivakumar (THS), Ragavarshini Venkatesh (THS), and Vinicius Zanta Leao da Silva (IAE).

**National Teacher Appreciation Week resolution.** Teacher Appreciation Week is observed nationally each May and was celebrated Monday, May 5th through Friday, May 9th this year. Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt, the resolution recites that teachers inspire, nurture and open children's minds to new ideas; that teachers promote and strengthen the principles of democratic equality, develop leaders and encourage critical thinking; that Troy teachers set the bar for excellence in education and continually exceed the highest standards in the profession; and that the goal of Teacher Appreciation Week is to raise national and local awareness of teaching excellence in building a better society. It resolves that the Troy School District supports National Teacher Appreciation Week, May 5-9, 2025 and encourages schools and community to recognize the vital and changing role of teachers. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

**Mental Health Awareness Month resolution.** Each year Oakland Community Health Network and its service provider network host initiatives promoting community awareness about mental illness, and school boards across Oakland County were asked to recognize May as Mental Health Awareness Month. Moved by Dr. Melton and supported by Mrs. Potts, the resolution recites that mental health is important for individual well-being and vitality as well as that of families, communities, and schools; that one in five of all Americans, including children, experience mental health issues that could lead to school difficulties, physical problems, and even suicide; and that May 8, 2025 is designated National Children's Mental Health Awareness Day and May 12 through May 18, 2025 is designated Children's Mental Health Acceptance Week. It resolves that the Troy Board of Education recognizes May 2025 as Mental Health Awareness Month and seeks to increase awareness and understanding of mental illness and the need to support all people seeking help. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

**Curriculum and Business.** No items were presented under either heading.

**Public communication and student representative reports.** Nine community members addressed the Board during public communication; no action was taken by the Board. Kristian Vitanovich, student representative for Troy College and Career High School, reported on events and activities at his school. Nurayda Albeez, student representative for International Academy-East, reported on events and activities at her school. Other comments congratulated the retirees again; expressed appreciation for public comments regarding the writing curriculum; invited attendance at the June 3rd Workshop for information on PA146 legislation; thanked teachers for another great school year; gave a shout out to 2025 graduates, with ceremonies for THS and AHS on 5/31, IA on 6/1, and TCCHS on 6/4; announced the upcoming SSAB Leadership Conference 5/23, Open Air Fest 5/28, and TFEE Golf Outing 6/10; welcomed new administrators; and thanked all who helped with 8th Grade Interviews. Official minutes of the Troy Board of Education meeting held January 16, 2024 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan. The document combines the Board's annual organizational meeting with the regular business meeting that followed.

ATTENDANCE AND CALL TO ORDER
President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart, and Wilson were present. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Harris, and West. Four high school student representatives attended along with approximately 25 members of the audience.

ELECTION OF ACTING CHAIRPERSON AND TEMPORARY SECRETARY
Mr. Schmidt explained that the evening's meeting is where the Board selects officers, appoints committee members for the upcoming year, and approves or authorizes items that must be considered on an annual basis, with the regular Board meeting to follow the organizational portion. It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mrs. Alic that Mr. Schmidt serve as acting chairperson to officiate the meeting until the election of a president was completed; the vote was Yes 7, No 0. Mr. Schmidt appointed Judy Holmes to act as temporary secretary until the secretary of the Troy Board of Education was elected.

NOMINATION AND ELECTION OF PRESIDENT
Acting Chairperson Schmidt declared nominations in order for the office of Board president. Mrs. Alic nominated Mr. Schmidt. A motion by Ms. Schmidt, supported by Dr. Wilson, closed nominations for president (Yes 7, No 0). It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Wilson that Mr. Schmidt serve as president of the Troy Board of Education until December 31, 2024. On roll call: Alic - Yes, Anne - Yes, Hauff - Yes, Haupt - Yes, Philippart - Yes, Schmidt - Yes, Wilson - Yes.

NOMINATION AND ELECTION OF VICE PRESIDENT
President Schmidt declared nominations in order for vice president. Dr. Wilson nominated Mrs. Anne. A motion by Mr. Schmidt, supported by Mrs. Alic, closed nominations (Yes 7, No 0). It was moved by Mr. Schmidt and supported by Mrs. Alic that Mrs. Anne serve as vice president of the Troy Board of Education until December 31, 2024. On roll call: Anne - Yes, Hauff - Yes, Haupt - Yes, Schmidt - Yes, Wilson - Yes, Philippart - Yes, Alic - Yes.

NOMINATION AND ELECTION OF SECRETARY
President Schmidt declared nominations in order for Board secretary. Dr. Wilson nominated Mr. Hauff. A motion by Mr. Schmidt, supported by Mrs. Alic, closed nominations (Yes 7, No 0). It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mrs. Alic that Mr. Hauff serve as secretary of the Troy Board of Education until December 31, 2024. On roll call: Hauff - Yes, Haupt - Yes, Philippart - Yes, Schmidt - Yes, Wilson - Yes, Alic - Yes, Anne - Yes.

APPOINTMENT OF SCHOOL BOARD TREASURER
It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt that Rick L. West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, be appointed Treasurer of the Troy Board of Education for the period January through December 2024. Yes 7, No 0.

FUND DEPOSITORIES AND INVESTMENTS
Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Dr. Wilson, the resolution recites that public monies belonging to or held for the State, County, or other political units of the State may come into the hands of Rick West, Treasurer of Troy School District, and that Michigan law requires the Board to provide by resolution for the deposit of all public monies including tax monies. The Treasurer is directed to deposit and/or invest all public monies in his name as Treasurer into the following depository institutions: Bank of America; Citizens Bank; JP Morgan Chase Bank; Comerica Bank; Huntington Bank; Fifth Third Bank; Flagstar Bancorp; MILAF (Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Plus, managed by PFM Asset Management, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank); and PNC Bank. Monies may be withdrawn by checks signed with a facsimile signature of Treasurer Rick West, and in emergencies by the handwritten signature of Rick West or Superintendent Richard M. Machesky, who may sign on the General Fund account and the Payroll account at Bank of America. Accounts established at PNC Bank for paying Troy Career Center expenses may be drawn on by checks with the handwritten signature of the Troy Career Center Manager, Assistant Manager, or Program Coordinators. The Treasurer may open or close accounts with the listed institutions when in the District's interest. District funds may be invested according to Board Policy 5000.06, and the Treasurer is authorized to combine money from more than one fund for the purpose of making an investment authorized by subsection (1)(h) of Section 380.1223 of the Revised School Code. The maximum amount to be invested with the above institutions is regulated by the school code. The certification reads: "I, Gary Hauff, Secretary of Troy School District, Oakland County, Michigan, certify that the Resolution was adopted by said Board at a meeting thereof held on the date specified above," given under hand and seal of the Troy School District in the County of Oakland in the State of Michigan this 17th day of January 2024. Yes 7, No 0.

DESIGNATION OF BOARD AND DISTRICT LEGAL COUNSEL
Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mrs. Alic to continue the designation of Clark Hill, PLC; Collins & Blaha, P.C.; Miller Johnson; Thrun Law Firm, P.C.; and Miller Canfield as legal counsel to advise and/or represent the Troy School District and Board of Education as necessary for the 2024 calendar year. The superintendent is authorized to consult additional counsel as needed with prior notification to the Board. Yes 7, No 0.

DESIGNATION OF SUPERINTENDENT AS DEPUTY SECRETARY
Moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mr. Hauff to continue the designation of the Superintendent of Schools as Deputy Secretary of the Board with authority to act for the secretary for the 2024 calendar year. Yes 7, No 0.

DESIGNATION OF PERSON FOR POSTING NOTICES OF MEETINGS
Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Anne that the person designated for posting notices of meetings for the 2024 calendar year shall be Judy Holmes, Secretary to the Superintendent of Schools. Yes 7, No 0.

MEETING SCHEDULE AND COMMITTEE ASSIGNMENTS
Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Troy Board of Education adopt the schedule of meetings for the 2024 calendar year as indicated on the attached calendar. Yes 7, No 0. Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Hauff that the Board adopt the Board Committee Memberships for the 2024 school year as attached. Yes 7, No 0.

RECOGNITION
President Schmidt announced that the TSD Mission Moment featuring the SSAB Executive Board, the Student Spotlight, and the Board Recognition Month item were all moved to the February 27, 2024 Board of Education Meeting due to the cancellation of school that day. Dr. Machesky nonetheless informally recognized the Board, thanked members for all they do for students and the community, and presented them with a gift of appreciation.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS
None.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (FIRST)
Mr. Jeff Zendler, Troy resident and parent of four students in the District, addressed the Board about the new playgrounds being designed for elementary schools and whether they will be accessible and inclusive for all students, including students with disabilities.

CONSENT AGENDA
Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Board approve items A, B, C, D, and E: minutes of the December 5, 2023 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the December 5, 2023 Closed Session Meeting; minutes of the December 5, 2023 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the December 12, 2023 Board of Education Meeting; and the Treasurer's Report for November 2023. Yes 7, No 0.

PERSONNEL (ELEMENTARY AND SECONDARY)
Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Philippart that the Board approve the personnel recommendations as stated, naming Jennifer Maxwell and Mallory Lyons. Yes 7, No 0.

CURRICULUM
None.

BUSINESS - FLOORING REPLACEMENT AND POLISHING PROJECT
Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Dr. Wilson that the bid for flooring replacement work be awarded as follows and approved as an expenditure of the Building Site & Sinking Fund: Shock Bros Floorcovering, flooring demo/replacement, $494,175.00; Diamond Shine Concrete & Stone, floor polishing, $26,000.00; Additional/Emergency Flooring, $30,000.00; TOTAL $550,175.00. Yes 7, No 0.

BUSINESS - PLAYGROUND EQUIPMENT PURCHASE
Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mr. Haupt that the bid for playground equipment and installation be awarded as follows and approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund: Sinclair Recreation/GameTime playground equipment, Contractor #1, $1,508,996.70; Midstate Recreation/Playworld playground equipment, Contractor #2, $1,183,777.90; TOTAL $2,692,774.60. Yes 7, No 0. Board members asked whether the playgrounds will be fully ADA compliant, especially for students with disabilities; Ms. Griffor indicated they have all been designed in alignment with ADA requirements.

BUSINESS - ATHLETIC COMPLEX UPGRADE
Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Dr. Philippart that the bid for the high school athletic renovations be awarded as follows and approved as an expenditure of the Building Site & Sinking Fund and the 2023 Capital Projects Fund: Cortis Bros Trucking & Excavating, site work, $8,505,700.00; City Contracting Services, architectural, $518,000.00; Contrast Mechanical, Inc., mechanical, $182,000.00; Innovated Energy Controls, electrical, $543,810.00; Shaw Integrated & Turf Solutions, Inc., synthetic turf, $2,292,305.00; Contingency (8%), $963,345.00; TOTAL $13,005,160.00. Yes 7, No 0. Board members inquired about past flooding issues with baseball fields and whether the upgrade will address that problem; Mr. West indicated the upgrade will fix several major problems.

BUSINESS - FIBER MAINTENANCE
Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Hauff that fiber maintenance services be awarded to Fiber Link, Inc. consistent with its submitted proposal to Bid #2324-05, with related expenditures approved as an expenditure of the General Fund. Yes 7, No 0.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (SECOND)
Mr. Jason Cichowicz, President of the Troy Education Association, addressed the Board about the TEA contract, which expires on January 31, 2024. He stated that working without a contract causes anxiety and frustration and that teachers feel disrespected, that many teachers are leaving the profession and choosing careers in surrounding districts, and that the association is ready to bargain and has offered many dates to negotiate.

OTHER
None.

BOARD COMMENTS
Dr. Wilson shared that the MLK Day event recognition for SSAB students will be held next month and gave a shout out to the students who worked at pulling it together; she also shared her excitement about the Student Equity Council kickoff and the way students are leading that work. Dr. Machesky thanked all the students and community members who came out to make the MLK Day event a success, noting several dignitaries attended and saw a showcase of service to the community. Mr. Schmidt announced that the next Board Workshop will be held Tuesday, February 6th at 6:00 p.m. in the Administration Building and the next Board Meeting Tuesday, February 27th at 7:00 p.m. in the Services Building.

**Standard terms and conditions.** Upon customer acceptance by signature or purchase order for the items, quantities and amounts indicated, KWL will proceed to fulfill available items. The customer agrees to pay for products fulfilled and services rendered; KWL invoices on net 30 terms upon fulfillment and may issue partial invoices for partial deliveries at the sale prices specified, each payable in full within 30 days of invoice date. The customer agrees not to infringe, reproduce without authorization, or distribute KWL copyrighted materials, including books, publications, computer software (object and source code), online curricula, web content, diagrams, photos, testing materials, exams, text, images and graphics. **Digital license and adoption terms.** All sales of licenses for digital books and materials are final, non-returnable and non-refundable after delivery. Within the adoption dates, July 1 2026 - June 30 2033, the customer may purchase additional quantities of licenses for the digital books and materials listed at the same sale price specified in the quote. Standard shipping, which may involve ground parcel and/or LTL freight shipments, will be billed at 8% of the sale price for print materials, net of any applicable discounts; expedited options are billed at cost incurred by Klett World Languages, Inc. Print and digital materials for teachers are provided free of charge at the rate of one set of teacher materials for each 25 sets of student materials.

**Professional development terms.** Sessions are facilitated by a trained content specialist or a member of the KWL Implementation Team; specific dates and topics are set in consultation between KWL and the school/district; the Implementation Team at pd@klettwl.com is the main point of contact. Virtual sessions may be rescheduled at no charge with at least 24 hours' notice. In-person sessions may be canceled or rescheduled at no charge and/or with a full refund with at least 2 weeks' notice; cancellation 13 to 4 days before the scheduled date makes the district responsible for 50% of the payment; cancellation with 3 days' notice or less, and any no-show regardless of format, makes the district responsible for payment in full. Virtual sessions may be recorded upon request and with KWL approval, with the recording shared afterwards; slide decks and presentations are not shared before or after a session unless a customized session has been purchased. Professional development sessions or products purchased upfront may be rolled over year to year through the life of the adoption, including renewals upon request, and expire when the adoption ends or if the district stops using KWL materials, whichever comes first.

**SIS integration terms.** To ensure accuracy and reliability of Skill Portfolio data within The KWL Hub ("the Platform"), the district agrees to use persistent, unique student identifiers such as SIS ID or UUID without reassigning or altering IDs mid-year; avoid duplicate or multiple accounts for a single student; preserve historical data when students change classes, sections or schools; give advance notice of SIS schema or roster changes affecting account mapping or data integrity; and monitor and schedule SIS syncs to avoid data loss or overwriting during active instructional use. The Platform is not responsible for data loss, broken reporting or Skill Portfolio inaccuracies resulting from failure to follow these practices, which must be maintained for the duration of the adoption. Inaccurate or missing student identifiers, account duplication, or unannounced schema changes may cause irreversible data inconsistencies or unavailability of key reporting features. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Presentation**: "PA 146 Legislative Overview," PowerPoint, 21 slides, presented to the Troy Board of Education, meeting date June 3, 2025.
**Presenter**: Kim St. Martin, Ph.D., Director, MiMTSS TA Center (mimtsstac.org). **Dated**: June 2025.

**Framing**
Bipartisan laws Public Act 146 and Public Act 147 of 2024 were signed by Governor Whitmer on October 10, 2024, to improve reading outcomes for K-12 learners, affecting in-service and pre-service teachers. They are frequently called the K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Law. The law is not focused on diagnosing learners with dyslexia.

**PA 146 components**
PA 146 includes Read by Grade Three, revising the 1280f statute. Individual Reading Improvement Plans (IRIPs) span K-3; 4th grade IRIPs are NOT included, though MDE is examining K-12 language to clarify requirements beyond 3rd grade. IRIP information must be reported to ISDs de-identified, then aggregated and sent to MDE. Diagnostic assessments are no longer referenced, and the term "district-identified coaches" is infused into the language.

**Assessment requirements**
K-3 requires reliable and valid screening and progress monitoring measures for phonemic awareness, letter-sound correspondences, single-word reading, nonsense word reading, rapid automized naming, oral passage reading fluency, and comprehension (retelling, cloze reading procedure). Rapid Automized Naming (RAN) identifies dyslexia characteristics by timing students naming known colors, objects, letters, or words; teachers should not be asked to teach students to improve RAN data (MDE Dyslexia Handbook).
In grades 4-12, only adolescents showing listed indicators need screening: escape or avoidance behaviors around reading or writing; effortful or laborious reading; comprehension difficulties caused by inaccurate or inefficient word reading; significant spelling or encoding difficulties not caused by fine or visual motor difficulties; low performance on approved English language arts standards or approved standardized literacy assessments; reading deficiency. Those students must be screened with an assessment from MDE's approved list; where data confirm the need for Tier 2 reading intervention support, students need access to intervention and are screened at least three times per year.

**Dyslexia definition and characteristics**
PA 146 defines dyslexia as both (i) a specific learning disorder neurobiological in origin, characterized by difficulties with accurate or fluent word recognition and poor spelling and decoding typically resulting from a deficit in the phonological component of language, often unexpected relative to other cognitive abilities; and (ii) a disorder that may include secondary consequences such as comprehension problems and reduced reading experience impeding vocabulary growth. Characteristics are sampled from Table 1 of the MDE Dyslexia Handbook, pg. 15 — K-3 examples include confusing letters with similar sounds and difficulty with handwriting; grades 4-12 include difficulty reading and spelling multisyllabic words and limited vocabulary.

**MTSS and code emphasis**
The law outlines Tier 1 class-wide reading instruction and adds language on Tier 1 curriculum resources and methods teaching decoding and word recognition through a "code-emphasis instructional approach"; Tiers 2 and 3 cover intensifying intervention. K-3 intervention support must be documented in the IRIP. Code emphasis means direct, explicit instruction on the code system of written English at the sound, syllable, morpheme, and word level so pupils develop automaticity in accurate sound-symbol associations.

**Prohibited methods, Sec. 23c (iii)**
Methods and resources must not minimize using letter-sound information to decode unknown words — including guessing from pictures, skipping words to use passage meaning, guessing from only the first sound, memorizing a word in its written form, and using predictable or leveled text for initial word recognition instruction — unless used to confirm meaning after decoding has been attempted.

**Science of Reading**
Per The Reading League (TRL, 2022), a large body of scientifically-based cross-disciplinary research conducted over the last 50 years worldwide, including multiple languages. It is not an ideology or philosophy, a fad or pendulum swing, a political agenda, one-size-fits-all, a program of instruction, or a single component such as phonics.

**MDE responsibilities**
Provide a coaching model, including expansion to grades 4-12; update a list of assessments by January 1, 2026; publish a list of evidence-based Tier 1 reading curricula and materials by January 1, 2026; and develop Technical Assistance on assessment selection and use, structured literacy, evidence-based methods and materials, and understanding dyslexia.

**Resources listed**
MDE K-12 Literacy and Dyslexia Laws; Section 35m and 35n; K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Research Network; and the 2025 Dyslexia Summit keynote "Building a New Brain City: Connecting Neuroscience & Educational Practices for Students with Reading."
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
"PA 146 Legislative Overview" is a 21-slide PowerPoint presented at the Troy Board of Education meeting of June 3, 2025, explaining Michigan's K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Law to the board.

PRESENTER AND SOURCE
The deck is authored by Kim St. Martin, Ph.D., identified on the closing slide as Director of the MiMTSS TA Center, and carries the web address mimtsstac.org and the date June 2025. Content is drawn from the statute itself and from the MDE Dyslexia Handbook, and the deck closes with a resources slide and a thank-you slide.

THE LAW
Bipartisan laws Public Act 146 and Public Act 147 of 2024 were signed by Governor Whitmer on October 10, 2024, with the stated goal of improving reading outcomes for K-12 learners and impacting in-service and pre-service teachers. The pair is frequently referred to as the K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Law. The presentation emphasizes that the law is not focused on diagnosing learners with dyslexia.

PA 146 COMPONENTS AND THE 1280f REVISION
PA 146 includes Read by Grade Three, revising the 1280f statute. The changes highlighted are: Individual Reading Improvement Plans (IRIPs) now span K-3; developing 4th grade IRIPs is explicitly not included in PA 146, although MDE is examining the language for K-12 to further clarify IRIP requirements beyond 3rd grade; PA 146 requires a level of IRIP information to be reported to ISDs, with student information de-identified, and then aggregated and sent to MDE; diagnostic assessments are no longer referenced; and the term "district-identified coaches" is infused into the language.

K-3 ASSESSMENT REQUIREMENTS
For kindergarten through 3rd grade, reliable and valid screening and progress monitoring assessment measures are required for phonemic awareness, letter-sound correspondences, single-word reading, nonsense word reading, rapid automized naming, oral passage reading fluency, and comprehension assessment (retelling, cloze reading procedure).

RAPID AUTOMIZED NAMING
A dedicated slide addresses Rapid Automized Naming (RAN). A RAN assessment measure is used to identify dyslexia characteristics. RAN measures cognitive processing speed by asking students to name known colors, objects, letters, or words, and the assessment is timed. The deck states that teachers should not be asked to teach students how to improve their RAN screening assessment data, and cites the MDE Dyslexia Handbook.

GRADES 4-12 ASSESSMENT REQUIREMENTS
Only adolescents who demonstrate any of the listed indicators need a screening assessment to confirm dyslexia consequences. The indicators are: escape or avoidance behaviors when asked to engage in reading or writing activities; effortful or laborious reading; reading comprehension difficulties caused by inaccurate or inefficient word reading; significant spelling or encoding (writing) difficulties not caused by fine or visual motor difficulties; low performance on approved English language arts standards; low performance on approved standardized literacy assessments; and reading deficiency. Students in grades 4-12 demonstrating any of these must be screened using a reliable and valid screening assessment from MDE's approved list. The screening assessment data confirms the need for Tier 2 reading intervention support, and where the data confirm that need, students will need access to reading intervention and will be screened at least three times per year.

DYSLEXIA DEFINITION AS WRITTEN IN PA 146
"Dyslexia" means both of the following: (i) a specific learning disorder that is neurobiological in origin and characterized by difficulties with accurate or fluent word recognition and by poor spelling and decoding abilities that typically result from a deficit in the phonological component of language that is often unexpected in relation to other cognitive abilities and the provision of effective classroom instruction; and (ii) a specific learning disorder that may include secondary consequences, such as problems in reading comprehension and a reduced reading experience that can impede the growth of vocabulary and lead to social, emotional, and behavioral difficulties.

DYSLEXIA CHARACTERISTICS
The characteristics presented are a sample from Table 1 of the MDE Dyslexia Handbook, page 15. For K-3, the listed characteristics are: confuses letters whose sounds are similar; repeatedly misspells words that include letter-sound combinations that have been taught; finds handwriting to be difficult (for example, pencil grip, letter formation); avoids reading-related activities; and difficulty finding the correct word when speaking. For 4th through 12th grade: demonstrates significant difficulties when trying to read and spell multisyllabic words; finds it challenging to understand new information from text due to underlying decoding and word recognition issues; limited vocabulary; lacks written expression skills compared to grade-level peers; and avoids reading and writing activities at school and at home.

MTSS AND TIERED SUPPORT
The law outlines the features of Tier 1, class-wide reading instruction, consistent with a portion of the language that was in the Read by Grade law. New language outlines Tier 1 curriculum resources and instructional methods to teach decoding and word recognition using a "code-emphasis instructional approach." Tiers 2 and 3 outline the methods to intensify literacy intervention instruction. Students in K-3 who need intervention support must have that support documented in the Individual Reading Improvement Plan. The deck notes that the term Individual Reading Intervention Plan is also used in PA 146 and that MDE will be clarifying how to interpret the language. The MDE web address WWW.MICHIGAN.GOV/MDE appears on this slide.

CODE-EMPHASIS INSTRUCTIONAL APPROACH DEFINED
"Code emphasis means direct, explicit instruction on the code system of written English at the sound, syllable, morpheme, and word level so pupils develop automaticity in accurate sound-symbol associations used for word recognition and for developing a robust sight-word vocabulary."

SCIENCE OF READING
Citing The Reading League (TRL, 2022), the Science of Reading is described as a large body of scientifically-based research across disciplines about reading and issues related to reading and writing; research conducted over the last 50 years across the world; and research that includes findings from studies in learning to read in multiple languages. The Science of Reading means there is substantial evidence to inform how proficient reading and writing develop, why some have difficulty, and how we can most effectively assess and teach to improve outcomes. A companion slide lists what the Science of Reading is not: not an ideology or philosophy; not a fad, trend, new idea, or pendulum swing; not a political agenda; not a one-size-fits-all approach; not a program of instruction; and not a single, specific component of instruction, such as phonics.

PROHIBITED INSTRUCTIONAL METHODS UNDER SEC. 23c (iii)
The statutory text quoted states that the instructional methods and curriculum resources described in that subparagraph must not include instructional methods or curriculum resources that minimize the importance of primarily using letter-sound information to decode or recognize unknown words, including but not limited to the following, unless used to confirm the meaning of unknown words after decoding has been attempted: (A) prompting pupils to guess unknown words using pictures and illustrations; (B) skipping over an unknown word or words to use the meaning of the passage to recognize the unknown word or words; (C) identifying only the first sound of an unknown word and then being prompted to guess the word using the word's initial sound and the meaning of the text surrounding the word; (D) memorizing a word in its written form; and (E) using predictable text and leveled text to provide initial word recognition instruction and practice in reading new learned letter-sound correspondences.

MDE RESPONSIBILITIES
As a result of this law, the Michigan Department of Education is required to: provide a coaching model, including expanding a coaching model to grades 4-12; update a list of assessments by January 1, 2026; publish a list of evidence-based Tier 1 reading curricula and materials by January 1, 2026; and develop Technical Assistance (TA) covering the selection and use of assessments (universal screener and progress monitoring assessments), structured literacy, evidence-based instructional method and curriculum materials, and understanding dyslexia.

RESOURCES CITED
The resources slide lists MDE K-12 Literacy and Dyslexia Laws; Section 35m and 35n; the K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Research Network; and the keynote from the 2025 Dyslexia Summit titled "Building a New Brain City: Connecting Neuroscience & Educational Practices for Students with Reading." A Questions slide precedes the resources, and the final slide reads "Thank YOU!" with the presenter's name and title, Director, MiMTSS TA Center.

RAPID AUTOMIZED NAMING

RAN measures cognitive processing speed by asking students to name known colors, objects, letters, or words, and the assessment is timed. The deck states that teachers should not be asked to teach students how to improve their RAN screening assessment data, and cites the MDE Dyslexia Handbook.

GRADES 4-12 ASSESSMENT REQUIREMENTS
Only adolescents who demonstrate any of the listed indicators need a screening assessment to confirm dyslexia consequences. The indicators are: escape or avoidance behaviors when asked to engage in reading or writing activities; effortful or laborious reading; reading comprehension difficulties caused by inaccurate or inefficient word reading; significant spelling or encoding (writing) difficulties not caused by fine or visual motor difficulties; low performance on approved English language arts standards; low performance on approved standardized literacy assessments; and reading deficiency. Students in grades 4-12 demonstrating any of these must be screened using a reliable and valid screening assessment from MDE's approved list. The screening assessment data confirms the need for Tier 2 reading intervention support, and where the data confirm that need, students will need access to reading intervention and will be screened at least three times per year.

DYSLEXIA DEFINITION AS WRITTEN IN PA 146
"Dyslexia" means both of the following: (i) a specific learning disorder that is neurobiological in origin and characterized by difficulties with accurate or fluent word recognition and by poor spelling and decoding abilities that typically result from a deficit in the phonological component of language that is often unexpected in relation to other cognitive abilities and the provision of effective classroom instruction; and (ii) a specific learning disorder that may include secondary consequences, such as problems in reading comprehension and a reduced reading experience that can impede the growth of vocabulary and lead to social, emotional, and behavioral difficulties.

DYSLEXIA CHARACTERISTICS
The characteristics presented are a sample from Table 1 of the MDE Dyslexia Handbook, page 15. For K-3, the listed characteristics are: confuses letters whose sounds are similar; repeatedly misspells words that include letter-sound combinations that have been taught; finds handwriting to be difficult (for example, pencil grip, letter formation); avoids reading-related activities; and difficulty finding the correct word when speaking. For 4th through 12th grade: demonstrates significant difficulties when trying to read and spell multisyllabic words; finds it challenging to understand new information from text due to underlying decoding and word recognition issues; limited vocabulary; lacks written expression skills compared to grade-level peers; and avoids reading and writing activities at school and at home.

MTSS AND TIERED SUPPORT
The law outlines the features of Tier 1, class-wide reading instruction, consistent with a portion of the language that was in the Read by Grade law. New language outlines Tier 1 curriculum resources and instructional methods to teach decoding and word recognition using a "code-emphasis instructional approach." Tiers 2 and 3 outline the methods to intensify literacy intervention instruction. Students in K-3 who need intervention support must have that support documented in the Individual Reading Improvement Plan. The deck notes that the term Individual Reading Intervention Plan is also used in PA 146 and that MDE will be clarifying how to interpret the language. The MDE web address WWW.MICHIGAN.GOV/MDE appears on this slide.

CODE-EMPHASIS INSTRUCTIONAL APPROACH DEFINED
"Code emphasis means direct, explicit instruction on the code system of written English at the sound, syllable, morpheme, and word level so pupils develop automaticity in accurate sound-symbol associations used for word recognition and for developing a robust sight-word vocabulary."

SCIENCE OF READING
Citing The Reading League (TRL, 2022), the Science of Reading is described as a large body of scientifically-based research across disciplines about reading and issues related to reading and writing; research conducted over the last 50 years across the world; and research that includes findings from studies in learning to read in multiple languages. The Science of Reading means there is substantial evidence to inform how proficient reading and writing develop, why some have difficulty, and how we can most effectively assess and teach to improve outcomes. A companion slide lists what the Science of Reading is not: not an ideology or philosophy; not a fad, trend, new idea, or pendulum swing; not a political agenda; not a one-size-fits-all approach; not a program of instruction; and not a single, specific component of instruction, such as phonics.

PROHIBITED INSTRUCTIONAL METHODS UNDER SEC. 23c (iii)
The statutory text quoted states that the instructional methods and curriculum resources described in that subparagraph must not include instructional methods or curriculum resources that minimize the importance of primarily using letter-sound information to decode or recognize unknown words, including but not limited to the following, unless used to confirm the meaning of unknown words after decoding has been attempted: (A) prompting pupils to guess unknown words using pictures and illustrations; (B) skipping over an unknown word or words to use the meaning of the passage to recognize the unknown word or words; (C) identifying only the first sound of an unknown word and then being prompted to guess the word using the word's initial sound and the meaning of the text surrounding the word; (D) memorizing a word in its written form; and (E) using predictable text and leveled text to provide initial word recognition instruction and practice in reading new learned letter-sound correspondences.

MDE RESPONSIBILITIES
As a result of this law, the Michigan Department of Education is required to: provide a coaching model, including expanding a coaching model to grades 4-12; update a list of assessments by January 1, 2026; publish a list of evidence-based Tier 1 reading curricula and materials by January 1, 2026; and develop Technical Assistance (TA) covering the selection and use of assessments (universal screener and progress monitoring assessments), structured literacy, evidence-based instructional method and curriculum materials, and understanding dyslexia.

RESOURCES CITED
The resources slide lists MDE K-12 Literacy and Dyslexia Laws; Section 35m and 35n; the K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Research Network; and the keynote from the 2025 Dyslexia Summit titled "Building a New Brain City: Connecting Neuroscience & Educational Practices for Students with Reading." A Questions slide precedes the resources, and the final slide reads "Thank YOU!" with the presenter's name and title, Director, MiMTSS TA Center.

Minutes of the regular meeting of the Board of Education of the Troy School District, Troy, Michigan, held December 13, 2022 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:0X p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present were Board members Anne, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, and Wilson; Mr. Gottlieb was absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Harris, and West. Approximately 35 members of the audience attended. The minutes were respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the typist notation GH/jh.

RECOGNITION — STUDENT SPOTLIGHT. The Student Spotlight celebrated the talents and achievements of students in the Creative Guild. The Board recognized a sophomore from Troy High School who had recently wrapped up editing on her directorial debut short film. Thomas Butcher, Creative Content Producer from the TSD Creative Guild, was invited up to share a clip and talk about the work that went into the student project from start to finish.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS. None.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (AGENDA ITEMS). Mr. Jeff Schaeper, Troy resident, addressed the Board about the District budget and future deficit and offered his assistance.

GENERAL — CONSENT AGENDA, RESOLUTION 22-086. It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Hammond that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B, C, D and E on the consent agenda: Minutes of the November 1, 2022 Board of Education Workshop; Minutes of the November 15, 2022 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report — October 2022; IA Letter of Understanding; and General Fund Budget Amendment #1. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Gottlieb.

PERSONNEL. None. CURRICULUM. None.

BUSINESS — BP 9952 2023 SITE WORK / RETENTION POND PROJECT, RESOLUTION 22-087. It was moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Mrs. Anne that the bid for site work projects be awarded to Simone Construction Services in the amount of $421,901.00 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the Building and Site Sinking Fund. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Gottlieb.

BUSINESS — PURCHASE AGREEMENT, SECTION 1 PRESERVATION, RESOLUTION 22-088. Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne. The recitals note that on March 20, 2018 the Board of Education passed a resolution that the School District property commonly known as Section 1 should be split into two parcels, so the front portion could be sold to a developer for residential purposes and the remaining portion would be preserved in perpetuity. The School District negotiated an Agreement of Purchase and Sale for the sale and preservation of the remaining 69.51 +/- acres of Section 1 with Six Rivers Land Conservancy, a Michigan non-profit corporation, whose mission is to conserve, sustain, and connect natural areas, lands, and waters that make the places we live special. The Agreement, already executed by Six Rivers, is attached as Exhibit A. The resolution authorizes the sale and preservation of the Premises on terms substantially similar to the attached Agreement and authorizes the Superintendent, or his designee, to execute the Agreement, any extensions, and all other documents necessary and incidental to the sale. Resolution declared adopted; certified by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Board of Education, that it is a true and complete copy of a resolution duly adopted at a regular meeting held on the 13th day of December, 2022, conducted in full compliance with the Open Meeting Act, Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Gottlieb.

BUSINESS — 2023 SCHOOL BUILDING AND SITE BOND SALE AUTHORIZING RESOLUTION (SERIES 1), RESOLUTION 22-089. It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Anne that the Board authorize the issuance of bonds designated the 2023 School Building and Site Bonds in an amount not to exceed $190,000,000, and that the attached resolution in its entirety be made part of the official minutes of the December 13, 2022 regular meeting.

The attached resolution, captioned TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT, COUNTY OF OAKLAND, State of MICHIGAN, RESOLUTION AUTHORIZING 2023 School Building and Site Bonds (UNLIMITED TAX GENERAL OBLIGATION), records a regular Board meeting held in the School District on December 13, 2022 at 7:00 p.m. local time. The preamble and resolution were offered by Member Gary Hauff and supported by Member Vital Anne.

Recitals: at the General School Election held November 8, 2022, qualified electors approved the issuance of bonds, in one or more series, in an amount not to exceed $555,000,000 (the 2022 Bond Proposal), for remodeling, equipping, re-equipping, furnishing and re-furnishing school buildings, athletic fields, playgrounds and other facilities; erecting and completing, equipping and furnishing a replacement middle school and classroom additions and other additions to existing school buildings and other facilities; acquiring and installing instructional technology infrastructure and equipment; acquiring sites, preparing, developing and improving sites; and the purchase of school buses. Under Section 6, Article IX and Section 16, Article IX of the Michigan Constitution of 1963, tax levies for the bonds are without limitation as to rate or amount. The Board authorized the first series in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $190,000,000. The Superintendent and the Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, either acting individually, are designated the Authorized Officer. The School District must either be granted qualified status under Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, as amended, or receive prior approval from the Michigan Department of Treasury.

Bond details: registered as to principal and interest in the denomination of $5,000 or integral multiples; dated as of the date of delivery or another date set by the Authorized Officer; maturing on May 1 or November 1, with final maturity not later than thirty (30) years from the date of issue; interest at rates determined upon negotiated sale not exceeding a true interest cost of six and one-half percent (6.50%) per annum, payable semi-annually on May 1 and November 1; underwriter's discount not to exceed 0.50% of principal. Interest is payable by check drawn on the Transfer Agent to the registered owner of record as of the fifteenth day of the month prior to each payment date. Bonds may be issued in book-entry-only form through The Depository Trust Company in New York, New York, as serial or term bonds, subject to optional or mandatory redemption as determined by the Authorized Officer.

Funds: the Treasurer shall open a special depositary account designated the 2023 School Building and Site Bonds Debt Retirement Fund, unless a Common Debt Retirement Fund is established, and a special depository account designated the 2023 School Building and Site Bonds Projects Fund (the Capital Projects Fund). Net original issue premium counts against the 2022 Bond Proposal. Commencing with the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2023, the School District must levy a tax annually sufficient to pay principal and interest, without limitation as to rate or amount. Arbitrage rebate obligations arise under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended.

Sale and professionals: the Board determined that a negotiated sale provides greater flexibility in structuring maturities and timing. Stifel, Nicolaus & Company, Incorporated was appointed senior managing underwriter, with authority for the Authorized Officer to appoint co-managing underwriters and to negotiate, award, execute and deliver a bond purchase agreement without further Board approval. Miller, Canfield, Paddock and Stone, P.L.C. was appointed bond counsel, with disclosure of Miller Canfield's periodic representation of Stifel in unrelated matters; PFM Financial Advisors LLC was appointed municipal advisor. The Authorized Officer may apply for bond ratings and municipal bond insurance, approve preliminary and final official statements, exercise authority under Section 315(1)(d) of the Act, apply to Treasury for prior approval or file a qualifying statement, request rating waivers, file a Security Report, and pursue qualification under the School Bond Qualification, Approval, and Loan Act, Act 92, Public Acts of Michigan, 2005, as amended. Continuing disclosure is covenanted under SEC Rule 15c2-12. Vote on the bond resolution: YES 6, NO 0, ABSENT Gottlieb; declared adopted and certified by Gary Hauff, Secretary, Board of Education, citing the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of 1976, as amended.

EXHIBIT A — BOND FORM. The form of the Troy School District 2023 School Building and Site Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation) provides interest computed on the basis of a 360-day year consisting of twelve 30-day months, payable semiannually, with principal payable at the corporate trust office of the Transfer Agent, changeable on not less than 60 days' notice. The bonds are issued under Act 451, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976, as amended, and Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, as amended, pursuant to the resolution adopted December 13, 2022, and constitute the first series authorized by the majority vote of qualified electors at the November 8, 2022 General School Election. The full faith and credit of the School District is irrevocably pledged. Redemption notice must be given at least 30 days and not more than 60 days prior to the redemption date; bonds are called in multiples of $5,000, and redemption is at par plus accrued interest. The Transfer Agent need not register transfers during the 15 days before the mailing of a redemption notice.

EXHIBIT B — FORM OF CONTINUING DISCLOSURE UNDERTAKING. Definitions include Audited Financial Statements (prepared by independent certified public accountants as required by Act 2, Public Acts of Michigan, 1968, as amended), Bondholders, EMMA (the MSRB's Electronic Municipal Market Access system), Financial Obligation, MSRB, Rule (SEC Rule 15c2-12 under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934), and SEC. The School District agrees to provide to the MSRB through EMMA, on or before the last day of the 6th month after the end of its fiscal year, commencing with the fiscal year ending June 30, 2023, annual financial information and operating data similar to Official Statement tables covering: ENROLLMENT — Historical Enrollment; STATE AID PAYMENTS; PROPERTY VALUATIONS — History of Valuations; MAJOR TAXPAYERS; SCHOOL DISTRICT TAX RATES (per $1,000 of Valuation); TAX LEVIES AND COLLECTIONS; RETIREMENT PLAN — Contribution to MPSERS; DEBT STATEMENT — DIRECT DEBT; SCHOOL LOAN REVOLVING FUND (SLRF) PROGRAM; and GENERAL FUND BUDGET SUMMARY in Appendix C, plus the Audited Financial Statements (unaudited statements filed if audited ones are unavailable). The undertaking requires notice of failure to disclose and, within ten business days, notice of sixteen listed events including payment delinquencies, unscheduled draws on debt service reserves or credit enhancements, adverse tax opinions and IRS notices such as Form 5701-TEB, bond calls and tender offers, defeasances, rating changes, bankruptcy or receivership, mergers or asset sales, and defaults under a Financial Obligation. Further provisions address materiality under federal securities laws, termination of the reporting obligation upon legal defeasance, enforcement limited to specific performance for the benefit of Bondholders, and amendment procedures consistent with the Rule.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (NON-AGENDA ITEMS). Mrs. Katie MacFarland, Troy resident and parent of students in the District, addressed the Board about emails exchanged between MASB and Board members regarding a court case from Maryland related to gender support. Mrs. Barb Yagley, Troy resident, addressed the Board regarding Covid and precautions to keep children safe and Covid funding, and recommended reading the book The Real Anthony Fauci. Mr. Edmund Rushton, Plymouth resident, addressed the Board about offering field trips for students to visit the Museum of African History in Detroit, located near the DIA, to learn about racism and history. Mr. Ollie Apahidean, parent of students in the District, addressed the Board about teachers teaching children how to pursue the truth and asked about the Code of Conduct and violations.

REPORTS FROM STUDENT REPRESENTATIVES. Yara Mashal, student representative for International Academy-East, reported on events and activities at her school. Sara Ali, student representative for Athens High School, reported on events and activities at Athens. Nish Palepu, student representative for Troy High School, and Alexi Papadelis, student representative for Troy College and Career High School, were not in attendance.

BOARD MEMBER COMMENTS. Board members wished everyone happy holidays and looked forward to coming together in the new year. Mrs. Hammond shared a heartfelt goodbye and members thanked her for her years of service to the board and community. Dr. Machesky congratulated the fine arts teachers for the numerous holiday concerts performed, gave a shout out to the SSAB Executive Board for bringing back the District's annual MLK Day event, and noted that donations of fleece are desperately needed for the event, along with a blood drive and other community activities. Mr. Schmidt announced that the next Board Workshop would be held January 10, 2023 at 6:00 p.m. at the Administration Building, and the Organizational and Regular Board Meeting on Tuesday, January 17th at 7:00 p.m. at the Services Building.

ADJOURNMENT. The meeting adjourned at 7:55 p.m.

Mr. Pagel read each name with the year service began: Ed Berky (Maintenance, All Schools, since 1993), Donna Black (Food Service, Wass Elementary, 2011), Carolyn Brown (Teacher, Wattles Elementary, 2002), Patrick Dawood (Teacher, Athens, 1999), Susan Fortuna (Teacher, Troy High, 1980), Tim Fulcher (Director of Athletics, Continuing Education and Enrichment, Troy Learning Center, 2008), Shelia Gannon (Transition Coordinator, Services, 1989), Mary Goetz (Teacher, Bemis, 1989), Todd Hensley (Purchasing Supervisor, Rankin, 2013), Susan Hill (Para-Professional, Martell, 2001), Joaquina Kapuscinski (Para-Professional, Bemis, 2007), Camille Lamesch (Teacher, Martell, 1996), Jill Martens (Para-Professional, Troy High, 2002), Mark Martin (Teacher, Boulan Park, 1999), Melven Moffett (Teacher, Leonard, 2011), Joni Pallas (Para-Professional, Larson, 2011), Joan Porter (Teacher, Barnard, 1987), Karen Reese (Teacher, Costello, 1996), Matthew Reimann (Teacher, Troy High, 2005), Tonia Romancheck (Teacher, Hamilton, 2003), Cheryl Rowley (Teacher, Hamilton, 2003), Pamela Russ (Teacher, Bemis, 1995), Kitty Schmidt (Teacher, Baker, 1985), Beth Soggs (Technology Director, Services, 2017), Luba Sordyl (Teacher, Athens, 2003), Roseann Sparbeck (Secretary, Athens, 1999), Sandra Tallant (Food Service, Larson, 1997), Ellen Talsma (Secretary, Troy High, 1999), Julie Tomasko (Para-Professional, Larson, 1995), Raymond Torres (Teacher, Smith, 2002), Bill Turner (Career and Technical Education Supervisor, Troy Learning Center, 2005) and Lynn Yagley (Para-Professional, Leonard, 1996). Retirees received a gift of appreciation for their years of service.

**Teacher Appreciation Week and Student Spotlight**
Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Hauff, the Board adopted a resolution supporting National Teacher Appreciation Week, May 6-10, 2024, reciting that teachers inspire and open children's minds, promote democratic equality and critical thinking, and that Troy teachers set the bar for excellence. Yes: 7, No: 0. For the Student Spotlight recognizing the TSD Creative Guild, Thomas Butcher returned to introduce Jayla Turner, a Troy High School senior and the Student Board Representative for Troy High, who shared her accomplishments and received a certificate of recognition.

**Mental Health Awareness Month**
Moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Dr. Philippart, the Board adopted a resolution recognizing May 2024 as Mental Health Awareness Month, in coordination with Oakland Community Health Network and other Oakland County school boards. The resolution states that one in five of all Americans, including children, experience mental health issues that could lead to school difficulties, physical problems and even suicide, and that May 9, 2024 is National Children's Mental Health Awareness Day while May 5 through May 11, 2024 is Children's Mental Health Acceptance Week. Yes: 7, No: 0.

**Additions, deletions and agenda-item public communication**
None reported for either item.

**Consent agenda**
Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Haupt, the Board approved items A, B, C, D, E, F and G: minutes of the April 2, 2024 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the April 16, 2024 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report - March 2024; approval of the Oakland Intermediate School District budget; a resolution to hold a public hearing on the proposed 2024/2025 school year budget; the Food Service Contract; and IA budget approval for the 2024/2025 school year. Yes: 7, No: 0.

**Personnel**
Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Alic, the Board issued a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure to Mr. Aurel Malutan, who begins duties as Finance Director as of July 1, 2024. Yes: 7, No: 0. Moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mr. Haupt, the Board issued a two-year administrative contract without tenure to Mr. Benjamin Cronin as Assistant Principal, Athens High School, commencing with the 2024-25 school year. Yes: 7, No: 0. Moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Alic, the Board issued a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure to Mrs. Kristin Crowe as Principal, Wass Elementary School, commencing with the 2024-25 school year. Yes: 7, No: 0. Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Anne, the Board approved elementary and secondary personnel recommendations for Victoria Auten, Sierra Dietz and Anna Greenblatt. Yes: 7, No: 0.

**Curriculum**
A brief presentation reviewed information given at the May 7 Board Workshop on the Algebra 1 math program. Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mr. Haupt, the Algebra 1 mathematics materials were adopted for the 2024-2025 school year. Yes: 7, No: 0.

**Business**
Smith MS ground stabilization improvements (Hauff/Alic): the bid for ground/soil stabilization and improvement work was awarded to CNC Foundations, Inc. in the amount of $370,920.00, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Yes: 7, No: 0. Wass oven purchase (Haupt/Philippart): the bid for two Electric Combi Ovens was awarded to Gold Star Products in the amount of $32,542.00, approved as an expenditure of the Food Service Fund. Yes: 7, No: 0. Epic Communication and Security Platform for Leonard and Bemis (Anne/Alic): purchase of the EPIC system was awarded to Inacomp TSG in the amount of $424,952, approved as an expenditure of the General Fund and the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Yes: 7, No: 0. iPads for freshmen (Anne/Haupt): the district will purchase iPads and cases from Apple Computers in the amount of $493,845, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Yes: 7, No: 0. Stadium scoreboards and audio systems (Philippart/Wilson): the district will purchase new scoreboards and audio systems for the Athens and Troy High School stadiums from Daktronics with installation by Johnson Sign Company in the amount of $170,500 inclusive of a 10% contingency, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Bond Fund. Yes: 7, No: 0.

**Board President comments - bargaining update**
President Schmidt read a statement on bargaining with the TEA. The district and TEA bargaining teams have had four bargaining sessions since April 16 and a total of 15 sessions to date, with recent meetings focused on the school calendar and significant progress reported. The administration seeks a competitive compensation package that is sustainable over time, and both parties agree Troy's pay schedule should be aligned and among the tops in Michigan. The statement attributed an elongated bargaining cycle statewide to several formerly prohibited topics such as evaluation and teacher placement. The Troy School District will utilize a portion of its fund balance to settle the contract. Both parties agreed to bring in a Michigan Employment Relations Commission (MERC) mediator; the district's two most recent contracts were also settled with the help of an independent mediator. The first mediation session was set for Wednesday, May 22, with additional sessions planned as needed. Schmidt stated the district cannot afford to replicate the financial situation in Ann Arbor, with 141 layoffs and $21 million in cuts, and called for more state funding for public education.

**Public communication (non-agenda items)**
Speakers were: Marianna Perakis, TSD parent, on the status of teacher contract negotiations and a fair and equitable settlement; Dr. Audra Melton, former TSD administrator and current parent, in support of TSD teachers, who announced her candidacy for the school board; Mrs. Stephanie Zendler, former TSD administrator and current parent, likewise announcing her candidacy; Mr. Alex Karpowitsch, Troy community member, on the state of negotiations and district climate, announcing his candidacy; Mr. Nik Didocha, TSD graduate; Ms. Karen Hunt, TSD parent, requesting a list of transition resources for special education students graduating out of the program because Project Search has only 8 spots open; Reagan Feld, a junior at Troy High School; Mrs. Emily Byrne, parent and teacher; Ms. Heather Kelly, teacher; Mrs. Pat Grandy, TSD preschool teacher, noting only 16 days left of school; Mrs. Angela Clemence, teacher; Mrs. Melissa Batts, teacher; Mr. Steve Dunneback, para-educator; Mr. Andrew Shipp, teacher; Mr. Rob Holder, teacher; Ms. Jennifer Bell, teacher; Mrs. Lara Cornish; and Mr. Jason Cichowicz, TEA president.

**Student representative reports**
Teagan Pruitt reported for Troy College and Career High School, Nurayda Albeez for International Academy-East, Marlien William, a senior, for Athens High School, and Jayla Turner for Troy High School, each covering year-end activities.

**Oakland Schools Board of Education election**
Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Anne, the Board adopted a resolution reciting Public Act 419 of 2004, which amended election procedures for Intermediate School Districts electing board members at a meeting of representatives from constituent district school boards, requires a constituent board to designate its representative and identify the supported candidate by resolution adopted not earlier than 21 days prior to the election, and requires consideration at not less than one public meeting; the Board previously considered the resolution at an open meeting under the Open Meetings Act on May 21, 2024. The Board designated Matt Haupt as its representative and Vital Anne as alternate to the 2024 electoral body for the Oakland Schools Intermediate School District Board of Education, supported candidates Carol Finkelstein and Marc Katz for the two positions, each for a term of six years ending June 30, 2030, and directed Haupt to vote for them at least on the first ballot at the June 3, 2024 election. Yes: 7, No: 0.

**Board comments, workshop date change and adjournment**
Board members shared appreciation of teachers and a desire to reach a contract agreement soon. Citing conflicts in board member calendars, it was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Anne that the June 4 Board of Education Workshop be rescheduled to Thursday, June 6 beginning at 6:00 p.m. Yes: 7, No: 0. Mr. Schmidt announced the next Board Workshop for Thursday, June 6 at 6:00 p.m. in the Administration Building and the next Board Meeting for Thursday, June 20 at 7:00 p.m. in the Services Building. The meeting adjourned at 9:49 p.m.

Meeting and Attendance
Regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education, October 14, 2025, held at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan. Vice President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mrs. Anne, Board members Alic, Haupt, Melton, Potts, and Zendler were present; Philippart was absent for all recorded votes. Superintendent Machesky attended along with administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Zawislak, Cottone, Vasovski, and Trudel. Approximately 12 members of the audience were present. The meeting adjourned at 8:06 p.m. Minutes were submitted by Emina Alic, Secretary, Troy Board of Education (notation EA/jh).

Recognitions
The agenda opened with a TSD Mission Moment and presentation of the Apple Distinguished School Award to Troy Union Elementary and Larson Middle School, a designation held by fewer than a thousand schools worldwide.

Resolutions Adopted
- Learning Disabilities Awareness Month, October 2025: moved by Dr. Melton, supported by Mr. Haupt, noting that 1 in 5 individuals have a learning disability and joining Governor Gretchen Whitmer in commemorating October 2025 as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.
- Principal Appreciation Month: moved by Mrs. Zendler, supported by Mrs. Alic, recognizing October as Principal Appreciation Month in Troy. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.
- 2026 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists: moved by Mr. Haupt, supported by Mrs. Zendler, honoring fifty-seven Troy students. More than one million students from some 21,000 high schools entered the program nationally and approximately 16,000 seniors were selected as semifinalists, by scoring in the top one and one-half percent on the PSAT with comparable SAT scores. A reception was set for November 13th. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

Consent Agenda
Moved by Mr. Haupt, supported by Mrs. Alic, approving items A through D: minutes of the September 2, 2025 Board Workshop; minutes of the September 16, 2025 Board Meeting; Treasurer's Report for August 2025; and second reading and adoption of Board Policy Revisions. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

Personnel
Moved by Mrs. Potts, supported by Mr. Haupt, that the Board issue a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Mr. Saso Vasovski, beginning duties as Technology Director on October 15, 2025.
