Official minutes of the regular meeting of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, held October 14, 2025 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. The minutes carry the notation EA/jh and are signed respectfully submitted by Emina Alic, Secretary, Troy Board of Education.

CALL TO ORDER AND ATTENDANCE
Vice President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mrs. Anne, Board members present were Alic, Haupt, Melton, Potts, and Zendler. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Zawislak, Cottone, Vasovski, and Trudel. There were approximately 12 members of the audience. Board member Philippart was recorded absent on every roll call vote of the evening.

RECOGNITION - TSD MISSION MOMENT / APPLE DISTINGUISHED SCHOOLS AWARD
The Board recognized two schools for earning designation as Apple Distinguished Schools, described as a recognition awarded to schools that are centers of innovation, leadership, and educational excellence, demonstrating a clear vision for learning with technology, a culture that supports continuous innovation, and compelling evidence of academic achievement and student engagement. Fewer than a thousand schools worldwide have earned the distinction. The Apple Distinguished School Award was presented to Troy Union Elementary and Larson Middle School, with congratulations to principals, staff, and students.

RECOGNITION - LEARNING DISABILITIES AWARENESS MONTH, OCTOBER 2025
The introduction noted that several national associations dedicated to supporting individuals with learning differences have designated October as a month of awareness, including organizations focused on Dyslexia, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), and Down Syndrome; that the U.S. Department of Education has recognized October as Learning Disabilities / Dyslexia / ADHD / Down Syndrome Awareness Month; and that Governor Whitmer declared October as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan. It was moved by Dr. Melton and supported by Mr. Haupt to adopt the resolution. The whereas clauses state that the term learning disabilities refers to differences in how brains work, which may affect the acquisition, organization, retention, understanding, or use of verbal or nonverbal information; that learning disabilities range in severity and may impact the acquisition and use of oral language, reading, written language, and mathematics; that 1 in 5 individuals have a learning disability; that learning disabilities may co-exist with other disabilities and conditions and can affect individuals regardless of race, gender, sexual orientation, or other intersecting factors; that disabilities are a natural part of human diversity though individuals may face discrimination or marginalization; that every person has strengths; that specialized assessments and interventions involving home, school, community, and workplace settings can significantly enhance quality of life; that appropriate supports and services allow individuals to achieve their goals and participate fully in society; and that understanding and celebrating unique abilities is essential to an inclusive society embracing the strengths of all Michigan residents. The resolving clause has the Troy School District Board of Education join Governor Gretchen Whitmer in commemorating October 2025 as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart. Resolution adopted.

RECOGNITION - 2025 PRINCIPALS APPRECIATION MONTH
The introduction noted that October has traditionally been celebrated statewide as Principal Appreciation Month in recognition of building-level educational leaders. It was moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Alic. The whereas clauses cite that energetic and inspiring school leadership is essential if teachers, schools, and districts are to ensure all Troy students are college and career ready; that K-12 principals play a vital role in student success and act as liaison between school and community; that Troy School District principals are dedicated, quality educational professionals committed to sound leadership and guidance; and that the district joins educators, parents, and students throughout Michigan to raise awareness of educational leadership. The resolution officially recognizes October as Principal Appreciation Month in Troy. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart. Resolution adopted.

RECOGNITION - 2026 NATIONAL MERIT SCHOLARSHIP SEMIFINALISTS
The narrative states that more than one million students nationwide from some 21,000 high schools entered the National Merit Scholarship Program and approximately 16,000 seniors were selected as semifinalists. Troy's fifty-seven semifinalists were named: Hasmita Anil Kumar, Fatima Ateeq, Matthew Batke, Shrish Bhandarkar, Mason Chiew, Sumehra Darafzin, Aarush Das, Arnav Dighrasker, William Dong, Lana Fargaly, Atul Ganesh, Vihaan Gehlaut, Aryan Goswami, Aaroosh Guduguntla, Anusha Gupta, Yeonjoon Ha, Kashifah Hossain, Aafla Ibraheem, Raghav Karur, Ryeo-Won Kim, Shlagha Kompelli, Aarush Kulkarni, Iniya Kumar, Ria Lattupalli, Phuong Le, Seungheon Lee, Sophia Li, Abigail Losey, Jing-Yi Ma, Jeeva Maridass, Joel Matthew, Aasrith Modem, Michael Molenda, Pratyush Neelakantan, Sameer Pai, Aayushi Parab, Kanghee Park, Sanjana Prabhu, Kristin Prakash, Akshiithi Prithiviraj, Tejaaswin Raja, Hansini Ramini, Sahas Ravoor, Ashwin Shrivastav, Divya Sovani, Chinmay Sujith Nair, Saanvi Thippireddy, Julia Triculescu, Yunis Turk, Matthew Vijayasegar, Akein Weerakoon, Anthony Wu, Casey Xin, Jonathan Xu, Alice Yang, Angela Zhang, and Eric Zhou. Copies of the resolution were to be presented to the students at a reception on November 13th. It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Zendler. The resolution notes that National Merit students reach semifinalist status by scoring in the top one and one-half percent on the National Preliminary Scholastic Aptitude Test (PSAT) and earning comparable scores on the Scholastic Aptitude Test (SAT). Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart. Resolution adopted.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS; PUBLIC COMMUNICATION ON AGENDA ITEMS
Both were recorded as None.

GENERAL - CONSENT AGENDA
It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Alic that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B, C, and D on the consent agenda: minutes of the September 2, 2025 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the September 16, 2025 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report - August 2025; and Second Reading and Adoption - Board Policy Revisions. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

PERSONNEL - ADMINISTRATIVE APPOINTMENT, DIRECTOR OF TECHNOLOGY
It was moved by Mrs. Potts and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Board of Education issue a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Mr. Saso Vasovski, who will begin his duties as Technology Director on October 15, 2025. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Potts that the furniture purchase for the Administration Building for an amount not to exceed $300,000 through pre-existing bid contracts (consortiums) be approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Bond Fund. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

Purpose and Framing
Presented to the TSD Board of Education in November 2025 under the title "Pieces of One Troy: Building Belonging Through Data and Action." Stated purposes: student performance on state assessments and how performance has changed over time; district-by-district performance; performance gaps between student groups; and areas of focus and celebrations. The deck notes that state assessments are summative snapshots, one part of a balanced assessment system, useful to policy and decision makers for identifying schools, groups, and students for support, and are not designed to be diagnostic or drive day-to-day teaching and learning.

County comparison bars for grades 3-7 show 71%, 70%, 67%, 66%, 66%, and 62% in ELA and 71%, 70%, 68%, 68%, and 65% in math.

PSAT 8 and SAT 11
ELA: 84.2% grade 8 and 77.3% grade 11 in 2024; 83.5% and 79.3% in 2025. Math: 64.3% grade 8 and 59.5% grade 11 in 2024; 64.3% and 60.7% in 2025. Eighth grade ELA over time for TSD: 87.1%, 81.0%, 85.6%, 84.2%, 83.5% across SY 19 through SY 25, versus Oakland 72.5%, 69.5%, 71.4%, 74.4%, 74.5% and statewide 61.9%, 59.7%, 59.7%, 64.5%, 65.3%. Eighth grade math TSD: 75.1%, 67.5%, 69.1%, 64.3%, 64.3%; Oakland 55.1%, 47.6%, 49.0%, 45.9%, 42.4%; statewide 41.4%, 36.2%, 36.3%, 32.6%, 30.4%. Eleventh grade ELA TSD: 82.9%, 75.3%, 76.9%, 77.3%, 79.3%; math TSD: 73.6%, 61.6%, 61.3%, 59.5%, 60.7%.

M-STEP Science and Social Studies (Grades 5, 8, 11)
Science 2025: 61.1%, 65.3%, 50.2%; 2024: 62.6%, 64.4%, 46.3%. Social studies 2025: 51.0%, 68.1%, 56.9%; 2024: 34.9%, 47.5%, 46.6%.

Gap Analysis
The deck frames the performance gap, also called an opportunity gap, for students with disabilities, economically disadvantaged students, and English learners. Multi-Tiered System of Support actions include coherence building, Professional Learning Communities at all schools, universal supports, progress monitoring for students on a plan, a district handbook, interventions taught by content-strong teachers, and a focus on Tier 1 instruction. Special education is called the largest and most persistent achievement gap; economically disadvantaged students outperform state and county peers though fewer than half meet proficiency; English learners perform strongly against county and state peers with a gap remaining.

Celebrations
Third grade ranked first in the county in both ELA and math, with a spring 2025 third grade ELA proficiency chart topped at 67.9%. Troy Public Schools ranked fourth statewide with 108 Seals of Biliteracy in 2024-25. AP students scoring 3 or higher rose across five years to 89.0% in 2024-25, and AP English 11 enrollment reached 45.3% of eleventh graders in 2025-2026. Middle school honors math enrollment was reported at 22% of grades 6-8 in both 24/25 and 25/26.

The deck states that historically districts have struggled to raise the performance of students with disabilities, economically disadvantaged students, and English learners on par with countywide and statewide rates of performance, commonly known as the performance gap, and that some refer to this as an opportunity gap wherein certain student groups have not been afforded adequate opportunities and support to perform on par with statewide and countywide peers.

MULTI-TIERED SYSTEM OF SUPPORT
Listed elements: district commitment to building coherence, in process; focus on systems that support all students; commitment to Professional Learning Communities, in process at all schools; universal supports; review of progress monitoring for any student on a plan; development of a district handbook; interventions taught by content strong teachers; and focus on Tier 1 instruction.

Official minutes of the Troy Board of Education regular meeting held Tuesday, March 21, 2023, at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, and Wilson were present; Dr. Philippart was absent. Assistant Superintendent Griffor was sitting in for Superintendent Machesky, who was in Washington, DC, advocating for special education programs. Administrators present were Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Haezebrouck, House, Detmer, Zawislak, Cross, Harris, Melton, and West. There were approximately 185 members of the audience. The minutes are signed by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the typist reference GH/jh.

RECOGNITION. President Schmidt changed the order of the Recognition items on the agenda. The first recognition was the Student Spotlight, in which students from the Creative Guild are recognized for creative achievements in TSD. The Board welcomed two seniors, Sophia Keil from Athens and Sonia Puri from Troy High. Assistant Superintendent Griffor invited Thomas Butcher to share about the students' work; the two students discussed their podcast productions and answered questions from Board members.

The Board then honored Leonard Elementary School and Athens High School for receiving the State School of Character Award, and Martell Elementary and Troy High for being named Emerging Schools of Character. Athens High School had earned the State School of Character designation during the height of the pandemic in 2021, but the district did not have a chance to honor the school at that time because meetings were not being held in person. Leonard was one of only 73 schools across the nation awarded the honor this year, with both Martell and Troy High recognized in 2023 as Emerging Schools. Character.org certifies schools and districts that embed character into all aspects of school life; the framework includes creating a caring school community, giving students opportunities to practice and reflect on their character strengths, and engaging families and communities as partners. Ms. Lori Soifer, Director of Schools of Character, spoke about each school and presented representatives from all four buildings with a certificate.

A Mission Moment recognized Baker Middle School 7th grade student Aryan Khedkar, who won the Oakland Schools' Scripps Regional Spelling Bee on Saturday, March 4th, at Oakland University. Assistant Superintendent DiPilato invited Mr. Jonathan Cross, Principal at Baker Middle School, to introduce Aryan and discuss the achievement; Aryan answered questions from Board members and shared tips on how to win a spelling bee.

A second Mission Moment recognized Baker classroom teacher Luchi Cacaj. Over the last 6 years the TSD middle school English Language Arts team has worked to improve reading and writing opportunities for students through partnerships with Teacher's College at Columbia University, implementing a new curriculum, embracing the workshop model, and forming partnerships within and across schools. Assistant Superintendent DiPilato asked Baker Principal Jonathan Cross to describe the opportunities provided in Mrs. Cacaj's classroom; Mr. Cross shared that Paula Tutman from Channel 4 News was so impressed with the classroom that she returned to do a story on it. Mrs. Cacaj received congratulations from the Board.

ADDITIONS & DELETIONS: None. PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (AGENDA ITEMS): None.

GENERAL - CONSENT AGENDA, item 23-021. It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Troy Board of Education take action to approve items A, B, C, D, and E on the consent agenda: Minutes of the February 7, 2023, Board of Education Workshop; Minutes of the February 14, 2023, Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report - January 2023; Furniture Pilot Purchase; and Adult Ed Laptops. The vote was Yes: 6, No: 0, Absent: Philippart.

PERSONNEL: None.

CURRICULUM. REPORT: Fielding/Middle School Design Update. Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent of Secondary Instruction, shared a brief PowerPoint and provided an update on the Fielding/Middle School Design project, including feedback from students and teachers about likes and dislikes, challenges and wants. She discussed teaching strategies, effective ways to learn, how to support 21st-Century learners, and how to evolve for the new middle schools' futures.

Early Middle College, item 23-022. The Troy School District is seeking to provide broad, rich, and robust course offerings that inspire, are intellectually challenging, and open more opportunities to future learning. The objective of the Early Middle College (EMC) is to offer students entering Grade 9 a five-year program that combines high school coursework with the first two years of college, culminating in attainment of a high school diploma and at least one of the five EMC on-track graduate outcomes, at no cost to the student or parents. The EMC will be located at Lawrence Technological University (LTU) and will utilize the resources of both LTU and TSD for students admitted to the program. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mrs. Alic that the Troy Board of Education approve the proposed Early Middle College partnership with Lawrence Technological University, with program elements to be developed beginning in the 2023/2024 school year. The vote was Yes: 6, No: 0, Absent: Philippart.

REPORT: Elementary Math. Natalie Haezebrouck, Director of Teaching & Learning, and Julia Alder, Curriculum & Instruction Specialist for PreK-5 Math, provided a brief report on the new elementary math program proposed to the Board. Bridges in Mathematics 2nd edition and Number Corner 3rd edition, by The Math Learning Center, for Grades K-5, were recommended for adoption. There was discussion among Board members regarding the new math program, which was piloted by 90 TSD teachers. Board members had the opportunity to visit classrooms in elementary buildings to witness the new student learning process and commented on how impressed they were seeing students' enthusiasm, excitement, and joy in doing math. It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mrs. Anne that the recommended mathematics materials for the elementary level be approved for the 2023-2024 school year. The vote was Yes: 6, No: 0, Absent: Philippart.

BUSINESS: None.

Reports from Student Representatives to the Board: Yara Mashal, student representative for International Academy-East, reported on events and activities at her school. Sara Ali, student representative for Athens High School, reported on events and activities at Athens. Nish Palepu, student representative for Troy High School, reported on events and activities at his school. Alexi Papadelis, student representative for Troy College and Career High School, was absent, but Mr. Schmidt shared that TCCHS held a Career Fair at the Troy Learning Center that day and that it was very successful and well-attended.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (NON-AGENDA ITEMS). Mr. Schmidt explained the guidelines for public comment and informed the audience that, due to the number of requests submitted to address the Board, each person would have only one minute to speak, which would allow a full hour of public comment. Every speaker addressed the removal of the honors program and supported keeping it as an option for students. Speakers were: Ms. Justine Perakis, TSD parent; Mrs. Bhargavi Kakasani, TSD parent; Mr. John Rollinger, TSD parent; Ms. Nitali Gandhi, TSD parent; Shivani Angadi, sophomore at Troy High School; George Perakis, senior at Troy High School; Ms. Vicki Mu, senior at Troy High School; Ray Zhang, senior at Troy High School; Mr. Yumin Sheng, TSD parent; Hengguang Li, TSD parent; Mr. Anupam Sule, TSD parent; Mrs. Peggy Chinoski, parent of TSD graduates; Jacqui Pursel, TSD parent; Mrs. Stella Kallis, TSD parent; Mr. Ollie Apahidean, TSD parent; Rp. Rocky Raczkowski, TSD parent; Ms. Shanshan Qiu, TSD parent; Ruihua Han, TSD parent; Fabrice Smielianskas, TSD parent; Mr. Bassam Salem, TSD parent; Mrs. Tracy Owens, TSD parent; Mrs. Disha Chablani, TSD parent; Arya Prasad, senior at Troy High School; Mrs. Shilpa Patel, TSD parent; Meaghan Kovacs, TSD parent; Ms. Katherina Mandia, junior at Troy High School; Mr. Krish Gupta, senior at Troy High School; Nikki Snyder, Dexter resident and member of the state board of education; Cynthia Lin, TSD parent; Mrs. Bo Yang, TSD parent; Aksheet Dutta, senior at Troy High School; Mr. Dale Murrish, former TSD parent; Dr. Changgong Zhou, TSD parent; the mother of Boulan Park Middle School student Ethan Wang; Helen Xu, TSD parent; Mr. Steven Sheng, TSD parent; and Weilong Hao, TSD parent.

OTHER - Portrait of a Graduate. Mr. Schmidt provided a brief update on the conversations and information gathering sessions being held with students throughout the district, noting that the common themes students are asking for align with the District's strategic plan and that good components are being gathered for building the portrait of a graduate.

Board Member Comments. Mr. Haupt thanked teachers for organizing events and reading opportunities for March is Reading Month. Mrs. Anne said she attended most of the student sessions for Portrait of a Graduate discussions and was impressed by what students shared; she noted the Board does not take curriculum changes lightly. Mrs. Alic spoke about how each student is met where they are academically to reach their highest potential, and announced that Ramadan starts on Thursday. Mr. Hauff discussed the Troy Times News supplement and his pride in students' leadership roles. Dr. Wilson spoke about changes to the curriculum program and the District's commitment to meeting students where they are; she congratulated Troy High for its recent performance of Curtains and the outstanding support staff winner and nominees. Ms. Griffor discussed the furniture pilot, shared that students have been invited to work with the team designing playgrounds, thanked parents for attending Parent/Teacher Conferences, and announced the next Board Workshop for April 4th and the regular meeting for April 18th. Mr. Schmidt said most students he spoke with would like longer deadlines to go in depth on projects rather than short deadlines, and enjoy experimentation as an exciting way to learn; he also spoke about the consideration given to every curriculum decision.

ADJOURNMENT. The meeting adjourned at 9:52 p.m.

Official minutes of the regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, held November 19, 2024, at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, and Wilson were present; Dr. Philippart was absent. RECOGNITION / MISSION MOMENT — NATIONAL BLUE RIBBON AWARD, HAMILTON ELEMENTARY SCHOOL. The Board recognized Hamilton Elementary School for its designation as a National Blue-Ribbon School, an award honoring the school as one of the very best schools in the United States. Hamilton was recognized by U.S. Secretary of Education Miguel Cardona at a ceremony in Washington, D.C. on November 7th and 8th. Only 356 schools from around the country were chosen for this honor in 2024. The minutes note that the award affirms the hard work of students, staff, parents, and the Hamilton community, and quote Secretary Cardona's press release statement that "The National Blue Ribbon Schools Award is a testament to the exceptional achievements of students and educators at each of these schools," that the 2024 National Blue Ribbon Schools are "raising the bar for our nation's students, serving as models for effective teaching and intentional collaboration in their schools and communities," and calling on the country to look to these schools for inspiration "as we champion education as the foundation of a brighter future for every child."

RECOGNITION — 2024 MICHIGAN SCHOOL PUBLIC RELATIONS ASSOCIATION (MSPRA) AWARDS. The Board recognized the Troy School District Communications Department and invited team members forward. The Communications team received 15 Michigan School and Public Relations Association (MSPRA) awards, the most the team has ever received. Staff thanked by name were Melissa Verduyn, Thomas Butcher, Adam Burns, Linda Alfonso, Patrice Rowbal, and newest team member Alison Hendry. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Presentation to the Troy Board of Education workshop of December 9, 2025 recommending adoption of new AP Spanish and AP French resources from Vista Higher Learning. The current materials, Abriendo Paso (2014) for AP Spanish and T'es Branche (2014) for AP French, were adopted in 2017, lack current cultural content and AP test preparation, and in the French case are a Level 4 textbook rather than an AP text. Vista was selected over Wayside and Klett because its rigor matches the AP exam, its authors are College Board trainers, and it holds 80 percent of the AP World Languages market share.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
Purpose
AP Spanish and AP French resource adoption, presented at the 12/9/25 Board Workshop of the Troy School District.

Context and Rationale
The World Language sequence runs Level 1 through Level 5 AP, and the AP exams are written at the intermediate high and advanced levels. The TSD World Languages vision describes learners who can communicate in an ever-expanding global community, discover and experience the heritage of another culture, become resilient risk-takers able to adapt to new environments, improve memory and problem-solving skills, enhance college applications and professional marketability, and open themselves to world travel. AP World Language and Culture is described as equivalent to an intermediate-level college course, in which students apply interpersonal, interpretive and presentational modes of communication while exploring family and communities, personal and public identities, beauty and aesthetics, science and technology, contemporary life, and global challenges. The exam assesses both language and culture, but the resources adopted in 2017 do not represent current culture.

Current State
World Languages operates on a 7-year adoption cycle. Under the PLC structure, Troy AP World Language teachers want a common resource to build cohesion among programs. Current resources are Abriendo Paso (2014) for AP Spanish, with outdated readings that are not updated, no interpersonal speaking practice and no AP test prep; and T'es Branche (2014) for AP French, which is a Level 4 textbook with outdated readings and listening resources. Teachers currently pull materials from a wide variety of sources, some at their own cost.

Selection Process
Guided by Jen Howe, Oakland Schools Heritage and World Language Consultant. Timeline: exploration of resources during the 24-25 school year; 8/11 leadership planning; 8/20 department kickoff and visioning; 10/2 and 10/7 rubric creation and vendor presentations; 10/20 pilot planning; 11/11 and 11/18 PLC planning and check-ins; 12/2 pilot feedback and synthesis.

Vendors Considered
| Vendor | Assessment |
| --- | --- |
| Wayside | French and Spanish; relatable content with a variety of authentic resources, but does not represent the rigor of the AP assessment and is only a textbook without assessment practice |
| Klett | No AP resource for French; Spanish has many authentic resources and AP practice but does not represent AP rigor, has fewer resources than Vista, and less user-friendly technology |
| Vista Higher Learning | French and Spanish; matches the rigor of the AP exam, culturally relevant resources and a large resource bank; resources may need scaffolding at the start of the year |

Recommended Resource
Vista Higher Learning. Its authors are also College Board trainers, and Vista holds 80 percent of the AP World Languages market share. The 26-27 AP exam will be updated; Vista agreed to provide an updated crosswalk for launching the 26-27 school year and, when it updates its textbooks, to provide updated electronic and physical resources free of cost. The district will bank its professional learning credit to support the change in August. Sample features shown included AP French culturally relevant resources with student supports, an AP Spanish cultural comparison in which a student named Maya contrasts the role of grandparents in the United States and El Salvador, and AP Spanish simulated conversations, a free response task; interpersonal communication practice supports the Free Response AP tasks, which are 50 percent of the exam.

Stakeholder Support and Timeline
Student quotations praised the online textbook for offering more listening and speaking resources, easier navigation, iPad access and speaking practice that built confidence for the heavily weighted speaking sections of the AP test. Student and caretaker surveys were referenced, followed by a financial request slide. Anticipated timeline: December, order placed; January, physical materials inventoried and pilot licenses extended into June; August, 7-year licenses begin and are rostered, with PD from Vista covering College Board changes.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Board workshop presentation titled AP Spanish and AP French Resource Adoption, delivered at the 12/9/25 Troy School District Board Workshop, proposing replacement of the district's AP world language instructional materials.

CONTEXT AND RATIONALE. The presentation situates AP within the district's world language sequence of Level 1, Level 2, Level 3, Level 4 and Level 5 AP, noting that the AP exams are written at the intermediate high and advanced levels. The TSD World Languages vision states that world language learners can communicate in an ever-expanding global community; discover and experience the rich heritage of another culture; become resilient risk-takers with a greater capacity to adapt to new environments; improve their memory and problem-solving skills for better overall academic performance; enhance their college applications and increase their professional marketability; and open themselves to opportunities for world travel. The AP World Languages vision is quoted as describing AP World Language and Culture as equivalent to an intermediate-level college course in which students cultivate their understanding of language and culture by applying interpersonal, interpretive and presentational modes of communication in real-life situations while exploring concepts related to family and communities, personal and public identities, beauty and aesthetics, science and technology, contemporary life, and global challenges. The presentation stresses that the exam assesses both language and culture, but that the resources adopted in 2017 do not have current culture represented.

CURRENT STATE. World Languages follows a 7-year adoption cycle. With the PLC structure in place, Troy AP World Language teachers desire a common resource to help build cohesion among programs. The current resources are Abriendo Paso (2014) for AP Spanish, criticized for outdated readings that have not been updated, no interpersonal speaking practice and no AP test prep; and T'es Branche (2014) for AP French, which is identified as a Level 4 textbook with outdated readings and listening resources that have not been updated. The stated current reality is that teachers are doing their best to pull resources from a wide variety of sources, some even at their own cost.

PROCESS OF RESOURCE SELECTION. Jen Howe, Oakland Schools Heritage and World Language Consultant, supported the process. The AP resources timeline was: 24-25 school year, exploration of resources; 8/11, leadership planning; 8/20, department kickoff and visioning; 10/2 and 10/7, rubric creation and vendor presentations; 10/20, pilot planning; 11/11 and 11/18, PLC planning and check-ins; and 12/2, pilot feedback and synthesis.

AP VENDORS CONSIDERED, PROS AND CONS. Wayside was evaluated for both French and Spanish; while the resource has relatable content for students with a variety of authentic resources, it does not represent the rigor of the AP assessment and is only a textbook without assessment practice. Klett has no AP resource for French; for Spanish, while the resource has many authentic resources and AP practice, it does not represent the rigor of the AP assessment, does not have the number of resources that Vista has, and its technology was less user friendly. Vista Higher Learning was evaluated for both French and Spanish and was found to match the rigor of the AP exam, providing meaningful, culturally relevant resources as well as a large resource bank; because of that rigor, resources may need to be scaffolded at the start of the year. Additional points favoring Vista: the authors of Vista are also College Board trainers; Vista has 80 percent of the AP World Languages market share; the 26-27 AP exam will be updated and Vista has agreed to provide an updated crosswalk for launching the 26-27 school year; when Vista updates its textbooks it will provide the district updated electronic and physical resources free of cost; and the district will bank its professional learning credit to support this change in August.

FEATURES OF THE RECOMMENDED TEXTS. Illustrative slides covered AP French culturally relevant resources, and AP French culturally relevant resources with student supports. For AP Spanish, a cultural comparison example was shown: on the AP test students must compare the country they are studying with the United States, and in the sample a student named Maya shares how the role of grandparents differs in the United States versus El Salvador. Another example showed AP Spanish simulated conversations, described as a free response task on the AP exam. The presentation notes that this is an example of interpersonal communication that fosters student confidence and practice for the Free Response AP tasks, which constitute 50 percent of the exam.

ADDITIONAL STAKEHOLDER SUPPORT. Two student quotations were included. One student said they like an online textbook because it has more resources such as listening and speaking, they can navigate the pages better and faster, and it is easier to have the textbook on an iPad. A second student said they have used the ebook many times in class and the variety of resources has been really helpful; that the hardest part of learning Spanish at this level is being able to speak their thoughts; that the ebook gave them speaking practice that already allowed them to feel more confident about their speaking abilities; and that the speaking sections of the AP test are huge, very important to the overall score and heavily weighted, so having these resources builds confidence in trying to get a good score. Slides for a Student Survey and a Caretaker Survey followed.

FINANCIAL REQUEST AND TIMELINE. A financial request section was included in the deck. The anticipated timeline moving forward is: December, order placed; January, physical materials inventoried and pilot licenses extended into June; August, 7-year licenses begin and are rostered, with professional development from Vista covering the College Board changes. The presentation closes with a questions slide.

ATHLETIC DEPARTMENT COMMUNICATION. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of February 14, 2023, held at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, called to order by President Schmidt at 7:00 p.m. before roughly 75 audience members and adjourned at 8:35 p.m. The Board recognized Fall 2022 All-State athletes, honored eight LitCon presenters, and adopted resolution 23-017 declaring February Principal Appreciation Month. Its most consequential action was resolution 23-020 awarding the Site Work Paving Program bid to Nagle Paving, at an amount printed as $2,2,46,617.00 inclusive of a 6% contingency, payable from the Building Site and Sinking Fund and Capital Projects Fund.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Meeting** \ Regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education, February 14, 2023, at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m.; the meeting adjourned at 8:35 p.m. Minutes submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary (GH/jh).

**Attendance** \ In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart and Wilson were present. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Fulcher, Haezebrouck and West. Approximately 75 members of the audience attended.

**Recognitions** \ Mr. Tim Fulcher, Director of Athletics, recognized Fall 2022 All-State athletes: Daniel Watkins, Carter Cusmano, John Palomino and Nick Worrell (Boys' Soccer); Olivia Hemmila, Ava Weeks and Riley Hayden (Girls' Golf); Derek Blackwell, Derrick Kim, Nish Palepu, Srihari Ananthalwan and Rushil Kagithala (Boys' Tennis); Vishvaa Ravishankar (Boys' Cross Country); and Darius Whiteside (Boys' Football). The Mission Moment honored the 8 teachers who represented the District at LitCon, the National Reading Recovery/Early Literacy Conference: Karen Bush and Holly Gordon, Ashley Pellosmaa and Sue Reid of Wattles, and classroom teachers Sara Provost, Alyssa Favot, Kristen Marcaccio and Erin Miller.

**Actions**

| No. | Item | Mover / Support | Vote |
|---|---|---|---|
| 23-017 | Resolution recognizing February as Principal Appreciation Month | Mrs. Anne / Dr. Wilson | Yes 7, No 0 |
| 23-018 | Consent agenda items A-F | Mr. Hauff / Mrs. Alic | Yes 7, No 0 |
| 23-019 | Adoption of the 2023-2024 High School Course Description Book | Dr. Wilson / Mrs. Anne | Yes 7, No 0 |

Official minutes of the Troy Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, for the Board Meeting of February 14, 2023, held at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present were Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Fulcher, Haezebrouck and West. There were approximately 75 members of the audience.

**Recognition - All-State Athletes Fall 2022.** Mr. Tim Fulcher, Director of Athletics, recognized students named All-State Athletes in their respective sports: Daniel Watkins (Boys' Soccer), Olivia Hemmila (Girls' Golf), Ava Weeks (Girls' Golf), Carter Cusmano (Boys' Soccer), John Palomino (Boys' Soccer), Nick Worrell (Boys' Soccer), Derek Blackwell (Boys' Tennis), Derrick Kim (Boys' Tennis), Nish Palepu (Boys' Tennis), Srihari Ananthalwan (Boys' Tennis), Rushil Kagithala (Boys' Tennis), Vishvaa Ravishankar (Boys' Cross Country), Darius Whiteside (Boys' Football) and Riley Hayden (Girls' Golf). The students came up to receive a certificate and congratulations from the Board.

**TSD Mission Moment - National LitCon Conference Presenters.** The Board honored the 8 teachers who represented the Troy School District at LitCon, the National Reading Recovery/Early Literacy Conference, at the end of January. Literacy specialists Karen Bush and Holly Gordon presented "How Intentional Coaching Leads to Transformation." Literacy specialist Ashley Pellosmaa and ELD specialist Sue Reid, from Wattles, presented ways to collaborate in order to accelerate the multilingual learner in literacy. Classroom teachers Sara Provost, Alyssa Favot, Kristen Marcaccio and Erin Miller presented on how a deeper understanding of literacy processing theory helped them provide more responsive instruction in the classroom.

**Principal Appreciation Month - Resolution 23-017.** Noting that February has traditionally been celebrated statewide as Principal Appreciation Month, it was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Wilson to adopt a resolution reciting that energetic and inspiring school leadership is essential if teachers, schools and districts are to ensure that all Troy students are college and career ready; that K-12 school principals play a vital role in student success and act as liaison between the school and the community it serves; that Troy School District principals are dedicated, quality educational professionals; and that during this month the District joins educators, parents and students throughout Michigan to raise awareness of the importance of educational leadership. The resolution officially recognizes February as Principal Appreciation Month in Troy. Vote: Yes 7, No 0. Mr. Schmidt offered a special thanks to the principals for their help in passing the bond and said the Board has appreciated their effort and support over the past six months.

**Additions & Deletions.** None. Mr. Schmidt moved the TCCHS student representative report up because Alexi had to leave early due to another obligation; Alexi Papadelis, student representative for Troy College and Career High School, shared a report on events and activities at her school.

**Public Communication (Agenda Items).** President Schmidt shared a statement providing the structure for the evening's public participation in compliance with the Open Meetings Act and reviewed the guidelines for public comment. Mrs. Tracy Owens, TSD parent, addressed the Board about the proposed changes to the High School Course Catalogue and the impact they will have on students. Mrs. Eleni Dilis, TSD parent, addressed the Board about honors classes being taken away and wanted parents to have a chance to share their thoughts on it.

**General - Consent Agenda, Resolution 23-018.** It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Alic that the Board approve items A, B, C, D, E and F on the consent agenda: minutes of the January 10, 2023 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the January 17, 2023 Board of Education Organizational & Regular Meeting; Treasurer's Report - December 2022; Schools Closed to Open Enrollment; Schools of Choice 105 & 105c; and OCSBA Legislative Priorities and Bylaw Amendments. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Personnel.** None.

**Curriculum - High School Course Catalogue 2023-2024.** Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent of Secondary Instruction, and Natalie Haezebrouck, Director of Teaching & Learning, shared a PowerPoint presentation and reported on the recommended changes to the 2023-2024 school year High School Course Catalogue. Resolution 23-019, moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mrs. Anne, resolved that the Board approves the proposed changes and adopts the 2023-2024 High School Course Description Book as presented. Vote: Yes 7, No 0. Board discussion addressed the changes made to the catalogue and the high school courses offered, how different teaching is today from the old way of teaching, a style that allows students to own their learning, the importance of demonstrating the workshop model of teaching, changes in ELA and Chemistry courses, team sports, and that all physical education classes are co-ed.

**Business - Site Work Paving Projects, Resolution 23-020.** It was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mr. Haupt that the bid for the Site Work Paving Program be awarded to Nagle Paving in the amount printed in the minutes as $2,2,46,617.00 (rendered with an extra comma in the source), inclusive of a 6% contingency, and that the amount be approved as an expenditure of the Building Site and Sinking Fund and Capital Projects Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Reports from Student Representatives to the Board.** Nish Palepu, student representative for Troy High School; Sara Ali, student representative for Athens High School; and Yara Mashal, student representative for International Academy-East, each shared reports on the events and activities at their schools.

**Public Communication (Non-Agenda Items).** None. **Other.** None.

**Board Member Comments.** Dr. Philippart congratulated and thanked the principals for their work and dedication to the District and said she is impressed with the charity weeks in the high schools and proud of the spirit in the community and the caring students show. Mr. Haupt also commented on the charity events and how hard the students work for such a good cause. Mrs. Anne congratulated the Teacher of the Year nominees and winners and shared that she attended the Advocacy Conference in Washington, DC to advocate for the District's schools and students. Mrs. Alic spoke about the tragedy at Michigan State University and the students from Oxford now attending MSU having to live through something like this again. Mr. Hauff shared that the TSD supplement in the Troy Times is out. Dr. Wilson also mentioned the tragedy at MSU, commended principals, teachers and students for advocating for kids who need help, and congratulated students for raising so much money during charity week. Dr. Machesky thanked Mrs. Alic and Dr. Wilson for their comments on the tragedy in East Lansing, reported that bond work in the District continues with design meetings happening on a daily basis, congratulated the Teacher of the Year winners and nominees and invited the community to watch the video on the District website, and announced that March is Reading Month with teachers looking for guest readers. Mr. Schmidt described attending the Advocacy Institute in Washington and the five main issues addressed with representatives: funding that had been promised to schools years ago, expanding free lunches, expanding Title 1 funding, staffing shortages, and expanding the pilot program for electric busses. He gave a shout out to Kerry Birmingham for the Troy Times insert and commented on the tragedy at MSU.

**Announcements and adjournment.** Mr. Schmidt announced that the next Board Workshop would be held March 7th at 6:00 p.m. at the Administration Building, the Board Winter Retreat on Saturday, March 11th at 9:00 a.m. at the Administration Building, and the next Board Meeting on March 21st at 7:00 p.m. at the Services Building. The meeting adjourned at 8:35 p.m. Minutes respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education (GH/jh).

**Item** — Agenda item 8.B., 24680 Troy School District-0625-AUD-Final, Board of Education meeting of November 18, 2025: the district's Annual Comprehensive Financial Report with Supplementary Information for the year ended June 30, 2025, prepared by the Business Office.

**Audit** — Plante & Moran, appointed by the Troy Board of Education for the 2024-2025 fiscal year, issued an unmodified opinion on the governmental activities, each major fund, and the aggregate remaining information. The auditor's Government Auditing Standards report on internal control and compliance is dated October 13, 2025. No findings or questioned costs for federal awards were reported for the year ended June 30, 2025. Federal awards supplemental information was issued under separate cover. The transmittal letter, dated October 13, 2025, is signed by Dan Trudel, CPA, Assistant Superintendent for Business Services, and Aurel Malutan, Director of Finance.

**Government-wide summary (in millions, per Management's Discussion and Analysis)**

| Current and other assets | $256.2 | $276.9 |
| Capital assets | 269.3 | 217.4 |
| Total assets | 525.5 | 494.3 |
| Deferred outflows | 71.1 | 101.4 |
| Total liabilities | 522.3 | 621.0 |

Total expenses were $200.3 million and total revenue $262.3 million, producing a $62.0 million increase in net position. Detailed statements report total expenses of $200,306,434, charges for services of $5,762,303, operating grants and contributions of $76,046,945, total general revenue of $180,461,987, a change in net position of $61,964,801, and an ending deficit of $(54,739,779).

**Funds** — Combined governmental fund balance was $177.6 million, a decrease of $51.9 million. The General Fund decreased by $3.1 million to $33.7 million, stated as 17.4 percent of 2025 general operating expenditures. Special revenue fund balance moved from $10.4 million to $10.0 million, with the Food Service Fund down $0.9 million, the Community Service Fund down $66 thousand, and the Troy School District Preschool Fund up $0.4 million. Debt service fund balances rose $1.4 million. The 2023 Capital Projects Fund spent $57.9 million on voter-approved construction and ended with $127.4 million; sinking fund millage collections were $5.1 million; capital project fund balances fell $49.7 million.

**Budget** — The final General Fund amendment was adopted in June 2025. Budgeted revenue was increased by $3.3 million, primarily state and federal sources, including roughly $5.0 million of Section 147a(4) MPSERS Reduced UAAL revenue. Actual General Fund revenue was $190,573,261 against a final budget of $194,857,883; actual expenditures were $193,633,993 against $198,648,733.

**Capital assets and debt** — Total capital assets were $502,829,646 less accumulated depreciation and amortization of $233,540,622, for $269,289,024 net. Additions were $63.1 million. General obligation bonds outstanding totaled $230,080,000 plus $21,275,050 of unamortized premium. Standard & Poor's affirmed an AA/Stable rating in January 2025. Remaining construction commitments were $32,677,915.

**MPSERS** — Net pension liability was $211,642,114 and the net OPEB asset $36,619,750, both measured as of September 30, 2024 at a 6.00 percent discount rate. Pension contributions for the year were $38,371,759 and OPEB contributions $3,410,390.

**Context** — Spring 2025 enrollment was 12,393; the 2025-2026 budget assumes 12,074 students and a $442 per pupil foundation allowance increase. The November 8, 2022 voter-approved bond totals $555 million.

DISTRICT PROFILE. The district enrolls more than 12,000 students in twelve elementary schools, four middle schools, two traditional and one non-traditional high school, and one International Academy. Troy covers just over 26.61 square miles, is the largest city in Oakland County and the 13th largest in Michigan, with a population of approximately 80,000, over 6,000 businesses with a market value over $12 billion, and more than 57 percent of residents holding a bachelor's degree or higher. Fourteen schools have received the National Blue Ribbon Award (Barnard, Bemis, Hamilton, Leonard, Martell, Schroeder, Troy Union, Wass, Wattles, Larson, Boulan Park, Athens, Troy High, and the International Academy). Athens High School, Troy High, and the International Academy were named among the top five percent of U.S. high schools by U.S. News and World Report; Athens and Troy High report graduation rates over 99 percent. Board recognitions listed include the Michigan Association of School Boards Visionary Leadership Award, ArtServe of Michigan School Board of the Year, a top-ten tech-savvy board designation from the Center for Digital Education, and the 2023/2024 MASB Standard of Excellence Award. The building inventory totals 448.74 acres and 2,185,181 square feet serving 12,393 students, with 128.30 acres of vacant property; entries include Athens High School (398,426 square feet, 1974, 1,457 students), Troy High School (343,207 square feet, 1992, 2,023), Troy College and Career High School (37,520 square feet, 200), Baker, Boulan, Larson and Smith middle schools, International Academy East (81,455 square feet, 541), the Preschool for Early 5's and ECP (72,000 square feet, 2019, 242), the Troy Center for Transitions (61), the Administration and Services buildings, the Transportation Building, and the Rankin warehouse.

ECONOMIC OUTLOOK. Enrollment as of Spring 2025 was 12,393; the 2025-2026 budget adopted in June 2025 estimates a September 2025 count of 12,074, with approximately 66.5 percent of total General Fund revenue coming from the foundation allowance and state sources. Legislation for 2025-2026 includes a foundation allowance increase of $442 per pupil, offset by reductions in other categorical funding. On November 8, 2022 voters approved a $555 million bond to be issued in three series over 6 years with projects planned for 10 to 12 years; the first series was issued in March 2023, and the district anticipates exhausting the 2013 voter-approved bond funds in the next fiscal year.

The Board recognized Troy High Colts who attended the Global Leadership Summit in Berlin, Germany during the prior summer. They were among 1,100 students from around the world studying water's impact in other European countries. During the summit, students were placed in teams and charged with solving a global problem related to the theme of water; using design thinking they ideated and created a prototype and delivered a one-minute pitch on the prototype to the judges. Communications Instructor and Global Leadership Summit Adviser Harriet Clark was invited to describe the competition and introduce her students, recognizing Ashley Carron, Anusha Gupta, Ava Fleming, Jake Baker, Josie Lido, Katerina Zak, Kate Bestul, Vivian Edoff, Nicole Gherase, Laith Hermiz, Nainika Jasti, Keira McComb, Shreyan Maini, Maya Saad, Neel Nagappala and Tia Tonelli.

Course Description Book, 2023-2024, Troy College and Career High School (TCCHS), Troy School District. Dr. Richard Machesky, Superintendent of Schools. Board item 5E; meeting date September 19, 2023.

**Nondiscrimination Policy (Revised August 2023)**
Cites Title IX of the Educational Amendments of 1972, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, and the Americans with Disabilities Act. Jordan M. Harris, J.D., Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, is named Title IX and Section 504/ADA Coordinator for employment and personnel matters; the District's Director of Special Education serves as Section 504/ADA Coordinator for handicapped and suspected handicapped students. Questions are directed to John Pagel, Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, Title IX and Section 504/ADA Coordinator.

**Credit Rules**
TCCHS students need 19.5 credits for a Troy School District diploma; a Troy High School or Athens High School diploma requires 22.5 credits. All TCCHS students must complete 8 semesters/4 years of high school and the 18 credits required by the Michigan Department of Education. The Inspire Online Program runs on the Edgenuity platform; the Intersect Online Program runs through the Pearson Connexus platform. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Course Description Book for 2023-2024, Troy College and Career High School (TCCHS), Troy School District, presented as board item 5E with a meeting date of September 19, 2023. The cover identifies Dr. Richard Machesky as Superintendent of Schools. The catalog opens with the district's Policy of Nondiscrimination, revised August 2023, then moves through credit rules, department course descriptions, online program course lists, Oakland Schools Technical Campus offerings, the antidiscrimination grievance procedure, and a graduation-requirement chart effective beginning with the Class of 2023.

**Nondiscrimination policy and coordinators.** The notice addressed to students, parents, and citizens of the Troy School District cites Title IX of the Educational Amendments of 1972, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, and the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Troy School District states it does not discriminate on the basis of sex or handicap in admission or access to, treatment or employment in, its programs and activities, and that it periodically reviews educational and employment programs for Title IX and Section 504/ADA compliance. A grievance procedure is available through any school office or the coordinator; a School District employee in a bargaining unit may instead use the grievance procedure in the collective bargaining agreement. In accordance with Federal regulations, the district has appointed Jordan M. Harris, J.D., Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, as Title IX and Section 504/ADA Coordinator for employment and personnel matters, and the District's Director of Special Education as Section 504/ADA Coordinator for handicapped and suspected handicapped students. Questions, suggestions, or concerns are directed to John Pagel, Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, Title IX and Section 504/ADA Coordinator, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, MI 48098-4799, (248)823-4000.

**School identification.** Troy College and Career High School is led by Mrs. Angela Milanov, Principal, at 1522 East Big Beaver Road, Troy, MI 48083, telephone 248.823.5156. A later page lists the Department of Teaching & Learning at 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098, 248.823.5221.

**Credit requirements and flexibility.** All students attending TCCHS must earn 19.5 credits to be eligible for a Troy School District high school diploma. Students seeking a diploma from Troy High School or Athens High School must meet the credit requirements in the THS and AHS course description book, totaling 22.5 credits. In alignment with the needs of alternative education students, TCCHS permits students with demonstrated need to deviate from the 19.5-credit requirement; any TCCHS student may request a meeting with a counselor or administrator about that option. All enrolled students must complete 8 semesters/4 years of high school and the 18 credits required by the Michigan Department of Education. Graduation Requirement Flexibility Options, updated 9.2015 under MCL 380.1278a and MCL 380.1278b, comprise: Personal Curriculum, allowing additional credits in some core academic areas in lieu of requirements in others; Physical Education Credit earned through athletics, extra-curricular activities, or a counselor-approved PE class; a World Language Requirement of 2.0 credits with flexibility for non-English heritage language proficiency, international study and residence, and substitution of Career & Technical Education or Visual & Performing or Applied Arts credits; and Career & Technical Education (CTE) Program Completion, whose credits may be exchanged on a 1:1 basis for required science or world language credits, or satisfy the Algebra 2 requirement when Algebra 2 content is embedded.

**Career Technical Education.** Woodworking Design & Fabrication 1, 2, and 3 each carry 1/2 credit per semester and each satisfies 1 credit of the math-related graduation requirement during the 12th grade year. Level 1 has no prerequisite and introduces designing, drawing, and manufacturing using CAD software, hand and power tools, power machines, and automation (CNC and 3D printing). Level 2 requires Woodworking Design 1 and emphasizes CAD design, CNC design and production, and advanced furniture and cabinet making. Level 3 requires Woodworking Design 2 and continues the curriculum with heavy industry influence.

**English Department.** Literature carries 1/2 credit per semester with 4 semesters required (2.0 credits total) and uses a competency-based skill framework across short stories, poetry, and novels, covering American literary eras, world literature, and forms of prose and verse. Informational Reading and Writing carries 1/2 credit per semester with 2 semesters required (1.0 credit total) and focuses on non-fiction, data mining, note taking, synthesis, summarizing, research, and position writing. Communications carries 1/2 credit per semester with 1 semester required and covers non-verbal, verbal, visual, written, and communal styles, elements of journalism, debate, and public speaking. Electives at 1 semester and 1/2 credit each include Creative Writing 1 (grades 10-12), Creative Writing 2 (prerequisite Creative Writing 1), Film and Literature, Literature of Suspense (authors named include Edgar Allan Poe, Mary Shelley, and Stephen King), Short Stories, Music Literature, and Science Fiction. Several electives require successful completion of freshmen year English. The Music Literature entry also carries text describing fundamental Pro Tools recording software concepts, original musical pieces, multi-track live audio, MIDI sequences, and virtual instruments.

**Fine Arts Department.** Offerings at 1 semester and 1/2 credit include Drawing 1; Advanced Drawing (prerequisite Drawing 1, with color as a focus); Painting 1 (water-soluble media); Advanced Painting (prerequisite Painting 1); Studio Art, with portfolio preparation as the goal and possible scheduling during Advanced Placement Art; Applied Arts and Design; Computer Graphics 1, teaching Photoshop alongside art history and theory; Principles of Photography 1, covering framing, composition, rule of thirds, light, texture, pattern lines, symmetry, depth of field, distance, perspective, culture, space, balance, color, and black and white photography; and Intro to Music Technology and Recording, using state-of-the-art studio gear and ProTools.

**Health Department.** Health is 1 semester, 1/2 credit, and is required for graduation. Topics include healthy lifestyles, violence, sexual harassment, nutrition, fitness and weight control (including steroids and eating disorders), alcohol and drug abuse, tobacco, human sexuality, birth control, and sexually transmitted diseases including HIV/AIDS. The course is taken online through the Edgenuity platform.

**Mathematics Department.** Business Math in Algebra A/B (Algebra 1 students) / Business Math A/B (Algebra 2 students) runs 4 semesters at 1/2 credit per semester; students operate an advanced fabrication lab business customizing textile products and manufacturing items of wood, metal, and/or plastic, with proceeds self-funding the venture and supporting community service or monetary gifts to local charities, and skill sets in sublimation, CNC operations, rapid prototyping, composite technologies, alternative energies, and automation robotics. Geometry by Design runs 2 semesters at 1/2 credit per semester and integrates geometry with building and construction trades. Personal Finance/Financial Well-Being runs 2 semesters at 1/2 credit per semester and is based on Michigan Personal Finance Competencies. Algebra 1 and Geometry each run 2 semesters at 1/2 credit per semester, with Algebra 1 a prerequisite for Geometry. Financial Management is 1 semester, 1/2 credit, satisfies 1/2 credit of the math-related graduation requirement, and includes a stock market game simulation and a budget challenge. School-Based Enterprise runs 2 semesters at 1/2 credit per semester, satisfies 1 credit of the math-related graduation requirement during the 12th grade year, and has students manage and operate a school store.

**Multi-Departmental.** Innovation Exploration (1 semester, 1/2 credit per semester) covers career research, resume writing, job applications, interviewing, mentors in trades and professional fields, a career portfolio, and an online educational plan. Innovation Learning (1 semester, 1/2 credit per semester) and Innovation Lab (prerequisite Innovation Learning 1, 1/2 credit) reference creatinginnovators.com and http://dschool.stanford.edu/, influenced by the "D school" at Stanford University, with the second semester devoted to a personal innovative project. **Antidiscrimination grievance procedure.** Any student or employee who believes he or she has been discriminated against, denied a benefit, or excluded from participation based on sex (including sexual harassment), race, color, religion, national origin, age (employees only), height, weight, marital status, or handicap files a written grievance with the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, the designated compliance administrator; forms are available in the Employee Services Department. Step 1 requires a written grievance form to the immediate supervisor or administrator within 10 workdays of the incident; not later than the next workday the administrator sends a copy to the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services; within 5 workdays of the filing date the supervisor meets the grievant; within 3 workdays of that meeting a written answer is given. Step 2: within 3 workdays of receiving the answer the grievant may appeal to the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services; within 10 workdays of the appeal the Assistant Superintendent (or Deputy Superintendent, if appropriate) meets the grievant; within 5 workdays of the meeting a written answer is given. Step 3: within 3 workdays of receiving that answer the grievant may appeal to the Superintendent; within 10 workdays the Superintendent meets the grievant; within 5 workdays the Superintendent gives a written answer, which is final and binding on all parties. The Superintendent, Deputy Superintendent, and Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services may designate representatives. A grievance not filed or appealed within the time limits is conclusively deemed abandoned; failure of an administrator to hold a meeting or render a decision allows automatic appeal to the next level; time limits may be extended only by mutual written agreement. Records are treated confidentially, and no record is kept in a staff member's personnel file if the final decision is that there was no reasonable basis for the grievance.

Online Learning Experience 0.0, a non-credit requirement embedded in Troy classroom experiences throughout middle and high school. State Assessments 0.0, requiring completion of the State of Michigan required assessments as administered during high school.
