**Document**
Attendance Area Review Community Feedback, Troy School District, presented for the May 6, 2025 Board of Education workshop (PDF version).

**Phases**
Phase 1 Discovery — committee formed; research, analysis and planning; potential recommendations developed. Phase 2 Recommendation (January) — committee provides the Board with options; Board determines whether to proceed. Phase 3 Feedback (March-April) — four listening sessions for families, one at each middle school, plus a community survey. Phase 4 Determination (May) — TSD provides the Board a summary of feedback and the Board determines any future changes.

**AARC goals**
Goal 1: right-size middle schools, equal student ratios. Goal 2: resolve double splits. Goal 3: no impact on high schools.

**Community meetings**
Five community meetings were held, one at each middle school with two at Larson due to spring break. Feedback themes: preferred time to split students (ES to MS or MS to HS), moving high school boundaries, reducing middle school splits another way, managing Somerset Apartments other than having them attend six schools, the duration of legacy status, mental health and social/emotional impact of an MS-to-HS split under Option C, and open enrollment for Larson, Smith and others.

**Feedback form (5 community meetings)**
31 responses; 74% of respondents from Troy Union. Open-ended tallies: TU to Larson 6; TU to Troy High 3; TU to Smith 3; consider other options 8; mental health impacts from splits 5; move HS boundaries 3; remove all splits 3; no MS to HS splits 5.

**Adult survey — 1,777 responses**
90.7% were a parent/guardian of a current student. Highest respondent student attendance: Troy High 328, Larson 327, Athens 297, Boulan Park 266, Hamilton 240; live in Somerset Apartments 53. 60.8% were familiar with the AARC process, most having read about it on the website and/or weekly newsletter. 70.1% favored some version of Option C, with Option C at 31.8%; 76.1% did not have an opinion or did not want the Board to consider any other option. Additional unlabeled percentage callouts: 73% and 52.3% important; 80.7% and 76% important; 81.3% and 76.5% important; ES to MS 72.7% and Yes & No Preference 51.5%; increase SOC 53% and allow open enrollment 63.2%.

**Student survey — 1,229 responses**
Optional for middle and high school students. Highest respondent attendance: Baker 344, Boulan Park 309, IA East 284, Larson 216. 547 students experienced a split after 5th grade, with 70% feeling neutral about the experience (Yes 44.5%, Neutral 31.3%). 300 students experienced a split after 8th grade, with 88% feeling neutral (Yes 24.4%, Neutral 21.4%). Further callouts: ES to MS 54.5% and Important 61.2%; Important 63.5% and Not Important or Don't Know 54.1%; Important 70.5% and Important 82.2%; Important 53.2%.

**Enrollment outcomes by scenario**

| Scenario | Baker | Boulan Park | Larson | Smith |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Existing Boundary (2024) | 631 | 847 | 863 | 599 |
| Maintain Existing Boundary/Policy (2027) | 517 | 793 | 750 | 466 |
| Option C | 616 | 603 | 625 | 682 |
| Option C — ONLY TU | 517 | 793 | 625 | 591 |
| Option C — ONLY SA | 616 | 603 | 750 | 557 |
| Option C — TU to Larson | 616 | 603 | 830 | 477 |

The four middle schools held 2,940 pupils in December 2024 and are projected at 2,526 pupils in 2027 (a 2027 reduction of 400+ students).

**Timeline and assumptions**
2025/2026 prepare for adjustments; 2026/2027 changes implemented. Students continue to have access to advanced programming; siblings enrolled in middle school at the same time may stay together; students currently in 5th, 6th, 7th or 8th grade (classes of 2032, 2031, 2030, 2029) are not impacted; current 5th or 6th graders slotted for a new school may move in 2025/2026. Curriculum and athletics are consistent across the four middle schools. Next steps in May: Board consideration and decision.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Attendance Area Review Community Feedback is a Troy School District presentation prepared for the May 6, 2025 Board of Education workshop summarizing community input on middle school attendance boundary options and presenting projected building enrollments under each scenario.

PHASES. Phase 1, Discovery: the committee was formed and research, analysis, and planning commenced, with the committee developing potential recommendations. Phase 2, Recommendation (January): the committee provided the Board of Education with a recommendation in the form of options, and the Board determined whether the district should move forward with the work. Phase 3, Feedback (March-April): TSD held four listening sessions for all families, one at each middle school, and sent out a community survey for additional feedback. Phase 4, Determination (May): TSD provides the Board with a summary of feedback and the Board determines any future changes.

ATTENDANCE AREA REVIEW COMMITTEE GOALS. Goal 1 is to right-size middle schools with equal student ratios. Goal 2 is to resolve double splits. Goal 3 is no impact on high schools.

AARC COMMUNITY MEETINGS. Five community meetings were held, one at each middle school, with two held at Larson due to spring break. Feedback questions and themes raised included: the preferred time to split students, if needed, whether elementary-to-middle school or middle-to-high school; whether to consider moving high school boundaries; whether the district could reduce middle school splits any other way; whether the district could manage Somerset Apartments some other way instead of having them attend six schools; how long the district would provide legacy status for a family and whether elementary students would be considered; whether other options could be considered; the mental health and social/emotional impact of the middle-to-high school split caused by Option C; and whether open enrollment could be offered for Larson, Smith and other buildings.

AARC FEEDBACK FORM. Feedback forms collected from the five community meetings yielded 31 responses, with 74% of respondents from Troy Union and the majority of open-ended feedback coming from Troy Union families. The tallied open-ended comments were: TU to Larson, 6; TU to Troy High, 3; TU to Smith, 3; consider other options, 8; mental health impacts from splits, 5; move HS boundaries, 3; remove all splits, 3; and no MS to HS splits, 5.

AARC ADULT SURVEY. The adult survey drew 1,777 responses. 90.7% of respondents were a parent or guardian of a current student. The highest numbers of respondents' students attended or had attended Troy High (328), Larson (327), Athens (297), Boulan Park (266), and Hamilton (240); 53 respondents live in Somerset Apartments. 60.8% of respondents were familiar with the AARC process, and most individuals read about it on the district website and/or in the weekly newsletter. The presentation notes that all collected data was shared with the Board of Education for review. On options, 70.1% of people were in favor of some version of Option C, with a callout of 31.8% for Option C itself, and a majority of respondents — 76.1% — either did not have an opinion or did not want the Board of Education to consider any other option. Several further adult survey slides display paired percentage callouts without the underlying question text: "Important 73%" with "Important 52.3%"; "Important 80.7%" with "Important 76%"; "Important 81.3%" with "Important 76.5%"; "ES to MS 72.7%" with "Yes & No Preference 51.5%"; and "Increase SOC 53%" with "Allow Open Enrollment 63.2%."

AARC STUDENT SURVEY. The student survey drew 1,229 responses and was optional for middle school and high school students. The highest numbers of respondents attended or had attended Baker (344), Boulan Park (309), IA East (284), and Larson (216). All collected data was shared with the Board of Education for review. On the experience of a split after 5th grade, the slide shows Yes 44.5% and Neutral 31.3%, with the note that 547 students experienced a split after 5th grade and 70% of students felt neutral about this experience. On a split after 8th grade, the slide shows Yes 24.4% and Neutral 21.4%, with the note that 300 students experienced a split after 8th grade and 88% of students felt neutral about this experience. Additional student survey callouts, again without accompanying question text, are: "ES to MS 54.5%" with "Important 61.2%"; "Important 63.5%" with "Not Important or Don't Know 54.1%"; "Important 70.5%" with "Important 82.2%"; and "Important 53.2%."

NEXT STEPS. In May the Board of Education takes the matter under consideration and a decision is determined.

AARC OUTCOMES — NO CHANGE. Under this scenario all Somerset Apartment students go to Boulan Park. The four middle schools held 2,940 pupils in December 2024, projected at 2,526 pupils in 2027, described as a 2027 reduction of 400+ students. Existing Boundary (2024) enrollments: Baker (Blue) 631 students, Boulan (Orange) 847 students, Larson (Green) 863 students, and Smith (Yellow) 599 students. Maintaining the existing boundary and policy in 2027 yields: Baker (Blue) 517 students, Boulan (Orange) 793 students, Larson (Green) 750 students, and Smith (Yellow) 466 students.

AARC OUTCOMES — OPTION C. Projected enrollments are Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 625, and Smith 682. This option was updated after the AARC concluded, based on questions asked by the group. Under it, all Troy Union students go to Smith; all students living in community housing follow their currently assigned elementary school to that elementary school's assigned middle school; and Somerset Apartments' 319 students go to Boulan Park from six elementary schools.

TROY UNION ELEMENTARY DETAIL. For Fall 2027, Troy Union Elementary is projected at 205 students. Middle school students from Troy Union total 205: Troy Union assigned to Smith, 100; Troy Union assigned to Larson, 105; Troy Union open enrolled from Smith to Larson, 20. Actual students from Troy Union to Smith would be 80, and actual students from Troy Union to Larson would be 125.

AARC OUTCOMES — OPTION C, ONLY TU. Projected enrollments are Baker 517, Boulan Park 793, Larson 625, and Smith 591. This option was updated after the Board of Education workshop on 1/14/25. All Troy Union students go to Smith; all students living in community housing go to Boulan Park Middle School under current policy; and Somerset Apartments' 319 students go to Boulan Park from six elementary schools.

SOMERSET APARTMENTS — ELEMENTARY. For Fall 2027, 319 students from Somerset Apartments are distributed across elementary schools as follows: Hamilton 0, Schroeder 60, Bemis 69, Martell 39, Leonard 52, Wattles 52, Morse 47, Troy Union 0, Costello 0, Wass 0, Hill 0, and Barnard 0. All Somerset Apartments students go to Boulan Park Middle School.

AARC OUTCOMES — OPTION C, ONLY SA. Projected enrollments are Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 750, and Smith 557. Updated after the Board of Education workshop on 1/14/25, this variant makes no changes for Troy Union; all students living in community housing follow their currently assigned elementary school to that elementary school's assigned middle school; and Somerset Apartments' 319 students go to Boulan Park from six elementary schools currently.

AARC OUTCOMES — OPTION C, TU TO LARSON. Projected enrollments are Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 830, and Smith 477. Also updated after the Board of Education workshop on 1/14/25, this variant sends all Troy Union students to Larson; all students living in community housing follow their currently assigned elementary school to that elementary school's assigned middle school; and Somerset Apartments' 319 students go to Boulan Park from six elementary schools.

TIMELINE AND ASSUMPTIONS. The 2025/2026 school year would be used to prepare for adjustments, with changes implemented in 2026/2027. Assumptions stated: Advanced Programming — students will continue to have access to advanced programming. Siblings — TSD will ensure that families with multiple middle school students enrolled at the same time will have the option to stay together, with siblings able to attend the same middle school. MS Legacy — students currently enrolled in 5th, 6th, 7th or 8th grade will not be impacted (classes of 2032, 2031, 2030, and 2029), and these students will have the option to continue in the building they are in during the Fall of 2025. Option to Move — a current 5th or 6th grader slotted to attend a new school may do so in the 2025/2026 school year, ahead of the proposed changes. Curriculum — the curriculum offered at all four middle schools is consistent across the district, and athletics are also uniform. The presentation closes with a Questions slide.

**Deck**

SLIDE 3 — COMMITTEE GOALS. Goal 1: right-size middle schools, equal student ratios. Goal 2: resolve double splits. Goal 3: no impact on high schools.

SLIDE 4 — COMMUNITY MEETINGS. Five community meetings were held, one at each middle school, with two at Larson due to spring break. Feedback captured: preferred time to split students, if needed, elementary-to-middle school or middle-to-high school; consider moving high school boundaries; whether middle school splits can be reduced any other way; whether the district can manage Somerset Apartments another way instead of having them attend six schools; how long the district will provide legacy for a family and whether elementary students would be considered; consider other options; consider mental health and social/emotional impact on the middle-to-high school split caused by Option C; and whether open enrollment could be offered for Larson, Smith, and others.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A Troy School District secondary mathematics update presented to the Board of Education on May 6, 2025, covering the district's math vision, professional learning supports for Illustrative Mathematics implementation, Honors Algebra 1 enrollment trends, NWEA MAP Growth assessment, and student and teacher perception survey results. Honors Algebra 1 enrollment reached 8% of grade 7 and 50% of grade 8 in 2024-2025. Student perception data from 1,932 respondents shows 93% saying their math class is a welcoming place for everyone, while 45% said they do not enjoy learning math.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Presentation**
Secondary Math Updates, Troy School District, May 6, 2025.

**Vision for mathematics**
All students are doers of mathematics; the program's purpose is to cultivate students' positive mathematical identities so that all students develop deep mathematical understandings, understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience the wonder, joy, and beauty of mathematics. Sourced to NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics.

**Professional learning**
The 2024 Math Summer Institute; back-to-school professional learning days; onsite learning with Illustrative Math and NWEA; monthly job-embedded professional learning with Honors Algebra 1; full days of learning during October, January, and March district professional learning; Math Specialists attending the IM coaching institute; and a full-time Math Specialist in each building to unpack units, co-plan, co-teach, coach teachers, and do intervention with struggling students.

**Support for families**
Every IM unit includes Family Support Materials describing the big ideas in plain language, with an overview of the mathematics, what to expect as learning deepens, and conversation-prompting questions. Every IM lesson includes a lesson summary in student-friendly language, useful for absences and for families. A Family Math Night was held for families with students in Math 7.

**Honors Algebra 1 enrollment**

| Course | 2021-2022 | 2022-2023 | 2023-2024 | 2024-2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Honors Algebra 1, Grade 7 | 2% | 1% | 1% | 8% |
| Honors Algebra 1, Grade 8 | 36% | 37% | 35% | 50% |

**NWEA MAP Growth**
MAP Growth is a computer-adaptive assessment used in K-12 schools by over 16 million students, nationally normed and standards aligned; MAP stands for Measures of Academic Progress. In 2024/25 all students in grades 6-8 and students enrolled in Algebra 1 took MAP Growth in the Fall and Spring, with Math 7 students also testing in Winter to provide an additional data point when choosing Math 8 or Honors Algebra 1. In 2025/26 all students in grades 6-8 and students in all levels of Algebra 1, Geometry, and Algebra 2 will test in Fall, Winter, and Spring. MAP Growth provides RIT (Rasch Unit) scores indicating instructional level, growth over time, projected growth against national norms, and disaggregated data. Next steps: use as a screener for intervention and extension, establish cohort data, compare Fall to Spring, use district data with teachers in late summer, hold a Summer 2025 Data Retreat with administrators, and continue professional learning in 2025-26.

**Student perception data (1,932 respondents)**
Celebrations: 93% said their math class is a welcoming place for everyone; 87% said they had lots of opportunities to interact with each other; 88% agreed it is important to try rather than to get things right the first time; 90% agreed with "I know I can be good at math"; 79% feel prepared for the next level of math; 59% said the lessons are "just right for them." Challenges: 34% would like more specific feedback on how to improve their work; 45% do not enjoy learning math; 24% said the lessons are too easy; 17% said the lessons are too hard.

**Teacher perception data (19 respondents)**
Celebrations: 95% say they are comfortable navigating the resource; 79% say they have the tools they need to accurately measure student progress. Challenges: 37% need more resources for families; 42% are using the IM Instructional Routines that support student access. Written comments request more support for ELD students and students with low reading/comprehension skills, more supplemental practice, closer alignment between assessments and learning activities, guidance on what can be combined or eliminated, and more at-home written examples.

**Distinguished math students**
In the 2025-26 school year a committee including a variety of stakeholders will be formed to investigate how to recognize distinguished middle school math students, considering extensions in and outside the classroom; information will be posted on the district website and communicated through the Troy Newsletter.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Secondary Math Updates is a Troy School District presentation delivered to the Board of Education on May 6, 2025.

VISION FOR MATHEMATICS. The presentation states that all students are doers of mathematics, and that the purpose of the mathematics program is to cultivate students' positive mathematical identities so that all students develop deep mathematical understandings, understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience the wonder, joy, and beauty of mathematics. The vision is attributed to NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics.

SUPPORTING IMPLEMENTATION THROUGH PROFESSIONAL LEARNING. Supports listed are the 2024 Math Summer Institute and, for the 2024/25 school year, back-to-school professional learning days; onsite learning with Illustrative Math and NWEA; monthly job-embedded professional learning with Honors Algebra 1; a full day of learning during October, January, and March district professional learning; Math Specialists attending the IM coaching institute; and a full-time Math Specialist in each building to unpack units, co-plan, co-teach, and coach teachers as well as do intervention with struggling students.

SUPPORT FOR FAMILIES. Every Illustrative Mathematics unit includes a section called Family Support Materials, which describes in plain language the big ideas students will encounter, provides an overview of the mathematics students are learning, gives details about what to expect as the learning deepens, and includes questions that promote conversation about the mathematics. Every IM lesson includes a lesson summary written to summarize the main mathematical points of a lesson, including any new vocabulary, in student-friendly language; these are meant for students to read on their own time or to catch up on a day they were absent, and are useful for families who want to understand in more detail what their student is learning. The district also held a Family Math Night for families with students in Math 7.

COHORT SLIDES. The deck includes slides for current 9th grade students, Class of 2028; current 8th grade students, Class of 2029; and current 7th grade students, Class of 2030.

ENROLLMENT IN HONORS ALGEBRA 1. The presentation reports the share of students enrolled in Honors Algebra 1 across four school years, 2021-2022, 2022-2023, 2023-2024, and 2024-2025. For Honors Algebra 1 in Grade 7, the figures are 2%, 1%, 1%, and 8%. For Honors Algebra 1 in Grade 8, the figures are 36%, 37%, 35%, and 50%.

ASSESSMENT AND NWEA MAP GROWTH. MAP Growth is described as a computer-adaptive assessment used in K-12 schools by over 16 million students to measure student performance and growth over time; it is nationally normed and standards aligned, and MAP stands for Measures of Academic Progress. In the 2024/25 school year, all students in grades 6-8 and students enrolled in Algebra 1 took the NWEA MAP Growth assessment in the Fall and Spring. Math 7 students also took MAP Growth in the Winter to provide an additional data point when choosing Math 8 or Honors Algebra 1 as their next math course. In the 2025/26 school year, all students in grades 6-8 and students enrolled in all levels of Algebra 1, Geometry, and Algebra 2 will take the NWEA MAP Growth assessment in the Fall, Winter, and Spring.

WHAT MAP GROWTH PROVIDES. RIT Scores (Rasch Unit Score): a RIT score indicates a student's instructional level, not tied to grade level but to a continuum of learning. Growth Over Time: MAP Growth can track how much a student has grown from fall to winter to spring, or year over year, supporting the study of learning trends and evaluation of the impact of instruction or interventions. Projected Growth: each student receives a growth projection based on national norms. Disaggregated Data: MAP Growth data can be analyzed by demographic subgroups, achievement levels, or custom student groups. The deck includes three slides headed NWEA Fall 2024-25 Achievement Data whose charts are not represented in the extracted text.

NEXT STEPS WITH NWEA. MAP Growth is established as a screener to identify students who may need intervention and students who may need extension; the district will establish cohort data to identify grade-level growth; comparisons from Fall to Spring will be made, with spring testing happening at the time of the presentation; the aim is maintaining high levels of performance and growing student performance; district data will be used late summer with teachers; a Data Retreat with administrators is planned for Summer 2025; and continued professional learning with teachers is planned for the 2025-26 school year.

STUDENT PERCEPTION DATA (1,932). Celebrations reported: 93% of students said their math class is a welcoming place for everyone; 87% of students said they had lots of opportunities to interact with each other; 88% agreed that in their math class it is important to try rather than to get things right the first time; 90% of students agreed with the statement "I know I can be good at math"; 79% of students feel prepared for the next level of math; and 59% said the lessons are "just right for them." Challenges reported: 34% of students would like to receive more specific feedback on how to improve their work; 45% of students do not enjoy learning math; 24% of students said the lessons are too easy; and 17% of students said the lessons are too hard.

STUDENT VOICE. Quoted student comments include enjoying interactions with peers and being at a level where "the math isn't too easy or too hard"; a teacher explaining math equations with real-life examples; appreciation that there are different ways to learn math; and feeling confident enough to raise a hand without being judged and working with friends. Suggestions from students include adding a difficulty level to assignments to show improvement, more interactive projects or activities so class does not get boring, a pre-test so the teacher understands what students know, more repetitive practice per activity to aid retention before tests, and learning more things that will be used in real life.

TEACHER PERCEPTION DATA (19). Celebrations: 95% of teachers say they are comfortable navigating the resource, and 79% of teachers say they have the tools they need to accurately measure student progress. Quoted teacher comments praise that there is not just one way to learn most content, that the curriculum figures out the "why," the conceptual content, the "are you ready for more" tasks, the collaborative tasks, the emphasis on getting students to talk and write math, the connection of math to real-life situations, and the low-floor approach that is inviting for struggling students. Challenges: 37% of teachers need more resources for families, and 42% of teachers are using the IM Instructional Routines that support student access. Teacher comments request more support for ELD students and students with low reading and comprehension skills, noting that reading a problem three times is not always doable or helpful; more supplemental practice to solidify concepts; assessments that match more of what the learning activities look like throughout lessons; more guidance on what can be combined or eliminated from lessons or units; and more at-home resources with written-out examples beyond the online workbook and videos.

RECOGNIZING DISTINGUISHED MATH STUDENTS. In the 2025-26 school year the district will form a committee that includes a variety of stakeholders to investigate how it might recognize distinguished middle school math students. As extensions are considered, the district will look to include opportunities in and outside of the classroom. Information will be posted on the district website and communicated through the Troy Newsletter.

Adam McManus, student representative for Troy High School, shared a report on his school. **Identification and attendance**
Regular meeting minutes of the Troy Board of Education, Tuesday, April 21, 2026, held at the Troy School District Services Building (Service Center), 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mrs. Anne, Board members Alic, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts and Zendler were present. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Smotherman, Brennan, Griffin, Algeier, Montante, Pagel and Trudel. Approximately 75 members of the audience attended. The Pledge of Allegiance opened the proceedings. The meeting was adjourned at 8:35 p.m. Minutes were respectfully submitted by Matt Haupt, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the typing reference MH/jh.

**Recognition: Outstanding Teachers of the Year**
The Board recognized the district's 2026 Outstanding Teachers of the Year. More than 49 Troy School District educators were nominated for the distinguished recognition, and from that group three educators were selected on the basis of passion, dedication, impact and excellence in teaching. A short video was shown capturing the administrative team surprising each winner in the classroom. A special reception for all nominees and winners was scheduled for Wednesday, April 29 at Troy High School, giving teachers an opportunity to connect with those who nominated them; each nominee was to receive a certificate, their nomination materials, and a small token of appreciation. Each of the three winners came to the podium as their name was called, shared remarks, and posed for a photo with members of the Board of Education.

The 2026 Outstanding Teachers of the Year are Lindsey Maliepaard, Elementary Teacher of the Year, Costello Elementary School; Tammy Gilbert, Middle School Teacher of the Year, Boulan Park Middle School; and Christina Rick, Troy High School, High School and Overall Teacher of the Year. All three winners were submitted to Oakland Schools to represent Troy in the countywide Outstanding Teacher Award program, and Christina Rick was named the 2026 Oakland County High School Teacher of the Year.

**TSD Mission Moment: Shamrock Shakedown**
The Mission Moment described the Shamrock Shakedown, which began as a shared passion for basketball between students and staff at Troy Center for Transition and grew into a school-wide tradition celebrating teamwork, inclusion and community. International Academy East (IA East) has been an essential partner, leading game-day setup and serving as master of ceremonies, with a soundtrack and halftime performances. Troy Center for Transition teacher Brynn Lawrence and International Academy East teacher Mark Chrzanowski were invited to the podium to introduce their students and describe the event. Ava Pittman from IA-East and Nathan Kohnert from TCT spoke about participating and shared a brief video.

**Autism Acceptance Month resolution**
April was designated Autism Acceptance Month. The resolution was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Alic. Its recitals state that Autism Spectrum Disorder affects more than five million people in the United States; that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report that 1 in 36 children may have autism; that autism is a neurological and developmental disorder characterized by social impairment and restricted interactive and communication behaviors that can affect anyone regardless of race, ethnicity, gender or socioeconomic background; that symptoms may present in a variety of combinations and can result in significant, lifelong challenges affecting learning, daily living, employment, social-interactive behaviors, and understanding verbal and nonverbal communications; that physicians, psychologists, behavior analysts, speech and language pathologists, occupational therapists, vocational rehabilitation professionals and educators can assist persons with autism and their families through early identification, education, intervention and recreation; and that the Troy School District is committed to fostering acceptance and belonging. The resolution recognizes April 2026 as Autism Acceptance Month in the Troy School District. The vote was Yes: 7, No: 0. A five minute recess followed. There were no additions or deletions to the agenda.

One community member addressed the Board during public communication on agenda items; no action was taken. Three community members addressed the Board during public communication on non-agenda items; no action was taken.

**Meeting**
Troy Board of Education special meeting, Tuesday, April 7, 2026, Service Center, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, held at the Troy School District Services Building. President Anne called the special meeting to order at 6:03 p.m.; adjournment at 6:22 p.m. Minutes submitted by Matt Haupt, Secretary, Troy Board of Education (MH/jh).

**Attendance**
Board: Anne (President), Alic, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts, Zendler. Also present: Superintendent Machesky and administrators Griffor, Pagel, DiPilato and Trudel. There was no one in the audience. The Pledge of Allegiance was recited. Public communication: none.

**Business Services, item a: Easement Agreement**
Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt. The resolution recites that Troy School District desires to grant a Sidewalk Easement and a Highway Easement to the Board of County Road Commissioners of the County of Oakland in order to construct, install, operate, use, maintain, repair, replace and remove a sidewalk and roadway for the new Smith Middle School on each Property. The Board authorized both easements on terms substantially similar to the attached documents (Exhibit A) and authorized the Superintendent, or his designee, to execute them and any necessary and incidental documents. A certification clause states the resolution was duly adopted at a special meeting held on the 7th day of April, 2026, with notice given in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976. Vote: Yes: 7, No: 0.

**Business Services, item b: Declaration of necessity and condemnation authorization**
Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Alic. The Board declared it necessary to acquire permanent highway easements and sidewalk easements along Livernois Road for the new Smith Middle School project, noting that negotiations with the Owner had not been successful and that the District has power to acquire interests in real property by condemnation under the Uniform Condemnation Procedures Act.

Key elements of the resolution:
- Project: construction and operation of the new Smith Middle School on Livernois Road, City of Troy, Oakland County, including driveway approaches and a deceleration lane on the east side of Livernois Road, road widening, traffic signal and sidewalk improvements (the Livernois Road Improvements).
- Property: owned in fee by Mirza Azam-Ali Baig and Juveria Baig, husband and wife; commonly known as 5836 Livernois Road, Troy, Michigan; Tax Parcel No. 20-10-101-033.
- Authority cited: Section 11a of Michigan Public Act 451, Public Acts of 1976 (The Revised School Code), MCL 380.11a; Uniform Condemnation Procedures Act, Public Act 87 of 1980, MCL 213.51 et seq.
- Authorizations: the Superintendent, or in his absence the Deputy Superintendent of Business Affairs, may execute documents, record the Statement of Necessity and Declaration of Taking of Private Property, retain appraisers, make good faith written offers, negotiate just compensation, and initiate proceedings in the Oakland County Circuit Court.
- The Deputy Superintendent of Schools of Business Affairs is authorized to establish an escrow account with First American Title Company for amounts estimated to be just compensation, and to select a real estate appraiser or other consultants.
- Clark Hill PLC, or another firm selected by the Superintendent in the event of conflict, is retained to initiate condemnation proceedings.
- The Board reserves the right to bring federal or state cost recovery actions against the Owner for costs from any release of hazardous or toxic substances on the Easement.

**Identification and attendance**
Special board meeting minutes of the Troy Board of Education for Tuesday, April 7, 2026, held at the Troy School District Services Building (Service Center), 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The Pledge of Allegiance was recited and there was no public communication. The meeting was adjourned at 6:22 p.m. Minutes were respectfully submitted by Matt Haupt, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, reference MH/jh.

**Business Services, item a: Easement Agreement**
Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt, the Board resolved to authorize the Sidewalk Easement and Highway Easement and to authorize the Superintendent of the School District, or his designee, to execute the Sidewalk Easement and Highway Easement as well as any and all documents necessary and incidental on behalf of the School District.

The recitals state that the Troy School District desires to grant a Sidewalk Easement and a Highway Easement to the Board of County Road Commissioners of the County of Oakland in order to construct, install, operate, use, maintain, repair, replace and remove a sidewalk and roadway for the new Smith Middle School on each Property (collectively the Properties), in accordance with the terms of the Sidewalk Easement and the Highway Easement; and that the School District desires to authorize the Superintendent, or his designee, to execute those easements on terms substantially similar to those in the attached documents, which are attached and incorporated by reference as Exhibit A.

The operative provisions are: (1) the School District authorizes the Sidewalk Easement and Highway Easement on terms substantially similar to those contained in the attached instruments; and (2) the Superintendent of the School District, or his designee, is authorized to execute the Sidewalk Easement and Highway Easement as well as any and all documents necessary and incidental on behalf of the School District.

A certification block headed RESOLUTION DECLARED ADOPTED follows, certifying that the foregoing is a true and complete copy of a resolution duly adopted by the Board of Education of Troy School District, County of Oakland, Michigan, at a special meeting held on the 7th day of April, 2026, and that the meeting was conducted and public notice given pursuant to and in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act, being Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976, and that minutes were kept and will be or have been made available as required by that Act. The certification is signed by the Secretary, Board of Education. The recorded vote is Yes: 7, No: 0.

**Business Services, item b: Declaring necessity to acquire highway and sidewalk easement and authorizing legal counsel to initiate condemnation proceedings for the Smith Middle School project**
Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Alic. The resolution states that negotiations with the Owner to acquire the easements have not been successful; that the District has power to acquire interests in real property by condemnation pursuant to the Uniform Condemnation Procedures Act; and that the Board finds it necessary to acquire permanent highway easements and sidewalk easements along Livernois Road.

The recitals identify the Troy School District as a Michigan general powers school district acting by and through its Board of Education, currently undertaking a project for construction and operation of the new Smith Middle School (the Project) located on Livernois Road in the City of Troy, Oakland County, Michigan, which includes roadway and sidewalk improvements necessary for the benefit of the public and to improve road conditions, safety, mobility and accessibility to the school and for road users. As part of the Project it is necessary to construct driveway approaches and a deceleration lane on the east side of Livernois Road, including widening the road and making traffic signal and sidewalk improvements, collectively the Livernois Road Improvements.

To undertake the Project the District must acquire permanent highway and sidewalk easements on, over, across and under certain real property owned in fee by Mirza Azam-Ali Baig and Juveria Baig, husband and wife (the Owner), situated in the City of Troy, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, commonly known as 5836 Livernois Road, Troy, Michigan, Tax Parcel No. 20-10-101-033. The Easements are set forth in the Declaration of Necessity and Taking of Property attached in substantial form as Exhibit A.

Statutory authority cited includes Section 11a of Michigan Public Act 451, Public Acts of 1976 (The Revised School Code), as amended, MCL 380.11a, under which the District has power to acquire interests in real property by condemnation, and the Uniform Condemnation Procedures Act, Public Act 87 of 1980, as amended, MCL 213.51 et seq. (the UCPA), which establishes procedures for the taking of property by eminent domain. The District reserves the right to bring federal or state cost recovery actions against the Owner for costs incurred as a result of the release of hazardous or toxic substances or materials that may have occurred on the Easement. The District will present the Owner a good faith written offer to acquire the Easement in exchange for payment of just compensation based on an appraisal by a state certified appraiser; if the Owner rejects that offer, the Clark Hill PLC law firm is authorized to institute a condemnation lawsuit for acquisition of the Easements, and the Superintendent of Schools or the Deputy Superintendent of Schools of Business Affairs is authorized to execute any documents needed for the condemnation lawsuit.

The operative provisions are numbered 1 through 6. (1) The Board declares that the Project is a public improvement and that acquiring the Easements in, on, over, under, across and through the Property for the Livernois Road Improvements is necessary and essential, since those improvements benefit the public and improve public safety. (2) The Board authorizes the Superintendent of Schools, or in his absence the Deputy Superintendent of Business Affairs, to take all action and execute documents necessary under the Revised School Code, the UCPA and any other applicable state or federal law, including acquiring the Easements, recording the Statement of Necessity and Declaration of Taking of Private Property in substantial form as set forth in Exhibit A, retaining qualified appraisers or other consultants to determine just compensation, making good faith written offers to property owners, entering negotiations, reaching agreements as to just compensation, presenting good faith offers to Owners and interested parties, and initiating appropriate proceedings in the Oakland County Circuit Court for condemnation of the Easements set forth in Exhibit A. (3) The Deputy Superintendent of Schools of Business Affairs is authorized to establish an escrow account with First American Title Company for the specific amounts estimated to be just compensation for the Easements to be condemned pursuant to the UCPA. (4) Clark Hill PLC, or in the event of conflict such other firm as the Superintendent may select, is retained to take all appropriate action regarding initiation of condemnation proceedings in the Oakland County Circuit Court for the taking of private property as indicated in Exhibit A. (5) The Deputy Superintendent of Schools of Business Affairs is authorized to select a real estate appraiser or other consultants, considering estimated appraisal cost, timing of services, professional services and expert witness qualifications, to prepare estimates of just compensation required for the Easement taken as described in Exhibit A. (6) The Board of Education for the Troy School District reserves the right to bring federal or state cost recovery actions against the Owner for costs incurred as a result of the release of hazardous or toxic substances or materials that may have occurred on the Easement.

**Other: rescheduling of the Board Workshop**
Moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Potts, the Board resolved to reschedule the May 5, 2026 Board of Education Workshop to the preceding week, April 28, 2026, at 6:00 p.m. No separate vote tally is printed in the minutes for this item or for Business Services item b; the only recorded tally in the minutes is Yes: 7, No: 0 on the Easement Agreement.

**Meeting**
Troy Board of Education regular meeting, April 16, 2024, Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. Called to order by President Schmidt at 7:00 p.m.; adjourned at 8:42 p.m. Minutes submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary (GH/jh).

**Attendance**
Present with Mr. Schmidt: Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart, and Wilson. Also present: Superintendent Machesky and administrators Montante, DiPilato, Griffor, Smotherman, Keyser, Pagel, Morse, Milanov, Keen, Pawlus, Hall, and West. Approximately 180 members of the audience attended.

**Recognition — Outstanding Teachers**
The District received 48 nominations, resulting in recognition of 41 outstanding teachers. All nominees were honored at a reception on Tuesday, April 9th at Troy High School and received a certificate, their nomination packets, and a token of appreciation; a video of the surprise classroom visits was shown. The top four were honored at the meeting:

| Teacher | Award | School |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Elizabeth Neuville | Preschool Teacher of the Year | TSD Preschool |
| Danielle Davenport | Elementary Teacher of the Year | Hill Elementary School |
| Eric Flessa | High School Teacher of the Year | Troy College & Career High School |
| Stephanie Hyska | Middle School Teacher of the Year and overall TSD Teacher of the Year | Boulan Park Middle School |

All winners were forwarded to Oakland Schools for the Countywide Outstanding Teacher Award program.

**Mission Moment — Autism Acceptance Month**
Moved by Dr. Wilson, supported by Mrs. Alic, a resolution recognizing April 2024 as Autism Acceptance Month in the Troy School District. Whereas clauses noted that Autism Spectrum Disorder affects more than five million people in the United States and that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report 1 in 36 children may have autism. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Student Spotlight and Volunteer Appreciation**
Mr. Thomas Butcher presented Cassandra Wilson, an Athens High School senior, recognized with a certificate for her TSD Creative Guild work. For Volunteer Appreciation Month the Board honored volunteers whose students graduate from TSD this year: Marti Steiner, Peggy Chinoski, Colleen Geyer, and Tara Colussi.

**Additions & Deletions / Public Communication (Agenda Items) / Personnel / Curriculum / Other**
None.

**Consent Agenda**
Moved by Mr. Hauff, supported by Mr. Haupt, to approve items A through F: minutes of the March 5, 2024 Special Meeting, Closed Session Meeting, and Board Workshop; minutes of the March 19, 2024 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report – February 2024; and Ancillary Fund(s) Budget Amendment. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Business — Smith Switch Gear**
Moved by Mrs. Alic, supported by Dr. Philippart, that the bid for the Smith Middle School Switchgear Package be awarded to Great Lakes Power and Lighting in an amount not to exceed $405,000.00, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Public Communication (Non-Agenda Items)**
Jordan Holsbeke (Martell teacher, 2022 Teacher of the Year), Jason Cichowicz (Troy Education Association president), Jacqueline Ciolek (Troy High), Jennifer Lee (Larson Middle School, 26-year teacher), Heather Kelly (Troy High), Jessica Craft (Troy High), and Mary Burns (Martell) addressed the expired teacher contract and fair and equitable compensation; Mrs. Craft also raised teachers not being given steps when they hire in. Ayesha Potts, a Troy resident and District parent, spoke about her candidacy for a seat on the Troy School Board in the upcoming elections.

**Student Representatives**
Jayla Turner (Troy High School), Saanvi Kapu (Athens junior, filling in for Marlien William), and Nurayda Albeez (International Academy-East) reported. Teagan Pruitt (Troy College and Career High School) was not in attendance.

**Board Comments and Announcements**
Dr. Philippart discussed the TSD Business Education Roundtable and the need for interviewers for the 8th Grade Interview Program; Mr. Hauff and Dr. Machesky praised the TSD Art Show at the Troy Community Center. Dates announced: Open-Air Festival Friday, May 17th, 4–9 p.m.; Board Workshop Tuesday, May 7th at 6:00 p.m., Administration Building; next Board Meeting Tuesday, May 21st at 7:00 p.m., Services Building. Mr. Schmidt updated the Board on District–Troy Education Association bargaining and cited the three R's — Recruit, Retain, and Respect.

Approved minutes of the regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, held April 16, 2024 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present were Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart, and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Montante, DiPilato, Griffor, Smotherman, Keyser, Pagel, Morse, Milanov, Keen, Pawlus, Hall, and West. There were approximately 180 members of the audience. The meeting adjourned at 8:42 p.m., and the minutes were respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the typist notation GH/jh.

RECOGNITION — TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT'S OUTSTANDING TEACHERS. The Board honored teachers described as having left an indelible mark on students, families, and colleagues, congratulating the Outstanding Teachers of the Year for the 2024 school year. The District received 48 nominations, resulting in the recognition of 41 outstanding teachers. Four of the nominees rose to the top due to their commitment, passion, impact, and dedication to their craft. A short video of the administrative team surprising the winners in their classrooms was shared with the Board and audience. All winners and nominees were recognized at a reception on Tuesday, April 9th at Troy High School, where teachers visited with those who nominated them and all nominees received a certificate, their nomination packets, and a small token of the District's appreciation. The top four winners were invited to the April 16 meeting to be honored, coming to the podium as their names were called to say a few words if they chose and to have their photo taken with members of the Board of Education. The Outstanding Teachers for 2024 are Elizabeth Neuville, Preschool Teacher of the Year, TSD Preschool; Danielle Davenport, Elementary Teacher of the Year, Hill Elementary School; Eric Flessa, High School Teacher of the Year, Troy College & Career High School; and Stephanie Hyska, Middle School Teacher of the Year and overall TSD Teacher of the Year, Boulan Park Middle School. All winners were sent on to Oakland Schools to represent Troy in the Countywide Outstanding Teacher Award program.

MISSION MOMENT — AUTISM ACCEPTANCE MONTH. April has been designated as Autism Acceptance Month. In honor of the month, the Troy School Board of Education acted on a resolution to celebrate the contributions of all neurodiverse people and to work toward ending disparities that autistic people experience when accessing employment, healthcare, and education, recognizing the need for public awareness to promote acceptance, celebrate differences, and be more inclusive toward autistic individuals. It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mrs. Alic. The whereas clauses stated that Autism Spectrum Disorder affects more than five million people in the United States; that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report that 1 in 36 children may have autism; that autism is a neurological and developmental disorder characterized by social impairment and restricted interactive and communication behaviors and can affect anyone regardless of race, ethnicity, gender, or socioeconomic background; that symptoms and characteristics may present in a variety of combinations and can result in significant, lifelong challenges in areas affecting learning, daily living, employment, social-interactive behaviors, and understanding verbal and nonverbal communications; that physicians, psychologists, behavior analysts, speech and language pathologists, occupational therapists, vocational rehabilitation professionals, and educators can assist persons with autism and their families by supporting early identification, education, intervention, recreation, and other opportunities vital to enhanced development and well-being; and that the Troy School District is honored to celebrate the many ways individuals with autism enhance the quality of the school community and is committed to fostering acceptance and a sense of belonging. The resolving clause recognized April 2024 as Autism Acceptance Month in the Troy School District. The vote was Yes: 7, No: 0.

STUDENT SPOTLIGHT. The Board recognized the creative achievements of students in the TSD Creative Guild. Mr. Thomas Butcher returned to present the featured student, Cassandra Wilson, a senior at Athens High School, described as having a familiar face. Butcher spoke about Cassandra and her special work, and Cassandra was invited up to share more about her accomplishments and to receive a certificate of recognition for her creative work.

VOLUNTEER APPRECIATION. The Board extended a thank you to Troy School District volunteers who dedicate their time and talents to the schools and community. In celebration of Volunteer Appreciation Month, the Board expressed gratitude for the contributions of dedicated volunteers whose students will be graduating from TSD this year. Marti Steiner, Peggy Chinoski, Colleen Geyer, and Tara Colussi were invited forward to accept a small token of appreciation for their outstanding service over many years.

ADDITIONS & DELETIONS. None. PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (AGENDA ITEMS). None.

GENERAL — CONSENT AGENDA. It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B, C, D, E, and F on the consent agenda: minutes of the March 5, 2024 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the March 5, 2024 Closed Session Meeting; minutes of the March 5, 2024 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the March 19, 2024 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report – February 2024; and an Ancillary Fund(s) Budget Amendment. The vote was Yes: 7, No: 0.

PERSONNEL. None. CURRICULUM. None.

BUSINESS — SMITH SWITCH GEAR. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Dr. Philippart that the bid for the Smith Middle School Switchgear Package be awarded to Great Lakes Power and Lighting in the amount not to exceed $405,000.00, and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. The vote was Yes: 7, No: 0.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (NON-AGENDA ITEMS). Mr. Jordan Holsbeke, Martell teacher and 2022 Teacher of the Year, addressed the Board about how Troy values teachers and how they deserve a fair and equitable contract. Mr. Jason Cichowicz, Troy Education Association president, addressed the Board regarding the expired teacher contract, fair and equitable compensation, and the importance of retaining teachers. Ms. Jacqueline Ciolek, Troy High teacher, addressed the expired teacher contract and fair and equitable compensation. Ms. Jennifer Lee, a Larson Middle School teacher of 26 years, addressed the expired teacher contract and fair and equitable compensation. Ms. Heather Kelly, Troy High teacher, addressed the expired teacher contract and fair and equitable compensation. Mrs. Jessica Craft, Troy High teacher, addressed the expired teacher contract, teachers not being given steps when they hire in, and the need for a fair and equitable contract. Mrs. Mary Burns, Martell teacher, addressed the expired teacher contract and fair and equitable compensation. Ayesha Potts, a Troy resident and parent in the District, addressed the Board about her candidacy in running for a seat on the Troy School Board in the upcoming elections.

REPORTS FROM STUDENT REPRESENTATIVES TO THE BOARD. Jayla Turner, student representative for Troy High School, reported on events and activities at her school. Saanvi Kapu, a junior at Athens High School, filled in as student representative because Marlien William was not in attendance, and shared a report on events and activities at Athens. Nurayda Albeez, student representative for International Academy-East, shared a report on events and activities at her school. Teagan Pruitt, student representative for Troy College and Career High School, was not in attendance.

OTHER. None.

BOARD COMMENTS. Dr. Wilson congratulated and thanked the teachers nominated for Teacher of the Year and encouraged participation in the Open-Air Festival, to be held outdoors on Friday, May 17th from 4 to 9 p.m. Dr. Philippart discussed the TSD Business Education Roundtable and the strong partnerships with businesses in the District that have a vested interest in students and schools, and mentioned the need for interviewers for the 8th Grade Interview Program. Mr. Haupt thanked the Teachers of the Year for their dedication and said he enjoyed the video. Mrs. Alic mentioned that the Troy Youth Association is celebrating Volunteer Appreciation Month and that there are opportunities to volunteer in the county, school district, and city. Mr. Hauff encouraged the community to visit the TSD Art Show at the Troy Community Center on Livernois and thanked teachers for supporting and encouraging the fine arts program in TSD. Mrs. Anne thanked the teachers and shared her appreciation of them, and mentioned attending the recent NSBA Conference and visiting schools in that community. Dr. Machesky echoed praise for the TSD Art Show, which he attended the reception for the previous night. Mr. Schmidt also mentioned the NSBA Conference and said the Board would discuss what they learned at the next workshop. He announced that the next Board Workshop would be held Tuesday, May 7th at 6:00 p.m. in the Administration Building and the next Board Meeting Tuesday, May 21st at 7:00 p.m. in the Services Building. He shared a brief update on the status of the District and Teachers Education Association bargaining sessions and mentioned the three R's — Recruit, Retain, and Respect — to sustain the District.

ADJOURNMENT. The meeting adjourned at 8:42 p.m.

Minutes of the regular meeting of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, held June 20, 2024 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The minutes bear the title M062024BdMtg and a meeting date of July 16, 2024, the date they were brought forward. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present were Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart, and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Montante, Pagel, Fulcher, Smotherman, and West. There were approximately 60 members of the audience. The meeting adjourned at 8:40 p.m. The minutes were respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, and carry the typist notation GH/jh.

**Business — Public Hearing on the 2024/2025 Proposed Budget.** Mr. West presented the details of the proposed budget to the Board and community and shared a PowerPoint presentation. He noted the proposed budget had been reviewed in great detail with the Board at the June workshop. His presentation covered tax values, homestead and non-homestead millage, and general fund adjustments and assumptions. He also spoke about ancillary funds, the sinking fund, and the capital projects fund, and reviewed student enrollment, the District's foundation allowance history, and revenues and expenditures. The Board indicated it had reviewed the proposed budget in its entirety at the June 6th Workshop. President Schmidt invited questions from the audience related to the proposed budget; no questions were asked.

**Recognition — Troy United Synchronized Swim Team, 2024 State Champions.** The Board congratulated the team on a successful season and invited Mr. Fulcher to the podium to introduce the team and present a team plaque. Swim team state champions from Troy High were Rebecca Austin, Erin Choi, Sonia De Donno, Jessica Deng, Ainsley Giorio, Shatakshi Gupta, Ana Sofia Hernandez Gomez, Nidhi Mody, Sei Park, Himasree Puppala, Lucie Rosati, Parker Silagy, Avani Singh, Cate Sivier, Kara Son, Isabel Thommana, Sritha Velireddy, Sasha Vivek, and Sia Wu. Swim team state champions from Athens were Greta Burt, Faith Frederick, Crystal Hensley, McKenzie Johnson, Sakura Mori, and Gwendolyn Schaefer. Coaches Lori Uchwal-Hollier, Erika Mooney, Beth Borland, and Nicole Cervantes were recognized and congratulated for their dedication and hard work.

**Recognition — ASBO Excellence in Financial Reporting for FY2023.** Mr. Schmidt recognized the Business Office team for again receiving the ASBO Award. The Association of School Business Officials International's Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting Program honored the Troy School District for excellence in the preparation and issuance of a high quality Comprehensive Annual Financial Report (CAFR) for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2023. Named for recognition were Rick West, Deputy Superintendent; Kandice Moynihan, former Finance Director; and the Finance team and staff.

**Resolution in Support of Gun Safety and Safe Gun Storage.** Moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mrs. Anne. The whereas clauses state that the safety and well-being of students, teachers, and staff is a top priority in the Troy School District; that firearm-related deaths are the leading cause of death among children and adolescents; that rates of death from firearms among ages 14 to 17 are now 22.5% higher than motor vehicle-related death rates, and that in the U.S. middle and high school age children are now more likely to die as the result of a firearm injury than from any other single cause of death; that according to a report from the US Secret Service, in incidents of gun violence on school grounds 76% of attackers acquired a firearm from the home of a parent or another close relative; that every year roughly 350 children under the age of 18 unintentionally shoot themselves or someone else; that nearly 22,000 Americans die by firearm suicide every year, including over 950 children and teens; that research indicates 47% of firearm owners who have children living in their homes do not safely store at least one of their weapons; that secure firearm storage is an essential component of any effective strategy to keep the community safe; and that keeping students, teachers and staff safe from gun violence should be the responsibility of all adult stakeholders within the district.

The resolved clauses direct the Superintendent to periodically communicate the importance of safe firearm storage and other firearm safety and violence prevention measures during gun violence awareness month, and to disseminate material on an annual basis stressing the importance of secure storage of firearms by including it in the District's annual notification materials. A further clause commits the Board and Superintendent to continue working with local law enforcement agencies, medical and mental health agencies, and non-profit organizations to collaborate and increase efforts to inform District parents of their obligations regarding secure storage of firearms in their homes as well as other gun violence prevention safety measures. A final clause states the resolution shall not be construed to conflict with any existing Michigan or federal law. The vote was 7 yes, 0 no, and the resolution was declared adopted.

Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Board of Education, certified that the resolution was duly adopted at a regular meeting held on the 20th day of June, 2024, and that the meeting was conducted and public notice given pursuant to and in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act, being Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976. Sources footnoted in the resolution include news.umich.edu (firearms as top cause of death among children and adolescents), labblog.uofmhealth.org, the US Secret Service report "Protecting America's Schools," everytownresearch.org (the "Not an Accident" map and a report on the rise of firearm suicide among young Americans), a Pew Research Center guns report, and David C. Grossman et al., "Gun Storage Practices and Risk of Youth Suicide and Unintentional Firearm Injuries," JAMA 293, no. 6 (2005): 707-14.

**Additions & Deletions:** None. **Public Communication (Agenda Items):** None.

**General — Consent Agenda.** Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, and I on the consent agenda: minutes of the May 7, 2024 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the May 7, 2024 Closed Session Meeting; minutes of the May 7, 2024 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the May 21, 2024 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report — April 2024; Michigan High School Athletic Association (MHSAA) Membership Resolution 2024/2025; the 2023/2024 Budget Amendment; the 2024/2025 Budget Appropriations Resolution; and Approval of Committee for Instructional Minutes. Vote: 7 yes, 0 no.

**Personnel — Administrative Appointment, Special Education Supervisor.** Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Hauff that the Board issue a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Mr. Trevor Harker, who will begin his duties as Special Education Supervisor effective July 1, 2024. Vote: 7 yes, 0 no.

**Personnel — Assistant Superintendent, Business Services.** Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Dr. Wilson that the Board issue a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Mr. Daniel Trudel, who will begin his duties as Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, effective July 1, 2024. Vote: 7 yes, 0 no.

**Personnel — TEA Contract Ratification.** A tentative agreement between representatives of the Troy Board of Education and the Troy Education Association/MEA/NEA (TEA) was reached on June 10, 2024. The TEA membership voted to ratify the agreement on June 19, 2024. The tentative agreement is a contract for the period February 1, 2024 through April 15, 2027, and the draft successor collective bargaining agreement with all modifications was attached for the Board's consideration. Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Philippart that the Board ratify and adopt the tentative agreement reached on June 10, 2024 for the period February 1, 2024 through April 15, 2027. Vote: 7 yes, 0 no.

**Curriculum:** None.

**Business — Serving Lines for Boulan, Larson and Wass Elementary School.** Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Alic that the purchase of serving lines be awarded to Stafford-Smith, Inc. in the amount of $317,179.00 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the Food Service Fund. Vote: 7 yes, 0 no.

**Business — UNOX Ovens for IAE, Larson and Smith Middle School.** Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt that the purchase of three UNOX ovens be awarded to Gold Star Products in the amount of $90,589.75 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the Food Service Fund. Vote: 7 yes, 0 no.

**Public Communication (Non-Agenda Items).** Mr. Walt Storrs, Troy resident, addressed the Board about flooding and poor drainage in the Sylvan Glen subdivision when the Troy Preschool was built; he had met with the City Engineer and requested to sit down with an engineer working on the new Smith Middle School regarding the issue. Alex Karpowitsch, Troy resident, addressed the Board about key performance indicators and provided Board members with copies of a PowerPoint from Detroit Public Schools titled Project 2026 Blueprint showing achievement data. Mrs. Tracy Owens, Troy resident, addressed the Board about special education in the District and informed them that her three children will not be attending Troy Schools next year.

**Other.** No other business items were listed. Board members shared sentiments about the end of the school year and wished everyone a wonderful summer. Dr. Machesky mentioned that several Board members were recognized by the Oakland County School Board Association for their achievements: he congratulated Nancy Philippart for 16 years of service on the Board, Karl Schmidt for serving 12 years on the Board, Emina Alic and Matt Haupt for becoming certified Board members receiving the Award of Merit, Vital Anne for receiving the Master Board of Education Member Award, and the entire Board for receiving the Standard of Excellence Award. He also acknowledged the entire bargaining team for their continued work in coming to an agreement. Mr. Schmidt talked about end of year celebrations and graduations, then spoke about legislative issues, the lack of funding for public schools in the governor's proposed budget, and how hard the MEA is working to get funds for public education. He announced the next Board meeting would be held on July 16th at Central Office at 9:30 in the morning.

**Adjournment.** The meeting adjourned at 8:40 p.m. Respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education.

The 2025 Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) Board of Directors candidate slate, packaged with MASB Bylaws Article IV (Membership) and the association's board-election and email-voting procedures. Included in the Troy School District Board of Education agenda for February 25, 2025. Incumbents are shown in bold in the original.

**Structure of MASB membership (Bylaws Article IV, Section 2)**
The board of education of any public school district in Michigan may become an active member. Active members are divided into eight regions designated by intermediate school district boundaries:
- Region 1: Copper Country ISD, Delta-Schoolcraft ISD, Dickinson-Iron ISD, Eastern Upper Peninsula ISD, Gogebic-Ontonagon ISD, Marquette-Alger RESA, Menominee County ISD

- Region 4: Bay-Arenac ISD, Clare-Gladwin RESD, Clinton County RESA, Gratiot-Isabella RESD, Midland County ESA, Saginaw ISD, Shiawassee RESD

Members are also divided into seven groups by pupil membership: Group I, all intermediate districts; Group II, 0-1,400; Group III, 1,401-2,500; Group IV, 2,501-5,000; Group V, 5,001-11,000; Group VI, 11,001-40,000; Group VII, more than 40,000.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Document and context.** MASB 2025 election materials placed before the Troy School District Board of Education for its meeting of February 25, 2025. The packet combines the Michigan Association of School Boards Bylaws, Article IV (Membership), the table of contents entry for "Board of Directors' Elections - Candidate Information and Email Voting Procedures" (page 4), and the candidate statements headed "2025 ELECTIONS - CANDIDATES FOR MASB BOARD of DIRECTORS." A note states that incumbents are bolded in the original.

**Bylaws, Article IV, Section 2 - Active Members.** The board of education of any public school district in Michigan may become an active member of the association. Active members are divided into eight regions designated according to intermediate school district boundaries. Region 1 comprises Copper Country ISD, Delta-Schoolcraft ISD, Dickinson-Iron ISD, Eastern Upper Peninsula ISD, Gogebic-Ontonagon ISD, Marquette-Alger RESA and Menominee County ISD. Region 2 comprises Alpena-Montmorency-Alcona ESD, Charlevoix-Emmet ISD, Cheboygan-Otsego-Presque Isle ESD, COOR ISD, Iosco RESA, Manistee ISD, Northwest Education Services and Wexford-Missaukee ISD. Region 3 comprises Ionia County ISD, Kent ISD, Mecosta-Osceola ISD, Montcalm Area ISD, Muskegon Area ISD, Newaygo County RESA, Ottawa Area ISD and West Shore ESD. Region 4 comprises Bay-Arenac ISD, Clare-Gladwin RESD, Clinton County RESA, Gratiot-Isabella RESD, Midland County ESA, Saginaw ISD and Shiawassee RESD. Region 5 comprises Genesee ISD, Huron ISD, Lapeer County ISD, Sanilac ISD, St. Clair County RESA and Tuscola ISD. Region 6 comprises Allegan Area ESA, Barry ISD, Berrien RESA, Branch ISD, Calhoun ISD, Heritage Southwest ISD, Kalamazoo RESA, St. Joseph County ISD and Van Buren ISD. Region 7 comprises Eaton RESA, Hillsdale County ISD, Ingham ISD, Jackson County ISD, Lenawee ISD, Livingston ESA, Monroe County ISD and Washtenaw ISD. Region 8 comprises Macomb ISD, Oakland Schools and Wayne RESA - the region in which Troy School District, an Oakland Schools constituent, votes. Active members are also divided into seven groups based on pupil membership: Group I, all intermediate districts; Group II, districts with pupil membership of 0-1,400; Group III, 1,401-2,500; Group IV, 2,501-5,000; Group V, 5,001-11,000; Group VI, 11,001-40,000; and Group VII, more than 40,000.

**Candidate slate.** Candidates are listed with their districts, counties and packet page numbers: TiAnna Harrison, Kalamazoo Public Schools, Kalamazoo County (page 5); Elizabeth O'Dell, St. Joseph County ISD, St. Joseph County (6); Guillermo Z. Lopez, Lansing School District, Ingham County (7); Cory McLaughlin, Jefferson Schools, Monroe County (8); Jack Temsey, Eaton RESA, Eaton County (9); Jason Babbage, Allen Park Public Schools, Wayne County (10); Dr. Anisha Hannah, Pontiac School District, Oakland County (11); Paul Kolin, Bloomfield Hills Schools, Oakland County (12); Roderick Means, Westwood Community School District, Wayne County (13); Randel Meisner, Fitzgerald Public Schools, Macomb County (14); Scott Wallace, Fraser Public Schools (15); Ursula (Wester) Rogers, Romulus Community Schools, Wayne County (16); and Lisa Valerio-Nowc, Clintondale Community Schools, Macomb County (17). The contests named are Region 6 (One-Year Term), Region 7 (Three-Year Term) and Region 8 (Three-Year Term).

**Dr. Anisha Hannah, Pontiac School District, Oakland County (Region 8, three-year term).** She describes education as "the key to unlocking the door of possibilities," argues that too much emphasis has been placed on test scores rather than the whole child, and notes that she is Director of Strategic Partnership & Initiatives with the Pontiac Collective Impact Partnership, leading collaboration among nonprofits, government agencies and educational institutions to improve economic and academic outcomes and supporting Oakland County's goal of 80 by 30. She cites experience as Board President with the City of Pontiac School Board of Education in managing complex budgets and engaging diverse stakeholders, and says she seeks the seat to provide a voice for minority students from lower socioeconomic backgrounds. Her credential block lists 3 years on the board, MASB Certified Boardmember, Award of Merit and Award of Distinction, and offices held as President and Secretary.

**Jason Babbage, Allen Park Public Schools, Wayne County.** An alumnus and lifelong resident of the Allen Park district, he holds a master's degree in automotive systems engineering and a bachelor's degree in mechanical engineering from U-M Dearborn and works at Ford Motor Company as an engineer in exterior automotive lighting, describing himself as one of the top experts in headlamp aim (HLA). He has two children in Allen Park schools, cites his MASB Level 2 award of merit, and identifies unfunded policies, declining enrollment, higher education standards and advances in educational technology as major issues, mentioning sensory rooms and the shift from textbooks to technology. His credential block lists 2 years on the board with the Certified Boardmember Award and Award of Merit.

**Roderick Means, Westwood Community School District, Wayne County.** He centers his vision on equity, innovation and community engagement, and names disparities in educational resources and technology integration as primary concerns. A single parent of two boys, he began as a little league baseball and football coach, served as a Cub and Boy Scout leader from Tiger Cub Coordinator to Cubmaster and assistant Boy Scout leader, and served on high school athletic and booster clubs. For the last 20 years he has worked as an Application Developer at the University of Michigan Ann Arbor. He has served on MASB committees including Government Relations, Bylaws and Policy, and Board Leadership and Training, and as an MASB Board Mentor. His credential block lists 28 years on the board; Certified Boardmember Award, Award of Merit, Award of Distinction, Master Boardmember, Master Diamond, Master Platinum and President's Award; and offices held as President, Vice President, Secretary and Treasurer.

**Paul Kolin, Bloomfield Hills Schools, Oakland County.** He describes education as the cornerstone of society, emphasizes equitable opportunity, removing barriers, supporting educators and innovative practice, and says MASB plays a pivotal role in providing leadership, governance and support to local districts. He references his background in Bloomfield Hills for the last 10 years and prior work as a teacher. His credential block lists 10 years on the board; Certified Boardmember Award, Award of Merit and Award of Distinction; and offices held as President, Vice President, Secretary and Treasurer.

**Randel Meisner, Fitzgerald Public Schools, Macomb County.** His stated concerns are sustainable funding for public education at all levels, teacher retention, teacher shortages, full funding for special education, and offsetting the MPSERS cost. His experience includes the MISD Legislative Committee, MISD Budget Review, annual legislative strategic planning sessions, and attendance at state Annual Leadership Conferences and National School Board Conferences; he has been awarded the MASB President's Award. His credential block lists 12 years on the board; Certified Boardmember Award, Award of Merit, Award of Distinction, Master Boardmember, Master Diamond, Master Platinum and President's Award; and offices held as Vice President, Secretary and Treasurer.

**Scott Wallace, Fraser Public Schools.** He notes that Region 8 includes many students of many different backgrounds, that he and his three children graduated from the district, that he is an Eagle Scout, has coached soccer and basketball, and served four years as an officer on the Board of Directors for the Fraser Soccer Club. He has been President of the Fraser Public Schools Board of Education since 2022 and a board member since 2017, and worked on the MASB legislative committee for three years. His credential block lists 8 years on the board; Certified Boardmember Award, Award of Merit, Award of Distinction and Master Boardmember; and offices held as President, Vice President and Treasurer.

**Lisa Valerio-Nowc, Clintondale Community Schools, Macomb County.** A librarian for over thirty years with school-library and classroom experience, she has been a School Librarian, Library Director of Baker College, and a leader in public libraries, and is currently Assistant Manager/Children's Librarian at the Chaney Branch of the Detroit Public Library. She describes classrooms changing daily with new technology, apps and tools and aims to make her district a safe place to learn and grow. Her credential block lists 2 years on the board, the Certified Boardmember Award and Award of Merit, and Secretary as the office held.

**Ursula (Wester) Rogers, Romulus Community Schools, Wayne County.** She cites disparities in funding, access to resources and growing student mental health needs as the central challenges, particularly for marginalized communities. Her career spans substitute teacher, secretary, human resources professional and school board member, with committee service in policy, human resources, school improvement and curriculum. She has been involved with the Romulus Athletic Club for 24 years as treasurer and cheerleading coach for a youth football organization. Her credential block lists 8 years on the board; Certified Boardmember Award, Award of Merit, Award of Distinction and Master Boardmember; and offices held as President, Secretary and Treasurer.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Administrative presentation to the Troy School District Board of Education on February 25, 2025 by Assistant Superintendents Christine DiPilato (Secondary Instruction) and Kristine Griffor (Elementary Instruction) recommending the Schools of Choice program parameters for 2025-2026. Using Plante Moran Cresa enrollment projections, the administration recommends accepting applications for 52 Section 105 and 6 Section 105C kindergarten students, 25 Section 105 and 1 Section 105C first graders, and 1 Section 105 plus 1 Section 105c student across grades 6-8. President Karl Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. with members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt and Wilson present, Dr. Philippart absent, and roughly 75 members of the audience.
