Meeting and attendance
Regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education, September 17, 2024, at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Present with him were Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt and Wilson; Dr. Philippart was absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Pagel, Jansen, Haezebrouck, Griffor, Trudel and Milanov. Approximately 75 members of the audience attended. Minutes submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary (GH/jh).

Recognitions
- Student representatives to the Board for 2024-2025: Kristian Vitanovich (Troy College and Career High School), Nurayda Albeez (International Academy - East), Diana D'Aloisio (Athens High School) and Adam McManus (Troy High School).
- All-State athletes for spring 2024, recognized by Mr. Jansen: Michelle Baik, Claire Balintfy, Ethan Bieniek, Louis D'Souza, Lauren DeJonckheere, Chase Duncan, Jacob Esser, Dylan Esser, Julian Farrell, Marin Fox, Jason Hamilton, Erin Humphrey, Olivia Jasniewicz, Nainka Jasti, Quinn Kelly, Hannah Lee, Michael Lim, Myles Linden, Nate Linden, Zach Macleish, Vishvaa Ravishankar, Kian Schneeweis, Nika Tananko, Sydney Taylor and Evan Watson.
- Student Spotlight: Thomas Butcher introduced Smith Middle School 7th graders Azra Yildiz and Seowoo Kim, recognized for work in the TSD Creative Guild.
- Michigan Association of School Boards awards presented by Dr. Machesky: Emina Alic and Matt Haupt, Certified Board Member Award and Award of Merit (all Level 1 courses and 45 education credits); Vital Anne, Master Board Member Award (Levels 1, 2 and 3 courses and a minimum of 368 education credits); Karl Schmidt, 12 years of service; Nancy Philippart, 16 years of service; and the TSD Board, Standard of Excellence Award.

Proclamation
On motion by Dr. Wilson, supported by Mrs. Anne, the Board adopted the Oakland Community Health Network proclamation recognizing September 2024 as National Suicide Prevention Month, citing World Suicide Prevention Day on September 10, CDC data that more than 48,000 people die by suicide each year, suicide as the second leading cause of death for ages 10 to 34, fourth for ages 35 to 54 and eighth for ages 55 to 64, and the work of NAMI and the 988 lifeline. Vote: 6 yes, 0 no, Philippart absent. Resolution adopted.

Section 1 update
Chris Bunch, Executive Director of Six Rivers Land Conservancy, updated the Board on the Section 1 Property, Turtle Woods Preserve, reporting that Oakland County Parks revised its new application and that the next Trust Fund Board meeting would be held in October.

Consent agenda
Moved by Mr. Hauff, supported by Mr. Haupt, approving items A through D: minutes of the August 20, 2024 Special Board Meeting, the August 20, 2024 Closed Session, and the August 20, 2024 Board of Education Meeting, plus the Treasurer's Report for July 2024. Vote 6-0, Philippart absent.

Personnel and curriculum
John Pagel, Assistant Superintendent for Employee Services, reported on the hiring process and the factors driving annual teacher hiring, including retirements and resignations, full-year leaves of absence, FTE status and student enrollment; the District hired 31 new teachers this year. The personnel recommendations were approved on motion by Mrs. Alic, supported by Mr. Hauff, 6-0 with Philippart absent. Natalie Haezebrouck, Director of Teaching and Learning, presented on summer professional learning, including curriculum development, the UDL Conference, the administrative kick-off, the TSD Math and Literacy Project for the Pre-K Institute and Troy Institutes K-12, New Teacher Orientation and restorative practices.

Other business
No additions or deletions, no agenda-item public communication and no business items. Three community members addressed the Board during non-agenda public communication, with no action taken. The Board certified Matt Haupt, Gary Hauff, Nicole Wilson and Karl Schmidt as delegates to the MASB 2024 Delegate Assembly on October 24 at 7:00 p.m., with Nancy Philippart as alternate, and approved delegations of no more than four members to the 2025 NSBA Advocacy Institute in Washington, D.C. (February 2-4, 2025) and the 2025 NSBA Annual Conference in Atlanta (April 4-6, 2025). Meeting adjourned at 8:51 p.m.

Minutes of the Troy Board of Education regular board meeting held Tuesday, September 17, 2024 at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan, carried on the October 15, 2024 agenda for approval. President Karl Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt and Wilson were present; Dr. Philippart was absent. Superintendent Machesky attended along with administrators DiPilato, Pagel, Jansen, Haezebrouck, Griffor, Trudel and Milanov. Approximately 75 members of the audience were present. The minutes are signed Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the typing notation GH/jh.

Recognition of student representatives. Mr. Schmidt introduced and welcomed the high school student representatives to the Board for the 2024-2025 school year. Kristian Vitanovich of Troy College and Career High School is a senior, AP student and student leader, a member of the TCC Student Council, a musician and songwriter active in the Music Club, and front man and lead guitarist of the TCC Rock House Band; he learned guitar one year earlier and has taken up cello and piano to advance his songwriting, and plans to attend college with aspirations of becoming a high school teacher. Nurayda Albeez of International Academy - East is a senior pursuing an IB Diploma, a member of the Superintendent Student Advisory Board since her freshman year and its president for the year, president of the IA Student Government, a former State Officer for the Michigan HOSA organization who facilitated statewide leadership conferences, and the recipient of the President's Volunteer Service Gold Award for three consecutive years after completing over 650 hours of community service; she is a former Barnard Bluejay and Baker Bobcat. Diana D'Aloisio of Athens High School is a senior scholar-athlete on the Athens Varsity Girls Golf Team, Vice President of the National Honor Society and a board member of the Athens Spanish Club, who plans to attend an in-state college and pursue a career in the medical field. Adam McManus of Troy High School is a senior serving as Student Government and Leadership Executive Board President, DECA Chapter President, Spanish Club President and a senior board member on the Principal-Student Advisory Board, and represents Troy High School and Oakland County on the Michigan Association of Student Councils and Honor Societies.

All-State athletes, spring 2024. Mr. Jansen and the Board recognized: Michelle Baik, senior, Troy High, girls' tennis; Claire Balintfy, senior, Athens, girls' lacrosse; Ethan Bieniek, freshman, Athens, boys' track; Louis D'Souza, senior, Troy High, boys' track; Lauren DeJonckheere, junior, Athens, girls' soccer; Chase Duncan, junior, Troy High, girls' lacrosse; Jacob Esser, senior, Athens, boys' track; Dylan Esser, senior, Athens, boys' track; Julian Farrell, junior, Athens, boys' track; Marin Fox, senior, Troy High, girls' tennis; Jason Hamilton, junior, Troy High, boys' track; Erin Humphrey, senior, Troy High, girls' lacrosse; Olivia Jasniewicz, sophomore, Troy High, girls' soccer; Nainka Jasti, sophomore, Troy High, girls' tennis; Quinn Kelly, junior, Troy High, boys' track; Hannah Lee, senior, Troy High, girls' tennis; Michael Lim, senior, Troy High, boys' lacrosse; Myles Linden, junior, Athens, boys' track; Nate Linden, sophomore, Athens, boys' track; Zach Macleish, junior, Troy High, boys' lacrosse; Vishvaa Ravishankar, senior, Troy High, boys' track; Kian Schneeweis, junior, Troy High, boys' track; Nika Tananko, senior, Troy High, girls' tennis; Sydney Taylor, senior, Troy High, girls' soccer; and Evan Watson, senior, Athens, boys' track.

Student Spotlight. The Board introduced the year's first Student Spotlight, which recognizes creative achievements in the TSD Creative Guild. Thomas Butcher was invited to the podium to introduce two 7th grade students from Smith Middle School, Azra Yildiz and Seowoo Kim, and to share their work.

National Suicide Prevention Month. Oakland Community Health Network asked school boards throughout Oakland County to partner with it by approving a proclamation designating September as National Suicide Prevention Month at their September board meetings. It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mrs. Anne to adopt the resolution, whose recitals note that September is known as National Suicide Prevention Month, that World Suicide Prevention Day is observed each year on September 10, that suicidal thoughts can affect anyone regardless of age, gender, race, orientation, income level, religion or background, that according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention each year more than 48,000 people died by suicide, that suicide is the second leading cause of death for people 10 to 34 years of age, the fourth leading cause among people 35 to 54 years of age and the eighth leading cause among people 55 to 64 years of age, that organizations such as the National Alliance on Mental Illness and the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, 988, work to help individuals in crisis, and that OCHN is committed to being a Zero Suicide organization. The resolved clause records that Oakland Community Health Network recognizes September 2024 as National Suicide Prevention Month and calls upon individuals, government agencies, public and private institutions, businesses, faith-based organizations and schools to recommit to increasing awareness and understanding of suicide prevention. Vote: yes 6, no 0, absent Philippart. Resolution adopted.

Michigan Association of School Boards awards. Dr. Machesky presented the Board with honors received during the past year. Trustees Emina Alic and Matt Haupt were recognized for the Certified Board Member Award and Award of Merit, requiring completion of all Level 1 courses and 45 education credits. Vital Anne was recognized for the Master Board Member Award, requiring completion of Levels 1, 2 and 3 courses and a minimum of 368 education credits. President Karl Schmidt was recognized for 12 years of dedicated service and Trustee Nancy Philippart for 16 years of dedicated service. The entire Board was congratulated for earning the Standard of Excellence Award, placing the Troy Board of Education among a handful of Michigan school district governing bodies demonstrating commitment to student achievement and exemplary leadership, with the minutes noting the Troy community is fortunate to have seven Board members committed to life-long learning and positive policy making.

Additions and deletions: none. Public communication on agenda items: none. Business: none.

Section 1 update. Mr. Chris Bunch, Executive Director for Six Rivers Land Conservancy, provided an update on the Section 1 Property, Turtle Woods Preserve. He indicated that Oakland County Parks revised their new application and that the next Trust Fund Board meeting will be held in October.

General consent agenda. Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B, C and D on the consent agenda: minutes of the August 20, 2024 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the August 20, 2024 Closed Session Meeting; minutes of the August 20, 2024 Board of Education Meeting; and the Treasurer's Report for July 2024. Vote: yes 6, no 0, absent Philippart.

Personnel, staffing update. John Pagel, Assistant Superintendent for Employee Services, shared a report on the District's hiring process and the factors influencing the number of teachers hired each year, including retirements and resignations, full-year leaves of absence, FTE status and student enrollment. This year the District hired 31 new teachers. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Hauff that the Board approve the personnel recommendations as stated. The new hires listed are Sara Abrin, Lauren Alarie, Hailey Ateek, Kelly Barker, Alyssa Baxendale, Benjamin Borglin, Britiany Bowers, Bradley Ciaramitaro, Isabella Contesti, Brittany Cwiertniewicz, Lillian DeLyon, Jenna Demeter, Riley Frazier, Heidi Haligowski, Lora Herbert, Tanille Hill, Madison Hutchins, Hannah Jackowicz, Steve Johansson, Monika Kitchen, Breanne Massie, Devron Minor, Alice Ochoa, Colleen Osis, Kirsten Paik, Stephanie Pindar, Shauna Pruess, Faith Pustover, Katie Schrepferman, Lauren Walkley and Kevin White. Vote: yes 6, no 0, absent Philippart.

Curriculum, summer learning. Director of Teaching and Learning Natalie Haezebrouck shared a PowerPoint presentation on the District's summer professional learning, covering summer curriculum development, participation at the UDL (Universal Design for Learning) Conference, the administrative kick-off meeting, and the TSD Math and Literacy Project for the Pre-K Institute and Troy Institutes K-12. She reported that New Teacher Orientation week went well and discussed restorative practices for building teams and future ready learning environments. Board members discussed the new calendar and their satisfaction that it is more culturally responsive; Ms. Haezebrouck noted that tool kits will be provided to help teachers respond to students and the diverse cultures in the school community. There was also discussion of the new furniture and the possibility of hosting job-embedded learning opportunities in buildings that have piloted it.

Public communication, non-agenda items. Three community members addressed the Board; no action was taken.

Reports from high school student representatives. Nurayda Albeez (International Academy - East), Kristian Vitanovich (Troy College and Career High School), Diana D'Aloisio (Athens High School) and Adam McManus (Troy High School) each reported on events and activities at their schools.

Other business. Moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Anne that the Troy Board of Education certify Matt Haupt, Gary Hauff, Nicole Wilson and Karl Schmidt as delegates to the MASB 2024 Delegate Assembly on October 24 at 7:00 p.m., with Nancy Philippart as alternate. Vote: yes 6, no 0, absent Philippart. Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mrs. Alic that the Board approve a delegation of no more than four Board members as representatives at the 2025 NSBA Advocacy Institute in Washington, D.C., February 2-4, 2025. Vote: yes 6, no 0, absent Philippart. Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Board approve a delegation of no more than four Board members as representatives at the 2025 NSBA Annual Conference for Public Education Leaders in Atlanta, Georgia, April 4-6, 2025. Vote: yes 6, no 0, absent Philippart.

Board comments and adjournment. Board members welcomed new staff and welcomed everyone back to the start of the school year. **Presentation:** HS Course Description Book Updates, Troy School District Board of Education, February 6, 2024.

**Course updates (existing offerings)**
- Alignment of Computer Science
- Renaming of Business courses: Marketing 2; Marketing Field Study Co-Op; Junior Business Field Study Co-Op; Senior Business Field Study Co-Op

**New courses proposed**
| Area | Courses |
|---|---|
| Art/History | AP Art History |
| Science | Chemistry 1 & Chemistry 2; Physics 1 & Physics 2; Engineering Physics; Environmental Science: Human Impact |
| English | English 10 |
| Social Studies | Stories of Yourself & Others |
| Business | Digital Business; Business Law & Management |

**Selected course specifications**
- AP Art History: Grades 11-12, 2 semesters, 1/2 credit per semester, no retake; prerequisite World History/Geography 1 and American History/Geography 1 & 2. Built on 250 works of art from prehistory to the present; equivalent to a two-semester introductory college art history survey.
- Stories of Yourself & Others: Grade 12, 1 semester, 1/2 ELA credit and 1/2 History credit, no retake; same prerequisites. Interdisciplinary, inquiry-based course on storytelling and narrative through the lens of Reconstruction history, using Socratic Seminar discussion and a culminating student research project.
- Digital Business: Grades 9-12, 1 semester, 1/2 credit, no retake, no prerequisite. Uses Microsoft Office (Word, Excel, PowerPoint), Wordpress, Canva, and responsible/ethical use of AI systems, with the goal of Microsoft Office Specialist certification.
- Business Law & Management: Grades 9-12, 1 semester, 1/2 credit, no retake, no prerequisite. Covers global trade, quality management, organizational structure, human resource law, workplace ethics, torts, negligence, contracts, fraud, and legal requirements for starting a business.
- English 10: 2 semesters, 1 credit, 1/2 credit per semester; required for all 10th grade students. Builds on English 9; multimodal texts, analytical lenses, real-world writing, book clubs, independent reading plan; summer reading required.

**Science**
New State of Michigan graduation requirements drove new course development, affecting the class of 2027 (this year's freshmen) and beyond. Board of Education visits were made to Athens High School and Troy High School. All graduation-required courses are designed for all students around NGSS standards, shifting toward "students figuring out science" with emphasis on inquiry and design.

**ELA pilot results (first quarter of 10 Honors)**

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Troy High | 154 of 190 | 117 (76%) | 28 (18%) | 9 (6%) |

**CommonLit assessment (grades 6-12 outcome measure)**
Each assessment has three reading passages with multiple-choice comprehension questions.

| Group | Submitted count | Pre-assessment (September) | Mid-year (December/January) |
|---|---|---|---|

HS Course Description Book Updates, presented to the Troy School District Board of Education at its February 6, 2024 meeting, sets out proposed changes to the high school course catalog across Computer Science, Business, Science, English Language Arts, Social Studies and Art, together with changes to graduation requirements.

OVERVIEW OF COURSE UPDATES
The overview section lists alignment of Computer Science and the renaming of Business courses, specifically Marketing 2, Marketing Field Study Co-Op, Junior Business Field Study Co-Op, and Senior Business Field Study Co-Op.

NEW COURSES
The new courses are grouped by department: Art/History - AP Art History; Science - Chemistry 1 & Chemistry 2, Physics 1 & Physics 2, Engineering Physics, and Environmental Science: Human Impact; English - English 10; Social Studies - Stories of Yourself & Others; Business - Digital Business and Business Law & Management.

AP Art History is offered in grades 11-12 over 2 semesters for 1/2 credit per semester with no retake, and carries the prerequisite of World History/Geography 1 and American History/Geography 1 & 2. The course description states that it welcomes students into the global art world to engage with its forms and content as they research, discuss, read and write about art, artists, art making, and responses to and interpretations of art. Students investigate 250 works of art characterized by diverse artistic traditions from prehistory to the present, developing in-depth, holistic understanding of the history of art from a global perspective, and apply skills of visual, contextual and comparative analysis. The course is described as the equivalent of a two-semester introductory college or university art history survey course.

Stories of Yourself & Others is a grade 12, one-semester course granting 1/2 ELA credit and 1/2 History credit, with no retake and the prerequisite of World History/Geography 1 and American History/Geography 1 & 2. It is an interdisciplinary, inquiry-based course exploring the power of storytelling, writing and narrative through the lens of Reconstruction history. Students investigate the role of identity in marginalized communities during the Reconstruction Era by evaluating and synthesizing primary and secondary resources; fiction and non-fiction narratives modeling self-reflection and storytelling are read and discussed in a Socratic Seminar format. The course culminates in a student research project into the student's own history and identity or a self-selected marginalized group, presented in a medium of the student's choice.

Digital Business is open to grades 9-12, runs one semester for 1/2 credit, has no retake and no prerequisite. Students work with hands-on business applications using Microsoft Office, blogging and website-building platforms such as Wordpress, online graphic design programs such as Canva, and the responsible and ethical use of AI systems. Coverage includes Word, Excel and PowerPoint, with the goal that students become certified through the Microsoft Office Specialist Program. Students use the three applications to create documents, presentations and spreadsheets in a "mock" business setting. Resumes, cover letters, interview skills, presentation skills and career search skills are discussed, along with introductory business topics such as data analysis for business decisions, planning tools to guide organizational and departmental activities, and developing policies and procedures to protect workplace security.

Business Law & Management is open to grades 9-12, runs one semester for 1/2 credit, with no retake and no prerequisite. Over a semester students study law and management topics relating to the business industry. Management content covers the impacts of global trade, managing internal and external business relationships to foster positive interactions, the nature and scope of quality management practices within a business, and designing organizational structure to facilitate business activities. Legal content covers current human resource laws and regulations, ethical behaviors in the workplace, torts, negligence, contracts and fraud, and legal requirements for starting a business.

SCIENCE UPDATES
The high school science course update section notes that new graduation requirements from the State of Michigan resulted in the development of new courses, and that this affects the class of 2027 and beyond - identified in the presentation as this year's freshmen. The section references Board of Education visits to Athens High School (AHS) and Troy High School (THS). All graduation-required courses are designed for all students around the NGSS standards, with a shift toward "students figuring out science" and an emphasis on inquiry and design. A slide titled HS Science Pathways accompanies the section.

ENGLISH LANGUAGE ARTS UPDATES
The ELA process review lists Class of 2027 ninth grade parent presentations in Spring 2023, publication of the pathway on the district website in March 2023, Board of Education visits in October 2023, teacher reflections, and input from ELA department heads, ELA coaches, ninth grade ELA teachers, tenth grade LC/LCH teachers and 11 AP teachers.

English 10 spans 2 semesters for 1 credit, at 1/2 credit per semester, and is required for all 10th grade students. Completion of both the ninth and tenth grade foundational English courses is intended to prepare students to engage with future English courses, including Advanced Placement courses. The course builds on foundational skills established in English 9, expands critical thinking using multimodal texts and analytical lenses, and engages students in real-world writing tasks to develop voice and argumentation with consideration for purpose and audience. In addition to whole-class selections and book clubs, students select reading goals to develop an independent reading plan. Summer reading is required.

REPORT CARD DATA FROM THE ELA 9 PILOT
Student grades in 10 Honors for students coming from the English 9 pilot were reported for the first quarter. At Troy High, 154 of 190 students who moved from the English 9 pilot to 10 Honors earned: A, 117 students (76%); B, 28 students (18%); C or lower, 9 students (6%). At Athens High School, 67 of 87 students who moved from the English 9 pilot to 10 Honors earned: A, 42 students (63%); B, 20 students (30%); C or lower, 5 students (7%). The presentation states that approximately 94% of students who participated in the ELA 9 ungrouped pilot and matriculated to 10 LC Honors earned an A or B for Q1.

COMMONLIT ASSESSMENT
CommonLit is presented as the measure of outcomes for students in grades 6-12. Each CommonLit Assessment is composed of three reading passages, each accompanied by a set of multiple-choice comprehension questions measuring reading comprehension. CommonLit is described as a data tool used to identify whether students are progressing in the attainment of grade level standards, to inform classroom instruction, and to create and measure goal setting for students. The reported figures cover submitted count, the pre-assessment scaled score in September, and the mid-year assessment scaled score in December/January. Tenth grade nationally across CommonLit: submitted count 98101, pre-assessment 196, mid-year 202. Tenth grade across TSD: submitted count 847, pre-assessment 200, mid-year 206. Tenth grade Honors currently in the pilot: submitted count 187, pre-assessment 206, mid-year 215.

DATA REVIEW GOING FORWARD
Additional measures identified include PSAT 9 data, to be reviewed this summer when released; continued monitoring of PSAT 10 and SAT 11 data as curriculum is built for tenth and eleventh grade; monitoring of AP Lit and AP Language enrollment and outcome scores as students progress into eleventh and twelfth grade; and student, teacher and parent surveys.

TEACHER REFLECTIONS AND IMPLEMENTATION PLAN
Staff met with teachers in grades 9, 10 and 11 AP to reflect on current implementation of ELA 9 and to plan implementation of ELA 10, with successes and challenges informing next steps. For ELA 10 development and implementation, the curriculum team has developed three comprehensive units, three additional units will be developed in the spring, summer work will include opportunities for revision, and all students will be enrolled in ELA 10 for the 2024-25 school year.

The plan of support includes, for spring: two days of job-embedded work for ELA grade 9, three planning days for the English 10 Curriculum Development Team, on-site visits with a staff developer, grade 9 lab learning, and grade 10 support for the writing process for units. Summer support includes the Homegrown Institute and unit unpacking. Next year includes continued job-embedded learning for ninth and tenth grade, continued support of coaching positions at both high schools, and continued partnership with staff developers.

GRADUATION REQUIREMENTS
Changes include the inclusion of Personal Finance for the class of 2028. Personal Finance standards will be embedded into Economics and AP Economics. Personal Finance must be indicated as a graduation requirement and grant 0.5 credit on a student's transcript, effective for the class of 2028; students do not enroll in economics until grade 11. On flexibility, the presentation cites high levels of flexibility at TCCHS, flexibility at AHS and THS, opportunities for a math-related fourth year, CTE, and the Personal Finance 0.5 credit, which can count in lieu of a variety of graduation requirements for the class of 2028, along with a commitment to continued learning and collaboration in making recommendations.

RESOURCES FOR FAMILIES
The presentation directs families to the Teaching and Learning website and notes an upcoming parent night for future tenth grade parents.

Item 4.a., Recommendations for Schools of Choice for the 2024-2025 School Year, was presented by Rick West, Deputy Superintendent, to the Troy School District Board of Education for the February 6, 2024 meeting. The packet includes a memorandum dated Tuesday, February 27, 2024, addressed to the TSD Board of Education from Rick West, Deputy Superintendent, on the subject of Schools of Choice Recommendations for the 2024-2025 School Year.

PROGRAM DESCRIPTION
Schools of Choice provides non-resident students with additional enrollment opportunities. Participation in Schools of Choice is optional for districts, and the degree and extent of participation are determined at the local level, including application enrollment dates, grade levels and building assignment.

ELEMENTARY ENROLLMENT PROJECTIONS SUBMITTED BY PLANTE MORAN CRESA
Projections and actuals for kindergarten and first grade are reported by school year. For 2021/2022, the kindergarten "Most Likely" projection was 845 (765 Kdg / 80 PreK) against an actual of 803 (723 Kdg / 80 PreK) as of 1/27/22, and the first grade "Most Likely" projection was 851 against an actual of 792 as of 1/27/22. For 2022/2023, the kindergarten "Most Likely" projection was 807 (737 Kdg / 70 PreK) against an actual of 881 (811 Kdg / 70 PreK) as of 1/27/23, with first grade "Most Likely" of 820 and actual of 762 as of 1/27/23. SUBGROUP DATA
By subgroup, English Learner students number 27 among SOC students (14.36% of SOC, change -4.07%) and 1,321 among non-SOC students (26.98% of non-SOC, change -0.91%). Free/Reduced Lunch students number 48 among SOC (25.53%, change 0.65%) and 803 among non-SOC (16.40%, change 2.52%). Special Education students number 24 among SOC (12.77%, change 2.17%) and 564 among non-SOC (11.52%, change 1.84%).

GRADE-LEVEL DATA
By grade for 2023-2024: TSD preK, 0 SOC and 90 non-SOC, 0.00%, change 0.00%; Kindergarten, 15 SOC and 712 non-SOC, 2.06%, change -0.65%; First, 22 SOC and 821 non-SOC, 2.61%, change -2.64%; Second, 38 SOC and 757 non-SOC, 4.78%, change -0.45%; Third, 39 SOC and 809 non-SOC, 4.60%, change 0.35%; Fourth, 34 SOC and 825 non-SOC, 3.96%, change -0.61%; Fifth, 40 SOC and 883 non-SOC, 4.33%, change 0.54%. Totals are 188 SOC (100%) and 4,897 non-SOC (100%), with change shown as NA.

NON-SCHOOLS OF CHOICE ENROLLMENT BY GRADE, 2023-2024
Non-SOC students by grade are reported as kindergarten 802*, first 821, second 757, third 809, fourth 825, fifth 883, sixth 948, seventh 918, eighth 885, ninth 869, tenth 956, eleventh 985 and twelfth 1008, for a total of 11,466. The asterisk indicates that the kindergarten total includes TSD PreK (Dev Kdg).

KINDERGARTEN AND FIRST GRADE HISTORY
A fifteen-year history of kindergarten and first grade enrollment is provided: 2009-2010, 739 and 817; 2010-2011, 752 and 785; 2011-2012, 727 and 832; 2012-2013, 768 and 795; 2013-2014, 766 and 814; 2014-2015, 700 and 787; 2015-2016, 755 and 728; 2016-2017, 798 and 769; 2017-2018, 812 and 845; 2018-2019, 800 and 871; 2019-2020, 792 and 845; 2020-2021, 734* and 785; 2021-2022, 764* and 744; 2022-2023, 859* and 722; and 2023-2024, 802* and 821. Asterisked kindergarten totals include TSD PreK (Dev Kdg).

SIBLING PREFERENCE PROJECTION
A survey was emailed to current Schools of Choice families requesting information on siblings who would be eligible for kindergarten, first grade, and sixth, seventh and eighth grade for the 2024-2025 school year. The results: 11 kindergarten students plan to attend, 1 first grade student plans to attend, and 7 middle school students plan to attend across sixth, seventh and eighth grades (2 in sixth grade, 4 in seventh grade, 1 in eighth grade).

MEMORANDUM AND RECOMMENDATIONS
The memorandum reproduces prior-year language describing factors considered for the 2016-2017 school year, which included current enrollment; enrollment projections, patterns and trends; numbers and percentages of Schools of Choice students currently in the district; projected numbers of Schools of Choice siblings age-eligible to enter the district in 2016-2017 if a "Limited" number of kindergarten, first and sixth through eighth grade students at Baker Middle School were admitted; and available elementary classrooms. That earlier recommendation was to use Fred Ignatovich's 1.5 enrollment projection numbers with his recommended formula (most likely + low/2) as the foundation; to accept SOC applications for 100 kindergarten and 30 first grade students, admitting 100 kindergartners initially with the option of admitting additional students in the third week of August if space allowed; to limit SOC kindergarten applicants to the full-day kindergarten program; and to accept "Sibling Preference" applications only for siblings of current SOC students, to attend Baker Middle School only, where estimated enrollment for the following year approximated 728 and accepting 15 applications during the initial application process would bring the district extremely close to an ideal total student population at Baker. It also noted that actual enrollment as of the February Count for both kindergarten and first grade was above both Mr. Ignatovich's "Most Likely" and "Low" 2015-16 projections, referenced in "Document 1."

For the 2024-2025 school year, the factors considered were current enrollment across the Troy School District; enrollment projections, patterns and trends; numbers and percentages of Schools of Choice students currently in the district; projected numbers of Schools of Choice siblings age-eligible to enter the district in 2024-2025 if a "Limited" number of kindergarten, first and sixth through eighth grade students were admitted under Schools of Choice; and available elementary classrooms.

After analyzing the data and factors, the recommendation is that the district use Plante Moran Cresa enrollment projection numbers as the foundation for determining the number of Schools of Choice students to admit for the 2024-2025 school year, and accept SOC applications for 11 kindergarten, 1 first grade and 7 middle school students. The memorandum states that based on the number of kindergarten applications received for the 2024-2025 school year, the district anticipates attracting many more than 11 applicants; this approach would allow the district to admit 11 kindergarteners initially, with the option of admitting additional students in the third week of August if space allows. Middle school students would be placed in a building according to available space.

Eight proposals, four in classroom instruction and four in non-instructional support, carry $3,229,885 in combined annual savings. The stated rationale is cost growth outpacing enrollment: special education costs rose 74%, from $16,744,610 in 2018–2019 to $29,210,999 in 2024–2025, an increase of $12,466,389, while the number of students served moved from 1,332 to 1,367.

Board Narrative Summary — Special Education Budget Reductions, Proposed Reduction Scenario, June 2026, Troy School District.

**Method**
Each proposal was evaluated across six weighted criteria: impact on student learning, equity, legal and compliance risk, cost savings, feasibility, and stakeholder support. Weighted scores placed each proposal into a tier. Tier 1 = strong candidate (4.0–5.0); Tier 2 = consider (3.0–3.9); Tier 3 = high risk, requires further study (below 3.0). Savings figures reflect actual FTE and actual dollar savings as entered in the scoring matrix.

**Why special education is in the reduction scenario**
Costs grew far faster than the population served over the six-year window cited.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Titled "Board Narrative Summary — Special Education Budget Reductions, Proposed Reduction Scenario" and dated June 2026, the paper explains to the Troy School District Board of Education how the proposed special education reductions were developed and how those specific reductions connect to the broader budget plan presented to the Board. It opens by stating that special education remains one of the district's highest priorities and one of its largest areas of investment.

SCORING METHOD AND TIER DEFINITIONS
The proposals were produced through the district's structured scoring process. Each was evaluated across six weighted criteria: impact on student learning, equity, legal and compliance risk, cost savings, feasibility, and stakeholder support. Weighted scores then determined tier placement. Tier 1 is defined as a strong candidate, scoring 4.0–5.0; Tier 2 as "consider," scoring 3.0–3.9; Tier 3 as high risk, requiring further study, scoring below 3.0. The summary states that savings figures reflect actual FTE and actual dollar savings as entered in the scoring matrix.

WHY SPECIAL EDUCATION IS PART OF THE CONVERSATION
The narrative attributes the inclusion of special education in the reduction scenario to six years of cost growth that is described as no longer sustainable within the district's structural budget. Between 2018–2019 and 2024–2025, special education costs rose 74% — an increase of more than $12.4 million — while the number of students served grew by only 3%. The accompanying comparison table reports Special Education Costs (IEP and non-IEP) of $16,744,610 in 2018–2019 and $29,210,999 in 2024–2025, a change of +$12,466,389 (74%); and Special Education Student Count of 1,332 in 2018–2019 and 1,367 in 2024–2025, a change of +35 (3%). The gap between cost growth and enrollment growth is identified as the central reason special education is included in the scenario.

A second driver is a state-led shift in how certain special education services are delivered. Several of the proposals align district staffing to new county-level service plans and county targets. Taken together, the reductions are described as intended to right-size staffing to current requirements while preserving the services students are entitled to.

COMMITMENTS TO STUDENTS
The summary states that the district's core obligations to students with disabilities do not change. All special education programs will continue to be staffed in alignment with state and county requirements, including certified teachers, paraprofessionals, and related service providers. Decisions are guided by each student's Individualized Education Program (IEP) and are mandated to comply with all legal and educational standards. As the district adapts to the state-led shift in service delivery, it will continue to provide services based on IEP needs and state requirements while making responsible adjustments to ensure the long-term sustainability of its programs.

SUMMARY OF PROPOSED REDUCTIONS
The proposed reductions fall into two categories, classroom instruction and non-instructional supports. Special Education – Classroom Instruction comprises 4 proposals with annual savings of $1,396,573 and a tier mix of 2 Tier 1 / 1 Tier 2 / 1 Tier 3. Special Education – Non-Instructional comprises 4 proposals with annual savings of $1,833,312 and a tier mix of 2 / 2 / 0. Total Special Education Reductions are stated as 8 proposals, $3,229,885 in annual savings, with a tier mix of 4 / 3 / 1.

CLASSROOM INSTRUCTION REDUCTIONS — $1,396,573
These proposals adjust instructional special education staffing to align with new county-level service plans and county staffing targets. Three of the four are described as strong or consider-level candidates; one — the adjustment of Teacher Consultant and Resource Room (TC/RR) staff to county targets — carries the highest risk in the special education set and is flagged for further Board discussion. The itemized proposals are:
• Adjust TC/RR staff to meet county targets (3.7 Elementary, 3.6 Secondary) — annual savings $635,100, weighted score 2.95, Tier 3, status "Flag for review."
• Teacher reduction based on new county level plan (3 L4, 1 ECP) — annual savings $348,000, score 4.10, Tier 1, status "Recommended."
• Paraprofessional reduction based on new county level plan — annual savings $236,270, score 4.10, Tier 1, status "Recommended."
• Elementary Resource Room paraprofessionals reduction — annual savings $177,203, score 3.85, Tier 2, status "Consider."
The subtotal for the category is $1,396,573. The narrative repeats that the TC/RR adjustment is the only Tier 3 proposal in the special education set, with a weighted score of 2.95, and that per the scoring framework it warrants further study before adoption.

NON-INSTRUCTIONAL REDUCTIONS — $1,833,312
These proposals reduce non-instructional support staffing. The largest single special education reduction in the entire scenario sits in this category: the reduction of general education Student Support Aides from 158 to 104 FTE, which the narrative says accounts for more than $1.3 million in savings. The remaining proposals adjust social worker, psychologist, and clerical staffing. The itemized proposals are:
• Student Support Aide – Gen Ed (from 158 to 104 FTE) — annual savings $1,334,362, score 4.15, Tier 1, status "Recommended."
• Social Workers reduction (from 24.4 to 21.4 FTE) — annual savings $348,000, score 3.90, Tier 2, status "Consider."
• Psychologist reduction (from 10 to 9 FTE) — annual savings $116,000, score 3.90, Tier 2, status "Consider."
• Special Education Secretary — annual savings $34,951, score 4.35, Tier 1, status "Recommended."
The subtotal for the category is $1,833,312. The narrative notes that the social worker and psychologist reductions are Tier 2 (consider) proposals and may benefit from phased implementation.

RISK AND PLANNING CONSIDERATIONS
Of the eight special education proposals, four are Tier 1 (recommended), three are Tier 2 (consider, with additional planning), and one is Tier 3 (high risk). In practical terms, the narrative states that the four Tier 1 proposals — totaling roughly $1.95 million — are strong candidates with low risk and high feasibility and are recommended for inclusion; that the three Tier 2 proposals — the Elementary Resource Room paraprofessional, social worker, and psychologist reductions — may be included with additional planning, communication, or phased implementation; and that the single Tier 3 proposal, the TC/RR staffing adjustment to county targets, is flagged for further Board conversation before it is adopted. It adds that proposals scoring below 4.0 may still be included if savings are critical to meeting the reduction goal, but that they require additional planning, communication, and mitigation efforts.

HOW THE REDUCTIONS FIT THE OVERALL PLAN
Because special education is governed by IEPs and by state and county requirements, the proposals were scored with particular attention to legal and compliance risk and to equity impact. The stated intent is to bring staffing back into alignment with current service requirements and the state-led delivery model — not to reduce services students are entitled to receive — while contributing meaningfully toward closing the structural budget gap.

Regular meeting minutes of the Troy Board of Education for Tuesday, June 16, 2026, held at the Troy School District Services Building (Service Center), 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:18 p.m. In addition to Mrs. Anne, Board members Alic, Melton, Potts, and Zendler were present; Mr. Haupt and Dr. Philippart were absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Moran, Anderson, Montante, Pagel, and Trudel. Approximately 50 members of the audience attended. The meeting opened with the Pledge of Allegiance and adjourned at 9:03 p.m.

PUBLIC HEARING: 2026/2027 PROPOSED BUDGET
Mr. Trudel shared an overview of the 2025-2026 final budget amendments as well as the 2026-2027 budget proposals. His presentation addressed taxable values, the Headlee amendment, homestead millage comparisons, general fund versus ancillary funds, the capital project fund, the common debt fund, the sinking fund, the capital maintenance fund, special revenue funds, the food service fund, the Troy Career Center fund, the community service fund, the Troy Preschool fund, and the student activities fund.

RECOGNITION: RESOLUTION IN SUPPORT OF GUN SAFETY AND SAFE GUN STORAGE
Moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Alic. The whereas clauses state that the safety and well-being of students, teachers, and staff is a top priority in the Troy School District; that firearms are now the leading cause of death among U.S. children and adolescents due to rising rates of homicide, suicide, and unintentional shootings, compounded by social inequities, increased access to guns, and insufficient safety measures; that rates of death from firearms among ages 14 to 17 are higher than motor vehicle-related death rates, and that middle and high school age children in the U.S. are now more likely to die as the result of a firearm injury than from any other single cause of death; that according to a report from the US Secret Service, in incidents of gun violence on school grounds 76% of attackers acquired a firearm from the home of a parent or another close relative; that since 2025 there have been over 240 unintentional shootings by children, resulting in 39 deaths and 72 injuries nationally; that more than 28,000 Americans are estimated to have died by suicide using firearms in 2025; that research indicates close to 5 million US children live in a home with a loaded and unlocked firearm; that evidence strongly suggests secure firearm storage is an essential component of any effective strategy to keep the community safe; that keeping students, teachers, and staff safe from the threat of gun violence should be the responsibility of all adult stakeholders within the school district; and that preventative measures require action now.

The resolved clauses direct the Superintendent to periodically communicate the importance of safe firearm storage and other firearm safety and violence prevention measures during gun violence awareness month, and to disseminate material on an annual basis stressing the importance of secure storage of firearms by including it in the district's annual notification materials; commit the Board and Superintendent to continue working with local law enforcement agencies, medical and mental health agencies, and non-profit organizations to inform district parents of their obligations regarding secure storage of firearms in their homes as well as other gun violence prevention safety measures; and state that the resolution shall not be construed to conflict with any existing Michigan or federal law. The vote was Yes 5, No 0, with Haupt and Philippart absent; the resolution was declared adopted. A certification by Matt Haupt, Secretary, Board of Education, attests that the resolution was duly adopted at a regular meeting held on the 16th day of June, 2026, conducted with public notice given in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act, being Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976.

RESOLUTION URGING PASSAGE OF THE 2026/2027 SCHOOL AID BUDGET BY JULY 1ST
Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Zendler. The whereas clauses note that with only two weeks remaining in the fiscal year for schools the Legislature had not yet passed a School Aid Budget; that last year the budget was not passed until after the Constitutional October 1 deadline, forcing districts to make critical staffing and programming decisions based on speculation rather than certainty, and that without a budget schools cannot responsibly plan for staffing, class sizes, transportation, or essential services; that Troy School District is legally obligated to complete its budget by the end of June and will fulfill that obligation, but without certainty from Lansing will again be forced to consider freezing programs, delaying hires, and laying off staff; that the framework for a responsible School Aid fund budget already exists within the three proposals under consideration; that focus should remain on passing a responsible, balanced budget rather than beginning discussions on major reforms, with significant property tax changes or other structural changes deserving thorough debate separate from the budget; and that policymakers must complete a School Aid budget including an inflationary increase to the foundation allowance, weighted funding for at-risk and ELL students, an end to the diversion of K12 dollars away from the classroom, and a fix to school safety and mental health funding. The resolved clauses call on the Legislature and the Governor to pass the School Aid Budget before July 1 and direct that a copy be forwarded to the district's representatives in the Michigan House of Representatives and the Michigan Senate as well as the Governor's office. The vote was Yes 5, No 0, with Haupt and Philippart absent; the motion was declared adopted, certified by Matt Haupt, Secretary.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A letter dated June 15, 2026 from Matt Jansen, Troy School District Director of Athletics, Continuing Education and Enrichment, asks the MHSAA Executive Board to waive the cooperative team enrollment limitation so Troy High School and Troy Athens High School may form a combined "Troy United" boys lacrosse program beginning in 2026-27. The two schools' combined enrollment of 3,936 students exceeds the enrollment cap established for cooperative agreements. The request is framed by a projected $12.1 million district budget deficit and by declining participation, with only 41 players projected to return across the two programs before incoming freshmen.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Document**
Letter dated June 15, 2026 to the Members of the MHSAA Executive Board, on Troy School District District Athletics letterhead — Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D., Superintendent of Schools; Matt Jansen, Director, Athletics; 1522 E. Big Beaver Rd., Troy, Michigan 48083; 248.823.5154, fax 248.823.5133. Signed by Matt Jansen, Director of Athletics, Continuing Education and Enrichment.

**Request**
Approval of a waiver to the current cooperative team enrollment limitation to allow Troy High School and Troy Athens High School to form a cooperative boys lacrosse program beginning with the 2026-27 school year, operating as a single "Troy United" program.

**Enrollment**

| School | Enrollment |
| --- | --- |
| Troy High School | 2,127 |
| Troy Athens High School | 1,809 |
| Combined | 3,936 |

The combined figure exceeds the enrollment cap established for cooperative agreements, which is why a waiver is sought.

**Financial context**
The district is facing a projected $12.1 million budget deficit entering the 2026-27 school year. As part of district-wide reductions, the Athletics Department has been tasked with reducing expenditures by approximately $100,000. The district recently discontinued financial support for non-MHSAA sanctioned sports, including synchronized swimming and boys and girls water polo; those programs moved to self-funded club status, generating approximately $50,000 in annual savings. A cooperative boys lacrosse program would provide an estimated annual savings of approximately $25,000.

**Participation**

| Measure | Troy High School | Troy Athens High School |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2026 season participants | 48 | 31 |
| Graduating seniors | 21 | 13 |
| Projected returning participants | 26 | 15 |

Combined returning participation is stated as 41 players before the addition of incoming freshmen. Of the 15 projected returners at Athens, only one participated at the varsity level during the 2026 season; the remaining 14 had never played lacrosse prior to 2026. Athens attempted to field both varsity and junior varsity teams but could not consistently maintain enough healthy student-athletes to sustain junior varsity competition through the season.

**Program stability**
Following the 2026 season, the Troy Athens varsity boys lacrosse coach informed the district of his decision to step down, citing as a significant factor the ongoing difficulty of building and sustaining a program with limited participation. Troy Athens has historically participated in a cooperative arrangement with Avondale Schools, which in recent years has yielded no more than two players annually and contributed no participants during the 2026 season; the letter concludes that partnership is no longer viable.

**Precedent cited**
Within the Oakland Activities Association and surrounding communities: Farmington and North Farmington; Royal Oak and Berkley; Birmingham Groves and Birmingham Seaholm; Waterford Mott and Waterford Kettering; Milford and Lakeland; the Livonia Public Schools combined program; South Lyon's combined program; Bishop Foley and Clawson; Brandon and Holly; the St. Clair Shores cooperative program; and Eisenhower and Utica.

**Position**
The letter states the request is not intended to create a competitive advantage but to preserve participation opportunities, maintain both varsity and junior varsity levels of competition, and sustain access to boys lacrosse. It notes the proposal has the full support and approval of Troy School District administration, including the Superintendent, Assistant Superintendent, both high school principals, and the Athletic Department.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Correspondence dated June 15, 2026, addressed to the Members of the MHSAA Executive Board, sent on Troy School District District Athletics letterhead listing Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D., Superintendent of Schools, and Matt Jansen, Director, Athletics, at 1522 E. Big Beaver Rd., Troy, Michigan 48083, telephone 248.823.5154, fax 248.823.5133. The letter is signed by Matt Jansen, Director of Athletics, Continuing Education and Enrichment, and carries the footer "An Equal Opportunity/Affirmative Action Employer."

THE REQUEST
On behalf of the Troy School District, the letter requests approval of a waiver to the current cooperative team enrollment limitation to allow Troy High School and Troy Athens High School to form a cooperative boys lacrosse program beginning with the 2026-27 school year. The combined enrollment of the two high schools is 3,936 students, with Troy High School enrolling 2,127 students and Troy Athens High School enrolling 1,809 students. The letter acknowledges that this total exceeds the enrollment cap established for cooperative agreements but argues that the circumstances warrant special consideration and approval.

FINANCIAL CONTEXT
The Troy School District is described as currently facing a projected $12.1 million budget deficit entering the 2026-27 school year. As part of district-wide reductions, the Athletics Department has been tasked with reducing expenditures by approximately $100,000. To address these financial challenges, the district recently discontinued financial support for non-MHSAA sanctioned sports, including synchronized swimming and boys and girls water polo. Those programs have transitioned to self-funded club status, generating approximately $50,000 in annual savings. The letter calls this a difficult decision and states that additional measures are necessary to maintain sustainable athletic opportunities for students. A cooperative boys lacrosse program between Troy High School and Troy Athens High School would provide an estimated annual savings of approximately $25,000 while preserving participation opportunities for student-athletes at both schools.

PARTICIPATION AND PROGRAM SUSTAINABILITY
The letter emphasizes that the request is driven more by participation numbers and program sustainability than solely by financial considerations. During the 2026 boys lacrosse season, Troy High School had 48 participants while Troy Athens High School had 31 participants. Troy High School is graduating 21 seniors and Troy Athens High School is graduating 13 seniors. This leaves projected returning participation numbers of only 26 student-athletes at Troy High School and 15 student-athletes at Troy Athens High School, for a combined total of 41 returning players before the addition of incoming freshmen.

The situation at Troy Athens is described as particularly concerning. Of the 15 projected returning players, only one participated at the varsity level during the 2026 season; the remaining 14 players had never played lacrosse prior to the 2026 season. Although Athens attempted to field both varsity and junior varsity teams in the spring, the program was unable to consistently maintain enough healthy student-athletes to sustain junior varsity competition throughout the season.

COACHING AND PRIOR COOPERATIVE ARRANGEMENT
These challenges are said to have affected program leadership and long-term stability. Following the 2026 season, the Troy Athens varsity boys lacrosse coach informed the district of his decision to step down, with a significant factor being the ongoing difficulty of building and sustaining a program with limited participation numbers. The letter presents this as further illustration of the challenges facing the Athens program and the need for a more sustainable model. Historically, Troy Athens has participated in a cooperative arrangement with Avondale Schools, but that partnership has not provided the participation numbers necessary to sustain the program: in recent years the cooperative agreement has yielded no more than two players annually, and during the 2026 season Avondale contributed no participants. The letter concludes that the Avondale partnership is no longer a viable long-term solution.

RATIONALE FOR A COMBINED PROGRAM
The letter states that one of the fundamental goals of interscholastic athletics is to provide meaningful participation and developmental opportunities for as many student-athletes as possible. A cooperative program would allow the district to maintain both varsity and junior varsity competition, ensuring that beginning and developing players have an appropriate environment in which to learn, improve, and remain engaged in the sport; without sufficient numbers to sustain a junior varsity program, opportunities for skill development and long-term participation are significantly diminished. Establishing a single "Troy United" boys lacrosse program is presented as a stable structure that supports program numbers while preserving access and opportunity for student-athletes from both schools, aligning with the educational mission of the MHSAA by prioritizing participation, student development, and the long-term viability of boys lacrosse within the community.

REGIONAL PRECEDENT
The letter argues the request is consistent with cooperative programs that already exist throughout the region. Within the Oakland Activities Association and surrounding communities, numerous school districts have been permitted to combine programs to preserve participation opportunities. Examples cited include Farmington and North Farmington, Royal Oak and Berkley, Birmingham Groves and Birmingham Seaholm, and Waterford Mott and Waterford Kettering. Additional area examples cited are Milford and Lakeland, the Livonia Public Schools combined program, South Lyon's combined program, Bishop Foley and Clawson, Brandon and Holly, the St. Clair Shores cooperative program, and Eisenhower and Utica. The Troy School District states it is simply seeking the same opportunity to preserve a viable boys lacrosse program for its students.

CLOSING POSITION AND APPROVALS
Approval of the waiver would allow the district to establish a single "Troy United" boys lacrosse program representing both Troy High School and Troy Athens High School, providing the participation numbers necessary to maintain both varsity and junior varsity opportunities while supporting the district's ongoing financial sustainability efforts. The letter states the request is not intended to create a competitive advantage but rather to preserve participation opportunities, maintain both levels of competition, and ensure that student-athletes in the Troy School District continue to have access to boys lacrosse in a sustainable and educationally sound manner. The proposal is reported to have already received the full support and approval of the Troy School District administration, including the Superintendent, the Assistant Superintendent, both high school principals, and the Athletic Department. The letter closes by respectfully requesting that the Executive Board grant the waiver to the cooperative enrollment limitation and approve the cooperative boys lacrosse program, thanking the board for its consideration and offering to provide any additional information the Council may require.

**Meeting**
Troy Board of Education regular meeting, June 13, 2023, held in the Media Center at Troy High School, 4777 Northfield Parkway. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:30 p.m. and it adjourned at 8:31 p.m. Minutes signed by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education (typist notation GH/jh).

**Attendance**
Present with Mr. Schmidt were Board members Alic, Anne, Haupt, and Wilson. Mr. Hauff and Dr. Philippart were absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Keyser, Foren, Young, Cross, Pagel, and West. Approximately 20 members of the audience attended.

**Recognition — TSD Mission Moment: Baker Student Civilian Award**
The Board recognized Baker 7th grade student David Kalaj for bravery in saving the life of a person who was drowning at the bottom of a pool the previous summer; the person was revived after receiving CPR. The Troy Police Department awarded David a Civilian Citation on May 18th at the Police Memorial Day celebration. Baker Principal Jonathan Cross introduced the student, who received a certificate of recognition.

**Personnel — Resolution 23-044**
Mr. Schmidt changed the order of the agenda to move Personnel up and invited Mr. Pagel to present. Moved by Dr. Wilson, supported by Mrs. Anne: a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure issued to Ms. Kristin Crowe as Special Education Supervisor, Services Building, effective July 1, 2023. Yes 5, No 0, Absent Hauff and Philippart. A brief recess followed.

**Public Hearing — 2023/2024 Proposed Budget**
Mr. West presented the proposed budget with a PowerPoint, covering tax values, homestead/non-homestead millage, general fund adjustments and assumptions, ancillary funds, the sinking fund and capital projects fund, student enrollment, foundation allowance history, and revenues and expenditures. The Board indicated it had reviewed the proposed budget in its entirety at the June 6th Workshop. There were no additions and deletions and no public communication on agenda items.

**General — Consent Agenda, Resolution 23-045**
Moved by Mr. Haupt, supported by Mrs. Alic, to approve items A through H. Yes 5, No 0, Absent Hauff and Philippart.

| Item | Description |
| --- | --- |
| A | Minutes of the May 2, 2023 Special Board of Education Meeting |
| B | Minutes of the May 2, 2023 Closed Session Meeting |
| C | Minutes of the May 2, 2023 Board of Education Workshop |
| D | Minutes of the May 2, 2023 Board of Education Meeting |
| E | Treasurer's Report — April 2023 |
| F | Vehicle Purchase |
| G | 2022/2023 Budget Amendment |
| H | 2023/2024 Budget Appropriations Resolution |

**Curriculum**
None.

**Business — Awards**

| Resolution | Item | Vendor | Amount | Funding |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 23-046 | Voice Communication System | Forerunner Technologies | $591,484.49 | 2023 Capital Projects Fund |
| 23-047 | Bid pack 38 — Bemis, Hill, Schroeder, AHS & THS Doors/Window Replacement | Daniels Glass Inc. | $457,297.00 | Capital Projects Fund and/or Building Site and Sinking Fund |

Resolution 23-046 was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Haupt; 23-047 was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Dr. Wilson. Both passed Yes 5, No 0, with Hauff and Philippart absent.

**Public Communication (Non-Agenda Items)**
Mr. Matt Sackrison, TSD parent, spoke on the District's Robotics program and suggested seeking a coordinator, especially at the elementary levels. Mrs. Katie MacFarland, TSD parent, spoke about pornographic books in District media centers and donated the book How Pornography Harms to the Board. Mr. Alex Karpowitsch, TSD parent, asked to see the data guiding the District's curriculum change. Mr. Jeff Schaeper, a TSD resident with graduates from Troy Schools, said the curriculum change design process did not include parents as stakeholders and provided a slide from the accountability presentation as an example.

**Other and Board Member Comments**
Other: none. Mr. Haupt congratulated graduates and all students; Mrs. Anne and Dr. Wilson shared the same sentiment. Dr. Machesky announced the TFEE Golf Outing on June 20th at Greystone Golf Club, a fundraiser providing grants for teachers; noted only half days remained and that IA-East's last day would be June 20th; and said work continues on the Athens principal position with a special meeting likely before the end of the month. Mr. Schmidt said the Section 1 application for the Natural Resource Trust Fund would be held the following morning at 9:15 a.m. and that he would attend, and announced the next Board meeting for Tuesday, July 18th at the Administration Building at 9:30 a.m., adding that summer Board meetings are not recorded.

Official minutes of the regular meeting of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, held June 13, 2023 at Troy High School, 4777 Northfield Parkway, specifically in the school's Media Center. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:30 p.m. The minutes are respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, and carry the typist notation GH/jh.

ATTENDANCE. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Alic, Anne, Haupt, and Wilson were present. Mr. Hauff and Dr. Philippart were absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Keyser, Foren, Young, Cross, Pagel, and West. Approximately 20 members of the audience attended.

RECOGNITION — TSD MISSION MOMENT: BAKER STUDENT CIVILIAN AWARD. The Board recognized David Kalaj, a Baker 7th grade student, for his bravery in saving the life of a person who was drowning at the bottom of a pool the previous summer. Thanks to David's quick response, the person was revived after receiving CPR. The Troy Police Department awarded David a Civilian Citation on May 18th at the Police Memorial Day celebration. Baker Principal Jonathan Cross was invited up to introduce the student and share more about his story. David received congratulations from the Board along with a certificate of recognition.

PERSONNEL — ADMINISTRATIVE APPOINTMENT, SPECIAL EDUCATION SUPERVISOR (CROWE), RESOLUTION 23-044. Mr. Schmidt changed the order of the agenda and moved Personnel up, inviting Mr. Pagel to present the administrative positions brought to the Board for consideration. It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mrs. Anne that BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that the Board of Education issues a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Ms. Kristin Crowe, who will begin her duties as Special Education Supervisor, Services Building, effective July 1, 2023. The vote was Yes 5, No 0, with Hauff and Philippart recorded absent. A brief recess followed.

BUSINESS — PUBLIC HEARING, 2023/2024 PROPOSED BUDGET. Mr. West presented the details of the proposed budget to the Board and community and shared a PowerPoint presentation. He noted the proposed budget had been reviewed in great detail with the Board at the June workshop. His presentation addressed tax values, homestead and non-homestead millage, and general fund adjustments and assumptions. He spoke about ancillary funds, the sinking fund, and the capital projects fund, among others. He also reviewed student enrollment, the District's foundation allowance history, and revenues and expenditures. The Board indicated that it had reviewed the proposed budget in its entirety at the June 6th Workshop.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS. None.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (AGENDA ITEMS). None.

GENERAL — CONSENT AGENDA, RESOLUTION 23-045. It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Alic that BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that the Troy Board of Education takes action to approve items A, B, C, D, E, F, G, and H on the consent agenda. The items were: minutes of the May 2, 2023 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the May 2, 2023 Closed Session Meeting; minutes of the May 2, 2023 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the May 2, 2023 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report — April 2023; Vehicle Purchase; 2022/2023 Budget Amendment; and 2023/2024 Budget Appropriations Resolution. The vote was Yes 5, No 0, with Hauff and Philippart absent.

CURRICULUM. None.

BUSINESS — VOICE COMMUNICATION SYSTEM, RESOLUTION 23-046. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Haupt that BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that the purchase of a voice communication system be awarded to Forerunner Technologies in the amount of $591,484.49, and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. The vote was Yes 5, No 0, with Hauff and Philippart absent.

BUSINESS — BEMIS, HILL, SCHROEDER, AHS & THS DOORS/WINDOW REPLACEMENT, RESOLUTION 23-047. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Dr. Wilson that BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that the bid for bid pack 38 be awarded as follows to Daniels Glass Inc. in the amount of $457,297.00 and that this be approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund and/or Building Site and Sinking Fund. The vote was Yes 5, No 0, with Hauff and Philippart absent. The agenda heading identifies the affected buildings as Bemis, Hill, and Schroeder elementary schools together with Athens High School (AHS) and Troy High School (THS).

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (NON-AGENDA ITEMS). Four speakers addressed the Board. Mr. Matt Sackrison, a TSD parent, spoke about the District's Robotics program and suggested seeking a coordinator to support the program, especially at the elementary levels. Mrs. Katie MacFarland, a TSD parent, addressed the Board about pornographic books in the District's media centers and gave the Board a book as a donation, How Pornography Harms. Mr. Alex Karpowitsch, a TSD parent, addressed the Board about the change in curriculum and asked to see the data that guided the District's decision to adopt the change. Mr. Jeff Schaeper, a TSD resident with graduates from Troy Schools, addressed the Board about the curriculum change design process and stated that it did not include parents, who are the stakeholders; he provided a slide from the accountability presentation as an example.

OTHER. None.

BOARD MEMBER COMMENTS. Mr. Haupt congratulated all the graduates and all students for completing another school year. Mrs. Anne and Dr. Wilson shared the same sentiment. Dr. Machesky announced that the TFEE Golf Outing would be held on June 20th at Greystone Golf Club and that the fundraiser would provide grants for teachers, putting money back into the classroom. He shared that only half days remained in the school year and that IA-East would have its last day on June 20th. He also reported that the District was working to punctuate the Athens principal position and would likely hold a special meeting before the end of the month to approve it. Mr. Schmidt shared that the Section 1 application for the Natural Resource Trust Fund would be held the following morning at 9:15 a.m. and that he would be in attendance. He announced that the next Board meeting would be held on Tuesday, July 18th at the Administration Building at 9:30 a.m., and added that summer Board meetings are not recorded.

ADJOURNMENT. The meeting adjourned at 8:31 p.m.

**Membership structure (MASB Bylaws, Article IV, Section 2)**
Active members are the boards of education of Michigan public school districts, divided into eight regions along intermediate school district boundaries. Region 1 covers Copper Country ISD, Delta-Schoolcraft ISD, Dickinson-Iron ISD, Eastern Upper Peninsula ISD, Gogebic-Ontonagon ISD, Marquette-Alger RESA and Menominee County ISD. Region 8 covers Macomb ISD, Oakland Schools and Wayne RESA, the region that includes Troy School District. Members are also divided into seven groups by pupil membership: Group I all intermediate districts; Group II 0-1,400; Group III 1,401-2,500; Group IV 2,501-5,000; Group V 5,001-11,000; Group VI 11,001-40,000; Group VII more than 40,000.

**Election rules**
The MASB Board of Directors has 24 members, including three at-large directors. Sixteen directors are elected from the eight regions, two per region, and one director each is elected from Groups V, VI and VII. The MASB President nominates the at-large director subject to board approval. Article VIII, Section 6 permits only one director from any one local or intermediate school district board. Article VIII, Section 8 provides that an unopposed nominee is declared elected without an election.

**Seats up in 2024**
Nine seats: Regions 1 (open seat), 2, 3 (one-year term), 4 (one-year term), 5, 6 (open seat), 7, 8, and Group V (one-year term). Region 1 is vacant because no nominations were received. Unopposed, with no ballots sent: Dawn Kaiser, Iosco RESA (Region 2); Rick Dernberger, Zeeland Public Schools and Ottawa Area Intermediate School District (Region 3); John Tramontana, DeWitt Public Schools (Region 4); Stephen Hyer, Clarkston Community Schools (Group V).

**Voting procedure**
Online balloting occurs in Regions 5, 6, 7 and 8. Each district received one ballot, emailed to the superintendent secretary on record with MASB on Jan. 26, 2024, and it cannot be forwarded. Ballots must be cast and confirmed by 1 p.m. on Wednesday, March 6, 2024. Unofficial results are posted on a voicemail recording at 517.327.5915, generally after 2 p.m. on the deadline date, and emailed that afternoon; official results are approved at the March 22, 2024 Board of Directors meeting. No local district or ISD funds may be used for campaigning, including district email accounts; questions go to MASB Legal Counsel Brad Banasik, J.D., bbanasik@masb.org or 517.327.5929, or to Cheryl Huffman at 517.327.5915 or chuffman@masb.org.

Active members are also divided into seven groups based on pupil membership: Group I, all intermediate districts; Group II, 0 to 1,400 pupils; Group III, 1,401 to 2,500; Group IV, 2,501 to 5,000; Group V, 5,001 to 11,000; Group VI, 11,001 to 40,000; Group VII, more than 40,000.

**Election framework.** Nine seats on the MASB Board of Directors are up for election. The board is comprised of 24 members, including three at-large directors. Sixteen directors are elected from the eight regions, two from each region, and one director per group is elected from Groups V, VI and VII. Directors are elected by active member school boards, and the MASB President nominates a member to serve as an at-large director subject to board approval. Under Article VIII, Section 6, only one director may be elected or appointed from any one local or intermediate school district board. Under Article VIII, Section 8, an unopposed nomination results in the candidate being declared elected without an election for the uncontested group or region.

**Seats up and unopposed representatives.** Seats up for election, one each and three-year terms unless otherwise noted, are Regions 1 (open seat), 2, 3 (one-year term), 4 (one-year term), 5, 6 (open seat), 7, 8 and Group V (one-year term). Region 1 has a vacant seat because no nominations were received. Region 2 continues with Dawn Kaiser, Iosco RESA; Region 3 with Rick Dernberger, Zeeland Public Schools and Ottawa Area Intermediate School District; Region 4 with John Tramontana, DeWitt Public Schools; and Group V with Stephen Hyer, Clarkston Community Schools, all unopposed and with no ballots to be sent.

**Voting procedures.** Voting in Regions 5, 6, 7 and 8 takes place via online ballot. Each district received one ballot, emailed to the superintendent secretary on record with MASB on Jan. 26, 2024, which cannot be forwarded. Completed ballots must be cast and confirmed by the superintendent secretary by 1 p.m. on Wednesday, March 6, 2024. Unofficial election results will be available on the voicemail recording at 517.327.5915, generally after 2 p.m. on the deadline date, and sent by email that afternoon; official results will be approved at the March 22, 2024 Board of Directors meeting, which newly elected directors should plan to attend. No local district or ISD funds can be used to campaign for anyone running for a seat, a rule that prohibits candidates from using their school district email account to message other board members, so a personal email account must be used. Questions about what constitutes an expenditure of school district funds go to MASB Legal Counsel Brad Banasik, J.D., at bbanasik@masb.org or 517.327.5929. An electronic file containing physical and email addresses for the voting group or region is made available to each candidate under a revokable license limited to contacting school board members about the election. Other questions go to Cheryl Huffman at 517.327.5915 or chuffman@masb.org.

ESTABLISH FUND DEPOSITORIES AND INVESTMENTS (23-006): Moved by Dr. Philippart, supported by Mr. Haupt, adopting the resolution for January through December 2023, with the attached resolution incorporated in full into the official minutes. Designated depository institutions: Bank of America, Citizens Bank, JP Morgan Chase Bank, Comerica Bank, Huntington Bank, Fifth Third Bank, Flagstar Bancorp, MILAF (Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Plus, managed by PFM Asset Management, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank), and PNC Bank. Monies may be withdrawn by checks bearing the facsimile signature of Treasurer Rick West, and in emergencies the handwritten signature of Rick West or Superintendent Richard M. Machesky, who may sign on the General Fund account and the Payroll account at Bank of America. RECOGNITION: The TSD Mission Moment honored the Superintendent Student Advisory Board Executive Committee, which leads the 60 members of the SSAB by planning and running meetings and setting agendas; it was the first year the group had an executive board. The committee organized and executed the District's MLK Celebration and Day of Service, attended by over 800 people, requiring hundreds of hours of planning, soliciting thousands of dollars in donations and supplies, and organizing volunteers with minimal staff support; a video by a Troy Schools Creative Guild student showed highlights. Recognized with a token of appreciation: Aanvi Arora, Allison Diebol, George Perakis, Akshitha Sahu, Aanya Shah, Marlien William and Ray Zhang. The Student Spotlight featured Troy High School sophomore Akshaya Rachamadugu, who wrapped up editing on her first directorial debut short film; Thomas Butcher showed a clip, and she answered Board questions and received a certificate of recognition.
