Meeting
Board of Education, Troy, Michigan. Regular board meeting, July 15, 2025, held at the Troy School District Administration Building, 4400 Livernois. Called to order by President Philippart at 9:35 a.m.; adjourned at 10:18 a.m. Minutes submitted by Emina Alic, Secretary, Troy Board of Education (notation EA/jh).

Attendance
Present: Dr. Philippart plus Board members Alic, Anne, Haupt, Melton and Potts. Mrs. Zendler attended via remote communications. Also present: Superintendent Machesky; administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Trudel and Pagel; and two members of the audience. Recognition, additions and deletions, and public communication were all recorded as none.

Consent Agenda
Moved by Mr. Haupt, supported by Mrs. Anne, to approve items A through G: minutes of the June 3, 2025 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the June 3, 2025 Closed Session Meeting; minutes of the June 3, 2025 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the June 17, 2025 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report for May 2025; settlement terms of Batista v Office of Retirement Services litigation; and rescheduling of the October 21st Board of Education Meeting and the December 2nd and January 6th Board Workshops. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent/Remote Zendler.

Personnel — Administrator Contract Extensions
Moved by Mrs. Anne, supported by Mrs. Alic, to extend the contracts of the listed administrators through June 30, 2026, or as otherwise indicated in the administrator's individual contract, without tenure in the administrative positions and subject to the layoff provision in the Administrative Handbook where applicable and as permitted by law. The list covered high school principals (Vernon Burden, Patrick Griffin, Remo Roncone), middle school principals (Ryan Brinks, Jonathan Cross, Anthony Morse, Brian Zawislak), eleven elementary principals, nine assistant principals, and five directors/supervisors. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent/Remote Zendler.

Assistant Superintendent Contracts
Moved by Mr. Haupt, supported by Mrs. Alic, to extend the contracts of Dan Trudel (Business Services), John Pagel (Employee Services), Kris Griffor (Elementary Instruction) and Christine DiPilato (Secondary Instruction) through June 30, 2027, without tenure in the administrative positions. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent/Remote Zendler.

Superintendent Evaluation and Contract
The board reported completing Dr. Richard Machesky's performance evaluation and shared an assessment rating him EXEMPLARY, having met or exceeded expectations in all evaluation categories. Points cited: continued execution of the strategic plan under the LEARNING FOR ALL vision; fiscal strength with sufficient fund balance to mitigate disruptions in state funding; a new business operations team integrated this year; bond projects tracking at or below budget; alignment and implementation of Multi-Tiered System of Support; new secondary assessments; math and literacy professional development; belonging, well-being and security initiatives; and all staff labor agreements negotiated and signed. The board committed to a more robust community-input process in curriculum evaluation and praised the Career Accelerator Program, run with the Business Roundtable, which provided 75 high school students with internships in local businesses. The minutes note that Dr. Machesky's contract then ran through June 30, 2029 and that the board planned to extend it by an additional year. Moved by Mrs. Alic, supported by Mrs. Anne, the extension was approved to be in effect July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2030, without tenure and subject to the provisions of the written Agreement. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent/Remote Zendler.

Other
Curriculum and Business items: none. Public communication on non-agenda items: none. Other items noted: summer work progress update, Data Dashboard update, and the MASB Conference in October. Dr. Philippart announced the next Board of Education meeting for August 19th at 6:00 p.m. in the Administration Building.

CONSENT AGENDA
It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Anne that the Troy Board of Education take action to approve items A through G on the consent agenda: minutes of the June 3, 2025 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the June 3, 2025 Closed Session Meeting; minutes of the June 3, 2025 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the June 17, 2025 Board of Education Meeting; the Treasurer's Report for May 2025; the settlement terms of Batista v Office of Retirement Services litigation; and rescheduling of the October 21st Board of Education Meeting together with the December 2nd and January 6th Board Workshops. The vote was recorded as Yes: 6, No: 0, Absent/Remote: Zendler.

PERSONNEL — EXTENSION OF ADMINISTRATIVE PERSONNEL CONTRACTS
It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mrs. Alic that the Troy Board of Education approve the extension of the contracts of the named administrators through June 30, 2026, or as otherwise indicated in the administrator's individual contract, without tenure in the administrative positions and subject to the layoff provision in the Administrative Handbook, where applicable and as permitted by law.

Middle school principals: Ryan Brinks, Principal, Smith Middle School; Jonathan Cross, Principal, Baker Middle School; Anthony Morse, Principal, Boulan Park Middle School; Brian Zawislak, Principal, Larson Middle School.

The vote was recorded as Yes: 6, No: 0, Absent/Remote: Zendler.

EXTENSION OF ASSISTANT SUPERINTENDENT CONTRACTS
It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Alic that the Troy Board of Education approve the extension of the contracts for Dan Trudel, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services; John Pagel, Assistant Superintendent, Employee Services; Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction; and Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction, through June 30, 2027, without tenure in the administrative positions. The vote was recorded as Yes: 6, No: 0, Absent/Remote: Zendler.

SUPERINTENDENT EVALUATION
The minutes record that the Board recently completed Superintendent Dr. Richard Machesky's performance evaluation and shared the resulting assessment with the community. The assessment states that Dr. Machesky is an EXEMPLARY superintendent who has met or exceeded expectations in all evaluation categories. It credits him with continuing to execute the district's strategic plan and driving high expectations for the vision of LEARNING FOR ALL as the basis for instructional decisions. It states the district remains fiscally strong under his leadership with sufficient fund balance to mitigate disruptions in state funding, that a new business operations team was integrated into the organization during the year, and that bond projects are tracking at or below budget. The district continues to focus on alignment and implementation of Multi-Tiered System of Support to address achievement gaps, particularly for special education students, English Language Learners and economically disadvantaged students. New assessments were put in place for secondary students to identify achievement gaps, and high-quality teacher professional development in math and literacy was provided for all grade levels. Several initiatives were put in place to increase students' sense of belonging, well-being and security. All staff labor agreements were successfully negotiated and signed during the year, providing the district with attractive compensation to retain and recruit staff. Going forward, Dr. Machesky and the board committed to developing a more robust process that gathers input and engages the community earlier in the curriculum evaluation process while still relying on the expertise of the district's educators for decision-making. The board also applauded Rich and the Business Roundtable for implementation of a growing, successful Career Accelerator Program that provided 75 high school students with internship opportunities in local businesses. The board expressed full confidence that he and his team have the capacity and capability to face future challenges.

EXTENSION OF SUPERINTENDENT CONTRACT
The minutes note that Dr. Machesky's contract at that time ran through June 30, 2029 and that the board planned to extend it by an additional year. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Anne that the Troy Board of Education extend the contract of the Superintendent of Schools as described, with the contract to be in effect from July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2030, without tenure in the administrative position and subject to provisions of the written Agreement. The vote was recorded as Yes: 6, No: 0, Absent/Remote: Zendler.

CURRICULUM, BUSINESS AND PUBLIC COMMUNICATION
No curriculum or business action items were recorded; the entries for these sections and for public communication on non-agenda items are marked none.

OTHER AND BOARD MEMBER COMMENTS
Items noted under other business and board member comments: a summer work progress update, a Data Dashboard update, and the MASB Conference in October.

ADJOURNMENT
Dr. Philippart shared that the next Board of Education Meeting would be held on August 19th at 6:00 p.m. in the Administration Building. The meeting was adjourned at 10:18 a.m. Respectfully submitted by Emina Alic, Secretary, Troy Board of Education; typist notation EA/jh.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Career Readiness and Technical Education is a slide presentation delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education on March 4, 2025, laying out a K-12 career-readiness continuum tied to the district's Portrait of a Learner: career awareness in grades K-5 built around Michigan's six Career Zones, career exploration in grades 6-8 organized around Michigan's 17 Career Clusters, and career preparation in grades 9-12 through pathway-specific programs. The deck reports five years of CTE enrollment by program cluster, with Marketing the largest at 548 students in 2023-2024 and 287 concentrators reported for that year.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Overview**
Presentation titled "Career Readiness and Technical Education" given to the Troy School District Board of Education on March 4, 2025. It maps a K-12 progression -- awareness (K-5), exploration (6-8), preparation (9-12) -- anchored to the district's Portrait of a Learner, then details career programs and CTE enrollment.

**Career Awareness (K-5): "Let the Journey Begin"**
Elementary awareness is described as helping students develop a sense of self, discover personal interests and strengths, and explore work beyond jobs held by family members. Best practices center on the six Michigan Career Zones, embedding them across the curriculum, and family engagement. Current practices: EDPs initiated in 1st grade and revised annually through Media; Talent Portfolios begun in 3rd grade; a STEMi Mobile field trip for 4th and 5th grade students; parent nights; and grade-level events with guest speakers and assemblies.

**Career Exploration (6-8): "The Journey Continues"**
Middle school is framed as a bridge for self-discovery rather than locking in a career choice. Best practices introduce Michigan's 17 Career Clusters to students and families and continue the EDP and Talent Portfolio. Current practices include an 8th grade parent night on the middle-to-high-school transition, career readiness activities in general education courses, career exploration electives, and a culminating 8th grade interview. Future growth: pacing plans to transition from Zones to Clusters, cluster-specific field trips, industry tours and job shadows, visits to high school CTE programs, and adding EDP and Portrait of a Learner components to the 8th grade interview.

**Career Preparation (9-12): "Multiple Pathways Ahead"**
Students update self-assessments, research labor market demand and postsecondary options, and build pathway-specific and employability skills while cultivating a Talent Portfolio. The EDP is revised annually into a 4-year plan. Counselors and the Career Facilitator assist students; programs cited include CTE, OSTC, Dual Enrollment, LTU EMC and CAP, plus an annual College and Career Fair. Future growth: staff work time to insert career components into lessons, a senior exit experience, career-related professional development, and further exploration of CAPS.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Career Readiness and Technical Education is a 32-slide presentation prepared for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of March 4, 2025 (file title "TSDCareerBOE3_4 - Read-Only (003)"). It presents the district's Career Readiness Pathway as a K-12 continuum grounded in the district's Portrait of a Learner, moving from career awareness in the elementary grades, to career exploration in middle school, to career preparation in high school, and closes with a program-by-program accounting of the district's career offerings and five years of Career and Technical Education enrollment data.

**Career Awareness, Grades K-5 ("Let the Journey Begin")**

The rationale slide, "Why Start Early?", states that career awareness at the elementary level helps students develop a sense of self, discover an awareness of personal interests and strengths, and explore the world of work beyond jobs held by family members. The stated goal is to provide students with a wide range of experiences that build confidence, challenge job stereotypes, and expand their view of the immense possibilities.

Best practices for K-5 are to familiarize students and families with the six Michigan Career Zones and provide opportunities for career discovery; to connect academic content to those zones and embed it across the curriculum; and to provide family engagement opportunities. Supporting resources referenced include K-1 Career Zone Slides, a Career Zone Coloring Example, 2-5 Career Zone Slides, and Career Zone Videos.

Current K-5 practices listed are: students initiate Educational Development Plans (EDPs) in 1st grade and revise them annually through Media; students initiate Talent Portfolios in 3rd grade; intentional Career Readiness projects and activities delivered through Media; a STEMi Mobile Field Trip for 4th and 5th grade students; parent nights; and grade-level career awareness events including guest speakers and assemblies.

Future growth for K-5 is organized under Career Zones (increase ways of familiarizing students and parents with the six Michigan Career Zones), Career Awareness (increase intentional and targeted activities providing awareness of career zones), and Family Engagement (additional activities supporting career awareness).

**Career Exploration, Grades 6-8 ("The Journey Continues")**

The "Career Exploration: The Bridge" slide states that middle school is the perfect time for career exploration, self-discovery, experiential learning, and seeing the relevancy between learning and future careers, and that rather than locking in a specific career choice, exploration allows students to consider possible roles for their future selves. A transition slide is labeled "Awareness to Exploration."

Best practices for grades 6-8: introduce Michigan's 17 Career Clusters to students and families; connect academic content in all classes to the Michigan career clusters and embed it across the curriculum; acquire career, postsecondary, and employment knowledge; provide family engagement opportunities to support career exploration; and continue and revise the Educational Development Plan (EDP) and Talent Portfolio.

Current practices for grades 6-8: continuation of EDPs and Talent Portfolios; an 8th grade parent night covering the transition from middle to high school; career readiness activities embedded in general education courses; career exploration electives; and a culminating 8th grade interview.

Future growth for grades 6-8 is grouped under Career Clusters, Career Exploration, and Family Engagement. Under Career Clusters: increase ways of familiarizing students and parents with the seventeen Michigan Career Clusters; develop pacing plans to transition from Zones to Clusters; and organize cluster-specific events such as field trips, industry tours, or job shadows. Under Career Exploration: engage with guest speakers and visit high school CTE programs; review current career electives to ensure alignment with future pathways provided in high school; and add components to the 8th grade interviews to include EDP information and the Portrait of a Learner. Under Family Engagement: provide additional family engagement activities supporting career awareness.

**Career Preparation, Grades 9-12 ("Multiple Pathways Ahead!")**

The career preparation narrative states that in high school students update self-assessments, refine evolving career goals, and engage in deeper career exploration; that students shift to a more focused pathway aligned with their career aspirations and increase their knowledge by researching labor market demand and postsecondary opportunities; and that this is the time for building pathway-specific skills and employability skills and cultivating a Talent Portfolio showcasing proficiencies, certifications, experiences, and accomplishments. A transition slide is labeled "Exploration to Preparation."

Best practices for grades 9-12: in-depth exploration of the Michigan career clusters and related career pathways; connecting academic content in all classes to those clusters and pathways to establish relevancy; increasing student knowledge about career options, job outlooks, training, and education opportunities and demonstrating career-ready practices (also referred to as employability skills or soft skills); providing family engagement opportunities; revising the EDP annually to help create a 4-year plan aligned with student goals; and recording information in a Talent Portfolio to demonstrate marketable skills to a prospective employer or admissions committee.

Current practices for grades 9-12: students review and revise their EDP each year; counselors and the Career Facilitator assist students in making informed choices about education, careers, and lifestyle options; various career-ready programs are available including but not limited to CTE Programs, OSTC, Dual Enrollment, LTU EMC, and CAP; general education teachers include Career Readiness lessons to show the relevancy of their content; and a College and Career Fair is open to all high school students on an annual basis.

Future growth for grades 9-12 is grouped under Building Target, Academic Connections, and Family Engagement: provide work time for staff to insert a career component in current lessons; create a senior exit experience; encourage teachers to connect content area curriculum to careers by participating in career-related professional development; further exploration of the CAPS program; and provide additional family engagement activities supporting career readiness.

**Career and Technical Education**

CTE is defined as an innovative approach to learning that combines academic instruction with hands-on, real-world experiences to prepare students for success in college, careers, and life, focusing on the knowledge and skills students need to excel in specific industries or fields while fostering 21st-century skills such as problem-solving, teamwork, communication, and adaptability. A subsequent slide addresses the components of CTE, followed by a slide headed "CTE Programs in TSD."

The CTE Enrollment 2019-2024 table reports enrollment by program cluster for five school years. Architecture & Construction: 16 (2019-20), 33 (2020-2021), 24 (2021-2022), 30 (2022-2023), 34 (2023-2024). Arts, AV Technology & Communication: 48, 65, 29, 46, 41. Education & Training: 46, 71, 56, 50, 45. Finance: 74, 88, 134, 62**, 62**. Hospitality & Tourism: 54, 65, 66, 83, 85. Information Technology: 172, 124, 101, 76**, 113. Manufacturing: ** for the first two years, then 15, 32, 30. Marketing: 383, 449, 336, 419, 548. Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics: 170, 187, 168, 138, 52**. Transportation, Distribution, Logistics: 95, 73, 77, 70, 71. A footnote explains that the double-asterisk numbers do not reflect total enrollment for the course, and that those numbers reflect the number of students enrolled in a CTE program taught by a CTE Certified Instructor. The slide is captioned "287 Concentrators in 2023-2024!"

**Dual Enrollment**

Dual enrollment is described as a program that allows students to take college courses while still in high school, with the courses counting for both high school and college credit, saving time and money and giving students a jump start on their college education. Enrollment is listed as 66 students at Troy High and 54 students at Athens.

**Oakland Schools Technical Campus (OSTC)**

OSTC is described as designed for any student who wants to graduate high school with industry certifications, on-the-job experiences, business connections, and college credits, seeking students who want a head start on their careers and desire cutting-edge, hands-on learning. Troy High enrollment is 22 students; Athens enrollment is 73 students, with an asterisk noting that 9 students are enrolled in OSTC and OCC EMC.

**Early Middle College with Lawrence Technological University (LTU)**

The LTU Early Middle College is a partnership between TSD and LTU in which a student earns a high school diploma with TSD, a certification in Cybersecurity with LTU, and an Associate's degree in Computer Science with LTU over a 5-year program. Five students are currently enrolled.

The five-year course sequence spans Year 1 (9th grade), Year 2 (10th grade), Year 3 (11th grade), Year 4 (12th grade), and Year 5 ("Superior"), each with fall and spring terms. High school courses in the grid include English 9A/9B, English 10A/10B, English 11A/11B, English 12A/12B, Algebra 1A/1B, Geometry A/B, Algebra 2A/2B, Biology A/B, Physics, Chemistry, World History A/B, US History A/B, Government, Economics, Health, Physical Education, and World Language 1. LTU courses listed include MCS 1142 Intro to Computers, MCS 1514 Computer Science 1, MCS 1111 Coding Club (Python and Java), MCS1003 Intro to Computer Applications, MCS 1243 Foundations of Computer Science, MCS 2513 Engineering 1, MCS 2514 Computer Science 2, MCS 5013 Web Server Programming, MCS 5813 Computer Security, INT 4023 Cybersecurity, COM 1103 College Composition, COM 2103 Tech and Professional Communication, COM1002 Pathways to Research Careers, HUM1213 Engaging Ancient Text, HUM1223 Engaging Modern Texts, LLT 2xx3 LLT 2000 Elective, SSC 2xx3 Elective, and NSC natural science elective lecture and lab options. Summer offerings MCS0054 and COM0094 are marked as courses a student may test out of. LTU credits by term are listed as 0, 0, 2, 5, 8, 8, 10, 10, 10, and 9, with a stated total of 60 LTU Credits.

**Career Accelerator Program (CAP)**

The Career Accelerator Program is described as designed for high school juniors and seniors to bridge the gap between education and the professional world by providing mentorship and exposure to various career opportunities for students within the community. The program consists of two parts: the Career Accelerator classes and the pre-internship.

**CAPS Program**

The Center of Advanced Professional Studies (CAPS) is described as offering high school students the opportunity to explore career paths and gain hands-on experience in a professional setting through real-world projects, collaboration with industry experts, and development of the skills needed to thrive in their chosen field. Further exploration of CAPS is listed among the district's high school future growth targets.

Overview
Two versions of a Food Services quote request for Wass Elementary School are included: a completed "REBID" form carrying a submitted price, and a blank original form. Both were issued by Troy School District, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48198, Food Services Department, and both are footed "Page 2 - Troy School Foodservice Bid - Wass Elementary."

Item 1 - Combi Oven, Electric (2 Ovens - One Double Stack)

| 2 ea | Water filter installation |

| 10 ea | "STEAM&FRY" basket, 18 x 26 inch, stainless steel |

Board packet material for agenda item 8.B., presented to the Troy Board of Education for the May 21, 2024 meeting, consists of foodservice equipment quote request forms for Wass Elementary School. The packet holds two versions of the same document: a completed form headed "Quote Request - Wass Elementary - REBID" bearing a submitted price and bidder signature, and a second, blank form headed "Quote Request - Wass Elementary" with the pricing and bidder fields left open. Both are issued under Troy School District, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48198, Food Services Department, and both carry the footer "Page 2 - Troy School Foodservice Bid - Wass Elementary."

Scope of the Request
The forms request a price for a single line, ITEM 1 - COMBI OVEN, ELECTRIC (2 Ovens - One Double Stack). The specified unit is UNOX USA Model XAVC-06FS-EPRM, described as a ChefTop MIND.Maps Plus Combi Oven, electric, countertop. Dimensions are given as 33.13 (h) x 33.88 (w) x 38.06 (d). Pan capacity is (6) 18 inch by 26 inch full size sheet pans or (12) hotel size pans. Additional specifications listed are MIND.Maps technology, programmable menu, 2-11/16 inch shelf spacing, glass door, right-to-left door opening, stainless steel interior and exterior, a 316L stainless steel cooking chamber, water line included for water connection within 3 feet, WIFI/USB for data transfer to HACCP software, and cMETus, NSF and ENERGY STAR designations.

Itemized Components
The bill of materials on both forms is identical. It comprises: 1 ea End User Data & Installation Confirmation Form; 1 ea 2 Year parts and 1 year labor warranty standard; 1 ea LONG.LIFE4-B1 extended warranty with certified installation; 1 ea LONG.LIFE4-B2 extended warranty with certified installation for the 2nd oven; 2 ea electrical configuration at 208v/60/3-ph, 42 amps, 14.5 kW, no cord and plug, with the dealer to verify prior to ordering; 2 ea UNOX Power Cable, 3 Phase 6 AWG, NEMA 15-60, for XAVC-06FS-EpxM and XAVC-1011-EPxM; and 1 ea Stacking Kit for ChefTop MIND.Maps Plus, which includes installation kits and stacking parts for stacking two ovens, for electric ovens, including floor stand XWARC-00-EF-F and casters XUC012.

Ventilation and Water Treatment
The request includes 1 ea Ventless Hood for ChefTop MIND.Maps Plus, dimensioned (WxDxH) 33-7/8 inches by 45-1/16 inches by 9-7/16 inches, with a 4-3/4 inch exhaust chimney diameter, including (1) 1-1/2 m hose and (2) hose clamps, rated 0.1 kW, 208-240v/60/1-ph, for models EPR and XAVC-06FS-EPLM, UL and NSF listed. The hood note states that it "reduces smoke, odors, grease latent vapors and lowers exhaust temperatures. Does not replace Type II exhaust hoods. Adhere to local codes." Also included is 1 ea ventless hood installation, which must be purchased with the corresponding unit LONG.Life4 and installed at the same time as the unit.

Two water-related acknowledgments are listed at 2 ea, placing sole responsibility on the owner, operator or purchaser to verify that the incoming water supply is comprehensively tested for Free Chlorine, Chloramine, TDS (Total Dissolved Solids), Silica, pH, TH (Total Hardness), Chlorides and Alkalinity, and if required to provide water treatment meeting the manufacturer's minimum water quality standards as outlined on the product spec sheet; non-compliance is stated to potentially damage the equipment or components and to VOID the original equipment manufacturer's warranty. The request further includes 2 ea UNOX.Finest Filtering System, which reduces carbonate hardness of water, with ChefTouch monitoring water consumption and notifying the user to replace the cartridge, and 2 ea water filter installation.

Consumables and Accessories
Listed are 1 ea UNOX Detergent & Rinse Eco, (10) 1 liter tanks, double concentrate, phosphate free, cleaning chemicals for Rotor.Klean; 10 ea CHROMO.GRID, 18 inch by 26 inch, stainless steel; and 10 ea "STEAM&FRY" Basket, 18 inch by 26 inch, stainless steel.

Extended Warranty Detail
The blank original form carries an expanded description of the LONG.LIFE4-B1 line. Pricing is based on a 100 mile radius from the installer, with additional charges possibly applying. The UNOX Long.Life4 program, subject to UNOX, Inc. terms and conditions, includes: (1) an extended warranty providing a 4 year/10,000 ON hours parts and 1 year labor warranty, with the oven required to be connected to the internet via Ethernet cable or WIFI and to remain accessible for remote login by UNOX; and (2) a pre-installation site inspection by an UNOX Certified Service Agent of the installation site, follow-up instructions advising the customer of any additional material needed for site preparation prior to installation, and assembly, setting and leveling of the UNOX equipment plus final hook-up by a Certified UNOX Service Agent. This applies to the 1st 06FS. LONG.LIFE4-B2 covers the extended warranty with certified installation for a 2nd or more unit(s) installed at the same time and location as the 1st unit (06FS).

Bid Conditions
Both forms state that the bid is to include all freight charges with the dealer delivering to the school, that installation by an authorized service agent is to be included, and that any utility rebates are to be included in the bid.

Bid Submitted
On the REBID form, the entry for "Bid for item #1" is $36,457.91. Bidder information given is Business Name: Great Lakes Hotel Supply; Address: 24101 W. Nine Mile Rd., Southfield, MI 48033; Phone: (248) 982-7283; Contact: Michael Trombley; Bidder's Signature: Michael Trombley. The blank companion form leaves the bid amount, business name, address, phone, contact and signature lines empty.

Deadlines and Contact
The REBID form instructs bidders to return the quote via e-mail or by 5:00 p.m., Friday April 26th, 2024, to Gayle Moran at gmoran2@troy.k12.mi.us. The blank original form gives the earlier deadline of 5:00 p.m., Friday April 12th, 2024, to the same contact, indicating the solicitation was reissued as a rebid with a later return date.

Pan capacity is (6) 18 inch by 26 inch full size sheet pans or (12) hotel size pans. Additional specifications listed are MIND.Maps technology, programmable menu, 2-11/16 inch shelf spacing, glass door, right-to-left door opening, stainless steel interior and exterior, a 316L stainless steel cooking chamber, water line included for water connection within 3 feet, WIFI/USB for data transfer to HACCP software, and cMETus, NSF and ENERGY STAR designations.

Itemized Components
The bill of materials on both forms is identical. It comprises: 1 ea End User Data & Installation Confirmation Form; 1 ea 2 Year parts and 1 year labor warranty standard; 1 ea LONG.LIFE4-B1 extended warranty with certified installation; 1 ea LONG.LIFE4-B2 extended warranty with certified installation for the 2nd oven; 2 ea electrical configuration at 208v/60/3-ph, 42 amps, 14.5 kW, no cord and plug, with the dealer to verify prior to ordering; 2 ea UNOX Power Cable, 3 Phase 6 AWG, NEMA 15-60, for XAVC-06FS-EpxM and XAVC-1011-EPxM; and 1 ea Stacking Kit for ChefTop MIND.Maps Plus, which includes installation kits and stacking parts for stacking two ovens, for electric ovens, including floor stand XWARC-00-EF-F and casters XUC012.

Ventilation and Water Treatment
The request includes 1 ea Ventless Hood for ChefTop MIND.Maps Plus, dimensioned (WxDxH) 33-7/8 inches by 45-1/16 inches by 9-7/16 inches, with a 4-3/4 inch exhaust chimney diameter, including (1) 1-1/2 m hose and (2) hose clamps, rated 0.1 kW, 208-240v/60/1-ph, for models EPR and XAVC-06FS-EPLM, UL and NSF listed. The hood note states that it "reduces smoke, odors, grease latent vapors and lowers exhaust temperatures. Does not replace Type II exhaust hoods. Adhere to local codes." Also included is 1 ea ventless hood installation, which must be purchased with the corresponding unit LONG.Life4 and installed at the same time as the unit.

Two water-related acknowledgments are listed at 2 ea, placing sole responsibility on the owner, operator or purchaser to verify that the incoming water supply is comprehensively tested for Free Chlorine, Chloramine, TDS (Total Dissolved Solids), Silica, pH, TH (Total Hardness), Chlorides and Alkalinity, and if required to provide water treatment meeting the manufacturer's minimum water quality standards as outlined on the product spec sheet; non-compliance is stated to potentially damage the equipment or components and to VOID the original equipment manufacturer's warranty. The request further includes 2 ea UNOX.Finest Filtering System, which reduces carbonate hardness of water, with ChefTouch monitoring water consumption and notifying the user to replace the cartridge, and 2 ea water filter installation.

Consumables and Accessories
Listed are 1 ea UNOX Detergent & Rinse Eco, (10) 1 liter tanks, double concentrate, phosphate free, cleaning chemicals for Rotor.Klean; 10 ea CHROMO.GRID, 18 inch by 26 inch, stainless steel; and 10 ea "STEAM&FRY" Basket, 18 inch by 26 inch, stainless steel.

Extended Warranty Detail
The blank original form carries an expanded description of the LONG.LIFE4-B1 line. Pricing is based on a 100 mile radius from the installer, with additional charges possibly applying. The UNOX Long.Life4 program, subject to UNOX, Inc. terms and conditions, includes: (1) an extended warranty providing a 4 year/10,000 ON hours parts and 1 year labor warranty, with the oven required to be connected to the internet via Ethernet cable or WIFI and to remain accessible for remote login by UNOX; and (2) a pre-installation site inspection by an UNOX Certified Service Agent of the installation site, follow-up instructions advising the customer of any additional material needed for site preparation prior to installation, and assembly, setting and leveling of the UNOX equipment plus final hook-up by a Certified UNOX Service Agent. This applies to the 1st 06FS. LONG.LIFE4-B2 covers the extended warranty with certified installation for a 2nd or more unit(s) installed at the same time and location as the 1st unit (06FS).

Bid Conditions
Both forms state that the bid is to include all freight charges with the dealer delivering to the school, that installation by an authorized service agent is to be included, and that any utility rebates are to be included in the bid.

Bid Submitted
On the REBID form, the entry for "Bid for item #1" is $36,457.91. Bidder information given is Business Name: Great Lakes Hotel Supply; Address: 24101 W. Nine Mile Rd., Southfield, MI 48033; Phone: (248) 982-7283; Contact: Michael Trombley; Bidder's Signature: Michael Trombley. The blank companion form leaves the bid amount, business name, address, phone, contact and signature lines empty.

Deadlines and Contact
The REBID form instructs bidders to return the quote via e-mail or by 5:00 p.m., Friday April 26th, 2024, to Gayle Moran at gmoran2@troy.k12.mi.us. The blank original form gives the earlier deadline of 5:00 p.m., Friday April 12th, 2024, to the same contact, indicating the solicitation was reissued as a rebid with a later return date.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Minutes of a Troy Board of Education meeting held at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, headed March 19, 2024, and carried on the April 16, 2024 agenda, record recognitions, public comment, and a series of unanimous 7-0 construction and technology awards. The Board certified an Operating Millage Renewal Proposal to the Oakland County Clerk for the August 6, 2024 election, with certification required no later than 4:00 p.m. on May 14, 2024. The largest action was the Smith Middle School foundations and steel contract package totaling $9,134,583.10 from the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m. before roughly 300 audience members, and it adjourned at 9:51 p.m.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
Meeting and Attendance
Held at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m. Board members present with him were Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart and Wilson. Superintendent Machesky attended along with administrators Montante, DiPilato, Griffor, Detmer, DiPonio, Zawislak, Henning, Bush, Recker, Jansen, Pagel, Fulcher and West. Approximately 300 members of the audience were present. Mr. Schmidt changed the order of Recognition items to allow additional time for guests to arrive for the Mission Moment. The meeting adjourned at 9:51 p.m. Minutes were submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education.

Recognitions
Larson Middle School received the 2024 State School of Character Award from Character.org, the only school in Michigan and one of only 87 schools in the country to earn it; it is Larson's third such recognition, following 2018 and 2019, and Larson may now apply for a National School of Character Award. Boulan Park instrumental music teacher Joe Havrilla presented 30 TSD musicians selected for the 2024 Michigan All-State Ensembles from four middle schools and three high schools, with 8 additional students named Honorable Mention; the students rehearsed and performed in Grand Rapids January 25-27. The Student Spotlight featured Troy High School senior Simmi Sharma of the TSD Creative Guild, introduced by Thomas Butcher. The Mission Moment honored winners of the Oakland County Water Resources Commission Kids' Clean Water Calendar Contest, drawn from nearly 600 county entries.

Consent Agenda and Personnel
Items A through D passed 7-0: minutes of the February 6, 2024 Workshop; minutes of the February 27, 2024 Board Meeting; Treasurer's Report - January 2024; and a Retention Pond Budget Modification. Personnel recommendations (Bryan Wietecha) passed 7-0. The Board issued a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure to Mr. Matt Jansen as Director, Athletics, Continuing Education and Enrichment, effective July 1, 2024, by a 7-0 vote. Curriculum: none.

Business Actions

| Item | Award | Amount | Fund |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Wattles abatement | Midwest Environmental | $36,500.00 | Building and Site Sinking Fund |
| Smith MS foundations | Simone Construction Services | $3,032,100.00 | 2023 Capital Projects Fund |
| Smith MS structural steel | B & A Structural Steel LLC | $4,838,848.00 | 2023 Capital Projects Fund |
| Site demolition and SESC | Blaze Contracting, Inc. | $587,000.00 | 2023 Capital Projects Fund |
| Smith MS bid total | | $8,457,948.00 | |
| Smith MS contingency | | $676,635.00 | |
| Smith MS TOTAL | | $9,134,583.10 | |
| Temporary fencing | Fence Connection | $51,036.00 | 2023 Capital Projects Fund |
| Cellular WAN (Cisco switches, Forti-Extender router, accessories) | People Driven Technologies | $790,132.15 | 2023 Capital Projects Fund |
| 2024 furniture package | Pre-existing bid consortium contracts | not to exceed $4,828,873.07 | 2023 Bond Fund |

Non-Homestead Renewal
A Resolution Certifying Operating Millage Renewal Proposal was adopted 7-0, certifying the Proposal (Exhibit A) to the Oakland County Clerk as School District Election Coordinator for the election of August 6, 2024, with filing required no later than 4:00 p.m. on May 14, 2024, and authorizing updates for any Headlee rollbacks applicable to the 2024 operating millage.

Public Comment and Reports
Agenda-item speakers addressed Honors courses and the New Solutions K-12 study. Non-agenda comment centered on restroom use and transgender student policy and on the expired teacher contract, with Troy Education Association president Jason Cichowicz among the speakers. President Schmidt reported on a Lansing trip with Dr. Machesky and David Randels of Oakland Schools regarding Governor Whitmer's proposed school funding budget, and Dr. Machesky summarized the New Solutions K12 report.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Minutes of the Troy Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, headed "BOARD MEETING MINUTES MARCH 19, 2024," held at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois. The document appears in the April 16, 2024 board packet, and its embedded certification by Secretary Gary Hauff attests that the millage resolution was adopted at a regular meeting held on April 16, 2024, conducted in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976. The minutes carry the typing notation GH/jh and are respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education.

Call to Order and Attendance
President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart and Wilson were present. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Montante, DiPilato, Griffor, Detmer, DiPonio, Zawislak, Henning, Bush, Recker, Jansen, Pagel, Fulcher and West. There were approximately 300 members of the audience. Mr. Schmidt changed the order of Recognition items to allow additional time for guests to arrive for the Mission Moment.

Recognition: State School of Character
Larson Middle School was honored for receiving the State School of Character Award. Character.org certifies schools and districts that have developed and implemented an intentional, proactive and comprehensive approach embedding character into all aspects of school life, including creating a caring school community, providing students opportunities to practice and reflect on character strengths, and engaging families and communities as partners. Larson was the only school in Michigan and one of only 87 schools in the country to earn the 2024 State School of Character Award, its third such recognition after 2018 and 2019, and it has now earned the right to apply for a National School of Character Award. Character Committee leaders Charlie Tull, Jen Rogers, Jackie Parker, Shannon Dziwanowski and Cindy Christianson, along with school administrators Brian Zawislak and Stephan Henning, were brought up to receive congratulations.

Recognition: All-State Band and Orchestra
Boulan Park instrumental music teacher Joe Havrilla spoke about the 30 Troy School District musicians chosen as members of the 2024 Michigan All-State Ensembles, representing each of TSD's four middle schools and three high schools. Additionally, 8 students were recognized as Honorable Mention. The students were in Grand Rapids January 25-27 to rehearse and perform with musicians from across the state. Michigan High School All-State Orchestra members recognized were Karen Jin (violin), Ryeo-Won Kim (violin), Jing Yi Ma (viola), Benjamin Sheng (viola), Emily Baek (cello), Jisoo Park (cello) and Danielle Leight (bass). Michigan High School All-State Band members were Halle Chen (oboe), Jay Shyn (clarinet), Angela Park (clarinet), Sahana Mukund (bass clarinet), Brian Feng (alto saxophone), Daniel Lee (alto saxophone), Sohum Kapoor (trumpet), Brian Liu (trombone), Sarbani Sengupta (trombone) and Brandon Mendoza (percussion). Michigan Middle School All-State Orchestra members were Chole Kim (violin), Sihyeon Jun (violin), Gabriella Murphy (violin), Suhana Reddy (violin), Ariel Song (violin), Brian Zhang (violin) and Leon Ma (cello). Michigan Middle School All-State Band members were Andy Zhao (clarinet), Aryan Khedkar (bass clarinet), Anson Pingree (alto saxophone), Pujah Raj (alto saxophone), Tanishi Swami (alto saxophone) and Landon Taylor (French horn).

Student Spotlight and Mission Moment
The Student Spotlight recognized creative achievement in the TSD Creative Guild, showcasing Troy High School senior Simmi Sharma for her video projects, editing and video production; Thomas Butcher introduced her work. The TSD Mission Moment honored Clean Water Calendar winners for 2024. Students at Barnard, Costello, Hamilton and Leonard Elementary Schools participated in the annual Kids' Clean Water Calendar Contest sponsored by the Oakland County Water Resources Commission, tied to the first unit in Michigan Studies on the Great Lakes ecosystem. There were nearly 600 entries in the county. Grand Prize Winner was Sally Huang, Leonard 5th grade, for "Save Life, Save Water, Save Nature." Calendar Winners were Matthews Baheena, Costello 5th grade, "Saying Doesn't Help...Doing Does"; Rishik Palla, Costello 5th grade, "No More Pollution"; and Samrath Singh, Barnard 4th grade, "Keep Our Lakes Clean, Please." Honorable Mentions were Erin Abraham (Barnard 5th grade), Mihith Arun (Barnard 4th grade), Emanuela Ivezaj (Barnard 4th grade), Nandini Sinha (Costello 5th grade) and Zidaan Akhtar (Hamilton 5th grade).

Additions and Deletions; Public Communication on Agenda Items
Additions and deletions: none. Alex Karpowitsch, Troy resident and Troy High graduate, addressed the Board about Honors courses and how the change will impact students, adding that the District has not shared the data. Dr. Audra Melton addressed the Board about the New Solutions K-12 study and its recommendations related to reading programs and expanding elementary reading specialists. Mrs. Stephanie Zendler, a former 12-year TSD administrator, addressed the Board about the Levinson report discussed at the recent Board workshop, speaking on the special education program, Reading Recovery, and Fountas and Pinnell Literacy.

Consent Agenda
Moved by Mr. Hauff, supported by Mr. Haupt, the Board approved items A, B, C and D on the consent agenda: Minutes of the February 6, 2024 Board of Education Workshop; Minutes of the February 27, 2024 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report - January 2024; and Retention Pond Budget Modification. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

Personnel
Moved by Mrs. Alic, supported by Mrs. Anne, the Board approved the personnel recommendations as stated (Bryan Wietecha). Vote: Yes 7, No 0. Moved by Mr. Haupt, supported by Dr. Wilson, the Board issued a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Mr. Matt Jansen, who will begin duties as Director, Athletics, Continuing Education and Enrichment as of July 1, 2024. Vote: Yes 7, No 0. Curriculum: none.

Business: Non-Homestead Renewal
A Resolution Certifying Operating Millage Renewal Proposal was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne. The recitals state that the Board determined it necessary for the continuing operation of the School District to renew the authority to levy certain operating mills as described in the Operating Millage Renewal Proposal attached as Exhibit A; that it is necessary and desirable to submit the Proposal to the School District's electors at an election to be held on August 6, 2024 (the August Election Date); and that the Board must certify the Proposal to the Clerk of the County of Oakland, State of Michigan (the School District Election Coordinator) as required by Michigan election laws not later than 4:00 p.m. on May 14, 2024. The operative provisions certify Exhibit A to the School District Election Coordinator and local clerks; individually authorize the Secretary of the Board and the Superintendent to file the Resolution and complete required forms, certificates or documents by no later than 4:00 p.m. on May 14, 2024; authorize the Secretary or Superintendent to update the Proposal prior to submission to reflect any Headlee rollbacks applicable to the current operating millage for the 2024 year; direct the Election Coordinator to post and publish notice of the last day of registration and notice of election and to have ballots prepared and printed in the form of Exhibit A or stated as a proposal on the voting machines, possibly alongside other matters presented to the electorate the same date; and rescind conflicting resolutions. Vote: Yes 7, No 0. RESOLUTION DECLARED ADOPTED, certified by Gary Hauff, Secretary, Board of Education.

Business: Contract Awards
Wattles Abatement - moved by Mrs. Alic, supported by Mr. Haupt: the bid for asbestos abatement awarded to Midwest Environmental in the amount of $36,500.00, approved as an expenditure of the Building and Site Sinking Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

New Smith MS Foundations and Steel - moved by Mrs. Anne, supported by Mr. Hauff: contract awarded as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund, with Foundations to Simone Construction Services at $3,032,100.00; Structural Steel to B & A Structural Steel LLC at $4,838,848.00; and Site Demolition and SESC to Blaze Contracting, Inc. at $587,000.00, for a Bid Total of $8,457,948.00, Contingency of $676,635.00, and a TOTAL of $9,134,583.10. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

New Smith MS Temporary Fencing - moved by Mr. Hauff, supported by Mrs. Alic: the bid for temporary fencing awarded to Fence Connection in the amount of $51,036.00, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

Cellular WAN - moved by Dr. Philippart, supported by Mr. Haupt: purchase of Cisco switches, Forti-Extender router and accessories awarded to People Driven Technologies in the amount of $790,132.15, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

2024 Furniture Package K-5 Classrooms, Baker, and IAE Classrooms - moved by Mrs. Alic, supported by Dr. Wilson: furniture purchase for Costello, Hamilton, Leonard, Schroeder, Wass and Wattles elementary schools along with Baker Middle School and IA-East, for an amount not to exceed $4,828,873.07 through pre-existing bid contracts (consortiums) as outlined in the memo from TMP dated March 15, 2024, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Bond Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

Student Representatives
Nurayda Albeez, student representative for International Academy-East, reported on events and activities at her school. Teagan Pruitt, student representative for Troy College and Career High School, was not in attendance. Jayla Turner, student representative for Troy High School, reported on her school. Mackenzie Sawyers filled in as Athens High School student representative since Marlien William was not in attendance and shared a report on Athens.

Public Communication, Non-Agenda Items
Mr. Peter Dungjen, a district parent, addressed a male student using the female restroom and the safety of all students. Mrs. Katie MacFarland, a district parent, supported Mr. Dungjen's daughter and asked the Board to invest bond monies in single stall bathrooms. Ms. Michelle Fox-Phillips, a Warren resident, spoke in support of transgender students using the restroom they choose and cited bullying and outing. Mr. Jason Cichowicz, Troy Education Association president, addressed the expired teacher contract, fair and equitable compensation, and retaining teachers. Ms. Justine Galbraith, a district teacher, spoke on upholding gender identity and student safety. Yvonne Tadajewski, P-Flag president of the Clinton Township Chapter, spoke in support of transgender students. Mrs. Emily Freeman, a district teacher, addressed the expired contract and the anxiety accompanying it. Kylie Wood, a district teacher, addressed the expired contract and teachers' need to be recognized and valued. Jennifer Smith, speaking on behalf of a non-tenured district teacher, addressed the expired contract, teacher burnout, and teachers working second jobs. Mrs. Jennifer Taylor, a district teacher, spoke on the expired contract and fair and equitable compensation. Ms. Audrey Carra, a first year district teacher, spoke on the expired contract and balancing work and life with student loan debt. Mr. Ollie Apahidean, a district parent, raised the restroom issue and pornography in the media center. Chris Kus, a district parent, raised the ongoing safety issue of a girl being bullied over the restroom issue and the removal of honors classes. Salwan Rabban, a Troy resident, addressed the female student bathroom being used by a male transgender student while stating respect for their choice and concern for student safety.

Other: Public Education Funding and NSK12 Levinson Report
President Schmidt reported that he, Dr. Machesky and David Randels from Oakland Schools traveled to Lansing the prior Friday to meet with the state senate appropriations committee chair about Governor Whitmer's proposed budget for public school funding. He shared a graph of per-pupil funding over the last 20 years showing that funding has not met the rate of inflation, expressed frustration at not getting the funding needed to support staff income, and said he will continue to push legislators to go beyond the governor's proposed PreK-12 budget. Dr. Machesky summarized the New Solutions K12 report, which would be available for public review on the TSD website, describing district challenges and values, the engagement of Mr. Levinson from NSK-12 to meet with stakeholders and gather data, the availability of data on MI-School Data via the transparency report on the TSD website, best practice professional development, a common understanding of MTSS across the organization, opportunities identified from the study and how to prioritize the work, the Guiding Coalition of stakeholders planning to meet quarterly, and review of student data at all levels to improve the achievement gap. Dr. Machesky and Board members shared about participating in district events, gave a shout out to volunteers who created sets for the spring high school plays, noted March is Reading Month and encouraged sign-ups to read to classrooms, and wished the TSD community a meaningful Ramadan, Happy Easter, Happy Holi and a Happy Spring Break. Mr. Schmidt spoke further about his Lansing trip and his conversation with the legislator about school funding.

Adjournment
The meeting adjourned at 9:51 p.m.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Exploring Our Data Story, a Troy School District Board of Education workshop presentation dated November 12, 2024, running 47 slides. Stated objectives are to review district goals, provide context to enhance understanding of data, and share how data is utilized to drive district systems and processes, under the framing heading Setting the Scene.

DISTRICT GOALS. Four numbered goal areas are presented: 1 Early Childhood to Career; 2 Equity & Well-Being; 3 Deep Learning; 4 Building Capacity.

ASSESSMENT INVENTORY. Under Beyond the Cover: Understanding Summative & Formative Assessment, the deck lists building a strong foundation and early childhood enrollment; district-level summative measures of M-STEP (grades 3-7), PSAT 8 / SAT 11, and College Board Advanced Placement; classroom-level formative measures of Fountas & Pinnell (K-5), Bridges Math (K-5), Common Lit (ELA 6-12), and NWEA Math (6 to Algebra 1); and exit data in the form of the TCCHS graduation rate. A slide titled Snapshots of Progress recognizes the limitations of summative M-STEP and PSAT/SAT data under three headings: cohort tracking (summative data helps monitor student cohort performance over time), comparative insights (performance can be assessed against other districts), and granularity issues (summative data lacks detailed analysis for specific performance insights).

M-STEP GRADES 3-7. The ELA chart plots school years 2018-19, 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24 with three series. TSD: 74.3, 68.9, 67, 65.6. OS (Oakland Schools): 53.6, 50.1, 49.7, 49.4. State: 44.3, 40.7, 40.7, 40.5. The mathematics chart, same years and series, plots TSD 70.1, 64.7, 65.7, 67.4; OS 48.9, 42.6, 43.7, 45; State 38.7, 33.3, 34.7, 35.6. Additional slides break out Elementary M-STEP grades 3-5 and Middle School M-STEP grades 6 and 7 for English language arts and mathematics, and two further slides present ELA M-STEP and Math M-STEP county comparisons with free and reduced lunch rate; these slides carry no extracted figures.

M-STEP SCIENCE. The science slide is organized by Elementary, Middle School and High School with series for 2021-22, 2022-23, 2023-24, OS Avg. and State Avg. The figures appearing on the slide are 20, 59.1, 48, 6.25, 63.72, 36.27, 27.27, 64.64 and 45.21, together with comparison averages of 47.8, 47.4 and 43.6 and of 40.4, 38.8 and 37.5.

M-STEP SOCIAL STUDIES. Organized the same way, the social studies slide shows 30.59, 45.13, 42.7, 36.12, 49.94, 33.72, 34.88, 47.59 and 45.95, with comparison values of 37.4, 44.7 and 24.1 and of 18.9, 29.7 and 39.6. A later slide is titled M-STEP Social Studies By School.

PSAT 8. The Evidence-based Reading & Writing chart covers 2018-19, 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24: TSD 87.1, 81, 85.6, 84.2; Oakland Schools 70.3, 67, 68.4, 71.4; State 61.9, 59.7, 59.7, 64.5. The mathematics chart for the same years: TSD 75.1, 67.5, 69, 64.3; Oakland Schools 52.5, 44.6, 45.5, 42.3; State 41.4, 36.2, 36.2, 32.6. A separate slide compares 2023-24 PSAT 8 results for the OS LEA average against TSD.

SAT. The SAT Overall Performance chart spans 2018-19, 2019-20, 2020-21, 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24 with an axis running 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80; plotted values are TSD 69.8, 58.8, 59.7 and 57; Oakland Schools 44.5, 37.3, 37.1 and 34.4; State 33.9, 28.1, 28.2 and 25.1. The SAT Total, met and/or exceeded expectations chart for 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24 shows AHS at 51.1, 53 and 50.3 and THS at 67.5, 70 and 67.2. The SAT EBRW percent met or exceeded chart for the same three years shows AHS 70.1, 76 and 72.7 and THS 81.7, 81.5 and 82.5. The SAT Math percent met or exceeded chart shows AHS 53.5, 54.6 and 53.8 and THS 70.6, 71.8 and 69.2. District-level SAT Evidence Based Reading & Writing across 2018-19, 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24 shows TSD 82.9, 75.3, 76.9 and 77.3; Oakland Schools 62.9, 59, 59.3 and 59.6; State 55.3, 51.6, 52.2 and 51.3. District-level SAT Math across the same years shows TSD 73.6, 61.6, 61.3 and 59.5; Oakland Schools 46.7, 39.3, 38.9 and 35.7; State 36.3, 30, 29.9 and 26.3. There are additional slides titled SAT Overall Performance By School and a 2023-24 SAT slide charting percent economically disadvantaged against EBRW and math, whose data labels extracted only partially.

REFLECTIONS AND USES OF SUMMATIVE DATA. The deck describes the MTSS process, collaboration and ongoing adjustments, and a partnership with NSK12 to evaluate supports and structure for students with services in ELD, special education and other areas. Areas of focus are access to Tier 1 (core instruction for all), access to content-strong staff (who is teaching the content and intervention), and additional time for learning (more time with content-strong staff). Ongoing professional learning is cited with the example of the October 31 and November 1 Trailguide. Further slides cover Using Data to Inform Instruction, MTSS Decision Making, and MTSS Time, the last listing building data and trends, MTSS is for ALL children, meeting on students with IEPs to discuss scheduling, reviewing progress monitoring of any student on a plan, working on team dynamics, starting with celebrations, and reviewing all data points.

FORMATIVE AND CLASSROOM-LEVEL TOOLS. Slides present the Fountas & Pinnell benchmark by grade level and a math benchmark by grade. The Math Recovery Assessment slide states that the elementary benchmark is utilized for universal screening, that diagnostic assessments about where to go with instruction are given by math specialists, and that next steps are determined for intervention and instruction; a sample class-level report follows. The NWEA update with mathematics states that a universal screener has been established for middle school mathematics, that middle school math specialists use it to identify which students need further, more diagnostic assessment within the MTSS process, and that it allows the district to participate in a third-party study with Illustrative Mathematics; a slide on NWEA informing classroom-level decisions follows. The Common Lit assessment slide organizes uses under assessment as a baseline (establishing a starting point for student performance), identifying needs (recognizing students who require immediate support), data-driven instruction (using assessment results to inform whole-class lessons and small group activities), monitoring growth (measuring student progress over time), and goal setting (engaging students in setting personal learning objectives based on assessment results), followed by a sample classroom report.

NEXT STEPS. Under Reading Between the Lines, district improvement needs are listed as examples of screening and diagnostic work to improve the MTSS process, formation of work groups to build capacity and continued partnership, and shared ownership of the MTSS process.

CELEBRATIONS. Investment in Early Childhood. International Academy East IB Diploma acquisition: 2024 81%, 2023 72%, 2022 88%, 2021 87%, 2020 90%, 2019 82%.

AP Honor Roll, with Athens High School and Troy High School compared for 2022-23 and 2023-24. School overall: Athens Silver then Gold; Troy Gold then Gold. College Culture: Athens 61% (232/378) then 70% (253/362); Troy 69% (364/527) then 75% (381/510). College Credit: Athens 50% (189/378) then 58% (209/362); Troy 65% (341/527) then 67% (341/510). College Optimization: Athens 27% (102/378) then 23% (83/362); Troy 30% (158/527) then 30% (153/510). Definitions given: College Culture is the percent of students in the graduating class who took an AP exam at any point in high school regardless of score; College Credit is the percent scoring 3 or higher on an AP exam in high school; College Optimization is the percent who took 5 or more AP exams where at least one was taken in 9th or 10th grade, with the note that research finds 6 or more APs do not improve college graduation rates beyond the optimal total of 5 such courses. Award thresholds are listed as College Culture Bronze 40%, Silver 50%, Gold 65%, Platinum 80%; College Credit Bronze 25%, Silver 30%, Gold 35%, Platinum 50%; College Optimization Bronze 2%, Silver 5%, Gold 10%, Platinum 15%.

Enrollment in AP 11 ELA by school year, showing 11 English AP enrollment, total 11th graders, and percent of 11th graders enrolled: 2020, 357 of 935, 38%; 2021, 307 of 905, 34%; 2022, 356 of 924, 39%; 2023, 315 of 932, 34%; 2024, 402 of 948, 42%. The slide quotes the College Board on AP courses helping students tackle college-level work, develop critical and useful skills for future AP courses, college and career, and stand out to scholarship organizations and in the college application process.

Seal of Biliteracy by year of graduation: 2019, 9; 2021, 3; 2022, 3; 2023, 5; 2024, 15; 2025, starred 18.

TCCHS 4-year graduation rate, percent of students who graduated in four years, charted for 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024 with values of 32, 48, 47, 64, 77 and 83.

Career and Technical Education completer status: more than 290 students from the Class of 2024 earned completer status in one of the district's CTE courses, with programs listed as Mechatronics, Computer Science, Automotive Technician, Cooking & Related Culinary Arts, Drafting & Design Technology, Finance & Financial Management Services, Education, Television & Radio Broadcasting, Woodworking, Merchandizing, Sales & Marketing Operations, and others. The deck closes with Sharing Troy's Success Stories and a thank-you slide.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Troy School District's June 2023 accountability report, presented to the Board of Education on June 6, 2023, reports progress under the Project 2026 Blueprint on the four World Class for All strategic pillars: Green (Early Childhood to Career), Red (Equity and Well-Being), Blue (Deep Learning) and Gold (Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families). Each pillar is reported through objectives, key results, celebrations, challenges and recommendations spanning November 2022 through June 2023. Among the most consequential items, the Portrait of a Graduate has completed Phases 1-3 following a January Board workshop and is awaiting Board adoption, and the district reports 2023-24 early childhood capacity of GSRP 80 max, PreK 90/100 and ECP 96 max.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Document**
June 2023 Accountability Report (PDF handout of the Project 2026 Blueprint presentation), Troy School District Board of Education meeting of June 6, 2023.

**Framing: Clarifying Our Foundation**
The foundation is presented as four elements: Mission (Why do we exist? / fundamental purpose / clarifies priorities and sharpens focus); Vision (What must our school become to accomplish our purpose? / compelling future / gives directions); Values (How must we behave to achieve our vision? / collective commitments / guides behaviors); and Goals (How will we mark our progress? / targets and timelines / establish priorities).

**(Re)Design Process: See, Engage, Act**
SEE draws on system-level data across demographic, process, academic and perception categories. ENGAGE means planning with key stakeholders including students, the BOE and staff. ACT means redesigning with Strategic Planning Teams, reviewing with the BOE, and finalizing strategic planning in June.

**Green Pillar - Early Childhood to Career**
Objectives: continue investing in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for universal preschool access for all three- and four-year-olds; expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students, including career and technical education, computer science access, connections for underrepresented students to in-demand careers, and work-based learning, credentials and college credit. Key results (updated June 2023) cover early and frequent 2023-24 recruitment, preschool-to-kindergarten transition, monitoring of preschool impact on achievement data and of access across the district, and Portrait of a Graduate adoption in progress. Celebrations include 2023-24 early childhood enrollment (full-day and half-day AM tuition full with additional sections opening in 23-24; GSRP 80 max with additional requested, income threshold expansion and a shift to Morse, Troy Union, Hill and Wass; Strong Beginnings free three-year-old program; PreK 90/100 with an added section; ECP 96 max), a Kindergarten Transition Committee, the January BoE workshop with Phases 1-3 complete, K-8 career readiness with Media Specialists and Maker Space growth, Early Middle College with LTU, a Business Round Table, and digital portfolio prep tied to Xello.

**Red Pillar - Equity and Well-Being**
Objectives: fund additional investments supporting the whole child, elevate Alignment, Access and Agency district wide, and assess needs to meet world-class learning environment demands. January-June 2023 results: re-energizing the Red Pillar, establishing the district JEDI Council and equity webpage, a Tier One elementary SEL curriculum pilot, CSTAG self-harm trainings for psychologists and social workers, a Middle School Advisory Study Team, a completed student code of conduct review, NEP Day of Learning/ILT, and the 2022-23 Equity Analysis Survey and listening tours. Hanover recommendations call for deeper equity professional learning, heavy focus on bullying, and prioritizing diversity resources and gender identities and expression.

**Blue Pillar - Deep Learning**
Objectives cover MTSS systems of support and student voice, technology access and training, global best practices (NPDL, The 6 C's, learning partnerships), and upgraded facilities. Title and setting: "June 2023 Accountability Report," a PDF of the Project 2026 Blueprint presentation prepared for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of June 6, 2023. The cover identifies the district as Troy School District and the initiative as the Project 2026 Blueprint.

Clarifying Our Foundation. The opening section lays out the foundational architecture of the plan in four parts. Mission answers "Why? Why do we exist?" and is described as the FUNDAMENTAL PURPOSE that clarifies priorities and sharpens focus. Vision answers "WHAT? What must our school become to accomplish our purpose?" and is described as the COMPELLING FUTURE that gives directions. Values answer "HOW? How must we behave to achieve our vision?" and are described as COLLECTIVE COMMITMENTS that guide behaviors. Goals answer "HOW WILL WE MARK OUR PROGRESS?" and are described as TARGETS AND TIMELINES that establish priorities.

(Re)Design Process: See, Engage, Act. The SEE phase uses system-level data spanning demographic, process, academic and perception data. The ENGAGE phase involves planning with key stakeholders, specifically students, the BOE and staff. The ACT phase involves redesigning WITH Strategic Planning Teams, reviewing with the BOE, and a June milestone to finalize strategic planning.

Accountability Plan. The report states that the World Class for All pillars hold the team accountable to Objectives and Key Results. Four pillars are reported: Green (Early Childhood to Career), Red (Equity and Well-Being), Blue (Deep Learning) and Gold (Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families).

Green Pillar objectives. Continue to invest in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for access to universal preschool for all three- and four-year-olds. Expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students, with a plan aimed at providing more students access to high-quality career and technical education programs that expand access to computer science; connect underrepresented students to careers in demand in high-growth industry sectors; and build partnerships with institutions of higher education, employers and other stakeholders that allow students to engage in quality work-based learning opportunities, earn a credential, and/or earn college credit.

Green Pillar key results, updated June 2023. Early childhood recruitment for 2023-24 described as early and frequent. Focus on meaningful transition from preschool to kindergarten. Monitoring of the impact of preschool on achievement data and monitoring of access across the district. Portrait of a Graduate adoption in progress. A slide titled "TSD Preschool Access Overtime" accompanies this section.

Green Pillar celebrations, November 2022 through June 2023. Under 2023-24 Early Childhood Enrollment: Tuition full-day and half-day AM programs are full, with additional sections opening in 23-24; GSRP is listed at 80 max with additional capacity requested, an income threshold expansion, and a shift to Morse, Troy Union, Hill and Wass to increase access; Strong Beginnings is described as a free three-year-old program; PreK is listed as 90/100 with an additional section added; ECP is listed at 96 max. A Kindergarten Transition Committee is noted along with a visual timeline. Under Portrait of Graduate: a January BoE Workshop was held, Phases 1-3 are complete, and BoE adoption is coming soon. Career readiness engagement opportunities for K-8 are partnered with Media Specialists and Maker Space growth. The district continues to prioritize post-secondary learning partnerships throughout K-12, including Early Middle College with LTU and a Business Round Table. Preparation for digital portfolios involves K-5 media, middle school innovation coaches and 6-8 English teachers, tied to Xello and future-ready exit discussions with students.

Green Pillar challenges, November 2022 through June 2023. Cohesion of programming during the 2023-24 shift; identifying barriers to preschool access; alignment of Media/Maker with Career Readiness, specifically training (time) and consistency (buy-in); shifting the mindset around the stigma of career readiness to prioritize relevance to learning in classrooms; supporting high school building leaders in embedding career readiness initiatives; and keeping Portrait of a Graduate on timeline while leveraging its connection to the current strategic plan.

Green Pillar June 2023 recommendations. Continue ongoing preschool recruitment and hold a Preschool Summer Institute 2023. Continue prioritizing messaging career readiness as a tool for students aligned with academic planning and college readiness with administrators, teachers and counselors. Continue focusing on business partnerships to enhance work-based learning for all high school students. Expand TSD Learning Portfolios to all students in Grades 3-9. Prioritize digital citizenship for K-8. Continue to expand embedded career readiness initiatives K-8 via media and elective classes. Jump start TSD's computer science K-12 curriculum collaboration with the Oakland Schools Computer Science team. Secure Portrait of Graduate board adoption and key stakeholder support.

Red Pillar objectives. Ensuring a focus on equity and well-being; funding additional investments to support the needs of the whole child; an elevated focus on Alignment, Access and Agency district wide; and assessing needs and taking action to meet the demands of a world class learning environment in all school communities.

Red Pillar celebrations and key results, January through June 2023. Re-establishing and re-energizing the district Red Pillar. Establishing a district level equity team, the JEDI Council, and an equity webpage. A Tier One SEL curriculum pilot at the elementary level. CSTAG self-harm trainings for school psychologists and social workers. A Middle School Advisory Study Team established and progressing. A completed student code of conduct review. Emphasis on adult learning in well-being and equity through the NEP Day of Learning and ILT. An Equity Analysis Survey for 2022-23 along with listening tours.

Red Pillar looking ahead to 2023-2024. Diversify and expand the Red Pillar team around Alignment, Access and Agency. Expand the SEL curriculum pilot. Transform adult SEL. Develop professional learning and community learning series models with an equity focus. Investigate wraparound services such as afterschool programs specific to SEL and equity. Partner with the Director of Security to review safety protocols. Conduct focused group work dedicated to establishing consistent MTSS structures. Run a book study and workshop series including Culturally Responsive Teaching and Street Data.

Red Pillar challenges and recommendations. Elevated concerns and needs include encouraging and implementing aligned structures, equity teamwork across buildings, and SEL and MTSS curriculum. Hanover recommendations are to dive deeper into professional learning for staff in the areas of equity, focus heavily on issues of bullying, and prioritize diversity including resources district wide and gender identities and expression. The report also calls for continued social work, psychologist and counseling support in all buildings and work toward more cohesive relationships and levels of support across all buildings.

Blue Pillar objectives. Create and sustain systems of support at all levels that deepen learning and empower student voice through MTSS, with access to deep learning described as imperative for all children. Improve technology access for students and families while providing quality training to leverage technology to deepen learning. Continue to pursue global best practices in all content areas, citing NPDL, The 6 C's and learning partnerships. Assess the need and take action for upgraded facilities to meet the demands of a world class learning environment in all school communities.

Blue Pillar key results. Elementary resource and teacher consultants trained in Math Recovery Training. Celebrations of Learning at middle schools. Continued pursuit of authentic assessments such as interviews and digital portfolios. Adoption of elementary and middle school math curriculum rooted in pedagogy. Elementary and middle school media teams continuing to develop curriculum using inquiry and maker-centered practices, with secondary engaged in this learning, in partnership with Dr. Edward Clapp. Elementary MTSS work continues to monitor benchmark data and develop capacity in math; secondary MTSS work continues to define roles on the MTSS team and consider data to be utilized.

Blue Pillar next year's work. Learning with outside experts on interdepartmental systems of support; a renewed commitment to instructional practices that foster deep learning across the curriculum; exploring quality interim assessment tools for core areas; continuing to grow digital portfolios for students to document learning over time; and continued elementary and middle school media team curriculum development using inquiry and maker-centered practices.

Gold Pillar objectives. Improving educator preparation, strengthening pipelines for underrepresented educators and supporting current educators; continuing to provide job-embedded professional learning experiences for all staff; and providing professional learning opportunities for staff, community and students with the goal of co-designing impactful experiences to better the OneTroy community.

Gold Pillar key results. Development of an Academics website for parent and community communication. A scholarship program currently being developed with Eastern Michigan University for existing employees. A Student Support Aide orientation, mentoring and training process. A sub-cabinet team for creating coherence covering budget, staffing and professional learning. Expanded partnerships with OU (secondary), EMU (special education) and WSU (social work). A years-of-service display lists the categories 15+, 20+ and 25+ alongside the figures 127, 114 and 78. Job-embedded tech learning for all core secondary staff. A hosted parent learning series with Celebrate Hope and Dr. Tony Wagner. High school 9th and 10th grade ELA teams continuing to develop curriculum. Learning with Dr. Jonathan Bostic and Illustrative Mathematics for middle school math teachers. Learning with Dr. Ted Coe for high school mathematics. Learning with Dr. Israel Tatou on design of physics curriculum. Use of late-start days to prioritize conversations with collaborative teacher teams around student learning.

Gold Pillar next year's work. Continued partnership with Celebrate Hope; job-embedded tech learning; implementation of professional learning in mathematics to support the new curriculum; enhanced learning opportunities for support staff; culturally and linguistically responsive teaching practices embedded into all job-embedded learning; continued investigation into attracting experienced staff from outside the district; retention strategies; and a "Grow Your Own" strategy for recruitment, both county and Troy-specific.

Closing. The report ends with a "What's Next?" quotation: "The world's best school systems ensure that all stakeholders understand the purpose, priorities, and goals of the system. Leaders clarify a few very specific non-negotiables that must be honored throughout the system and at the same time they encourage autonomy and creativity at all levels to foster ownership and innovation."
